editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: There is a certain island called Diomedeia, and it holds many herons. These, they say, neither harm the barbarians nor approach them; but if a Greek puts in as a stranger, they come up to him by some divine gift, spreading their wings like hands held out in welcome and embrace. And when the Greeks touch them they do not shrink away, but keep still and endure it, and when the men sit down they fly into their laps, as though invited as guests to a feast. These birds are said to be the companions of Diomedes, who shared with him in the campaign against Ilium; and afterwards, when they changed their former nature into the form of birds, they still even now preserve their character as Greeks and lovers of Greece.

When the cranes leave behind the country of the Thracians and the Thracian frosts, they gather at the Hebrus, and each, having swallowed a stone to serve both as food and as ballast against the onset of the winds, attempt their migration and their rush toward the Nile, out of longing for warmth and for the winter quarters there. When they are about to rise and hold on their forward way, the oldest crane goes round the whole flock three times, and then, falling, gives up its life. There the rest bury the dead one, and then make straight for Egypt, crossing the greatest seas on the spread of their wings, and they neither anchor anywhere nor rest. They come upon the Egyptians sowing, and finding in the fields, as one might say, an abundant table, they then share, uninvited, in the hospitality.

With a man of Mauretania the lion shares the road and drinks the water of the same spring. And I hear that the lions even visit the houses of the Mauretanians, when they meet with no game and a strong hunger seizes them. And if the man is present, he wards the lion off and drives it back, chasing it with all his might; but if he is away and only the woman is left, she holds it from advancing with reproachful words and brings it to order, admonishing it to master itself and not to flame up with hunger. And the lion understands the Mauretanian speech, and the sense of the woman's rebuke to the beast is, as they say, of this kind: "Are you not ashamed, being a lion, the king of the animals, to come to my hut and to need a woman to be fed, and, like a man maimed in body, to look to a woman's hands, that by her pity and mercy you may obtain what you need? You, who ought to hasten to the mountain haunts after deer and antelopes and all the rest that is the lion's glorious dinner. Yet you are content to be fed on scraps like a wretched little dog." And while she chants such things, the lion, as though stricken in soul and filled with shame, quietly and with downcast eyes departs, overcome by what is just. And if horses and dogs, through being reared with us, understand and cower when men threaten, I should not wonder that the Mauretanians, being reared and brought up together with lions, are understood by the very lions. For they testify of their own infants that they think the lions' cubs worthy of the same and like fare, of one bed and one roof; and that from this the beasts understand the aforesaid speech is neither incredible nor strange.

The partridge is the most lascivious of birds. They love the females fiercely, and being overcome by lust they couple most constantly. So when those who keep fighting partridges goad them on to battle against one another, they set beside each one its mate, having discovered this device against cowardice and weakness in the contest. For the partridge will not endure to appear beaten before either his beloved or his wife; he will rather die under blows than, when his adversary comes against him, turn away and shamefully let her see this, before whom he wishes to win esteem. This was just what the Cretans had in mind concerning their beloved boys. For I am told that a certain Cretan, a good lover and brave in war and in all else, had as his favourite a noble youth of outstanding beauty, manly in spirit and well and finely endowed by nature for the noblest studies, but on account of his age not yet called to arms (I have given elsewhere the name both of the lover and of the boy). The Cretans say that this young man displayed great deeds of valour in the battle, but that when the enemy's phalanx pressed upon him in a mass he stumbled over a corpse lying there, and they say he was overturned. One of the enemy, the nearest, raised his weapon and was about to strike the man across the back; but he turned and said, "Do not deal me a shameful and unmanly blow, but strike me full in the breast, so that my beloved may not convict me of cowardice and refuse to lay out my corpse, not daring to approach me when I lie disgraced." That a man should be ashamed to be seen a coward is no great wonder; but that a partridge should partake of shame—this is a most august gift of nature. Yet Aristodemus the trembler, and Cleonymus who threw away his shield, and Pisander the coward, felt no shame before their fatherlands, nor before their wives, nor before their children.

They say that there are black birds, dark to look at, which inhabit the land of the Parians and neighbouring Cyzicus; you would call them hawks by their shape. They do not taste flesh, and are temperate as to the belly, and seeds suffice them for a meal. When autumn begins, a flock of these birds (they call them Memnons) goes straight to the Trojan land, to the tomb of Memnon. Those who still dwell in the Troad say that there is a mound consecrated to Memnon the son of Eos; and that his very corpse, carried by his mother to Susa—the place so famously hymned as Memnonian—was raised on high from the field of slaughter and received the burial befitting him, while the monument there bears his name in another sense. So the birds named after the aforesaid hero come every year, and they divide and split into enmity and difference, and they fight a fierce battle, until half of them die, and the others, the victors, go off whence indeed they came. Now how this is done, and whence, I have no leisure now to philosophize, nor to track out the secrets of nature; but this shall be said. The aforesaid birds wage this contest every year as a funeral game for the son of Eos and Tithonus. The Greeks honoured Pelias once with a contest, and Amarynceus, and indeed Patroclus too, and Achilles, the rival of Memnon.

Men need a word to urge and persuade them to be brave, and to drive out cowardice and instil confidence—athletes for the running-track, soldiers for the fight with arms; but animals need no encouragement from outside. They sharpen their own courage for themselves, and rouse and stir themselves up. The boar, when about to go into battle, whets its tusks against the smooth rocks. And to this Homer too plainly bears witness about the creature. And indeed the lion stirs itself up by lashing itself with its tail, and does not allow itself to grow slack or to rest. This too the poet knew, and sings of it concerning the lion. And the elephants strike themselves with their trunks, kindling themselves to the contest when the time for it comes, and they need no one to sing to them and say, "This is no work for sitting or delay," nor do they wait for the verses of Tyrtaeus. And the bull that leads the herd, when conquered by another leader, withdraws himself to another place, and becomes his own trainer, and practices every exercise, rolling in the dust and rubbing his horns against the trees, and in every other way disciplining himself to the training of his strength; and indeed he abstains from love and is temperate, like Iccus of Tarentum, whom Plato the son of Ariston celebrates as having remained, throughout the whole time of his training, ignorant and untried of any intercourse at all. Now for Iccus, being a man and longing for the Olympic and Pythian crowns, conscious of fame and greedy for glory, it was nothing great to sleep with restraint and temperance; for the prizes were both in fact and in reputation glorious—the Olympic wild olive and the Isthmian pine and the Pythian laurel, and to be looked upon while alive and well spoken of when dead. And indeed I hear that the lyre-player Amoebeus, having married a most beautiful wife, abstained from her throughout the whole time during which he went to the theatres to compete. And Diogenes the tragic actor renounced the licentious bed altogether and entirely. And Clitomachus the pancratiast, if ever he saw dogs coupling, turned away, and if at a banquet he heard any licentious and amorous talk, he rose and departed. That men should do these things, either for the sake of gaining money or for the sake of sharing in fame and glory, is no great wonder; but for a bull that conquers a rival bull, what proclamations, O son of Ariston, do they make, and what prizes do they set apart?

I have learned that the cows of Susa are not without a share of arithmetic. That this is no idle boast, the account itself bears witness, which says that in Susa many cows draw water for the king's parks, into the higher-lying ground, each one a hundred buckets. They perform with the greatest readiness the toil that has been laid upon them or in which they have long been trained, and you would never see one of them shirking; but if, beyond the hundred already mentioned, you should press one of them to draw up so much as a single further bucket, you will not persuade or compel her, whether you strike or coax. So Ctesias says.

Indian tales teach us these things too. The hunters lead their hounds—the well-bred ones, good at picking out the tracks of beasts and swiftest in running—to the regions full of game, and tying them to trees, they then depart, having simply, as the saying goes, thrown the dice. When tigers come upon them, if they have fallen into a lack of prey and are hungry, they tear the hounds to pieces; but if they arrive in heat and well-fed, they mate with them, and even those beasts, in their fullness, remember love. From this union, they say, not a hound but a tiger is born. From this in turn, and from a bitch, a tiger might still be born; but the offspring of this one and of a bitch reverts to its mother, and the seed slips down toward the worse, and a hound is born. To these things Aristotle will not object. These hounds, then, which can boast a tiger for a father, disdain to hunt a deer or to close with a boar, but rejoice to dart upon lions, thereby displaying their lineage from above. To Alexander the son of Philip the Indians gave proof of the courage of these hounds in this way. They let loose a deer, and the hound stayed quiet; then a boar, and it remained motionless; then a bear after these, and the bear did not vex it at all; but when a lion was let loose, then, as it saw it, the more did anger sink into it, and, having beheld its true adversary, it neither hesitated nor stayed still, but darting at the lion it held on with a powerful grip, squeezing and throttling. The Indian, then, who was furnishing the king with this spectacle, knowing well the dog's tenacity, ordered that its tail be cut off. The tail was cut off, but it took no notice. Then the Indian ordered one of its legs to be cut off too, and it was cut off; but the hound held on as it had from the first, and did not let go, as though some other leg, a stranger's, were being cut off. And another was cut off, and the hound did not relax its bite; and a third one besides, and it held fast; and the fourth after these, and it was still master of its bite. And at last they cut away the rest of the body from the head; but its teeth still hung from the original grip, and the head was held aloft from the lion, even though the biter himself was no longer there. Alexander then was distressed, astonished at the hound, that having given proof of itself it had perished, suffering the opposite of cowards, and bartering death for its courage. So the Indian, seeing him distressed, gave him four hounds like that one. And Alexander was pleased to receive them, and gave gifts in return such as was fitting, and the son of Philip, on receiving the four, forgot his grief for the first.

The lion, when it is already advanced in age and has grown heavy with years, is least able to hunt, and gladly rests in cavernous or bushy haunts, and does not venture even against the weakest of beasts, mistrusting its years and mindful of its body's weakness. But those born from it, taking courage in the prime of their age and in their inborn strength, go out to the hunt, and take along the one now grown old, urging him on; then, leaving him behind at the middle of the road they must travel, they set about the hunt themselves, and when they have got as much as will suffice both for themselves and for him who begot them, with a noble and piercing roar the young call the aged one, the sons their father, as hosts call a guest to the feast. And he comes quietly and at a walk, and as it were creeping, and embracing his young, and fawning a little with his tongue, as though praising them for their good hunting, he sets to the meal, and feasts with his sons. And Solon does not command these things to the lions, but Nature teaches them, Nature that cares nothing for human laws; and she becomes an unalterable law.

The elephant rarely falls in love, they say, for it is a chaste creature, as I have said above. Yet I have heard of an erotic passion among elephants that is worth marvelling at. What I have learned is this. A man not unpractised in hunting these animals, having received authority from the emperor of the Romans and been sent out to hunt according to a certain custom native to the Moors, reports in a written account that a young she-elephant, in the bloom of her beauty as it seemed to those people, mated with a young and handsome bull; but another, older bull, whether he was her mate or her lover, grew indignant, as though he had been dishonoured. Kindled with a violent rage he rushed forward, and coming upon the young and handsome bull and closing with him, he then fought, as one who grieves over a bride or a beloved. And they dashed against each other so hard that both lost their tusks. Neither won, but the hunters by their missiles turned them away from one another, since by now, stripped of their weapons, they were useless. So this contest of love between elephant lovers, equally matched to the end, came to rest there. And Paris was being dragged by Menelaus and was choking as the strap of his helmet pressed upon him, and the son of Atreus would surely have hauled him away and won boundless glory, had not the strap snapped, and had not the daughter of Zeus and Dione snatched him away, after he had fought a most shameful and unmanly fight; and the coward went off and slept with the adulteress.

The race of the Hyperborean men and the honours paid to Apollo there are celebrated by the poets and sung also by the prose-writers, among them Hecataeus too — not the Milesian, but the Abderite. The many other solemn things he says it does not seem to me my present purpose to bring forward, and so I shall postpone to another time the telling of each, when it will be more pleasant for me and better for my hearers; but those things which this work alone summons me to relate are these. There are priests of this god, sons of Boreas and Chione, three in number, brothers by birth, six cubits in height. So whenever these perform the customary rite at the usual season for the god aforesaid, there fly down from the mountains which they call the Rhipaean clouds of swans, irresistible in their multitude, and having circled the temple and, as it were, purified it by their flight, they then descend into the precinct of the temple, which is very great in size and most fair in beauty. So when the singers sing to the god with their own music, and the harpers join the chorus with an all-harmonious melody, then the swans too sing along, keeping time in unison, and in no way anywhere do they sing harshly or out of tune, but as though having taken the keynote from the leader of the chorus, they sing together with the native masters of the sacred songs. Then, when the hymn is finished, the swans withdraw, having rendered their customary service in honour of the god, and having celebrated the god, the aforesaid winged choristers, so to call them, singing and chanting throughout the whole day.

Of Myra in Lycia there is a gulf, and it has a spring, and there is a temple of Apollo there, and the priest of this god scatters about the flesh of calves sacrificed to the god, and the orphus-fish swim up in shoals and eat the flesh like invited banqueters. And those who have sacrificed rejoice, and believe that the feasting of these fish is for them a good omen, and they say the god is gracious, because the fish have been filled with the flesh. But if they cast it out upon the land with their tails, as though dishonouring it and judging it abominable, this is believed to be the wrath of the god. And the fish recognize the voice of the priest too, and when they obey, they gladden those by whom they have been summoned, but doing the contrary, they grieve them.

I am told that an eagle foretold to Gordius the kingship of his son Midas. While Gordius was ploughing, the eagle flew down, perched upon the yoke, and spent the whole day there; nor did it leave before evening, when Gordius gave over his ploughing at the hour when oxen are unyoked. And when Gelon of Syracuse was still a boy, an enormous wolf sprang into the schoolroom and snatched the writing-tablet from his hands with its teeth. Gelon leapt up from his seat and pursued it, not cowering before the beast but clinging fast to his tablet. But as soon as he had got outside the schoolroom, the building collapsed and buried the boys together with their teacher, while by divine providence Gelon alone survived. And here is the marvel: a wolf did not kill a man but saved one — the gods not disdaining to use even creatures without reason, to reveal a kingdom to the one and to save the other from impending danger. This love of the gods, then, is also a property peculiar to animals.

In the Ionian Sea, near Epidamnus, where the Taulantii dwell nearby, there is an island called Athena's, and fishermen live there. There is also a lake on the spot, and shoals of tamed and domesticated mackerel are reared in it. The fishermen throw food to these, and there is a truce between them, and the fish are free and have been granted exemption from being hunted, and they live on to a great age, and even old mackerel dwell there. Yet they do not feed in idleness, nor are they ungrateful for their keep; rather, when they have taken their morning food from the fishermen, they then go off to the hunt themselves, as though paying for their nurture. Going forth from the harbour they set out against the foreign mackerel, and when they meet them, as it were a troop or a battle-line, they swim up to them as to fellows of their own kind and nature; and neither do those flee these, nor these turn away from those, but they come together. Then the tame ones, surrounding the newcomers and forming a ring and packing themselves close, cut off a great multitude in the middle and do not let them slip away, but wait for their keepers; and in return for the food on which they were fed they feast the fishermen in turn. For the fishermen come up and take the foreign fish and work a great slaughter. The tame ones then go off in haste to the harbour, and slipping into their own hollows await their afternoon meal. And the fishermen come bringing it, if they wish to have fellow-hunters and faithful friends. And this is done day by day.

I know from hearsay of a Macedonian way of catching fish, and this is the manner of it. Between Beroea and Thessalonica runs a river called the Astraeus. There are in it fish of a mottled colour; what the natives call them it is better to ask the Macedonians. These fish feed on flies native to the river, flies in no way like those elsewhere, nor resembling wasps in appearance, nor could one fairly liken this creature in form to the so-called anthedons, nor to bees themselves; yet it has a share of something peculiar to each of the aforesaid. It resembles a fly in boldness, while in size you would call it an anthedon; it has taken the colour of a wasp, and it hums like the bees. The whole country there calls it the hippurus. So these flies, settling on the stream, seek out the food dear to them; yet they cannot escape the fish swimming below. When one of these sees a fly floating on the surface, it swims up quietly and underwater, fearing to stir the water above lest it scare off the prey. Then, coming near, in the fly's shadow, it gapes and swallows the fly, as a wolf snatches a sheep from the flock or an eagle a goose from the yard; and having done this, it slips back beneath the ripple. So the fishermen know what happens; yet they do not use these flies as bait for the fish at all. For if a human hand touches them, they lose their natural colour, their wings wither, and they become uneatable by the fish; and for this reason the fishermen do not go near them, having by some secret instinct come to hate the ones that are caught. So they get round the fish by a fisherman's craft, devising for them a trick of this sort. They wrap the hook with crimson wool, and to the wool are fitted two feathers of a cock, those that grow beneath the wattles and are like wax in colour. The reed is a fathom long, and the line is of the same length. So they let down the trick, and the fish, drawn by the colour and goaded, comes to meet it, supposing it will get a wonderful banquet from the beauty of the sight; then, gaping wide, it is caught on the hook, and has enjoyed a bitter feast, taken captive.

When a purple-fisher has caught the murex — not for men's food, but for the dyeing of wool — then, if the colour drawn from the creature is to remain fast and hard to wash out and able to produce a genuine, undeceiving dye, he destroys the murex, shell and all, with a single blow of a stone. But if the blow falls too lightly and the creature is left still breathing, the murex, when it is struck a second time with the stone, is useless for the dye; for in its pain it has used up the colour, which has either been absorbed into the mass of its flesh or has otherwise flowed away. This, they say, Homer too knew, when he says that those who die suddenly are overtaken by the death of the purple, chanting in his own verses the well-known line: "Then purple death seized him, and mighty fate."

Alexander, in his Periplus of the Red Sea, says that he saw snakes forty cubits long, and a kind of crab whose shell had a circumference of a foot on every side, while very large claws hung from it and projected; and these were plotted against by no one. The reason is that they are said to be sacred to Poseidon. They are dedicated to the god, so that the crabs are, as it were, his votive offerings, unharmed and unplotted against.

The parrot-wrasse feeds on sea-grasses and seaweed; but it is the most lustful of all fish, and its insatiable desire for the female is the cause of its capture. The clever fishermen, knowing this about it, attack it in the following way. When they have caught a female, they tie a fine cord of broom-fibre to the very tip of its mouth and drag the living fish through the sea; for they know the lairs of these fish, their haunts, and where they gather in shoals. They make for the purpose a lead weight, heavy and round in shape, three fingers long, fastened at each end with a rush-cord, and this drags the captured female along. And one of the men in the boat carries a basket-trap with a wide mouth, turned toward the captured wrasse, and the basket is weighted gently with a measured stone. So the males, like young men who have caught sight of a beautiful bride, are driven mad and rush after her, each striving to outstrip the others, to come close and to touch her, like men sick with love hunting after a kiss or a caress or some other amorous theft. The man who leads the female along quietly and sparingly, lying in wait and laying his ambush straight at the trap, leads, you might say, the lovers along with their beloved. And when they have come up to the trap, the fisherman lets the lead drop inside; and the female, falling in with the cord, drags the male down too. So they have swum together into capture, and the wrasses pay this penalty for the impulse of their desire.

That living creatures should be born in the mountains, in the air, and in the sea is no great wonder; for material, nourishment, and nature are the cause of these. But that there should be winged offspring of fire, the creatures called the fire-born, and that they should live and flourish in it, and flit about here and there — this is astonishing. And the still greater wonder: whenever they swerve out of the fire that is their element and partake of cold air, then at once they are dead. And let others say what the cause is, why they are born in fire and perish in air.

About the Libyan mare I hear the Libyans say such things. They are the swiftest of horses, and either feel weariness little or not at all. They are lean and not well-fleshed, yet fit also to endure their master's neglect. For their masters give them no tending — neither stroking them, nor making a rolling-place, nor cleaning out their hooves, nor combing their coats, nor plaiting their manes, nor washing them when weary — but as soon as they have finished the appointed course, they dismount and turn them loose to graze. And the Libyans are lean and squalid, and on such horses they ride. But the Medes are stately and luxurious, and so too are their horses. You would say that they live softly along with their masters, both in the size of their body and in their beauty, and now too in their finery and the tending from without. These same things come to my mind too about dogs. The Cretan hound is light and good at leaping and bred to mountain-ranging; and indeed the Cretans show themselves to be such men, as the report sings. The most spirited of dogs is the Molossian, since the men too are most spirited. And the Carmanian man and his dog are both most savage and unbendingly fierce, they say.

At Eryx in Sicily there is a festival which the people of Eryx themselves, and indeed all who dwell in Sicily, call the Anagogia, the Departure. The reason given is that on those days they say Aphrodite sets out from there to Libya. They infer this from the following evidence. There is a very great multitude of doves in that place. Now during those days they are not to be seen, and the people of Eryx say that the goddess has departed with them as her escort; for that doves are the playthings of Aphrodite both they sing and all men believe. After nine days have passed, one of surpassing beauty is seen flying in from the sea that brings her from Libya—not like the rest of the common pigeons, but purple, just as Anacreon of Teos sings of Aphrodite to us, calling her somewhere "the purple one." And she might be likened to gold as well, in keeping with Homer's goddess of the same name, whom he hymns as golden. The clouds of the remaining doves follow her, and again there is a festival and a great gathering for the people of Eryx, the Katagogia, the Homecoming—this name too taken from the event.

They say that in Crete the owl is not bred at all, but that if one is brought in from outside it dies. Euripides seems to have written without examination when he made Polyidus, seeing this bird and inferring from it that he would find Glaucus. For my part I learn that the Cretans sing and teach stories besides those already related. The Cretan land received a gift from Zeus, since it was, of course, his nurse and concealed him in the famous hiding-place: that it should be free of every wicked beast born for harm, and should neither breed such itself nor rear one brought from outside. And it displays the power of the gift; for it is barren of the aforesaid creatures. And if anyone, by way of test or proof of the favour from Zeus, should bring in one of those foreign beasts, it dies the moment it merely touches the land. So those who hunt snakes in nearby Libya contrive as follows. These charmers tame and bring as a spectacle many of the venomous beasts, and bring with them a load of Libyan earth, enough for their need. They do this through forethought for the snakes, so that they may not perish; and for this reason, whenever they come to the aforesaid island, they do not set down the animals before they have first scattered beneath them the foreign earth they bring. And upon this they gather the crowds, and indeed they astonish the foolish and the many. Now so long as each of them remains in its place, coiled and settled, and rises up but does not pass beyond its own familiar dust, so long it lives; but if it ventures out onto the foreign earth that is strange to it and hostile, it dies, and with reason. For if the nod of Zeus was not unfulfilled toward Thetis, nor would be toward anyone else, it will surely not appear void toward his own nurse.

The irrational animals love often to spare and refrain even from those that have become familiar to them. I hear, at any rate, this tale. A hunter had tamed a leopard from infancy and kept it, loving and cherishing it strongly, as one would a friend or a beloved. So he used to bring it a live kid and give it to it, devising at once both food and a kind of pleasure for the beast in tearing the kid apart, that it might not seem to eat carrion and a dead thing. And when a kid was brought, the leopard held itself in check, choosing to go without food because of fullness. And it did this on the second day too; for it still needed hunger as a remedy. But when the third day came on, it was hungry, and showed this as usual by its voice; yet it did not touch the kid that had been its friend for two days, but let it go and took another. But men have betrayed even their brothers and their parents and old friends, and many men often.

At the foot of Atlas—this mountain is celebrated both by the prose writers and by the poets—there are wonderful pastures and very deep woods, and their thickets resemble groves that are altogether shady and overarched with leaves. It is here, they say, that the elephants now grown old come, weighed down with age; for Nature leads them as it were into a colony, having given them rest at last and revealed to them a kind of haven and a longed-for harbour, where they may live out the remainder of their lives. A spring of fresh and very pure water, in great abundance, is set apart for them; they are accounted sacred and are left inviolate; and from the barbarians of that country they have received a treaty against being hunted. They are celebrated in song as gods of the woods and dells, and are made an object of the greatest concern as masters of the place. There is also a story current about them, that one of the local kings, longing for the beauty and the size of their tusks, desired to kill some of them, so that he might gain a choice possession; for, through their many years and the great length of their lives, these animals' weapons are the largest of all. When this desire came upon him, he sent out three hundred picked men to spear this sacred herd. They covered the road as fast as their feet would carry them, fully armed, and were now drawing near the place, when a plague suddenly seized and laid them low; and all of them perished except one, who returned and described the disaster to the man who had sent them—a most pitiable tale. In this way too the elephants were revealed to be beloved of the gods.

Every hunting hound that has itself taken a beast is pleased, and treats the catch as a prize, if its master grants it to him; but if not, it keeps the prey alive until the hunter comes and decides about the captured creature whatever he wishes. But coming upon a dead hare or boar, it would not touch it, not inscribing itself upon another's labours, and least of all deeming it right to appropriate what does not belong to it. From this it seems to have within itself something of natural ambition; for it has no need of meat, but is in love with victory. And it is worth hearing what the hunting hound does at the time of the hunt. It goes before the huntsman, fastened to a long leash, and follows the scent while holding back its voice with self-control. And as long as a lack of game meets it, and it lights upon nothing, it goes on, to all sight and judgment, rather downcast; and indeed, going forward, the hound draws the hunter on eagerly and most steadfastly. But if it traces a scent and lights upon the smell of some beast, there it stands still. The huntsman comes near, and the hound, overjoyed at its success, fawns upon its master and kisses his feet, and again takes up the tracking from where it began, and goes forward step by step until it reaches the lair, and no farther does it advance. The hunter understands, then, and with a low cry he signals to the net-keepers, and they spread the nets around. And then, at the right moment, the hound barks; and its cry now means to rouse the boar to start up, so that it may break out in flight and be caught in the nets. When the beast is taken, the hound cries out a kind of victory paean, and rejoices and skips about, like soldiers who have conquered their enemies. These things the hounds do in the hunting of boars and deer.

The eagle, the king of birds, the other birds fear and cower before when it appears—not only while it survives and lives, but even if one should mix its feathers with those of other birds, the eagle's remain whole and untouched, while the others rot away, not enduring the company of those.

Fish are not all eager for love at the same season; some are roused to mating in spring, others have received this impulse in summer, others in autumn, and some are kindled to the aforesaid purpose through the winter. Most of them, having brought forth once in the year, then cease; but I hear that the sea-bass also breeds a second time, and the red mullet is accused of conceiving three times, as its very name, they say, declares.

The Epirotes too sacrifice to Apollo in another way, both they themselves and all the strangers who are sojourning among them, and to him they hold the greatest festival of one day in the year, solemn and magnificent. There is a grove sacred to the god, and it has an enclosure round about, and within there are serpents, and these are a plaything of the god. The priestess, an unmarried woman, comes alone, and brings food to the serpents. They are said by the Epirotes to be descendants of the Python at Delphi. If, then, these serpents look gently upon the priestess as she comes and take the food eagerly, they are agreed to signify a fruitful and disease-free year; but if they frighten her and do not take the offerings she holds out, some divine the contrary of what was said, and others expect it.

At the old Bambyce (it is now called Hierapolis, since Seleucus named it thus) there are sacred fish, and they swim in troops and have leaders, and these eat first of the food thrown to them. And they keep their friendship toward one another most of all fish, and they are always at peace, either because the goddess breathes concord upon them, or because, being filled with the food thrown to them, they thus remain without taste and without knowledge of devouring one another.

The Carians catch the sea-bream in this way. When the south wind blows gently and sends a softer breeze, when the swell has subsided and laps quietly upon the sands, then the fisherman has no need of a rod at all. He takes a switch of juniper, a very strong one, fastens a line to its tip, and threads upon the hook a half-salted fish with a mouth like a wolf's, and lets it down into the sea. He sits at the stern of his boat and works his bait, while a boy rows gently for him, deliberately learning beforehand to keep the stroke slow, and brings the boat in toward the land. Many sea-bream leap about, darting up out of the burrows where they live, and gather around the hook; for the fish, long since dead but dressed up to catch them, draws them on as though by a magic charm. Then, when they have come near the shore, they are easily taken, bound fast by the greed of their bellies.
If you give a man suffering in the liver and afflicted with jaundice the gall of a parrot-fish to eat, he will be saved, as the skilled fishermen teach.

The sea-rams — whose name reaches the many, but the account of them is not very clear, except in so far as it is shown by the catching — pass the winter about the Cyrnian and Sardinian strait, and they are even seen above the water. Dolphins of the greatest size swim about them. Now the male ram has a white band running round its forehead (you would say it was the diadem of Lysimachus or Antigonus or some other of the kings in Macedon); but the female ram, just as cocks have wattles, so this too has tresses hanging beneath its neck. Each of these rams seizes dead bodies and makes them its food. But it also seizes the living, and with the swell of its swimming, being huge and prodigious, it even overturns ships, working for them so great a storm from itself. It seizes also those who stand on the nearby land. The people of Cyrnus say that, when a ship was wrecked in a storm, a man very skilled at swimming, after crossing a great stretch of sea, took hold of a headland of theirs, and climbing up stood there very fearlessly, as one now free of all dangers and in safety and command of his life. But a ram, swimming alongside, saw the man standing there, and inflamed by hunger coiled and arched itself, and with its tail drove much water, and then raised itself, lifted by the swelling wave, and reached up onto the headland and, like a squall or whirlwind, snatched away the man. So much for the Cyrnian seizing and hunting of the ram. The dwellers about the Ocean tell as a tale that the ancient kings of Atlantis, of the seed of Poseidon, wore on their heads the bands of the male rams, as a token of their rule; and that their wives, the queens, wore the tresses of the females, as a proof of their rule. This creature is exceedingly strong in the nostrils, and breathes in a great breath, and draws to itself a vast quantity of air, and hunts the seals too in this way. The seals, perceiving that a ram is somewhere near and brings them destruction, swim off as fast as they can, and reaching the land and slipping beneath the cavernous rocks they hide. But the rams, aware of their flight, pursue, and standing opposite the cave they understand by the smell of the flesh that their prey is within, and as by some most violent magic charm they draw with their nostrils the air between themselves and the seal. And the seal, like an arrow or a spear-point, swerves from the assault of the breath, and at first withdraws, but at last, by the most violent drawing, it is dragged out of the cave, and follows unwilling, as though stretched along by thongs or ropes, and squeaks, and becomes a dinner for the ram. Those skilled in examining such things say that the hairs growing from the ram's nostrils are good for many purposes.

In India, I learn, there are birds called parrots, of which I have already made mention above; but what I did not say of them before, this it now seems most fitting to say. There are three kinds of them, I am told; and all of them, having learned as children do, themselves become talkative and utter human speech. In the forests they give out a bird's cry, but no clear and articulate voice do they produce; they are untaught and not yet talkative. There are also peacocks in India, the largest anywhere, and green-plumaged pigeons; a man seeing one for the first time, and without skill in judging birds, would say it was a parrot and not a pigeon. They have lips and legs resembling in colour those of the partridges in Greece. Cocks too grow there of the greatest size, and they have a crest not red, as ours have, but variegated like garlands of flowers. The feathers of their tails are not curved nor bent into a spiral, but flat, and they trail them, as peacocks do, when they do not raise and erect them. The feathers of the Indian cocks have a colour golden and dark-gleaming, like the emerald stone.

Cleitarchus, in his work on India, says that there are snakes sixteen cubits long. He celebrates also another kind of snake, not like the others in appearance; for they are much shorter, but are seen variegated in colour, as though painted with dyes; for some have bronze-coloured bands running down from the head to the tail, others bands like silver, others crimson, and indeed some gold-gleaming. He says that they are terrible at biting and killing most swiftly.

The grey mullet is one of the fishes that live in the marshes, and it is believed to master its belly and to live very temperately. For it does not attack any living creature, but is by nature at peace with all the fishes; whatever it finds lying dead, that becomes its dinner. And it does not touch the thing before it has stirred it with its tail; if it stays still, the mullet takes it for food, but if it moves, the mullet retreats.

The other birds, as the story goes, are covered by the male; but the swallows are not, but their union is the opposite. The reason nature knows. The more common account is that they shudder at Tereus and fear lest he should one day creep up secretly and then enact a new tragedy. But this too, it seems, was a gift to the swallow from nature, and as I judge the most precious one: if it happens to be blinded with pins, it sees again. Why then do we still sing of Tiresias, even though he was wisest not only here but also in Hades, as Homer says?

These too, it seems, were peculiarities of the nature of animals. Ctesias says that neither a wild nor a tame pig is found among the Indians, and he says somewhere that their sheep have tails a cubit broad.

Wolves go in pairs, and so do horses; but lions no longer do so. For the lioness and the lion do not take the same path, whether they go to the hunt or to drink. The reason, as the older authorities say, is that each, trusting in its own bodily strength, has no need of the other.

The river Indus is without beasts, but in it alone, they say, is bred a worm. And its form is such as those that are born and bred in wood; but those of that river grow to seven cubits in length, though larger and smaller might be found; and their thickness is such that a boy of ten years would scarcely be able to clasp them with his arms. They have one tooth growing above and another below, and both are square, a span in length. So great is the strength of their teeth. Whatever they take in them they crush most easily, whether it be a stone or a tame or wild animal. By day they remain below in the depth of the river, delighting in the mud and slime, and so are not visible; but by night they come out onto the land, and whatever they meet—horse or ox or ass—they crush it, then drag it to their own haunts and eat it in the river, and gnaw all its limbs except the belly of the animal. And if hunger presses them even by day, when a camel or ox drinks at the bank they creep up beneath and seize it very warily by the tip of the lips, and by a most violent rush and a firm pull drag it into the water, and make it their dinner. A hide of two fingers' thickness covers each of them. The taking and hunting of them is contrived in this way. They let down a stout and strong hook fastened to an iron chain, having tied to it a rope of white flax a talent in weight, and wrapped both with wool here and there so that the worm may not gnaw through them; and having fixed a lamb or kid upon the hook, they then let it down into the water of the river. As many as thirty men hold the rope, each with a javelin slung ready and a sword at his side. And there lie at hand serviceable clubs to strike with if need be; these are of cornel-wood, exceedingly hard. Then, when the worm is caught upon the hook and has swallowed the bait, they haul it up, and having caught it they kill it and hang it in the heat for thirty days. And from it a thick oil drips into earthenware vessels; each animal yields ten cotylae. This oil they bring to the king of the Indians, sealed with seals; for no one else is permitted to have so much as a drop of it. The rest of the creature's carcass is useless. The oil has this power. Whatever heap of wood you wish to set ablaze and reduce to embers, you will kindle it by pouring on a cotyle of this, without first putting under it any seed of fire; and if you wish to burn a man or animal, you pour it on, and at once he is consumed. With this, they say, the king of the Indians takes the cities that have come into enmity with him, and waits for neither rams nor tortoises nor the other siege-engines, since he has taken them by burning; for he fills earthenware vessels, each holding about a cotyle, with the oil, and stops them up above, and slings them at the gates. And when they hit the windows, the vessels are dashed and broken, and the oil pours down, and fire is poured over the gates, and is unquenchable. It burns armour too, and men in battle, and its strength is boundless. It is put out and made to vanish by a great quantity of rubbish thrown over it. So Ctesias of Cnidus says.

That the bear brings forth a shapeless lump of flesh and then articulates it with its tongue and as it were moulds it, has been said above. But what I have not yet said shall be said now, and in a very fitting place. It gives birth in winter, and having given birth keeps to its den, and fearing the frosts awaits the coming of spring, nor would it ever bring out its young before three months are fulfilled. And when it perceives itself to be pregnant, regarding this as a sickness, it seeks a den. Hence indeed the affliction has been called "denning" for the bear. Then it enters not walking but on its back, hiding its tracks from the hunters; for it drags itself along on its back. And having got inside it rests, and in a way wears down its condition, and does this for forty days. And Aristotle says that for twice seven days it remains motionless and still, but for the rest of the time only turns over. So for all forty days it remains without food and without nourishment, and it is enough for it to lick its right paw. And from the excessive wasting its intestine has folded together and closed up. Knowing this, when it comes out it eats what is called wild arum; and this, being flatulent, opens up its intestine for it and widens it, and renders it capable of receiving food. And when it is full again, it eats ants, and is emptied most easily. So have I described the natural emptyings and the timely fillings of bears, which need, O men, neither physicians nor mixtures.

There is a Paeonian animal, called the monops, resembling a shaggy bull in size. When it is pursued, then, being agitated, it discharges a fiery and pungent dung, so I hear, which, if it should fall upon any of the hunters, kills him.

Dolphins too, it seems, were more righteous than men at repaying a favour, and are not liable to that custom of the Persians which even Xenophon praises. What I mean is this. A man named Coeranus, of Parian descent, when certain dolphins had fallen into a net at Byzantium and been caught, gave money like a ransom to those who had caught them, and set them free; in return for which he received their gratitude. He was once sailing, as the story goes, in a fifty-oared ship carrying certain Milesians, and in the strait between Naxos and Paros, when the ship had capsized and the others had perished, the dolphins saved Coeranus, repaying in equal measure the kindness they had first received. And the place where they swam carrying him to shore is shown as a headland and a cavernous rock, and the spot is called Coeraneus. Some time later, when this Coeranus was dead, they burned him near the sea. Then the dolphins, somehow perceiving it, gathered, as though come to the funeral, and as long as the pyre blazed and burned they remained, like a faithful friend to a friend; and then, when it was quenched, they swam away. But men, indeed, court the living and the rich and those who seem to prosper, but turn their backs on the dead or on those in misfortune, that they may not have to pay any gratitude for benefits received.

Mice are in any case a prolific creature, and bring forth many at a single birth; but if they happen to taste salt as well, then indeed they bear a great many, far more than usual. The crocodiles, when they have laid their eggs, test the genuine from the spurious in the following way. If, the moment it is hatched out, the young one seizes something, it counts thereafter as belonging to the race, and is loved by its parents, and is believed to be one of the crocodiles and is reckoned among them; but if it is sluggish and lazy and does not catch from somewhere either a fly or a gnat or an earthworm or a young lizard, the father tears it to pieces as worthless and counterfeit and in no way belonging to him. And it seems that, like these beasts, the eagles too test their genuine offspring by the ray of the sun, and love their young by judgment and not by feeling.
Herodotus says that camels have four thighs in their hind legs, and as many knees besides, and that their joints, through the hinder legs, are turned toward the tail.

In Etna of Sicily a temple of Hephaestus is honoured, and there is an enclosure and sacred trees and a fire unquenchable and unsleeping. There are dogs about the temple and the grove that are sacred, and on those who enter the temple and the grove modestly and as is fitting and proper, these dogs fawn and wag their tails, as though showing friendliness and recognizing them; but if anyone be polluted in his hands, this man they both bite and tear, while those who come merely from some unchaste intercourse they only chase away.

The Egyptians say (and they do not at all persuade me, but they say nevertheless) that a lamb both eight-footed and two-tailed was born in the time of that famous Bocchoris, and that it broke into speech. And they sing that the lamb had two heads, and they say the same was four-horned. Now to Homer, who gave a voice to the horse Xanthus, it is fair to grant pardon, for he is a poet; and Alcman too, imitating Homer in such things, would not bear blame, for he has a sufficient excuse toward respect in being the very first to dare; but how is it possible to give heed to Egyptians boasting such things? Still, the peculiarities of this lamb have been told, even if they are fabulous.

Fish have many haunts: some live among the rocks, some in the sands, others among the grasses. For there are indeed sea-grasses, and some of them are called moss, others vines, and certain ones grapes, and others seaweed. There is even a kind of sea-grass called cabbage; and certain growths among them are called lichen and hairs. The food of these is different for different fish, and one accustomed to its own native and kindred grass would not, one might say, taste of another.

Fish are caught even without weels and hooks and nets, in this way. Many sea-gulfs end in certain shallows, and these can be waded into. So when there is calm and a peace of the winds, the expert fishermen lead many men there, and bid them walk and trample the sand, pressing down their soles as hard as they can. Then deep footprints are left behind, which, if they are kept — provided the sand does not collapse and confuse them, and the water is not stirred up by wind — the fishermen wait a little, then, wading in, find lying at rest in the hollows of the steps and in the footprints the flat fish: plaice and turbot and sole and torpedo-fish and the like.

In the Bibonian gulf there are countless tribes of tunny. Some of them, like wild boars, are solitary and swim by themselves, being very large; others go in pairs and feed together like wolves; others in herds, like flocks of goats, ranging over broad pastures. As the Dog-star rises and its ray is keenest at its height, they set out for the Euxine; and as the wave seems to them fiery, they swim woven into one another, and by the joining of their bodies they get somehow a share of some shade.

There is also another bird in India, the size of a starling; it is variegated, and when trained it can imitate a man's voice, and it is more talkative and quicker-witted than the parrots. It does not, however, gladly endure to be fed by men, but out of longing for freedom and desire for the open speech that goes with living among its own kind, it embraces hunger rather than slavery with luxury. The Macedonians who settled among the Indians, in the city of Bucephala and the country about it, and in the city called Cyropolis, and in the others which Alexander son of Philip founded, call it the kerkion; and it got this name in the following way, since it too shakes its rump, as wagtails do.

In the ninth of his books about Ptolemy, Nymphis says that in the land of the Troglodytes there are vipers of an unmatched size, if they be compared with other vipers; for they are even fifteen cubits long; and that the tortoises there have a shell so great that it holds even six Attic medimni.

Fishes avenge one another like faithful men and just comrades in arms — the fish which the experts in sea-fishing like to call the anthias, creatures of the open sea by their character. Whenever any of these perceive that one of their fellows has been caught, they swim up most swiftly, then set their backs against him, and falling upon him and pushing with all their strength they prevent his being drawn up. The parrot-wrasses too are good defenders of their own shoal. They come up and

The creatures called day-flies are so named, taking their name from the measure of their life; for they are born in wine, and when the vessel is opened they fly out and see the light and die. So nature gave them entrance into life, but rescued them most swiftly from the evils within it, since they perceive neither any of their own misfortunes nor
The Indian ants that guard the gold
Wolves do not loose themselves from the pangs of birth easily, but only in twelve days and as many nights, since the Delians say that it took Leto just so long to come from the Hyperboreans to Delos.

The porpoise is an animal like the dolphin, and it too has milk. In colour it is not black, but resembles the deepest dark-blue, and it breathes not by gills but by a blowhole; for so they call the passage of its breath. Its haunt is the Black Sea and the sea there; and the porpoise is least apt to wander beyond those haunts.

When snakes are about to taste autumn fruit, they suck up the juice of what is called the sow-thistle; and this benefits them against being filled with any wind. And when they are about to lie in wait for someone, whether man or beast, they eat the death-bearing roots and the herbs of that kind. Nor was even Homer ignorant of their food. He says, at any rate, how a snake awaits a man, coiling about its den, having first filled itself with much venomous and evil food.

It seems that obedience too is proper to the bull, when it has been tamed and changed from its wild nature to gentleness. They remain motionless even upon litters, whether you wish them to stay still on their backs or face downwards, kneeling on their forelegs and carrying upon their necks either a boy or a girl. You will also see a bull bearing a woman upon its back, standing erect upon its hind legs, and propping its whole body lightly upon whatever support it finds. I have myself seen men dancing upon bulls while the bulls stood motionless and unmoved.

There were fishes too at once gentle and tame, and of such a kind as to obey when called, and to receive food readily from those who gave it—such as the sacred eel at Arethusa. They sing too of the lamprey of Crassus the Roman, which was adorned with earrings and little necklaces set with jewels, like a girl in her bloom, and when Crassus called it recognized the voice and swam up, and whatever he held out it ate eagerly, taking it readily. This lamprey, indeed, Crassus wept for, so I hear, when it ended its life, and buried it. And once when Domitius said to him, "Fool, you wept for a dead lamprey," he replied, "I wept for a beast; but you, who buried three wives, did not weep." I hear the Egyptians say that the sacred crocodiles are gentle, and that when their keepers touch and stroke them they endure it and bear it lightly, and gape when those men put in their hands

I hear that the teeth of the asp—which one might rightly call venom-bearing—have, as it were, very thin coverings wrapped about them, like membranes, by which they are enwrapped. So when the asp fixes its mouth upon someone, they say the little membranes part, and the venom is poured out, and again those membranes run together and unite. And the sting of the scorpion, they say, has a kind of hollow fold, not

Herodotus says that the sheep of Arabia have tails unlike those of other sheep. The same writer teaches, I believe, that there are two breeds of them, and indeed he says that some of them have very long tails, so that, if one measured them, they are not less than three cubits. If, then, one were to let these tails drag, they would be utterly chafed,

The people of Hermione revere Demeter, and sacrifice to her magnificently and grandly, and call the festival Chthonia. At any rate I hear that very great cows are led by the priestess of Demeter to the altar from the herd and offer themselves to be sacrificed. And Aristocles is my witness for what I say, who says somewhere: "Demeter rich in fruits, you are manifest both among the Sicilians and among the children of Erechtheus. But this one great thing is judged among the people of Hermione: for the wild bull from the herd, whom not even ten men can master, this one an old woman, walking alone, leads alone by the ear to this altar, and he follows like a child its mother. Yours is this, Demeter, yours is the strength; gracious may you be, and may the lot flourish wholly in Hermione."

This too I know I have heard about hawks. Before the Nile spreads over Egypt and rises onto the ploughlands, they cast off the feathers that are already growing old, just as the branches of plants cast off their dry leaves, and the hawks grow fresh and fine plumage, as the trees their blossom. There were, it seems, several kinds of hawks, and Aristophanes too seems to hint at this. At any rate he says: "But we sent three thousand hawks, mounted archers. And every one comes with hooked talons, kestrel, buzzard, vulture, owl, eagle." They are distributed and assigned to many gods. The partridge-catcher and the swift-winged is, they say, a servant of Apollo; the sea-eagle and the falcon they assign to Athena; of Hermes they say the dove-slayer is the plaything; of Hera the long-winged, and the so-called buzzard of Artemis. To the mother of the gods the merlin, and another to another god. So the kinds of hawks are very many.

You may hear fishermen speaking of a fish called the callionymus. About it Aristotle says that it has a large gall-bladder lying upon its right lobe, and that its liver is carried on the left side. Menander also bears witness to this, in the Messenia I think, where he says, "I declare you have more gall than a callionymus"; and Anaxippus in the Man under Judgement, "If you provoke me and make all my gall boil up like a callionymus's, you will see I am no whit different from a dogfish-swordfish." Now there are some who say it is good to eat, but the greater number contradict them. The poets who have taken pains to give a lawful place in their verse to fish that are of some account do not readily mention it in their banquets of fishes — Epicharmus in The Marriage of Hebe and in Earth and Sea and besides in The Muses, and Mnesimachus in The Isthmian Victor.

About the sea-urchin I have spoken above, and now too I will tell what I have further heard. It is good for the stomach; for one who was before a poor eater and loathed everything whatever, this restores. It is also an emptier of the bladder, as those skilled in these matters say. And if you smear it on a body that is scaly with itch, it makes whole one who before was suffering the said disease. Burnt in its very shells, it cleanses away the foulness of wounds. And the ash of a land-hedgehog burnt, mixed besides with pitch and smeared on the bald parts, makes the hairs that were before fugitive (to add a little jest) grow up again. Drunk in wine it is good for the kidneys, and saves those who are dropsical when it is drunk, as I have already said. And the liver of this hedgehog, dried in the sun, heals those who are seized

Demostratus, a man skilled in the science of fishing — and, by Zeus, good at expounding it too — says that there is a fish fair in form, and that this is called the "moon," small in size, blue in form, broad in shape. He says it has crests on its back and raises them; and that they are soft and neither resistant nor rough. So, when this fish swims below, it parts these crests and shows a half-circle, and there is, to look upon, the shape of the moon when halved. And this the Cypriot

I hear too that there grows in India a bird called the kela; it is three times the size of the bustard, and has a mouth fearfully strong and long legs; it bears also a crop, and that a very large one, like a leather bag, and it has a voice exceedingly harsh. In the rest of its plumage it is ash-grey, but at the tips of its wings it is pale yellow.

There is also a kind of snake called the prester, which, if it bites, first makes its victims sluggish and least able to move, then little by little weak and unable to breathe; and indeed the bite pours forgetfulness over the mind, and stops the bladder, and makes the hair fall out; then follows suffocation, and it causes convulsions, and the end of life is most painful.

strive to bite through the line, so as to save the one that has been taken; and often, having cut it through, they have saved their fellow and set him free, asking no ransom for his life. But often they have failed, and missed their aim; yet they did their own part most readily and eagerly. They say that a wrasse has even fallen into a basket-trap and thrust out its tail, and those swimming free outside have bitten it and led their comrade out. And if the mouth of the trap was open, one of them held out its tail to him outside, and he, gaping wide, followed it. These creatures do such things, O men, not having learned to love, but being so by nature. The fish called the nibbler is accused by its nature, its name, and now also by its mouth: it has teeth set close together and many, and is very strong at cutting through whatever falls in its way. So, when caught by a hook, alone of all fish it does not draw itself backward, but presses forward in its eagerness to bite through the line. The fishermen counter this with a contrivance: they have the shanks of their hooks forged long. But the fish — for it is also good at leaping — has often leapt even above these and, cutting the line that holds it, has swum back to the haunts of the fishes. This fish, taking the shoal that feeds with it, goes together with them straight at the dolphins; and when one dolphin somehow becomes separated, they surround it and then set on the beast vigorously, for they know that it is not indifferent to their bites. They cling to it most firmly, and the dolphin leaps up and turns somersaults, and shows by its writhing that it is tormented with pain; for they fasten on with a tenacious grip and are lifted up as it leaps. And while it strives to shake them off and beat them away, they do not let go but eat it alive. Then, whatever part each one has bitten off, with that he makes off; and the dolphin gladly swims away, having feasted these uninvited guests, as one might say, with its own pain.

become witnesses of those of others. A man, indeed, has sometimes in a long time healed the wound or sting of an asp, either by taking the knife, or enduring fire most patiently, or by setting against the evil the necessary drugs, that wretched man, lest it should creep further. The basilisk is a span in length; and indeed even the longest of serpents, on seeing it, not after any delay but at once, from the very assault of its breath, is withered. And if a man is holding a staff, and the basilisk bites that, the master of the staff is dead.

would not cross the river called Campylinus. And the Issedones who dwell with these ants are so called, and are so. A tortoise that has eaten a serpent and then bitten off some marjoram is freed from the harm which would otherwise have destroyed it utterly. And the dove I hear men say is the most chaste of birds and most restrained in love; for they are never torn from one another, neither the female, unless by some chance she is bereft of her mate, nor the male, unless he is widowed. But partridges are without self-control in love; and so they destroy the eggs that are laid, that the females may not, by rearing their young, bring a distraction from intercourse with them.

The tortoise and the partridge are creatures at war; so too the stork and the corncrake against the gull, and the falcon and the heron against the seagull; the lark regards the goldfinch as its enemy, and there is enmity between the turtledove and the redstart; the kite and the raven are foes; the siren against the hawk, and the hawk against the buzzard are found to differ not only in kind but also in nature. The channa is a most lustful fish. And white ants may be heard of at Pheneus in Laconia.

The hen that has conquered the male in battle grows proud with pleasure and lets down its wattles—not so far as the cocks do, yet it lets them down, and is filled with spirit, and steps out more largely.

When deer have shed their horns, they enter and withdraw into the thickets, guarding against those that attack them, and with reason; for being bereft of their weapons they believe that they have been deprived of their strength for the time. They are said also to take care lest, while their antlers are new, the sunbeam falling upon them before they have set and gained what are called the knobs should rot the flesh.

The land of Libya is the parent of many and varied beasts, and the so-called catoblepas too it seems to bring forth. In appearance it is much like a bull, but its face looks more savage. Its brows are high and shaggy, and its eyes lie beneath them, not very large like an ox's, but smaller and bloodshot; and they do not look straight ahead, but down at the ground, from which it gets its name catoblepas, the "down-looker." A mane begins above from the crown of the head and, resembling horsehair, comes down over the forehead and covers the face, making it more terrifying to anyone who meets it. It feeds on deadly roots. When it casts a sidelong glance like a bull, it bristles at once and raises its mane; and as this rises and stands erect, and the lips around its mouth are bared, it sends out through its throat a sharp, heavy, foul-smelling breath, so that the air above its head is poisoned, and the animals near it, breathing this in, are grievously harmed and fall into loss of voice and deadly convulsions. This beast understands its own power; the animals know it too, and flee from it as far away as they can.

and clean their teeth and remove the bits of flesh that have got in. The Egyptians say, moreover, that these crocodiles aforesaid have a share of prophecy too, and they bring forward this proof. When Ptolemy—ask the Egyptians which one this was—called the gentlest of the crocodiles, they say it did not obey, and when he held out food it did not approach; and the priests understood that the crocodile, knowing that the end was coming upon Ptolemy, therefore disdained to take food from him. I hear that some men prophesy by birds, and sitting in observation of fowl examine their flights and their perchings. And celebrated for this wisdom are the Teiresiases and Polydamases and Polyidi and Theoclymeni and many others. And there were others skilled at judging the dispositions of entrails—Silani and Megistiae and Euclidae, and after these a long list. I hear, however, of some who say that certain men prophesy by barley-meal and by sieves and by little cheeses. And I have learned of a certain Lycian village between Myra and Phellus, named Sura, in which some prophesy by sitting over fish, and they know what the fishes' coming, when summoned, and their withdrawal mean, and what they reveal when they do not obey, and what they signify when they come in numbers. You will hear from these wise men prophecies drawn both from a fish that leaps and one that floats up from the deep and one that takes the food offered, and again from one that does not take it.

very visible because of its extreme thinness. And they say that the poison both exists and is engendered there, and at the same moment as the blow goes forward through the sting and flows out. And the opening through which it issues you will not see either, observable as it is. But if a man spits saliva upon it, the sting is blunted and numbed and becomes powerless to strike. The bitch, even if she bears many puppies, yet the first that comes from the mother and is eldest of the litter convicts the father; for it is born most like to him in every way, while the rest are as it may chance. Nature seems to philosophize in this, preferring the sower to the receiver.

rubbed against the ground. The shepherds, he says, are skilled enough to do no more than fashion little carts which support the tails of these animals, so as to keep off the chafing from them. The other breed of sheep, he says, carry broad tails, and these grow broad even to a cubit. Snails know that the partridges and the herons are their enemies, and they flee from them; nor would you ever see snails creeping where these birds feed. But the kind of snails called the "stronger" deceive and outwit, by a certain natural cleverness, the birds just mentioned. For they come forth from the shells that have grown over them, and feed in great safety, while the birds I have mentioned swoop down upon the empty shells as though upon the snails themselves; and finding nothing, they cast them away as useless to them and depart. Then the snails return, and each goes back into his own house, filled from his feeding and saved by the very deception with which he tricked his foe.
In the land of Daunia they celebrate a temple of Athena of Ilium; and they sing that the dogs reared there fawn upon those of the Greeks who arrive, but bark at the barbarians.

The Egyptians, then, revering and deifying various kinds of animals, incur ridicule among most people; but the Thebans, being Greeks, revere, as I hear, the weasel, and they say it was the nurse of Heracles — or rather not the nurse at all, but that when Alcmene was in labour and unable to give birth, the weasel ran past and loosed the bonds of her travail, and Heracles came forth and was now creeping. And those who inhabit Hamaxitus of the Troad revere the mouse; from this, they say, they also call the Apollo honoured among them Sminthian. For still the Aeolians and the Trojans call the mouse "sminthos," just as Aeschylus too in his Sisyphus: "But there is some field-mouse, sminthos, thus monstrous." And in the Sminthium tame mice are reared, receiving public maintenance, and white mice lurk beneath the altar, and beside the tripod of Apollo a mouse stands. And this fable too I have heard concerning this worship. The crops of the Aeolians and the Trojans were assailed by many myriads of mice which, coming upon them, mowed them down unripe and rendered the harvests unfinished for the sowers. So when they inquired of the god at Delphi, he said that they must sacrifice to Apollo Sminthian, and they, obeying, were freed from the plot of the mice, and their wheat came to the appointed harvest. And they add these things too. When the colonists sent out from home to a settlement of Cretans were overtaken by some misfortune, they begged the Pythian god to show them a good place, profitable for their settlement. An oracle came forth: where the earthborn should make war on them, there they should remain and raise a city. So they come to this Hamaxitus and encamp to rest, and an unspeakable multitude of mice creeping up gnawed through the handles of their shields and ate through the strings of their bows; and they conjectured that these were the earthborn, and indeed, coming to be at a loss for their weapons of defence, they settle this place, and found a temple of Apollo Sminthian. So the mention of the mice has led us to a piece of theology, but we have been no worse for ourselves for having heard such things too.

The sea-frog also, like the birds, lays an egg. For it does not bring forth living young within itself; for even at birth its young have a head both large and rough, and on this account it is least able to receive its offspring back in fear; for they would gall and injure it if they re-entered. And likewise, when born and going forth, they would do much the same. So sea-frogs are neither easy in childbirth for the bringing of living creatures to birth, nor are they good refuges for their young. The eggs of frogs do not agree with the nature or peculiar character of other eggs; theirs too is rough, and has scales, and to one who touches it will seem resistant.

by the disease called the elephant's. The female elephant — the wise ones celebrate that her tusks are the more valuable, and they teach us this too. In the land of Mauretania the elephants are wont to shed their tusks invariably in the tenth year, just as deer shed their horns, only deer do so every year. These elephants, then, choose out level and dewy ground in preference to the rest, and set their tusks into it, crouching down on bended knees, exceedingly eager to be rid of them. They thrust them so far in as to hide them completely; then, smoothing the place with their feet, they leave it standing guard over their treasure. And since the ground is most fertile, it very quickly grows grass over it, and conceals the sight of what has been done from those who pass that way. But those who track down these hidden hoards, and have a certain cunning against the elephants' stratagem, bring water in goatskins, and then scatter the filled skins about in different places, while they themselves remain there. And one of them sleeps, another drinks, and one perhaps, even while sipping from his cup between draughts, sings a little, and through his song calls to mind the girl he loves. Nor should I be surprised if one of them also makes advances to a handsome youth who is present and a partner in the search; for the Moors are both beautiful and tall, and have a manly look, and apply themselves to the works of hunting, and indeed they inflame many to love, being still mere boys and of that age. So if the tusks lie buried near, by some secret and marvellous attraction they draw that water out of the skins, and prove them empty. Thereupon, with mattocks and pickaxes, they dig up the place, and have their quarry, having tracked it by scent without hounds. But if the skins stay full where the hunters of these tusks set them down, they go off to another hunt, and indeed carry off the skins and water again, the instruments of the said chase.

fishermen say; and this account too is from Demostratus. When the moon is full, this fish, when caught, is itself full, and fills the trees too, if you bring and fasten it to them; but when the moon is waning, it is itself melted away and fails, and brought to plants it withers them. And when wells are dug, if one throws this fish into the water found, at the time when the month is beginning to show, the water will be ever-flowing and will never fail; but if at the waning, the water will cease. And indeed if you throw the same fish into a rising spring, you will have it either full or the place from then on empty. How the tunny swim into the Propontis, and how they swim out, I know I have said somewhere above in these discourses; but let one here think of Heraclea and Tius and Amastris, cities of Pontus. So those who dwell in this whole region know best the visit of the tunny, and indeed they come at that season of the year, and many weapons are made ready against them — ships and nets and a high watchtower. This watchtower stands fixed on some beach, in a position with a very open view; and to describe its construction is no labour for me, and to you, the hearer, it brings a delicacy for the ears. Two tall trunks of fir stand divided by broad cross-beams, these woven close together and very good for the watcher to climb and stand upon. The ships have, each, six rowers on either side, young men who row well; and the nets are long, not too light or held up by floats, but rather weighted with lead. The shoals of these fish swim in all together. As spring shines forth and the winds now blow peacefully and the air is bright and, as it were, smiling, and the wave is at rest and the sea is smooth, the watcher, seeing by some secret skill and a most keen-sighted nature, tells the hunters from where they are coming; and if the nets must be stretched out toward the shore, he teaches this too; and if further in, he gives, like a general, the signal, or like a chorus-master the keynote; and indeed he will often even tell the whole number, and will not miss his mark. And it goes thus. When the shoal of tunny has thrust itself out into the open sea, the man keeping watch on the tower and observing closely the movements of the aforesaid fish, crying out very sharply, says to pursue there and to row straight out to sea. So they, having hung from one of the firs that hold the watcher a very long rope attached to the nets, then row their ships one behind another in a line, and hold to one another, since the net is divided among each. And the first, casting out its own portion of the net, withdraws; then the second does this, and the third, and the fourth must let down hers; but those rowing the fifth still hold off, and those after her must not yet let down; then others row off this way and that and carry their portion of the net, and then they rest. The tunny, being sluggish and unable to do any deed requiring boldness, stay penned in and keep still; and the rowers, as of a captured city, take a populace of fish, a poet would say. So, dear Greeks, the Eretrians too know these things, and the Naxians by report, having learned about such hunting all that Herodotus and others tell. The rest of the hunting you shall hear from others.

I hear also that there is an Indian hoopoe twice the size of ours and fairer to look upon. And Homer says that a horse's bridle and trapping lie stored up as a treasure for a Greek king, but this hoopoe is a plaything for the king of the Indians, who carries it about in his hands and delights in it, and continually gazes at it, marvelling at the bird's splendour and its natural beauty. The Brahmans tell a tale also of this bird, and the tale that is told is this.
