A son was born to a king of the Indians, and he had brothers, who, when they came to manhood, became most lawless and most wicked. They despised this one as the youngest, and they mocked their father and mother, scorning their old age. So the parents shrank from living with these sons, and fled away, the boy and the old people together. But when a hard journey overtook them, the old people gave out and died; yet the boy did not neglect them, but buried them within himself, cutting open his head with a sword. And the all-seeing Sun, the same people say, marvelling at the excess of his piety, made him a bird, fairest to look upon and long-lived in his span; and a crest has risen up from the top of his head, as a memorial, as it were, of what he did when he was fleeing. Some such tale the Athenians too told in their marvelling about the crested lark, attending to a certain myth, which Aristophanes the comic poet seems to me to have followed when he says in the Birds: "For you were born ignorant and no busybody, nor have you pored over Aesop, who used to say in his tale that the lark was the first of all birds to be born, before the earth, and then her father died of sickness; and there was no earth, and he lay unburied on the fifth day. She, at a loss in her helplessness, buried her father in her own head." It seems, then, that the tale, told among the Indians of one bird, flowed over to the Greeks also of another. For the Brahmans say that it was an immeasurable length of time ago that these things were done by the Indian hoopoe, while he was still a man and a boy in age, to his parents.

Phylarchus, in his twelfth book, sings such things about the Egyptian asps. He says that they are greatly honoured, and that from this honour they become very tame and gentle to handle. So, reared among the children, they do no harm, and when called they crawl out of their holes and come. Their summons is the snapping of the fingers. The Egyptians offer them gifts of hospitality besides. For when they have finished dinner, they soak barley-groats in wine and honey and set them on the table at which they happened to have dined; then, snapping their fingers, they call them as it were as guests. And the asps, as though at a signal, appear, and crawl out one from one place, another from another, and standing about the table they leave the rest of their coil on the floor, but raising their heads they lick all round, and quietly and little by little they fill themselves with the groats, and consume them. And by night, if anything presses the Egyptians, they snap their fingers again; and this sound signifies to the asps to withdraw and depart. So they understand the difference of the sound and for what purpose this is done, and at once they draw back and vanish, crawling into their crannies and holes. And the man who rises neither treads on any of them nor falls upon them.

I hear that a dog fell in love with Glauce the lyre-player; others say it was not a dog but a ram, and others a goose. And in Soli in Cilicia a dog fell in love with a boy named Xenophon; and at Sparta a jackdaw sickened with love for the beauty of another handsome youth.

The love of music in dolphins and their amorous nature — the one the Corinthians sing of, and the Lesbians agree with them, the other the men of Ios: those tell of Arion of Methymna, while the others tell what happened in Ios concerning the beautiful boy and his swimming and the dolphin. And a man of Byzantium too, named Leonides, says that he himself saw, while sailing along the Aeolian coast, in the city called Poroselene, a tame dolphin that lived in their harbour and treated the people there as his own private hosts. And in addition to this, the same man says that an old woman and an old man living with her raised this fosterling, holding out to it baits, and very alluring ones. Moreover the son of these old folk was reared together with it, and the two of them tended both the dolphin and their own boy; and somehow, from their being reared together, the man and the creature came unawares into love of one another, and — this is the famous tale — a most august mutual love was honoured in the persons aforesaid. So the dolphin loved Poroselene as his fatherland, and cherished the harbour as his own home; and indeed he repaid to those who reared him the cost of his rearing. And this was his manner. Being full-grown, he needed least of all to be fed from the hand; but now, swimming out further and ranging about and looking for sea-catches, he had some as a dinner for himself and brought others back to his household; and they knew this, and indeed gladly awaited the tribute from him. And this was one source of income; here is another. The dolphin's name had been given by those who reared him, as to the boy; and the boy, confident in their rearing together, would call him by this name, standing on some jutting place, and at the same time as the call would coax him. And the dolphin, whether he was racing against some rowing-boat, or diving and gambolling among the other dolphins that wandered in shoals about the place, or hunting as his belly drove him, would come back most swiftly, like a ship driven on with much foam, and when he came near his favourite he would be his playmate and frolic with him, now swimming beside the boy, now, like one challenging him, the dolphin would then draw his favourite into a contest with himself. And the still greater wonder: he would sometimes give up even the first place and swim behind him, as though pleasantly beaten. These things, then, were proclaimed abroad, and to those sailing by it seemed a spectacle, along with the other good things the city had, and it was a source of income to the old folk and the lad.

Wolves swimming a river, that they may not be violently overturned by the rush of the stream, nature, devising a peculiar ballast for them, has taught a salvation easy out of difficult straits. Biting one another's tails, they then resist the current, and so swim across painlessly and safely.

That horses delight more in marshes and meadows and windy places, men skilled in the rearing of horses and foals agree. Hence too Homer—being, as it seems to me, clever at observing such things—said somewhere that "three thousand mares pastured along the marsh." And horse-keepers testify that mares are often made pregnant by the wind and flee before the south wind or the north. So the same poet, knowing this, said, "Of these even Boreas grew enamoured as they grazed." And Aristotle too, as I understand it, taking his cue from this, said that they, stung by the aforementioned winds, run off.

The dolphin is believed to be a creature that loves its own kind. And the proof is this. Aenus is a Thracian city. It happened that a dolphin was caught and wounded, not to death, but so that life was still possible for the captive. So blood flowed, and the others not yet taken perceived it, and a whole shoal came to the harbour, and leaped about, and seemed bent on doing something not good. So the people of Aenus were afraid and released the captive. And the others, having recovered it as one of their kindred, went off and departed. But rarely is a man a partner in zeal and care for a kinsman or kinswoman in misfortune.

Horses that go into war are suspicious both of leaping over trenches and of vaulting a pit and crossing palisades and stakes and such things. And one may hear Homer too speaking about such matters: how "Hector, going through the throng, besought his comrades, urging them to cross the trench. But his swift-footed horses dared it not, but loudly neighed, standing on the very brink; for the wide trench frightened them, neither easy to leap over near at hand nor to cross."

Those skilled in hunting elephants sing to us that, when these beasts are pursued, they rush and are borne along with an irresistible force and an ungovernable impulse, checked by nothing, and that they drive even through the largest trees as though through a cornfield, snapping the trees like so many stalks of grain; and in some places the trees stand higher than they and overtop their crests, while in others they themselves are taller than the trees. So they run at full speed and, taking shortcuts, cut off their pursuers along the roads, and reasonably so, for they are familiar with the country. And when they have drawn far away, and have got beyond the cavalry that came after them, and have taken heart as though they were in shelter from danger and at liberty, they stand and rest, gladly casting off the anxiety that came from their fear. Then too the memory of food comes upon them; and I hear that they feed on the mastich that grows thickly about the trees, and on wild ivy that creeps over the plants and is very dense, and on the soft, fresh foliage of palms, and on the shoots of other plants and the more tender twigs. But if the pursuers draw near again, they turn once more to flight. The pursuers, however, encamp when evening overtakes them, and setting fire to the wood and so in a manner walling off the road behind, they take their stand against the elephants. For elephants fear fire no less than lions do.

Easily mastered, too, and most easily caught, were asses by wolves, bees by bee-eaters, cicadas by swallows, and snakes by deer. The leopard catches most creatures by its smell, and the ape still more so.

Of the shell-backed and shell-skinned creatures this too is peculiar. They are wont to become somewhat emptier and lighter as the moon wanes. And among the shell-backed, the purple-fish and whelks and sea-snails and their kindred prove what I say; among the others, the rock-crabs and crayfish and lobsters and crabs and whatever is akin to these. It is said too that the young of beasts of burden born while the moon wanes are feebler than the others and weaker; and indeed those skilled in these matters advise that what is born in this part of the month should not be reared, for it is of no worth. At the new moon, as I learn, animals either utter something with their natural voice or fall down; but the lion alone, as Aristotle says, does neither of these.

The Pontic mackerel imitate the king of the Persians, who winters in Susa but passes the summer in Ecbatana. For these fish too winter in the so-called Propontis, since that region is warm; but in summer they live by the Aegialus, for the sea I have named provides them with gentle breezes.

In the land of Arcadia there is a sanctuary of Pan; "the Court" is the name of the place. So whatever animals take refuge there, the god, holding them in reverence as suppliants, then saves them with the greatest safety; for the wolves that pursue them shudder to enter within, and are checked merely by seeing whither the prey has fled. These too, it seems, have their own good means toward safety.

Dolphins, it seems, are mindful of their dead too, and in no way betrayers of their fellows when they have departed from life. At any rate, having gone beneath one of their own that has died, they then carry it borne up to the land, trusting that men will bury it, and Aristotle bears witness to this; and another multitude follows, as though honouring it, or, by Zeus, even fighting on its behalf, lest some other sea-monster run up and, seizing the corpse, then devour it. So those who are just and have a sense of music bury them out of reverence for the dolphins' love of music; but others say that they neglect them, with no concern from Muses or Graces. And forgive, dear dolphins, the savagery of men, since even the Athenians cast out unburied the good Phocion. And Olympias too lay naked, she who bore the son of Zeus, as she herself boasted and as he too declared. And the Egyptians, having killed the Roman Pompey, surnamed the Great, who had done so much and won most august victories and celebrated three triumphs and saved the father of his murderer and restored him to the kingdom of the Egyptians, left him cast out, deprived of his head, beside the sea — him too, as they often leave you. For this all-devouring creature, man, does not spare even you, but they dare to make even you into salt-fish, and they do not perceive that they are doing this in anger against the Muses, the daughters of Zeus.

Octopuses too in time grow to great size, advancing toward the bulk of sea-monsters, and they too are reckoned among them. At any rate I am told that at Dicaearchia in Italy an octopus grew to a prodigious bulk of body and came to scorn and despise its food in the sea and the pastures there. This creature would even go forth onto the land and plunder some of the things on shore. Now there was a hidden conduit that carried the refuse of the said city out into the sea; up this the octopus would swim, climbing into a certain house by the shore, where there was a cargo belonging to Iberian merchants and salted fish from those parts stored in stout vessels. Then, wrapping its tentacles about the earthenware and squeezing it, it would break the jars and devour the salt fish. And when the merchants came in and saw the broken pottery, and found a great quantity of their cargo gone, they were astounded and could not guess who was plundering them: for the doors were seen to be untampered with, the roof unbroken, and the walls not dug through; yet the remains of the salt fish, left over by the uninvited guest, were plainly to be seen. So they decided to leave the boldest of their household indoors, armed, to lie in wait. That night the octopus crept up to its accustomed feast, and wrapping itself about the vessels — like an athlete in the wrestling clinch gripping his adversary firmly and very warily — it then crushed the pottery; for the octopus, one may say, was as easy a robber as ever was. It was the time of the full moon, the house was lit up, and everything was clearly visible. But the man would not set upon it alone, fearing the beast — for indeed the enemy was too great for one man — and at dawn he related to the merchants what had been done; and they, hearing it, would not believe him. Then some, remembering the magnitude of their loss, ventured the risk and hastened to engage the foe, while others, thirsting for the strange and incredible spectacle, shut themselves in along with them as volunteer allies. Then in the evening the thief came again and made for his accustomed table. At this point some blocked off the conduit, others armed themselves against the enemy, and with sharpened cleavers and razors they cut through its tentacles, as vine-dressers and woodcutters cut the topmost branches of an oak. And having lopped away its strength they brought it down at last, late and with difficulty, after no little labour; and — the strangest thing — merchants hunted a fish on dry land. So the malice and craftiness of this creature has been revealed to us as a property peculiar to it.

The elephant is said to have a double heart and to think with two minds, raging with the one and growing gentle with the other; and I follow Moorish accounts in saying this. For the same men celebrate this too, that there are lynxes there. They say the lynxes are even more snub-nosed than the leopard, but shaggy at the tips of their ears. This beast is a terrible leaper, and powerful to grip its prey most forcibly and firmly. Euripides too seems to bear witness to this beast, even when he does not name it, where he somewhere says: "He comes upon his shoulders bearing a weight, either of a boar or of the misshapen lynx, a hard-to-bear creature." But what he means by "hard-to-bear" it is better to ask the critics.

When the tunny have been caught in the Pontic hunt (and I should say in the Sicilian too; or with what purpose would Sophron have written his charming Tunny-Hunter? but certainly there are catches of these tunny elsewhere as well) — when they are now entangled in the net, all then pray to Poseidon the averter of evil. And — to tell whence I think fit to give this god his name, demanding it of myself and wishing to speak well of him in this — they beseech the brother of Zeus, who rules the sea, that neither the swordfish come as a fellow-traveller with this shoal, nor the dolphin. For the noble swordfish often cuts through the net and lets the herd escape free. And the dolphin too is a creature that plots against the net; for it is terrible at biting through.

In India there is born a creature like a land-crocodile to look at; in size it would be like a Maltese lapdog. It is covered with scales so rough and so close-set that, when it is flayed, men use the skins for files. It cuts through bronze and gnaws away iron. They call it the phattages.

The crocodile often grows very long. In the time of Psammitichus, king of the Egyptians, a crocodile of twenty-five cubits is said to have appeared, and in the time of Amasis one of twenty-six cubits and four palms. Sea-monsters, I hear, grow to the greatest size about the Laconian sea, and some of the critics say that it was from this that Homer called Lacedaemon "full of sea-monsters." About Cythera they celebrate still greater sea-monsters as growing. Their sinews too, it seems, are useful for the twisting of strings for harps and other instruments, and indeed for engines of war. In the Red Sea, besides those already mentioned, there are bred scorpion-fish and gobies two cubits long, and even three. Amometus says that in Libya there is a certain city in which the priests, charming crocodiles out of a lake with very alluring incantations, lead out crocodiles sixteen cubits long. Theocles, in his fourth book, says that about the Syrtis there are bred sea-monsters greater than triremes. And about the country of the Gedrosii (which is a part of the land of India by no means inglorious) Onesicritus and Orthagoras say that there are bred sea-monsters half a stade in length. They say that these have such power that often, when one of them blows through its nostrils, it throws up so great a swell of the sea that to the ignorant and inexperienced these appear to be waterspouts.

They say that the jackal is a most man-loving creature. When it meets a man anywhere, it turns aside out of his way, as though out of respect; but when it sees him being wronged by some other beast, then it comes to his defence.

In Libya Archelaus says that many mules, either wounded or worn out by thirst, are cast out dead. And often a very great tribe of serpents, flocking together, eat the flesh; but whenever they hear the hiss of a basilisk, those under their dens and the sand vanish most swiftly and hide, while it, coming up in great peace, dines, then hisses again and departs, and the mules and the dinner from them are thenceforth marked, as the saying goes, with stars.

To she-asses nature did not assign braying, they say. But the same nature granted that dogs are made voiceless by hyenas. Sweet scent and perfume are causes of death to vultures. To swans hemlock is destruction. And how the horse fears the camel both Cyrus and Croesus learned, as they say.

I am told that the king of the Scythians (I know his name but pass it by; for what profit is it to me?) had a mare of high quality possessing every excellence that mares are required to have and to show, and that he had also a son of that very mare surpassing all the others in excellence. Now not finding any worthy mate to pair with her, nor any good mare to bring to the son so as to take seed from him, for these reasons he brought the two together to the act. They for their part welcomed and showed affection to each other in every other way, but would not come together. So since the animals were wiser than the Scythian's scheme, he covered both the male and the female with cloaks, and they performed that lawless and unjust act. But when both perceived what had been done, then indeed they atoned for the impiety by death, leaping over a cliff.

In Egypt, as Eudemus says, a monkey was being pursued, and cats were the pursuers. So fleeing with all its might it made straight for a certain tree, and they too sprang up most swiftly; for they cling to the bark, and trees are climbable for them too. But when it was being caught, being one against many, it leaped from the trunk, and seized with its hands the tip of a branch that hung overhead, and held on firmly for no short time; and the cats, since it was no longer within their reach, ran off to another hunt. And it, with much effort, was saved, owing to itself, as was fitting, its rescue.

In Egypt, by the lake called the lake of Moeris, where Crocodilopolis stands, the tomb of a crow is shown, and the Egyptians tell this reason. The king of the Egyptians (this one was called Mares) had a crow as a pet, very tame, and whatever letters he wished conveyed somewhere quickly, this bird carried, and it was the swiftest of messengers, and on hearing it knew where it must direct its flight, and what place it must pass by, and where, on arriving, it must rest. In return for which, when it died, Mares honoured it with a monument and a tomb.

I hear Aristotle saying that cranes flying from the sea to the land give warning to the man who understands of the threat of a severe storm. But when these same birds fly quietly, they promise fair weather and a peaceful sky; and even by their silence the same birds remind those not unskilled that the weather will be calm. But if they fly down and cry out and are troubled and cause trouble, they too in this case threaten a severe storm. A heron crying at dusk seems to indicate the same. A heron flying straight out to sea hints that rain will burst from the sky. But if the weather is wintry, an owl that sings prophesies fair weather and a bright day; whereas if it is fair and the owl gives a low cry, one must expect a storm. The raven that calls quickly and beats and claps its wings was the first to judge that a storm is coming. Again, the raven and the crow and the jackdaw, if they cry in the late evening, teach that some visitation of storm is at hand. Jackdaws screeching like hawks, as he says, and flying now higher, now lower, signify frost and rain. The crow that gives a low cry at suppertime invites fair weather for the morrow. Birds appearing many in number and white in colour teach that there will be much storm. Ducks and gulls that flap their wings indicate a strong wind. Birds flying eagerly from the sea to the land bear witness to a storm. The robin that comes into the farmyards and dwellings clearly is fleeing the visitation of a storm. Cocks too and the domestic fowl, when they beat their wings and bluster and twitter softly, indicate a storm. Birds threaten wind by bathing, and hint at certain onsets of winds. But in stormy weather, birds flying toward one another and darting through one another signify fair weather. Birds that gather about lakes and the banks of rivers are not ignorant that a storm is coming. Again, the birds of the sea and of the marsh, when they go to the land, are not ignorant that there will be much storm; while the land birds hastening to the watery places are messengers of fair weather, provided they keep silent.

I hear Megasthenes say that in the Indian sea there is born a little fish, and that while it lives it is invisible, swimming somewhere below and in the deep, but when dead it floats up. Whoever touches it grows faint at first, and then dies. As for the chelydrus, anyone who treads on it, even if he is not bitten, as Apollodorus says in his treatise On Venomous Creatures, dies in any case; for it has something putrefying, and he says that the mere touch of the creature is enough. And indeed, he who tries somehow to treat and aid the dying man gets blisters on his hands, since he has touched only the man who trod on it. And Aristoxenus somewhere says that a man killed a certain snake with his hands and, though not bitten, nevertheless died; and the garment which he happened to be wearing when he killed the snake also rotted not long after.

Aristotle says that the bass is keenest in hearing, and likewise the chromis and the saupe and the grey mullet. And I learn that the bass knows well that there is a little stone in its head. And in winter this becomes very cold, and pains it severely. For this reason, in that season of the year, it warms itself, and contrives this remedy against the chill from the stone, a most effective one. And the chromis does the same, I have learned, and the sea-bream and the maigre; for these too have a similar stone. There were parasites, it seems, even among the kinds of fish. The one called the "louse," at any rate, nibbles at the dolphin's catch; and the dolphin is pleased with it and willingly shares. For this reason it is very fat, as though stuffed full from a rich and abundant banquet. And Menander's Theron prides himself that he led men by the nose and made them his own manger; while Cleisophus even bound up one of his eyes with a bandage, doing a favour to Philip, whose own eye had been struck out in the siege of Methone. But there is, it seems to me, friendship and fellowship between the louse and the dolphin; for to flatter, as also other evils, a man knows, but the irrational creatures do not know it.

I learn that those cooks who are exact in their craft, whenever they wish the bellies of red mullets not to burst while roasting, kiss the fishes' mouths; and when this has been done, they remain whole, so they say.

In Curias the deer (there is a multitude of these beasts there, and many hunters are intent upon hunting them), whenever they take refuge in the sanctuary of Apollo there (it is a very great grove), the dogs bark indeed, but do not endure to come near; and the deer, gathered together, feed an untroubled and fearless feeding, by some secret nature entrusting to the god their own safety.

Lions they revere in Egypt, and a city is named after them; and it is worth telling the peculiarities of the lions there. They have temples and abundant places of resort, and they have beef every day, and it lies torn in pieces, bare of bones and sinews, and as they eat the Egyptians sing over them in the Egyptian tongue. And the burden of the song is, "Let no one of those looking on bewitch you," and the song is, as one might say, in place of amulets. Many of them are deified among them, and dwellings facing one another are set apart for them. And some windows opening toward the dawn, others toward the evening, make their abode more agreeable to them. They have also gymnasia for the sake of health, and near are wrestling-floors, and the well-fed calf is their adversary. And having exercised against this, if it overthrows it (it does this slowly, from idleness and lack of hunting), it gorges itself and returns to its own den. And the creature is intensely fiery, and from this the Egyptians dedicated it to Hephaestus too; and the fire from outside it shrinks from and flees, they say, owing to the abundance of the fire within. And since it is exceedingly fiery, they say it is the house of the Sun; and when the sun is hottest and most summery in itself, they say it draws near to the Lion. Moreover, those who inhabit the great city of the Sun rear these lions in the gateways of the god's temple, as having a share, the Egyptians say, of a more divine portion. For indeed, standing over those to whom the god is gracious in a dream, they foretell certain things, and those who have sworn falsely they punish, not with delays but at once, the god breathing his just anger upon them through them. And Empedocles too says that the best transmigration of a man is, if his lot should lead him into an animal, to become a lion; if into a plant, a laurel. And what Empedocles says is this: "Among beasts they become mountain-couching, ground-bedded lions, and laurels among the fair-leaved trees." And if one must, of the wisdom of the Egyptians who turn even such things into nature, take account (and one must), they assign the front parts of this animal to fire, but the hinder parts to water. And the double-natured sphinx the Egyptian craftsmen carving and the Theban myths boasting try to show us as of two forms, glorifying it by the mixture of the maiden's face and the lion-like body. This Euripides too hints at, saying: "Curling her tail beneath her lion-footed tread, she sat." And indeed they say the Nemean lion fell from the moon. At any rate the verses of Epimenides say: "For I too am of the race of fair-haired Selene, who, shuddering terribly, shook off the wild beast, the lion, in Nemea, bringing him up at the bidding of revered Hera." But let us assign these things to the myths; the peculiarities of lions have been told both above and now sufficiently.

The Indians heal the wounds of captured elephants in this way. They bathe them with warm water, just as Patroclus did for the wound of Eurypylus in the fair pages of Homer; then they anoint them with butter. If the wounds are deep, they soothe the inflammation by applying and inserting pieces of pork, warm and still bloody. Their eye-diseases they treat by warming cow's milk and pouring it into them; the elephants open their eyelids, and being helped they take pleasure and feel it, just as men do. And they keep flushing them so long as they keep the rheum running; the proof that the inflammation has ceased is this. As for whatever other diseases befall them, dark wine is their remedy. But if a creature is not delivered from its sickness by this medicine, it is past saving.

About the great ostrich one might say this too. When it is killed, its stomach is found, when cleaned out, to hold stones, which the ostrich swallows and keeps and digests in time within its gizzard. These stones would also be good for men's digestion, and the bird's sinews and fat are good for men's sinews. The ostrich is caught by horses; for it runs in a circle, but circling round on the outer side, while the horsemen cut across by the inner circle, and going round a shorter course they catch it in time, when it gives out from running. It is taken also in this way. It makes a low nest on the ground, scooping out the sand with its feet. The very middle of it is hollow, but it builds the edges round about high, walling them off in a manner, so that the rain from heaven may be kept out by the rims and may not flow into the nest and flood the ostrich's chicks, which are tender. It lays even more than eighty eggs, yet does not hatch them all at once, nor do they all come to the light at the same time; but some are already hatched, others are still forming within the eggs, and others are being kept warm. So when the ostrich is engaged in this, a man who is not foolish but practised in such hunting, having observed it, fixes sharpened spear-points about the nest, setting them upright on their butt-ends, and the iron gleams; then he withdraws and lies in wait for what happens. So the ostrich comes back from feeding, loving its chicks strongly and thirsting for their company. At first it looks about this way and that and rolls its eye, fearing lest someone see it; but then, overcome by longing and goaded, spreading its wings like a sail, borne along at a strained pace and with a rush, it leaps into its own nest, and most pitiably, entangled and impaled upon the spear-points, it dies. So the hunter comes up and has taken the offspring along with the mother.

The land of the Indians is rained upon in spring with liquid honey, and still more the country of the Prasii, which, falling upon the grasses and the foliage of the marsh-reeds, furnishes wondrous pasture for the oxen and the sheep; and the animals feast on this most pleasant feast (for the herdsmen lead them chiefly to the places where the sweet dew settles when it has fallen); and the animals in turn feast the herdsmen, for they yield a milk exceedingly sweet, and have no need to mix honey with it, as the Greeks do.

The Syrian partridge is found about Antiochia in Pisidia, and it eats even stones; it is smaller than the partridge and black in colour, but tawny in the beak. It is not tamed like the other, nor does it become domesticated, but remains wild forever. It is not large, pleasanter to eat than the other, and its flesh seems somehow firmer.

Aristotle, in the eighth book on animals, says that elephants eat nine Macedonian medimni of barley, and on top of these six of barley-groats — or, if you give it, even seven; and the same writer says that they drink fourteen Macedonian measures, and again in the afternoon drink eight more. He says that elephants live two hundred years, and that some go on even to three hundred. Clear and pure water is most hateful to the camel to drink, but muddy and filthy water it counts the sweetest of drinks. And indeed, if it comes to a river or a lake, it does not stoop to drink before it has stirred up the mud with its feet and destroyed the beauty of the water. If it remains without drink, it can hold out even eight days.

A certain Nicias, one of a hunting party, was unexpectedly carried off course and fell into a charcoal-burners' kiln; and the dogs that were with him, seeing this, did not leave him, but at first whined and howled about the kiln; in the end they did all but lead the passers-by to the disaster, taking hold of their cloaks gently and sparingly with their teeth and dragging them, as though the dogs were calling the men to help their master. And so one man, seeing what they did, suspected what had happened, and followed and found Nicias burned to death in the kiln, inferring from the remains what had occurred.

Accounts of the Euboeans that come this way say that the fishermen there assign to the dolphins of those parts an equal share of the catch; and I hear that the fishing is of this kind. There must be a calm, and if this is so, they hang from the prow of their boats certain hollow braziers with fire blazing in them; and these are transparent, so as both to enclose the fire and not to hide the light. They call them lanterns. So the fish fear the glare and are dismayed by the brightness; and some, not knowing what the thing they see intends, draw near, wishing to learn the cause of what frightens them; then, struck with terror, they either rest in throngs by some rock, quivering with fear, or are thrust out onto the shore, and resemble men thunderstruck. And when they are in such a state it is then very easy to strike them even with a trident. So when the dolphins see the fishermen kindle the fire, they make themselves ready. And while the men gently row over, the dolphins frighten and push the fish on the outside and check them from escaping. So those fish, pressed on every side and in a way encircled both by the men's rowing and by the dolphins' swimming, understand that there is no escape for them, and they stay and are caught, a very great quantity. And the dolphins come up as though demanding the profit of the common toil owed them from the gathering, and the fishermen faithfully and fair-mindedly yield to their fellow-hunters the just portion, if they wish their allies to be present again, uninvited and without excuse. For the seamen there believe that if they transgress they will have as enemies those whom they had before as friends.
When horses' foals are left by their mothers before their rearing, like orphans, the other mares rear them together with their own young, taking pity on them.

Eudemus relates that a groom fell in love with a young mare, the best of the herd, as one might with a beautiful girl, the loveliest in the whole estate; and that at first he held himself in check, but at last ventured upon the strange union and had intercourse with her. She had a foal, itself also beautiful, which, seeing what was being done, was grieved, as though its mother were being tyrannized by its master, and it leapt upon the man and killed him; and afterwards it watched where he was buried, and going there it dug him up and outraged the corpse and mangled it with all manner of mutilation.

Aristotle says that the land of the Astypalaeans is hostile to snakes, just as the same author agrees with us that Rheneia is hostile to weasels. And the crow cannot climb up to the Athenian acropolis. And you will not call Elis the mother of mules—or what is said is false.

Each kind of animal possesses also a peculiar name for the care taken in rearing it. There is, at any rate, what one might call colt-breaking, and puppy-rearing, and elephant-tending, and lion-rearing, and bird-rearing, and the like.

I hear the Egyptians say that the oryx perceives the rising of Sirius first, and bears witness to it by sneezing. The Libyans too boast vigorously, asserting that among them even the goats foreknow this same thing. These animals also foreshow rain when it is coming; for when they have gone out of their folds, they rush at a run, and very swiftly, to the fodder; then, when they have eaten their fill, they turn back toward home, and standing there with their faces toward it they remain still, waiting for the shepherd to drive them in as quickly as possible. Hipparchus, in the time of the tyrant Hieron, sitting in the theatre and wearing a leather cloak, astonished men because he foreknew the coming storm from the present clear sky; and Hieron admired him, and congratulated the Nicaeans of Bithynia that Hipparchus was their fellow citizen. At Olympia too Anaxagoras, watching the Olympic games in a leather cloak, when rain burst forth, was celebrated by all Hellas, and boasted that he understood things too divine for mortal nature. That an ox, if Zeus is about to send rain, lies down on its right haunch, but if there is to be fair weather, again on the left, scarcely anyone wonders at. And these things too I have heard, which are enough to astonish. If an ox bellows and sniffs the air, rain must follow. Cattle that eat their fill and beyond their custom indicate a storm. Sheep that dig the earth with their hooves seem to signify a storm; and these same, if they mate early in the season, agree that an early winter is coming. Goats that lie down all together signify the same. Swine appearing in the cornlands teach that rain is to be avoided. Lambs and kids that leap upon one another and skip about agree that a bright day is coming. Weasels squeaking, and mice doing the same as they, betoken that there will be a severe storm. Wolves that flee the wilds and go straight toward inhabited places bear witness by their behaviour that they have shuddered at the onset of a coming storm. A lion's visitation in the fruitful regions indicates drought. Beasts of burden that frisk and bray more than their custom indicate that a wet storm is coming; and if a beast throws up dust with its hooves, this too signifies the same. But hares seen in numbers in these same regions indicate fair weather. In all these matters men are left behind, and learn of such things only when they have happened.
Nicander says that the skin of the amphisbaena, wrapped around a staff, drives off all snakes and the other creatures which kill not by biting but by striking.

The elephant has this strong love too toward its offspring. The hunters of these beasts dig trenches, into which these animals fall, and some are taken and some are killed. And what the manner of such trenching is, and what its shape, and how great its depth, and what the approaches are—you will learn elsewhere; but I come to uncover and to prove their affection. A mother, seeing her own calf fallen into one of the trenches, neither hesitated nor lingered idly, but rushing with all the impulse she had, eagerly and with overwhelming feeling, she thrust herself down headlong upon her young, and both met the same end together; for the calf, crushed by the mother's weight, was shattered, while she perished darting down headlong. Ridiculous, then, are those who

The female dolphin has breasts like a woman's, and suckles her young with milk most abundant and plentiful. They swim together, but separated according to age: the young and tender ones are stationed in the first rank, and the full-grown follow them in the swim. For the dolphin is a creature loving to its offspring and full of affection, and it is anxious for its young. And for the sake of protection, as in a soldiers' battle-line, some belong to the first rank, some to the second, some to the third; the young swim in front, the females swim behind them, and the males bring up the rear, watching over and guarding the swimming of their offspring and their mates. What has Nestor to say to this, fair Homer, whom you celebrate in song as the best tactician of the heroes of his time?

I have said somewhere above that the flies in Olympia, at the coming of the festal assembly, willingly withdraw and, as one might say, go off together with the women to the opposite bank of the Alpheus. In Leucas there is a high headland, and a temple is founded to Apollo, and those who honour him name him Actian. So when the assembly is about to gather, at which they also perform the leap for the god, they sacrifice an ox to the flies, and these, filled with the blood, disappear. The flies of Leucas, then, depart when bribed, but those of Pisa are unbribed. Those, therefore, are the better, doing what is needful out of reverence for the god, and not for a wage.

There is a creature, the moth, which delights in the brightness of fire and flies to lamps when they are at their height, and falling upon them by its rush it is then burnt up. Aeschylus too, the poet of tragedy, mentions it, saying: "I greatly fear the foolish doom of the moth."

For an elephant of the herd, though tamed, water is its drink; but for one trained for war the drink is wine — not the wine of the vine, but one they make by craft, one from rice, another from cane. They also go out to gather flowers for them; for elephants are lovers of fragrance, and they are led into the meadows to be broken in by the sweetest of scents. The elephant chooses out the flower, judging by its smell, and the trainer, holding a basket, holds it out as the beast gathers and casts in. Then, when it has filled the basket, it bathes, as though it had been plucking fruit, and delights in the bath like the more luxurious sort of men. Afterward, on returning, it longs for the flowers, and cries out if they are slow in coming, and will not take its food before someone brings it what it gathered. Then, taking the flowers from the basket with its trunk, it strews them over the edge of its manger, devising in this way, through their sweet scent, a relish for its food, so to speak. It also scatters many of the flowers over the place where it lodges, eager to win a sleep made sweet. The Indian elephants were nine cubits in height and five in breadth. The greatest of the elephants there are those called the Prasian, and second to these would rank the Taxilan.

There is a city in the western regions of Italy; its name is Patavium. They say the city is the work of Antenor the Trojan. He founded it, having been saved from his home when he departed after his fatherland Ilium was taken, the Greeks having shown him respect, since he had saved Menelaus when he came on embassy with Odysseus concerning Helen, though Antimachus advised that they be killed. And Antimachus gave this advice having received Alexander's gold, splendid gifts, as Homer says. Now another city neighbours this Patavium, and they call it Vicetia, and a river flows past it named the Eretaenus, and this river passes a good deal of country and then falls into the Eridanus, and shares its water with it. Now in the Eretaenus there are eels of the greatest size, and by far fatter than those elsewhere; and they are caught in this way. The hunter sits upon a jutting rock in some bay-like spot, where the stream spreads out wider, or he sits upon some tree that has been thrown roots and all near the bank by a strong wind, which rots beneath but is useless to cut up and burn. So this eel-fisher, taking his seat, and taking the gut of a newly slaughtered lamb, three or four cubits long and very fat, lets one end of it down into the water, and it is whirled about, turning in the eddies; but the other end he holds in his hands, and into it has been inserted a piece of reed, as long as a sword-hilt. The food does not escape the eels; for they delight in this gut. And the first one that comes up, goaded by hunger and gaping wide, fixes in its teeth, which are curved and hooked and hard to disengage, and continually leaps about and tries to drag the bait down. The man, perceiving from the trembling of the gut that the eel has hold, puts into his own mouth the reed to which the gut is attached, and blowing down it with all his might, inflates the gut very strongly, and from the inrushing breath it swells and grows distended. So the wind slips down into the eel and fills its head with breath and fills its throat, and stops up the creature's breathing. And unable to breathe, nor yet to draw out from the entrail the teeth fixed in it, the eel is choked, and is hauled up, caught by the gut and the breath and the reed as a third agent. Now this is done day by day, and many eels are caught by many fishers. Let these things too be told by me as peculiar to these fishes.

The Indian pearl (for above I spoke of the Red Sea pearl) is got in this way. There is a city ruled by a man named Soras, of royal race, at the time when Eucratides ruled the Bactrians; the city's name is Perimula, and Fish-eaters dwell in it. From there, they say, the said men set out with their nets and enclose with great arms a fair-sized circle of shore; and the said stone is formed in a shell like a large whelk, and the pearl-oysters swim in herds and have leaders, as in the hives the bees have those called kings; and I am told that this leader too is distinguished both in colour and in size. The underwater divers make it a contest to catch this one; for when it is taken, they take the whole herd, which is then, as one might say, left desolate and without a champion; for it keeps still and goes no further, like a flock that has lost its herdsman by some hostile chance; but the leader escapes and very cleverly winds away, and goes before and saves its subjects. Those that are caught they are said to salt in jars; and when the flesh rots and runs off, the pebble is left behind. The best is the Indian and that of the Red Sea. It is found also in the Western Ocean, where the island of Britain is; but it seems somehow more golden to look upon, and to have its lustre duller and dimmer. Juba says it is found also in the strait by the Bosporus, and is inferior to the British, and that it cannot at all be compared with the Indian and the Red Sea pearl. The land-pearl in India is said to have no peculiar nature of its own, but to be an offspring of crystal — not of the crystal that forms from frosts, but of the mined kind.
The Indian sea breeds sea-snakes broad in the tail; and the lakes too breed water-snakes of the greatest size. The sea-serpents seem to have a bite that is jagged rather than venomous.

Pythagoras, in his work on the Red Sea, says that there comes into being a certain land animal about that sea, called the kepos. The name fits it, for it has many colours. The full-grown one is the size of the Eretrian dogs. I wish to go over its variegated nature and show it in words, as he writes. The parts about its head, and its back, and the spine ending in the tail, are pure tawny, and you may see also certain golden hairs scattered about; its face is white as far as the cheeks, but from there golden bands run down to the neck. The parts below this, as far as the breast, and the forefeet, are all whitish. There are two breasts, dark, each filling the hand; the belly is all white, and the hind feet are black. As for the shape of the face, you will speak truly, be sure, if you compare it to a baboon's.

The drone that is bred among the bees hides by day in the honeycombs, but by night, when it has watched for the bees to fall asleep, it visits their work and damages the hives. When the bees have observed this, most of them sleep, being worn out, but a few of them lie in wait. Then, when they have caught the thief, they strike him sparingly and thrust him out and cast him forth into exile. But even so he is not disciplined; for he is by nature both idle and greedy — two evils. So he hides himself outside the combs, and then, when the bees set out
The deer conquers the serpent, by a certain wonderful gift of nature; and the hated enemy cannot escape its notice when it is in its hole, but applying its nostrils to the entrance of the lair

Crows are most faithful to one another, and when they come together into partnership they are exceedingly fond of each other, and one would not see these creatures mating loosely and at random. And those who are exact about these matters say that if one of them dies, the other remains widowed. And I hear that the ancients in their marriages, after

Most fish during the spring are eager for love, and they betake themselves rather to the Black Sea; for it has, in a way, chambers and resting-places—these being nature's gifts to fishes—and moreover it is free of such beasts as the sea feeds. Dolphins alone roam there, slender and weak; and indeed it is barren of the octopus and produces no crab, and

For the people of Rhegium and the Locrians it is by treaty allowed to pass into each other's land and till it. Yet the cicadas of the one and of the other do not agree with these terms, nor are they of one and the same mind; for you will find the Locrian cicada most silent in Rhegium, and the Rhegian most

These too were wise acts of the bear. If it is pursued together with its cubs, it pushes them on as far as it can; but when it perceives that one has given out, it carries one on its back and one in its mouth, and laying hold of a tree leaps up; and the one clings to its back with its claws, while the other is carried in its teeth as it runs

Concerning hawks I have heard this too. The servants of Apollo in Egypt say that there are certain men called hawk-keepers, who are the rearers and tenders of the god's hawks. Now the whole tribe is dedicated to this god; but some there are reared as sacred with carefully prepared food, and they seem to be in no way different from the offerings dedicated to the god.

A dog troubled by repletion knows a grass that grows in the stone walls, and having tasted of it, it vomits up all that pains it, with phlegm and bile, and a great deal of refuse passes from it, and it procures its own deliverance, without needing physicians as allies at all. And it discharges, moreover, a quantity of black bile, which, if it remained, would produce in dogs madness, a grievous disease. And when full of worms, they eat the beards of grain, as Aristotle says. When wounded, they have in their tongue a remedy, with which, licking around the wounded part, they bring it back to health, having bidden a long farewell to bandages and dressings and compounds of drugs. And this too has not escaped the dog, that the fruit of the manna-ash fattens swine, but brings on hip-pain for itself; and seeing a sow stuffing herself with the fruit aforesaid, it keeps away from it very firmly, even from what seems pleasant. But men

are in doubt whether there is a natural affection toward offspring. The seals give birth on the land, but little by little they bring their pups to the wet, and give them a taste of the sea, then lead them back to the place of their birth, and again

As to the male and female viper, some say that they differ in kind but not in nature, the one being male and the other female; others think they differ in nature as well, the one being one sort of creature and the other another. I hear some say that those bitten by the male viper are seized with convulsions, but not those bitten by the female. Others say that the bite of the female is white, but that of the male is not so, but livid. Nicander says that from the bite which the male viper inflicts there appear the marks of two teeth, but of more, if the female should bite.

There is an island, Icarus, and it lies in the Red Sea. There, then, is a temple of Artemis, and multitudes of wild goats and of gazelles very well-fed, and hares too. If, then, anyone, having asked leave of the goddess to take them, then attempts to hunt as many as he can with success, he does not fail of his eagerness, but both takes them and rejoices in the gift; but if he does not ask, he neither takes them and pays penalties, which others tell.

The wagtail is a winged creature, weak in its hinder parts, and for this reason they say it is unable to weave a nest privately or by itself, but lays its eggs in those of others. From this the proverbs of the countryfolk called beggars "wagtails." It moves its tail-feathers, like the halcyon in Archilochus. Aristophanes too mentions this bird in his Amphiaraus, saying: "Wag your loins from the tips like a wagtail, of an old man, and you will work a good charm." And in his Old Age: "the wagtail-stepping rhythm of one stooping." And Autocrates in his Drummers: "as the dear maiden daughters of the Lydians play, lightly leaping their hair, and clapping with their hands, before Ephesian Artemis the fairest, and lifting one hip downward and the other again upward, as a wagtail leaps."

To hold and check an Indian horse as it springs and bolts forward was not within every man's power, but only of those trained in horsemanship from boyhood. For it is not their custom to govern these horses with a bit, to keep them in rhythm and steer them, but with spiked muzzles; for the horses have an unruly tongue and an untried palate. Nevertheless these masters of horsemanship compel them to wheel about and turn round in a circle, revolving on the same spot. Whoever would do this needs both strength of arm and a thorough knowledge of horsemanship.

That the sea-lion resembles the crayfish in a way, we too know; but we see that it is slighter in the build of its body, and somewhat tinged with blue, and that it is sluggish and has very large claws, like in shape to those of crabs. It is said by the more skilled fishermen to have certain membranes attached to its shell, beneath which membranes are tender little pieces of flesh, and these are called the fat of that lion. And men derive this benefit from them: it cleanses muddy complexion from the face, and mixed with oil blended with roses and made into an ointment it lends to beauty and brightness. I have also heard this further: that the lion on land is greatly afraid of the strange look of the sea-lion, and cannot bear its smell; and that the same lion fears the cock, I have said above. They say too that, when its shells are crushed and the powder cast into water, the land-lion that drinks it is delivered from a sickness troubling its belly. Let these too be told by me as peculiar to the sea-lion.

Now about the cranes among birds I well know I have spoken in earlier discourses; but I declare I have heard of a sea-crane, a fish bred in the Corinthian sea. This sea, where this crane was tracked down, slopes toward the sea facing Athens, on the side of the isthmus that looks toward them. In length, then, it ran to about fifteen feet, measured by a just measure, and it had, as I hear, the thickness of an eel, though not of the largest.
In India of wild horses and of asses of this kind

There is a creature they call the onocentaur, and whoever has seen it would not disbelieve that there were also tribes of Centaurs, and that the craftsmen did not lie against nature, but that time brought forth those too, united from bodies that were not alike. But let us leave them, whether they really came to be at one and the same appearing, or whether rumour, which is more pliable and more persuasible than any wax, moulded them, and mixed half-parts of horse and man by some divine joining, and gave them a single soul. But this creature, about which the present account has set out to speak, came to my hearing in the following way. It is likened in the face to a man, and deep hair runs round it. A neck beneath the face, and breasts, and these too human; nipples raised and standing on the chest, and shoulders and upper arms and forearms, and besides hands and breast down to the loins, and these too human; but the spine and the ribs and the belly and the hind feet are very like an ass's, and ash-coloured

to their pastures, he forces his way in and does his own work, gorging himself and ravaging the bees' sweet treasure. And they, returning from the pasture, when they come upon him, no longer strike him sparingly nor merely enough to put him to flight, but falling on him most violently they crush the robber; and undergoing no light penalty, he pays with his life for his gluttony and greed. The bee-keepers say this, and they convince me. There are also among the bees certain idle bees, yet not drone-like in their ways; for these do not damage the combs nor plot against the honey, but feed from the flowers, themselves flying about and grazing with the others. And even if they are unskilled in the work and the gathering of the honey, still they are not wholly idle. For some of them bring water to the king and to the elder bees, those that attend the king and have been set apart as his bodyguard; others have this task, to carry outside the bees that are dying — for their combs must be kept clean, and they do not tolerate a dead bee within; and others keep watch by night, like guards keeping a small city, the building of the combs.

of the venomous creature, it breathes in most violently, and draws it as with a spell by its breath, and brings it out against its will, and as it peers out begins to eat it; and most of all it does this through the winter. A man, too, has shaved a deer's horn, then cast the shavings into the fire, and the smoke rising drives the serpents from everywhere, since they cannot bear even the smell. The horse is otherwise a proud creature; for its size and speed, the loftiness of its neck, the suppleness of its legs, and the striking of its hooves lift it into haughtiness and vanity; and especially a long-maned mare is most dainty and most luxurious. So she disdains to let asses mount her, but delights to be wedded to a horse, and counts herself worthy of the greatest. Knowing this, those who wish to get mules for themselves shear off the mare's mane carelessly and at random, and then bring the asses to her; and she submits to the now inglorious bridegroom, ashamed at first. And Sophocles seems to mention this experience.

the wedding-song, used to sing the crow, giving this as a token of concord to those who come together for the begetting of children. But those who watch the seats and flights of birds say it is an ill omen for a single crow to answer. And since the owl is its enemy, and by night plots against the crow's eggs, the crow by day does this same thing to the owl, knowing that the owl's sight is then weak. The land-hedgehog nature has made not unwise nor unlearned in storing up for use. For since it needs food for the whole year, but not every season gives the fruits in season, it rolls itself, they say, in the drying-floors, and the dried figs that get stuck on it — many fix themselves on its spines — it quietly carries off, and having laid them up in store keeps them, and can take from its den, at a time when it is not possible to procure them from outside.

it does not breed the lobster; but these are the destruction of small fish. I learn that when the new moon first appears, the elephants, by some natural and mysterious instinct, take freshly plucked branches from the wood in which they pasture and then raise them aloft, and look up toward the goddess, and gently wave the branches, as though holding out to the goddess this supplication on behalf of her being gracious and kindly to them.

voiceless among the Locrians. And what the reason for such an exchange is, I do not know, nor does anyone else, unless he is idly bold; but Nature alone knows, O men of Rhegium and Locri. At any rate a river runs between the land of the Rhegians and Locris, and the banks are not parted even by the distance of a plethron, and yet neither kind flies across it. And in Cephallenia there is a river which is the cause of the fruitfulness of the cicadas on one side and their barrenness on the other. As for their king, the bees, when he leaves them—being gentle and tame and very nearly stingless—pursue and chase him as a fugitive from his rule. They track him by scent in a secret way, and seize him from the smell about him, and bring him back to his kingship, willingly and of their own desire, admiring his character. But the Athenians drove out Pisistratus, and the Syracusans Dionysius, and others others, since they were tyrants and lawless and unable to display the kingly art, which is indeed humanity and the protection of subjects.

up. And when it meets a bull while hungry, it does not fight by main force and in a straight line, but it wrestles, and seizing the neck-tendon it bends it down and tightens its grip. And the bull is pressed and bellows, and at last gives out and lies down, and the bear fills itself. We have recognized that animals are good at learning in this respect too. In the time of the Ptolemies the Egyptians taught the dog-faced baboons letters and dancing and flute-playing and harp-playing. And a baboon would exact payment for these things, and putting what was given into a little pouch hung from it would carry it, like those clever at gathering alms. And that the Sybarites taught horses even to dance, has long been proclaimed. And the docility of elephants to learning and their readiness I have spoken of above. And dogs, too, are capable of serving in the house those who have trained them, and it is enough for a poor man to have a dog as a slave. There were, however, even of such men, some without slaves, like the Troglodytes among the Arabians, and the Nomads among the Libyans, and that part of the Ethiopians who live by the lakes, who have learned to eat nothing at all beyond their food from fish. And the animal remembers what it suffers, and needs for its memory no art—not Simonides, not Hippias, not Theodectes, nor any other of those proclaimed for this profession and this skill. Where the cow has been robbed of its calf, at any rate, coming there it laments its affliction with familiar lowing. And oxen about to go under the yoke, some smile, others retreat step by step. And a horse, when it hears the rattle of bits and the clink of the bridle, and beholds the breast-pieces and frontlets, snorts thereat, and prancing strikes its hooves and is filled with rapture; the shout of the grooms rouses it, and it pricks up its ears and dilates its nostrils, by the memory of the course and by the irresistible spell of habit.

Those, then, who have been entrusted with the care of these hawks tell the ignorant that they all lay their eggs in their nests—for they are reared in a sacred grove—and it is agreed that, while this is true of other hawks, it is still more so of these. To the newly hatched they offer the brains, extracted from birds that have been caught, a soft food for tender chicks; but to those that are full-grown they set out flesh and sinews, all that makes strong nourishment for birds of prey; while to those between the newly hatched and the already full-grown, hearts are set out, and the remains of these are seen. And the difference of food just mentioned proves that the hawks know what is suited and proper to each age, and observe it very precisely, and would not touch food unsuited to their age. In season, moreover, there are visitations of quails to them, and flocks of other birds come, and those sacred hawks have a feast from these too. The boundless goodwill of dogs toward those who feed them is shown by this also. In one of the civil wars at Rome, when Calvus the Roman had been slain, none of the man's enemies was able to cut off his head, though countless men made it their contest and their boast to do so, until they had killed the dog that stood beside him—a dog reared by him, which most faithfully preserved its goodwill toward him and fought in defence of the fallen man, like a good comrade-in-arms and tent-mate and a friend to the last. And it is worth learning what was done by another—not a man, by Zeus, but a good dog, strong of purpose. Pyrrhus of Epirus was travelling, and came upon a murdered man, with a dog standing beside him and guarding its master, so that no one might do further outrage to the slaying and the corpse. The dog happened to be on the third day without food, keeping its laborious and most steadfast watch. When Pyrrhus learned of this, he pitied the dead man and gave him burial, and ordered that the dog be cared for; and he gave it from his own hand all that a dog longs for, in plenty, and enough to draw it into friendship and goodwill toward himself, Pyrrhus winning the dog over little by little. So much for that. Then, not long afterward, there was a review of the soldiers, and the king of whom I spoke was watching, and that dog was beside him. In all else it kept quiet and was very gentle; but when it saw its master's murderers in the review of the soldiers, it could not bear to remain still, but leaped at them and barked, tearing at them with its claws, and turning often toward Pyrrhus, it called him, as best it could, to witness that it had found the murderers. So suspicion came upon the king and those around him, and they took to heart the dog's barking at the men aforesaid. They were arrested and tortured, and confessed all that they had dared to do. To those who, having trampled upon the law of Zeus the god of comradeship and friendship, have betrayed their friends both living and dead, this seems a mere fable; but I do not believe those who think ill of the noble gifts of Nature, which, if it gave goodwill and affection to the irrational creatures, surely gave them all the more to this rational creature, man. But men do not use the gift. And why should one go on to recount all the other evils that men have wrought against their own friends for the sake of base gain, weaving plots and betraying them? For my part, it grieves me if a dog has been proved more faithful and more loving than men.

are often overcome, quite without self-control, by those who persuade them to eat against their will. Not easily would an ambush escape the elephants. At any rate, when they come near the trench which those hunting them are accustomed to dig, whether by some natural understanding or, by Zeus, by a secret prophetic sense, they are checked from advancing farther, and turning themselves about they then stand their ground, as in war, most stoutly, and try to overturn the hunters and, having forced their way through them, to procure their safety by flight, becoming the stronger over their adversaries. There then arises, at that moment, a fierce battle, and slaughter on both sides. The manner of this battle is as follows. The men hurl strong spears, aiming at them, while the elephants seize whoever comes within reach, and dashing him to the ground and trampling him and wounding him with their tusks, they bring upon him a most pitiable and most painful end. The beasts advance, in their fury, spreading out their ears like sails, after the manner of the great ostriches, which spread their wings and either flee or advance; and the elephants, curving up their trunks and folding them under their tusks, like the ram of a ship borne along with a great surge, fall upon them with most violent rush and overturn many, trumpeting a piercing and shrill note like a trumpet. And as those caught are trampled and crushed by the knees, a great crash of bones being shattered is heard even from afar, and as their eyes are squeezed out of their faces and their noses crushed and their foreheads broken, the distinctness of their appearance is lost, and they often become unrecognizable even to their nearest kin. But others are unexpectedly saved in this way. The hunter is caught, but the beast in its rush overpasses him, and drives its knees into the ground, and fixes its tusks fast into a bush or a root or some such thing, and is held, and only with difficulty pulls them out and frees them; and in the meantime the huntsman slips out and gets away. So in such a battle the elephants often prevail, but often too are defeated, when the men bring against them terrors devised by stratagem and varied fears. For trumpets sound, and they make a din and a clatter, striking their spears against their shields, and some fire they kindle upon the ground, and some they raise aloft, and other fire they sling, hurling blazing brands and shaking violently against the faces of the beasts long torches of fire at its height. And the beasts, fearing these and confounded, are pushed back, and sometimes are even forced to fall into the trench which till then they had guarded against.

lead them down to the sea, and quickly lead them out; and when they have done this many times, in the end they make them most accomplished swimmers. And easily does the pup slip into the sea-life, instruction leading it on, while Nature compels it to love its mother's ways and habits and customs. The eagle is a grasping creature, and they make their food by plunder, and eat flesh; for they snatch hares and fawns and a goose from the yard and other things. But one alone among them, the very one that is called "of Zeus," touches no flesh, but grass suffices it; and though it has heard nothing of Pythagoras of Samos, yet it abstains from living things.

When the hunting of elephants has been successful, it is worth telling what men do to tame them and make them gentle. First they lead them, bound, into some wood a little way from the trench in which they were caught, gripping them with ropes and allowing them neither to rush forward nor again to draw back and pull away. Then they fasten each one to a great tree at a measured distance, so that it can neither leap forward nor again retreat far with freedom to caper and run riot; and by starvation and hunger they break down their excessive strength and vigour, and gently wear away their spirit and the stubbornness of their souls, so that the elephants come to forget their once invincible ferocity and are released from their former fury. Then the trainers of such beasts approach and offer them food from the hand, and the elephants, compelled by need, take it and do no harm, and already look gentle and worn out. But the very strong and full-grown among them break their bonds, and with the points of their tusks and with their trunks tear up the trees, or even snap them off by their rush and fall upon them; these are tamed only with difficulty and after long time, some by hunger, some by sweet food, some by the goad. The food for these animals while they are being tamed is the largest loaves, barley, dried figs, raisins, onions, garlic, honey in abundance, bundles of mastich and palm and ivy, and every kind of edible vegetation that is also their natural fare and therefore dear to them.

So then, since I made mention of the Rhipaean swans among the Hyperboreans, because they serve the son of Zeus and Leto every day with devotion, shall we not tell the peculiarities of the sacred bull which the Egyptians deify? And how would not both this work and Nature blame us, of whom this too is a work and a gift? But the account shall be not careless on this side either, and fittingly this piece of theology too shall be told. Apis is believed by the Egyptians to be a god most manifest. He is born of a cow, into which a heavenly light, falling, is the cause of his conception. And the Greeks call him Epaphus, and trace his mother to be Io the Argive, the daughter of Inachus; but the Egyptians reject this account as false, and use time as their witness. For they say that Epaphus was born late and recently, but that the first Apis took up his sojourn among men many myriads of years earlier. The signs and tokens of him are told by Herodotus and by Aristagoras, but the Egyptians do not agree with them; for they say there are twenty-nine of them and that they are conspicuous on this sacred bull. What these are, and how they are scattered over the body of the animal, and in what way they are, as it were, spangled upon him, you will learn elsewhere; but as to which of the stars each sign by symbols hints at its nature, the Egyptians are competent to give proof. For indeed they say that the signs reveal the rising of the Nile and the shape of the cosmos; and there is a certain sign and symbol, as they say, which hints that darkness is older than light. And the crescent shape of the moon declares another sign to the one who understands, and besides these there are other riddles of other things, not easy to read with the eyes for the profane and the ignorant of divine lore. When the report spreads abroad saying that the god has been born to the Egyptians, some of the sacred scribes, to whom the exact knowledge of the test concerning the signs has been handed down as a study from father to son, come there, where the calf of the god-beloved cow was born, and according to the most ancient direction of Hermes they raise a house, where surely it shall live for the first time, looking toward the risings of the sun and receiving the food of the calf in sufficient measure; for this calf must be at the milk for four months. And when it has been reared up, then, as the new moon rises, sacred scribes and prophets come to meet it, and indeed each year they adorn for this purpose a ship sacred to this god, and in it they ferry him to Memphis, where are his dearest haunts and welcome dwellings and pleasure-grounds and runs and wrestling-floors and gymnasia and homes of fair cows and a well and a spring of drinkable water; for the attendants and priests say it does not always profit him to drink of the Nile, since one grows fat on this sweet stream, which is good for a bulk of flesh. The processions which they conduct, and the sacred rites which they perform, sacrificing the epiphany-offerings of the new god — the Egyptians — and the dances they dance, and the feasts and assemblies they hold, and how every city and village goes through with mirth, it would be long to tell. And he in whose herd this divine animal was born seems blessed and is so, and the Egyptians hold him in wonder. And Apis was a good seer, not, by Zeus, by seating maidens or older women upon any tripods, nor by filling them with a sacred draught, but — what one prays for to this god — children playing outside and frisking to the pipes, becoming inspired, foretell in rhythm each several thing, so that what they say is truer than the words at the Sagra. The Egyptians liken him also to Horus, whom indeed they have believed to be most of all the cause of the bearing of crops and of all good seasons. From this too they philosophize about his many colours, hinting through symbols at the variety of the crops. And a certain account of the prophets, not known to all, says that Menis the king of the Egyptians devised to revere a living animal, and then chose the bull, having believed it to be the fairest of all and going in the footsteps of Homer's judgment about these matters, says Menis. For Homer too says in the Iliad: "As a bull stands forth pre-eminent among all in the herd; for he is conspicuous among the gathered cattle." But the things to which the Egyptians who have written about the animals turn aside into mythology about this beast do not seem to me agreeable.

Mice that die by themselves and from no plot, their limbs flowing away from them, depart little by little from life. From this the proverb says "according to a mouse's destruction," and Menander mentions it in his Thais. They used to say "more talkative than a turtle-dove"; for the turtle-dove both utters sound unceasingly through its mouth, and already, as they say, very much also from its hinder parts. The same poet mentions this proverb too in his Necklace. And Demetrius in his play Sicily mentions that the turtle-doves talk with their rump too. They say that mice are most lecherous, and they bring forward Cratinus as witness, who says in his Runaway Women: "Come now, let me flash for you, out of a clear sky, the lewdness of Xenophon's mouse." And still more they used to say the female was raging mad for venery. And again in Epicrates' Chorus: "But the accursed bawd quite took me in, swearing by the Maid, by Artemis, by Pherrephatta, that she was like a heifer, like a virgin, like an unbroken filly. But she was a whole mouse-warren." And wishing to call her lecherous to excess, he named her a whole mouse-warren. And Philemon: "a white mouse — when anyone — but I am ashamed to speak — the accursed creature cries out so loudly at once that it is often impossible to escape notice."

Those who have reached the height of this skill try to wheel and drive a chariot about in the same way; and it would be no contemptible feat to turn a team of four ravenous horses round with ease. The chariot carries two fighters beside the driver. The war-elephant, upon what is called its little tower, or indeed upon its bare and unencumbered back, carries three warriors, two hurling missiles on either side and the third behind, and a fourth who holds the goad in his hands and with it steers the beast, as a skilled steersman and master of the ship steers a vessel with the rudder. The hunting of leopards would be a Moorish practice. They have a building made of stones, resembling a kind of cage; this is the first enclosure. As for the second, further in, they hang from a longish cord a portion of rotten and stinking flesh, and they set up a flimsy door of reeds and certain canes, and through it the smell of the said flesh streams out and disperses. The beasts catch the scent — for somehow they take pleasure in foul smells — for the air bearing those odours strikes upon them, whether they are on the mountain-tops, or in a ravine, or even in a glen. Then, inflamed at meeting the smell, and by its overpowering urge, the leopard rushes headlong to the beloved banquet, drawn on by it as though by a magic charm. It falls upon the door, overturns it, and lays hold of its ill-fated dinner. For along with the said cord a very cunning snare has been woven in, which is set in motion as the flesh is eaten and closes about the greedy leopard. And she is caught — the unhappy creature paying the penalty for her ravenous belly and her loathsome feasting.

The Moorish asses, swiftest to run, are at their first onset most keen, so that one might think there was some rush of a breeze, or, by Zeus, the very wing of a bird; but they soon tire, and their feet give out, and their breath fails, and they forget their swiftness and stand fettered, and let fall plentiful tears — not, it seems to me, so much over their coming death as over the weakness of their feet. So the men, leaping down from their horses, then throw nooses about their necks, and each, fastening the captive to his horse, leads it off as a prisoner. That the Libyan horses are small to look at but swiftest to run, I have said above.

Its head and mouth are those of the winged crane, and its scales — these too you would call a crane's feathers. It does not move with a winding swim, like those of the fish that are narrow and long after the manner of eels. It has a strength very apt for leaping; at any rate it springs like an arrow shot from a bowstring.
