Now the Epidaurian accounts say that this creature is the offspring of no fish, but that the winged cranes, fleeing the Thracian frost and the other western cold, fall in with the wind; and the females are goaded to mating, and the males are inflamed for them, and indeed swell toward union with them, and for this reason wish to mount them, but the females do not endure it, for they cannot bear mating aloft; and the males, unable to master their desire, cast forth their seed. And if they chance to be borne over land, it falls upon nothing, but perishes idly; but if they fly over the sea, then the sea, receiving the embryo as it were a treasure, guards it, and brings this creature to birth, and does not destroy it as though it had fallen into some barren and sterile womb. And this account, the Epidaurian, has now been told. But another, whose race I do not know, taking a different road, then does not agree with the same things; and that I may not seem ignorant of it, that account too shall be told. Demostratus, of whom I made mention above also, said: "I saw the fish, and wonder at it came over me, and I wished to make it into a salted specimen, that it might be there for another also to see. So while the cooks were busy and opening it, I myself examined the entrails. I saw spines from either side coming together and inclining their ends toward one another, and they were three-cornered like the official tablets; and a liver lay within, running out in length, and beneath it lay a gall-bladder with a long passage along the pouches; and seeing the gall you would have said it was a moist bean. So when both were taken out, the gall and the liver, the one swelled up and was like the liver of a very large fish, while the gall, having melted the stone (for it chanced to be set upon a stone), then vanished." And here we set bounds to both accounts. To tell of the catching of the bonito, a thing not very commonly told, is not outside this endeavour. Ten young men in the prime of their bloom board a light and therefore very swift ship; dividing themselves equally to either side, and having eaten their fill, they then each set to the oars, wandering this way and that. One sits at the stern, and from this side and that lets down trailing lines; and from these others hang, and to all the hooks are joined, and each hook bears a bait wrapped in a tuft of Laconian purple, and a gull's feather is attached to each hook, so that it shakes gently with the inrushing water. So in longing for these the bonito swim up; and when the greediest one fixes its mouth, the rest come too, and the hooks are shaken at the same moment, impaled upon the fish. So the men leave off rowing and let go the oars, and standing up they haul up the lines, well-caught and indeed weighted with fish; and when these fall into the ship, the proof of the good catch shows from the multitude of the fish taken.

there are herds. So when the asses mount the mares, the mares, they say, submit and take pleasure in the union, and bear mules tawny in colour and very swift, though otherwise hard to bridle and ticklish. Men catch these with foot-traps and then bring them up, they say, to the king of the Prasii; and those caught when two years old do not refuse breaking-in, but the older ones differ not at all from jagged-toothed and flesh-eating beasts. Among the Indian Prasii, they say, there is a kind of ape that thinks like a man; in size they are like Hyrcanian hounds, and a forelock is seen growing naturally on them; one who did not know the truth would say they were ascetics. A satyr-like beard grows beneath their chins, and the tail is like a lion's brush. The whole of the rest of their body is white, but the head and the tip of the tail are tawny. They are temperate and tame by nature; they live in the woods, and feed on the wild produce of the season. They come in throngs to the outskirts of Latage (Latage is an Indian city), and eat the boiled rice set out for them by the king; and every day this feast is set ready before them. When they have eaten their fill, they go back again to their woodland haunts, they say, in good order, and harm nothing in their path.

like it is the hue, while the parts below the flanks are gently whitish. The hands serve this creature a double use; for where speed is needed, they run before the hind legs, and it is not surpassed in running by the rest of the four-footed beasts; but when again it must take something up, or set it down, or grasp and grip it, then the feet that before were hands become hands again, and it does not walk, but sits. The creature is exceedingly ill-tempered. If indeed it is caught, then, not bearing slavery and longing for its former freedom, it refuses all food and dies of hunger. Pythagoras says these things too, as Crates of the Mysian Pergamum confirms. The land of the Boeotians is free of moles, and this creature does not burrow it about Lebadea; and if somehow they are brought in from elsewhere, they die. About the land of the Orchomenians, however, there are many of them. In Libya there is a scarcity of wild boars and of deer. In Pontus neither soft-bodied creatures nor shell-fish are bred, save rarely and a few. Deinon says that in Ethiopia there are bred the single-horned birds, and four-horned pigs, and sheep bare of wool but with the hair of camels.

The age of bees one might discern in the following way. Those a year old are smooth and resemble oil in colour; the older ones become rough both to see and to touch, and appear wrinkled with age; but these are more experienced and more skilful, for time has taught them the wisdom of honey-making. They also have something prophetic, so that they foreknow the coming of rains and frost; and when they reckon that one or both of these will happen, they do not extend their flight to a great distance, but flutter about their hives and, as it were, hover at the doorways. From this the bee-keepers, taking it as an omen, foretell to the farmers the coming onset of winter. Now the bees fear not so much the frost as heavy rain and snow. They often fly against the wind, carrying a small stone in their feet, just so large as is easy for them to carry as they fly; and in a way they devise this as ballast for themselves against the wind that strikes them, so that the breeze may not turn them aside from their course.

About the wisdom of elephants I have spoken elsewhere, and indeed about their hunting too I have said a few things out of the many that others have told. But for the present I am minded to speak of their love of music, their docility, and their readiness for learning — things hard for even a man to attain, let alone for so great a beast and one hitherto so very savage to have in him. For the elephant has learned, and knows, dancing and the dance, to step in rhythm, to listen with pleasure to the pipe, and to understand the differences of sounds, whether to slow down when they yield or to quicken when they spur him on; and he does it exactly and does not err. So nature made him greatest in size, but learning has shown him most gentle and easily led. Now if I were going to write of their docility and aptitude for learning among the Indians, or in Ethiopia, or in Libya, perhaps I should seem to someone to be making up some tale and boasting, and then on the report of the beast to be slandering nature with falsehood — which a man who loves wisdom and is an ardent lover of truth ought least of all to do. But I have chosen to tell what I myself saw and what others have recorded as done before in Rome, running over a few things out of many, by this too no less demonstrating the peculiar character of the creature. The elephant, when tamed, is most gentle, and is led most easily to whatever one wishes. And honouring time, I will speak first of the oldest events. Germanicus Caesar was producing shows for the Romans; he would be the nephew of Tiberius. So there came to be in Rome several full-grown males and females, and from them home-born young were begotten. And when their limbs began to set firm, a man wise at dealing with such beasts trained them, handling them with a marvellous and astonishing instruction. He led them on at first quietly and gently to his teachings, applying certain baits and the sweetest and most varied foods to allure and draw them, so that whatever was savage in them might be cast out, and they might desert to the gentle and somehow human. And the lessons were: not to go mad on hearing the pipes, not to be disturbed when the clattering noise of drums beat, to be charmed by the syrinx, and to endure also discordant sounds, the tramp of feet stepping, and mingled song; and they were trained too not to fear a crowd of men. There were also these manly lessons: not to grow angry at the descent of a blow, nor, when compelled to bend and curve some of their limbs in dancing and choric fashion, to be then kindled to rage, and that too when they were well-endowed with strength and force. Now by nature this is already an advantage, and a most noble one, not to be disorderly or unruly toward human teachings; but when the dancing-master had shown them most skilful, and they had made exact the lessons of their training, they did not, they say, belie the labour of the teaching when need, with the occasion, called on them to display their lessons. For this chorus was twelve in number; and they came forward, distributed from this side of the theatre and from that, and entered with delicate steps, swaying their whole body luxuriously, and they were clothed in choristers' robes of flowered work. And at the mere signal of the chorus-leader's voice, they would go into a row, they say, if the master so bade; then again they would wheel round into a circle, when he signalled to go that way; and if they had to deploy, they did it; and indeed, scattering flowers, they adorned the floor, doing this with measure and sparingly, and they would even beat time somewhat with their feet, the same beasts keeping a choral and tuneful rhythm together. Now that Damon and Spintharus and Aristoxenus and Philoxenus and others understood music most excellently and were reckoned among the few in this wisdom is wonderful, but in no way incredible or unreasonable. The reason: man is a rational creature, capable of mind and reckoning; but that an inarticulate creature should understand both rhythm and melody, and keep a figure and not pervert the tune, and fulfil the demand of what it has been taught — these are gifts of nature, and at the same time an astonishing peculiarity in each case. And what followed these was enough even to drive the spectator mad. Low couches were set with mattresses on the sand of the theatre, and these received bolsters, and on them a richly worked covering, clear tokens of a most prosperous house of ancient wealth; and costly cups lay beside them, and mixing-bowls of gold and silver, and in them a great quantity of water, and tables of citron-wood and ivory, very stately, stood by, and on them were meats and loaves, enough to fill the bellies of the most omnivorous creatures. And when the preparations were full and abundant, the banqueters came forward, six males and an equal number of females; and the males had a manly robe, the females a womanly one, and they reclined in order, paired male and female. And at the signal they stretched out their trunks as hands, modestly, and ate most temperately; and not one of them seemed gluttonous, nor a glutton greedy beforehand, nor a snatcher of the larger portion, like the Persian in Xenophon's Golden. And when they had to drink, a mixing-bowl was set beside each, and drawing up the drink with their trunks they drank decorously, then sprinkled it about in play and not in insolence. Many other such things, wise and astonishing, of the peculiar nature of these creatures men have recorded. And I myself saw one writing letters on a tablet, in Roman characters, with its trunk, without swerving or wandering; only the hand of the teacher lay upon it, guiding it to the outline of the letters, until the creature had finished writing; and it looked fixedly downward. You would have said that the creature's eyes were educated and literate.

Indeed even the fiercest of animals are at peace and at truce with those that can help them, their inborn malice being loosed for the sake of need. The crocodile, for instance, swims and at the same time gapes. So the leeches fall upon it and trouble it. Knowing this, it needs a physician, the plover; for when it has become full of them, it comes forth to the bank and gapes toward the sunbeam. Then the plover, inserting its beak, draws out the said leeches, and the crocodile, being helped, endures and keeps still. And the one has the leeches for its dinner, the other is benefited, and reckons it the plover's wage that it does it no harm.

I am told that of all animals only mares endure the union of the males even when pregnant; for they are the most lustful. For this reason the more dissolute among women are called "mares" by those who censure them in more dignified terms.

It is the king's care among the bees that the swarm be ordered in this way. Some he commands to carry water, others within to mould the honeycombs, while the third part goes out to forage; and then they change their tasks in rotation, having most beautifully divided them. But the king himself—it is enough for him to have taken thought for these things and to legislate as I have said, after the manner of the great rulers whom the philosophers like to name the same men, statesmen and kings—as for the rest he rests and is exempt from working with his own hands. And if it is better for the bees to move, then the ruler too departs. And if he is still young, he leads, and the rest follow; but if he is older, he goes carried, borne by other bees. The bees turn to sleep at a signal. When it seems time to sleep, the king commands one to sound the signal for slumber. And she, obeying, has proclaimed it, and the others turn thereupon to rest, having until then been humming. So long as the king survives, the swarm prospers, and all disorder is banished; and the drones rest contentedly in their own cells, and the older bees dwell apart, and the young apart, and the king by himself, and the larvae are by themselves, and their food and their evacuations are kept separate. But when the king perishes, all is full of disorder and anarchy; for the drones lay eggs in the bees' cells, and the rest, being thrown into confusion among one another, no longer permit the swarm to prosper; and they die out at last for lack of a ruler. The bee lives a pure life, and would never feed upon any animal; and it needs no Pythagoras as counsellor, but the flowers suffice it as food. It is also of the highest temperance. At any rate it has hated luxury and softness. And the proof is this: it pursues and drives away one anointed with perfume as an enemy who has done it deadly harm. And it knows too one who has come from licentious intercourse, and pursues him also as a deadly foe. And they are well endowed with courage and are not to be turned. They flee no animal at all, nor yield in cowardice, but go to meet it. And toward those who do not trouble them nor begin unjust acts nor approach the swarm with mischief and treachery, they are peaceful and at truce; but a truceless war, as the saying is, is kindled against those who harm them, and whoever comes to ravage their honey is reckoned among their enemies. They smite the wasps badly too. And Aristotle says that once, meeting a horseman near the swarm, the bees killed him, falling upon him in force, horse and all. Yet at times they differ even among themselves, and the stronger overcome the weaker. And there overcome them, as I hear, both the toads and the frogs from the marshes and the bee-eaters and the swallows, and often the wasps too. But whoever overcomes them wins, so to speak, a Cadmean victory; for being struck and stung they come off badly; for the bees are armed no less with spirit than with stings. Nor are they without a share of providential wisdom, and Aristotle gives proof of what I say. It is this. Some bees came to a swarm not their own but another's, and then plundered the honey that in no way belonged to them. But the others, although robbed of their own labour, nevertheless endured quietly, keeping still, and then waited firmly to see what would come. And when the beekeeper had killed most of the enemy, those within, judging that they could be a match for an equal fight, came forth and then defended themselves, and exacted a vengeance for what they had been robbed of that was by no means to be blamed.

The deer gives birth beside the roads, and seems to do this from wisdom; for it fears the wild beasts and their plots, but takes courage at men. And it believes itself weaker than the beasts, but does not doubt that it can escape men. But when grown fat it would no longer give birth beside the roads; for it knows that it is more sluggish at running. So it gives birth in the glens and the woods and the valleys.

This too has come to my ear about the octopus. There was a rock that jutted out, though not very high. Now an octopus once crept up upon it and spread out its tentacles, and was very gladly warming itself—for the weather seemed somehow wintry—though it had not yet turned its own colour to that of the rock. Octopuses are by nature accustomed to do this, both to guard against plots against themselves and themselves to lie in wait for fish. An eagle, then, seeing the prey—sharp-eyed, but not seeing what was good for itself—leaped upon the octopus with all the speed and strength of its wings, reckoning that it would have a ready meal for itself and its young. But the octopus's coils wrapped themselves around the eagle, and clinging fast they dragged the hated foe down; and the eagle, having gaped like a wolf, as one might say, then floated dead upon the sea—over its supper. Countless such things, indeed, do birds suffer, but men suffer more. Among the tales told by Herodotus is that of Cyrus the son of Cambyses among the Massagetae—the other Cyrus—and of Polycrates, who hastened to Oroetes to seize the gold, and of another who, contriving evil for another, contrives it for his own liver. These things the irrational creatures do not know; but men, though they know, do not guard against them. And what need is there of tongue and arguments and teachers and blows, O Cyrus and Polycrates? The rest I pass over; for why should I counsel what is most profitable to the deaf and the senseless?

Hegemon, in his Dardanian verses, says of Aleuas the Thessalian many things, and among them that a serpent fell in love with him. That this Aleuas had golden hair is a marvel he tells in the saying; for me let it be fair. And he says that Aleuas herded cattle on Mount Ossa, as Anchises did on Ida, and pastured the cows by the spring called Haemonia. The spring too would be Thessalian. A serpent of the greatest size, then, fell in love with Aleuas, and crept up to him, and kissed his hair, and licking the face of its beloved with its tongue cleaned it, and brought him many gifts of its hunting. And if a ram was overcome by Glauce the lyre-player, and a dolphin at Iasus by a youth, what prevents a serpent too from falling in love with a beautiful herdsman, since it has become, with its keen sight, a good judge of conspicuous beauty? It was, then, peculiar to animals to fall in love not only with one of their own kind and nature, but even with what was least akin to them, provided it was beautiful.

If one merely touches the venomous spider, they say, it kills him without his even being severely pained. And that the bite of the asp too is most gentle Cleopatra proved, when, as Augustus drew near, she tested painless death at her banquets, and found that by the sword it was painful, the wounded confessing this, and that by drugs it was distressing—for they brought on a kind of convulsion and forced the heart to suffer—but that the death from the bite of the asp was gentle, and, to put it in Homer's words, "feeble." There are some creatures that kill merely by being touched and by their belching too, such as the centrines and the toad.

Those are ignorant of the nature of fish who condemn them all utterly to silence; for some both hiss and grunt. The lyre-fish grunts, and so does the chromis and the boar-fish, as Aristotle says; the smith-fish hisses; and the cuckoo-fish, imitating in its voice the bird of the same name, utters sounds like it.

"But come now, change your strain," the discourse might say, and sing not, by Zeus, a horse nor the ambush within it, but Mneuis the bull. And this bull the Egyptians say is sacred to the Sun, since they say that Apis is an offering to the Moon. And to this bull too there is, they say, a peculiar token of his being neither base nor spurious but dear to the god aforesaid. Of these matters another shall speak; but the Egyptian account I have heard concerning the trial and test of this bull, whether he is of a higher conception or not, this I wish to tell. Bocchoris the king of the Egyptians, having somehow snatched a false renown and a report saying nothing sound, seemed both just in his judgments and adorned in soul toward holiness; but in truth he was of a contrary nature. And most of the rest I now pass over, but concerning Mneuis, wishing to grieve the Egyptians, see what he does to him. He brings against him a wild bull as adversary. So Mneuis bellows, and the newcomer bellowed in answer. Then, carried away by his rage, the stranger, wishing to fall upon the god-beloved bull, stumbles, and falling against the trunk of a persea tree his horn was caught, and Mneuis, wounding him in the side, killed him. Bocchoris is put to shame, and the Egyptians hate him. And if anyone thinks it most shameful to fall from natural discourse into myths, he is a fool. For I say all that is done to these bulls and all that has been done, and I hear the Egyptians telling it. But it was not so; thus hateful is falsehood to those people.

The Egyptians revere a black bull too, and they call it Onuphis. And let Egyptian accounts tell us the name of the place where it is reared; for it is harsh. Its hairs grow the contrary way to those of others; for these things too are peculiar to it. And this was the greatest of cattle, beyond even the Chaonian, which the Thesprotians and the Epirotes call "larini," tracing them in their genealogy from the breed of the cattle of Geryon. And this Onuphis feeds on Median grass.

Hares are caught by foxes too, and by craft no less but even more; for the fox is clever at deceiving and knows tricks. Whenever by night it comes upon the track of a hare and perceives the creature, it steps up silently and with noiseless foot, holding back its panting, and coming upon it in its form tries to take it as one secure and unsuspecting. But the hare is not given to luxury, nor does it sleep heedlessly; the moment it perceives the approaching creature it leaps up from its bed and runs. And it accomplishes its course very swiftly, while the fox too darts upon its track and keeps to the chase. The hare, having run a long way and thinking itself now the stronger and beyond capture, plunges gladly into a thicket and rests; but the fox comes up and does not let it stay still, but rouses it again and drives it off on another course, blown along by the wind. Then this second course, no less than the first, is run to its end; and when the hare longs to rest once more, the fox comes up and, shaking the bush, works wakefulness upon it. And the hare runs off again, and the fox is not left behind. When course follows course upon it without break, and sleeplessness succeeds, the hare gives up, and the fox, coming upon it, takes it — not by speed, by Zeus, but mastering it by time and by craft. Now this account, running ahead, has been put off concerning the hare's running, and the rest it will be more seasonable to tell in what follows. So I return to the point from which I digressed. This, then, was the reason for scattering its offspring and rearing them apart, one here, one there. The hare is exceedingly fond of its young, but it fears the plots of hunters and the raids of foxes, and shudders no less at the assaults of birds, and at the voice of ravens and eagles most of all; for with these among winged creatures it has no truce. It hides itself either in a leafy bush or in deep standing corn, or sets some other necessary and unassailable shelter before itself.

The herd of Libyan oxen was indeed beyond number, and the wild and free among them are swiftest. The hunters often go astray pursuing one and fall in with others that are fresh; for one slips into a thicket or a glen and vanishes, while others appear, like it, and deceive the eye. And if one should set about pursuing one of them, his horse will give out before the ox; for he will catch in time the one already tired, but those that are just beginning their run, his horse having worn itself out beforehand, he will not catch. Many are caught and killed every year, yet their breeding succeeds them most abundantly. The bulls roam together with the calves in common, and the females too, some pregnant, some newly delivered. If one should catch a calf still young, and not kill it at once, he will have a double gain; for he has caught its mother along with it, by doing what it is not absurd to relate. He ties the calf with a rush-rope and leaves it and withdraws; and the mother, worn with longing for her young and inflamed and goaded, wishing to loose it and lead it away, drives her horns at the rope to fray and burst the bonds. And whichever of her horns she thrusts into the twist of the rush-rope is held fast, and fettered along with the calf she remains, not having loosed it, but having flung about herself an inescapable bond. So the hunter takes out her liver for himself, cuts out the udders still swelling, flays off the hide, and leaves the flesh as a feast for birds and beasts. But the calf he carries home whole; for it is most pleasant to eat, and will furnish curd for the cheese-making, yielding rennet.

That the land-marten was once a human being I have heard; and that this was her name, and that she was a sorceress and witch, and that she was terribly licentious and sick with a lawless lust — this too has reached my ears; and that the wrath of the goddess Hecate turned her into this evil creature, this also has not escaped me. May the goddess be gracious; but I leave tales and storytelling to others. That it is a most plotting beast, and that martens set upon dead men and leap upon them when unguarded, and rob and gulp down their eyes, is plain. They say too that the testicles of a marten, fastened upon a woman by a plot or with her consent, keep her from becoming a mother again, and check her from mating. And the inwards of a marten, taking on a certain preparation which those skilled in these things know, and cast into wine by a plot, set friendship at variance, as the story goes, and cut off goodwill that was hitherto united. But concerning these things let us leave it to dear Ares to punish and bring to justice the sorcerers and witches. There is also a fish called the marten, a small one, having nothing in common with the so-called dogfish. For those are cartilaginous and of the open sea, and advancing to great size then resemble a dog; but the marten — you would say it is the so-called hepatus. This fish is small, and its eyes are half-closed; it has pupils likened to the colour of blue. And it has a chin larger than the hepatus, but again is inferior to the chromis in this respect. Being a rock-fish and feeding on seaweed, I am told that it too, like the land-marten, eats the eyes of all the dead bodies it meets. Fishermen use it for similar purposes, all those along Epirus who deal in poisons, wicked men, sophists in evil. And since the tribe of these fish is raw-eating, all the kind that share life with the water-hunters and go down to the lowest hiding-places blacken their own feet and the hollows of their hands, trying to do away with the gleam from them; for the limbs of men, shining most brightly in the water, draw on these fish.

There is a grass-eating creature in India, and it is twice the size of a horse. It has a very bushy tail of an absolutely black colour, and these hairs would be finer than human hairs, and the women of India set great store by having them; for they plait them in and adorn themselves very becomingly, fastening them on beneath their own natural tresses. The length of each hair reaches even to two cubits, and from a single root some thirty grow out together like a tassel. Of all creatures this is the most cowardly; for if it is seen by anyone and perceives that it is being watched, it flees with all the speed of its feet, and relies on its eagerness rather than on the swiftness of its legs. It is pursued by horsemen and by hounds good at running; but if it sees that it is going to be caught, it hides its tail in some thicket and stands facing about, watching the hunters, and takes a little courage, thinking it will no longer be an object of desire when its tail is not seen; for it knows that the tail is its beauty. But it holds an empty notion about this; for someone shoots it with a poisoned arrow, and having killed it cuts off the tail, the prize of the hunt. And having flayed the whole body — for the hide too is good — he leaves the carcass; for the Indians have no use at all for its flesh.

In Zacynthus those skilled at testing and tracking out such matters say that to those bitten by venomous spiders there befall not only as many symptoms as to those bitten elsewhere, but more than those. For their whole bodies become full of numbness and somehow trembling and exceedingly cold, and there are vomitings that breed convulsions, and the bladder is distended; and their ears too ache violently, and the sole of each foot pains them as well. And those who lay their hands on them feel each of the things I have mentioned. But what is astonishing even to hear, and still more wonderful to see, is that, when some of the unbitten either step into the bath-water of those who were bitten or, indeed, wash their feet (such things as are wont to happen often; and such things also befall through certain plots of enemies), all the same pains come upon them too as upon those who were bitten.

Many kinds of fish too have known the strength of love, the god so great that he has not overlooked or despised even those below in the depths of the sea. Among his servants is the grey mullet — not every kind, but the one which those who have studied the kinds and differences of fish call the sharp-snouted. Many of them, I hear, are caught about the Achaean gulf. There are different ways of catching them; but it is chiefly their frenzy for sex that this kind of hunting exposes. A fisherman, having caught a female and tied her to a long reed or a long cord of broom, walks quietly along the shore and drags the fish swimming and struggling beside him; and on his track follows another carrying a net, and this netsman watches carefully where and how the event will fall out. So the female is led along, and however many of the males catch sight of her, like unbridled youths who have ogled some lovely girl running past, they rush after her, maddened with desire for union. Then the man with the net casts it, and often, by the impulse of their lust, he meets with a fine catch of fishes coming on. But the female chosen by the first hunter must be in her prime and well-fleshed, so that more may rush upon her, taking the alluring bait of her beauty; for if she is thin, most of them despise her and go away. But whichever of them is sick with love does not depart, enslaved not, by Zeus, to her beauty, but to the longing for union.

The hare too has peculiarities born in it. For it sleeps with its eyelids open, and betrays its years by showing certain hollows. And it carries in its womb some young half-formed, others it is in labour with, and others already born to it.

The Thessalians and the Illyrians and the Lemnians count jackdaws benefactors, and have voted them public maintenance, since the jackdaws destroy and ruin the eggs and the offspring of the locusts, which damage the crops of the aforesaid peoples. So the clouds of locusts are greatly diminished, and the fruits in season remain unharmed for the aforesaid peoples.

Partridges, while still dwelling within their eggs and confined by the shells that have grown about them, do not wait to be hatched out by their parents, but by their own efforts, as though knocking at a door, break out of the eggs, and peeping forth then push themselves up, and having shattered the shell of the egg they at once run, and if the half toward the tail clings to them they shake it off and cast it away, and they seek for food and leap most swiftly.

This too is a proof of the industriousness of bees. In the most wintry of places, from the setting of the Pleiades to the spring equinox, the bees keep continually within doors and rest indoors quietly, out of longing for warmth and flight from cold; but all the rest of the year they hate idleness and rest, and are good at toil. And you would never see a bee loitering outside that season in which their limbs are numbed.
The land-tortoise, having chewed marjoram, makes nothing of the viper. And if it lacks the marjoram, having eaten rue it is armed against its enemy. But if it fails of either, it is destroyed.

Let the Paeonian women be proud and take on airs, doing the deeds that are celebrated. They are these. On their head they carry a pitcher full of water, holding their neck erect, so that as they walk the pitcher remains unmoved and unswerving; and hanging an infant at the breast they suckle it; and fastening the leading-rein to their arm they lead their husband's horse to water; and with their hands they spin flax. These things Darius too admired, when some Paeonian youths, having so equipped their sister, brought her before him as he was giving judgment, so that, falling in love with such concentrated industry, he might take the Paeonians. But how much more imposing is Nature than the Paeonian women! A hound that had been hunting—a hare was her quarry, and the hound was pregnant—when she had accomplished the task before her, left the prey to her master, and withdrawing she gave birth, they say, to nine puppies, and then reared them. And if the women of the Ligurians are proud because they too, when they have been delivered of their labour pains, rise up and take up the work of the household, when they hear of the deed of the hound aforesaid they will assuredly cease from their boasting and hide their faces.

The pareias, or parouas—for so Apollodorus would have it—is reddish in colour, fair to look upon in the eye, broad of mouth, not dangerous to bite, but gentle. For this reason they dedicated it as sacred to the most humane of the gods, and those who first traced these things out gave it the name of attendant of Asclepius.

You will tell me that the fox is a cunning creature—I mean the one nourished from the land; but hear too the devices of the sea-fox, and learn what sort of things she too does. For either she does not approach the hook at all from the first, or, having swallowed it, at once turning inside out the inner part of herself, she turned it outward, unrolling her body like a tunic, and in this manner, of course, she thrust out the hook.

The elephant is, to look at, a mass of flesh, and a very great one; but its flesh is not edible, except the trunk and the lips of the mouth and the marrow of the tusks. The fat of the elephant is most hateful to venomous creatures; for if one anoints oneself with it or burns it as incense, they flee very far away.

The dolphins — their love of music and their earnestness and devotion about song has been proclaimed and gone abroad to many, and that they are friendly to man others have said, and we too have set forth somewhere above in our account; but here it is no worse to speak of their intelligence. Whenever, at any rate, a dolphin falls into a net, at first it keeps quiet and gives no thought at all to flight, but feasts on the fish caught along with it, and as though come as an invited guest to a banquet, it then fills itself with them; but when it perceives, as it is being dragged, that it is coming near the land, then, gnawing through the net, it gets free and is at liberty. And if ever it is caught, the more gracious of the fishermen, threading a rush through its nostrils, let it go; and the dolphin, as though ashamed at the reproach, no longer comes near a net thereafter. And Aristotle says that even if it is caught and bound and is in the boat, many dolphins swim round the fishing-vessel, and leap and frisk to such a degree, like suppliants, until the fishermen are moved to something and pity the prisoner, and yield to those that beg and release the captive to them.

The dolphin was the swiftest and most leaping of fish, and indeed of all land creatures too. At any rate it leaps over even a ship, as Aristotle says, and he tries to add the cause, and it is this. It holds its breath, just as the underwater divers do; for they too, having braced the breath within like a bowstring, then let the body go like an arrow. And what is compressed within, he says, pushes and shoots them forth.

I have heard an account from a hunter who in other respects too was a good man, the kind who would not lie, and I have believed him, and for that reason it shall be told. He said that the male hare also gives birth, and at the same time begets and is in labour, and does not lack a share in either nature. And he said it rears its young after bearing them, and that it brings forth perhaps two or three; and he affirmed this, and indeed he added that crowning instance to the whole account. A male hare, he said, was caught half-dead, and its belly was swollen as though it were pregnant. He admitted that it was cut open, and that a womb was found, and three leverets. These at first lay motionless when taken out, and lay there like mere lumps of flesh; but when, warmed by the sun and gradually heated, they had lain a while, they came round and revived, and one of them stirred and afterward looked up, and presently even put out its tongue and opened its mouth in longing for food. So, as was natural, milk was brought to such little creatures, and little by little they were reared — a proof, as it seems to me, of the marvellous nature of the parent that bore them. Yet I cannot persuade myself not to believe the account; and the reason is that the man's tongue knew neither falsehood nor boasting.

The sea-dragon is like the other fishes in the rest of its body, but in its head it resembles the land-dragon, and in the size of its eyes (for these too are large), and indeed its jaws also present somehow the form of those of land-dragons. It has scales too, and they are rough, and seem not far from the dragon's skin, if one should touch them. There grow upon it dangerous stings, and the stings bear venom, and they are no good thing to one who touches them.

Sea-cockles too are a varied creature; for some of them are by nature rough, others quite smooth; and some you will crush by pressing with the fingers, others you will break with a stone; and some of them are very black in colour, others you would say were like silver, and others wear the said colours blended together. Their kinds are various and their beds quite diverse; for some lie scattered in the sands of the shores, and rest on the mud; some lie beneath the moss; others, fastened to the rocks, then cling to them very firmly. In the so-called Istrian sea these cockles, in the summer season, when the harvest is beginning, come together like a herd to one another, and swim up lightly — at first heavy and burdensome and not swimming up, but at that time no longer such. They flee the south wind, and shun the north, and do not endure the east either. They delight in a waveless sea, and in the pleasant and soft breezes when the west wind blows. So under these breezes, leaving their own mud, still shut and closed fast, they come up from the depths, and the sea being waveless they swim; and then, opening their own roofs, they peep out, like brides from their own chambers, or roses warmed by the sun and peeping out of their buds. So, taking heart little by little, very gladly they keep still and remain at rest, awaiting their companion the wind; and one shell they spread beneath, the other they raise upright, and the cockles sail, using the one for a sail and the other for a hull. And they go forward in this way, there being quiet and fair weather (you would say, seeing them from afar, it was nothing but a fleet of ships); but if they perceive the approach of a ship or the onset of a beast or the swimming of a large fish, folding themselves up with a single clap of their shells, they slip down all together and vanish.

There were, it seems, monsters in the Indian sea five times the size of the largest elephant. At any rate a single rib of one of these whales extends as much as twenty cubits, it has a lip fifteen cubits long, and the fin of each gill is seven cubits broad. There are conchs and purple-shells big enough to hold an heap of earth most easily; and even the shells of the sea-urchins there could contain as much. The sizes of the fishes are beyond reckoning, especially of the basses, and there are bonitos and gilt-heads. I hear that in the season, when the rivers come down in flood, rushing violently and pouring out over the land, these fishes too overflow upon the fields and are carried about and wander in the shallow water. And when the rains that overfill the rivers cease and the streams go back again and return to their natural courses, in the low-lying and marshy and level places — where indeed the so-called fallows are wont to have certain hollows — fish even eight cubits long are left behind. And the farmers catch them while they swim feebly, since they are carried not in the deep but on the surface, and barely and with difficulty keep themselves alive in the little water.

There is a kind of toad, I hear, terrible both to drink and bitter to look upon. To drink: if anyone, having crushed it, then gives the blood to someone to drink, casting it by way of a plot either into wine or into other drinks, of which the accursed contrivers of such things judge the mixture with that blood to be suitable, it kills, somehow, not after delay but at once. To look upon, the toad is an evil in this way. If anyone gazes at the beast, then looks it full in the face with a keen look, and it too looks back boldly, after its own nature, and breathes out a certain breath connatural to itself but hostile to human skin, it makes him pale, very pale, so that one who did not see it but met the man first would say he had seen a sick man. And the pallor remains for not many days, then vanishes.

There were also, it seems, fishes good at chastity. The one called the Aetnaean, when it has been paired with its mate, as with a lawful wife, and has obtained its marriage-bed, touches no other; and it needs no contracts to guarantee fidelity, no dowry, nor does the Aetnaean fear a suit for ill-treatment, nor stand in awe of Solon. O noble and venerable laws, which unbridled men are not ashamed to disobey!

All the great whales, except the dog-fishes, need the guide, and are led by his eyes. It is a small and slender fish, with a long head; and its tail is narrow, as the experts in these matters say. Whether nature has assigned each whale this particular fish, or whether it comes to it willingly out of friendship, I do not know; but I rather believe that what is done is a compulsion of nature. For this fish never swims for itself, but goes before the whale's head, and is its guide and, so to speak, its rudder. It sees ahead for the whale all things, and perceives beforehand with the same eyes, and teaches it everything with the tip of its tail, touching it with this, and giving a signal, and it checks the whale from dangers, but leads it on toward what will feed it, and teaches it of the hunters' plot by some untraceable sign, and forewarns it of the places upon which so great a beast must not venture, lest it should ever be caught utterly on a reef and perish. So the foundation of life for the greatest is the smallest. And the creature, when fattened, seems no longer to see or to hear, but the mass of its flesh is a barrier both to its sight and to its hearing. And it is not seen bereft of the whale, but of necessity, when the cause of all the aforesaid things for it has perished first, that one too must perish.

Cranes are born in Thrace, which is the most wintry of regions and the most frosty of those I hear of. So they love the land in which they were born, but they love themselves too, and assign part to their ancestral haunts and part to their own safety. For in the summer they stay in their place, but when autumn is already half over they depart to Egypt and Libya and Ethiopia, as though they knew the circuit of the earth and the natures of climates and the differences of seasons. And having passed a spring-like winter, again, when the air begins to be calm and peaceful, they turn back. They make as leaders of the flight those already experienced in the journey; and these would naturally be the elder ones. And to bring up the rear they appoint birds of like age; and the young are stationed in the middle of them. Having watched for a wind favourable and friendly to them and flowing behind, using it as an escort and one that thrusts them forward, they then form the figure of their flight into an acute-angled triangle, so that, striking the air, they may cleave it most easily, and they hold to their course. So do cranes summer and winter. But men have thought the wisdom of the king of the Persians wonderful in his knowledge of the mixture of climates, singing of Susa and Ecbatana and the much-talked-of removals of the Persian to this place and that. And when the cranes see an eagle coming on, forming a circle and gathering into a hollow mass they threaten as though to set themselves against it; and it is beaten back, wing and all. And resting their beaks on one another's rumps, they then in a way bind their flight together, and make their toil easy toil for themselves, the same birds sparingly resting upon one another. And when, in a long stretch of land, they chance upon a spring, they rest by night and sleep; but three or four keep guard over the rest, and, that they may not let their watch fall asleep, they stand on one leg, while with the lifted foot they hold a stone in their claws very firmly and carefully, so that if ever they should without knowing it slip into sleep, the stone, falling and striking, may force them to throw off slumber. And the stone which a crane swallows to have ballast is a touchstone of gold, when, having as it were come to anchor and put in, it then brings it up again.

Among partridges, the clear-voiced and tuneful trust in their own fine singing; and the warlike and contentious ones likewise are confident that they are not fit to be wasted once caught; and for this reason, when taken, they struggle less against their captors in order not to be caught. But the others, and still more the Cirrhaean partridges, conscious of being good neither at fighting nor at singing, and knowing well that once caught they will become dinner for their captors, contrive by a certain natural cunning to render themselves uneatable; and they abstain from all other food that gratifies and fattens them, and eat garlic most eagerly. Now those who have learned this beforehand make a willing truce of non-pursuit with them; but whoever has not previously encountered the catch of these birds, having taken and boiled one, wastes both his time and his pains upon it, finding that he has got a wretched piece of meat.

Geometry, and beauty of shapes, and lovely formations the bees display without art or rule or what the wise call the compass. And when there is increase and the swarm thrives with bees, they send out colonies just as the greatest and most populous of cities do. The bee knows too when rain threatens to visit, and when a harsh wind is to come. And if the wind should come upon it contrary to its expectation, you will see each carrying a stone with the tips of its feet for ballast. And what the divine Plato says about the cicadas and their love of song and of music, one might say also about the choir of bees. At any rate, whenever they frisk about or stray, then the beekeepers clap a certain rhythmic and harmonious clapping; and the bees, as though drawn by a Siren, indeed turn back to their own haunts again.

The deer, as I hear, is content with what it has, and does not desire more, but is more temperate as to the belly than men. About the Hellespont, at any rate, there is a hill, and deer pasture upon it, and one of their ears is slit, and they do not pass beyond the hill, nor do they desire strange pasture, nor long for other meadows out of need for more abundant grass; but what they have suffices them the whole year through. What, O men, do you say to this—you whom not all that "the stone threshold of the Archer encloses within" could ever fill up until death?

The story of the industrious mule Aristotle told, and we too somewhere above; and there is nothing strange in telling this story of the dog as well, which also happened at Athens. A temple-robber came into the temple of Asclepius, having watched for the very middle of the night and waited for the soundest sleep of the sleepers, and then he stole many of the offerings, and, as he supposed, had escaped notice. But there was within a good watchman, a dog, better than the sacristans at keeping awake, which followed him in pursuit and never ceased its barking, bearing witness to the deed with all the power it had. At first the man himself and his partners in that wicked deed pelted it with stones; but at last they held out loaves and barley-cakes. These they brought along as a bait for dogs, providently, as they supposed. But when the dog kept barking both as the man entered the house where he was lodging and again as he came out, it became known where the dog had come from; and the pictures and the places where they had been dedicated longed for the offerings that were missing. So the Athenians inferred that this man was the thief, and putting him to the torture they convicted him of the whole affair. He was punished according to the law, while the dog was honoured with public maintenance and care, as a faithful guardian, in no way inferior in vigilance to any of the temple-keepers.

In Ethiopia the scorpions called Sibritae—for so the natives are likely to call them—I hear feed on lizards and asps and millipedes and water-beetles and every creeping thing, and whoever treads upon their droppings, I have learned, breaks out in sores. About Corcyra there are born the so-called hydrae, which turn upon their pursuers and, breathing out a strange breath, then check them in their rush and turn them back. The typhlops, which they also call typhline and besides "the deaf one," has a head much like a lamprey's, so one account says, but exceedingly small eyes. And one of its two names it has from this; the other, "deaf one," because it is dull of hearing. It has a strong hide, very slow to be cut through. The acontias they say is an amphibious snake, and spends much of its time on dry land, and lies in wait for every creature. The cunning of its plot is of this kind. It hides somewhere unseen along the highways, and often, having crept up onto a tree, then coiling itself up and hiding its head in the coil, it eyes quietly the passers-by; then it launches itself at whatever passes, whether it be an irrational animal or a man. It is a leaping creature, able to spring across even twenty cubits, if need be; and as it leaps it at once fastens on.

Men say that there are certain love-charms; and the frog gives, as a token of amorous union, a kind of cry to the female, like a lover singing some serenade, and this cry is called the ololygon, as they say. And when he has won the female, both wait through the night; for they cannot come together in the water, and by day they shrink from coupling on land. But when night falls, with much security they come out and enjoy one another. And when frogs cry more loudly and more clearly than usual, they signify a visitation of rain.

The variety of colour and form among the animals of Arabia is enough to confound every painter, and this not only in the strong and noble kinds, but already even in the meaner sorts. For the locusts and the serpents are spangled with gold-like images upon them; and the fish, partaking of still more of this richly adorned colouring, are then astonishing to behold. Nor are the shellfish of the Red Sea without a share of the same splendour; for fiery bands run round them, and on seeing them you would say that they imitate the rainbow in their blending of colours, being marked out by Nature in parallel lines. The pearl, so famed among the foolish and so marvellous among women, is also a nursling of the Red Sea; and they tell the marvel that it is born when the lightning flashes upon the shells as they lie open. These shells, the mothers of the pearls aforesaid, are hunted when the weather is fine and the sea calm; and the hunters, having caught them, then take out this thing that bewitches the souls of the wanton. A small pearl may be found in a very large shell, and a large one in a small shell; one shell has none, another no more than one, and many have many; there are those who say that as many as twenty grow attached to a single shell. The shell is the flesh, and the pearls grow upon it like a thorn. If one were to open the shells before the proper time and before the full birth, one would find flesh indeed, but would not have the prize of the hunt. The pearl is like a stone that has been hardened, and is by nature unable to hold and keep moisture within itself, not even a little. To the dealers in pearls and to the buyers the very white and the large ones seem most beautiful and most precious, and not a few, by Zeus, have grown rich from them, men whose livelihood comes from this. Nor am I ignorant of this either, that when the stones have been taken out, the shells are released again, having paid, as it were, the much-sought prize as a ransom for their own safety, and then they grow it again. But if the creature that nourishes the pearl dies before the pearl is taken out, as one account says, the pearl too rots together with the flesh and perishes. By nature it has a smooth and well-rounded surface. And if one of those that have grown otherwise should be wished, by the craft of skill, to be rounded off and made smooth, the stone exposes the design; for it does not yield, but grows up roughnesses, and in this way declares that it has been plotted against to make it beautiful.

When Daphnis the cowherd of Syracuse suffered at the hands of the nymph these things that are celebrated in song, his five reared dogs — Sannos and Podargos and Lampas and Alcimos and Theon — beholding the sufferings of their master, chose death over him, they say, and lamented much first, and wept exceedingly.

The physa is an Egyptian fish worthy of wonder. For it knows, they say, when the moon wanes, and knows its waxing too. And indeed its liver waxes together with the goddess or wanes together with her, and at one time it is well-nourished, at another thinner.

The hare is also knowing about winds and seasons; for there is something clever in it, though not gracious. In winter, then, it makes its bed in spots that face the sun; for it is plain that it gladly takes warmth and is hostile to cold; but in summer it inclines toward the north out of longing for cool. Its nostrils are its gauge of the difference of the seasons. The hare does not close its eyes when it sleeps — this it has alone among animals — nor are its eyelids overcome by sleep; they say it sleeps with its body, but at that time sees with its eyes. I write what the skilled hunters say. Hares feed by night, partly perhaps from a desire for strange food, but I should say it is for the sake of exercise, so that even then, when it holds out vigorously against sleep and stays active, it may keep up its speed. It loves the way back exceedingly, and is overcome by attachment to every familiar spot; and for this reason it is mostly caught, since it cannot bear to abandon its accustomed haunts.

It would be for me to tell also what is peculiar to animals. The king of the Indians eats for his dessert such things as the Greeks ask to nibble — the fruit of the ground-palm; but he dines on a certain grub bred in that plant, roasted, sweetest of all, as the Indian accounts say; and those who tell of so great a pleasure from eating it win even me over by what they say. He has these too as side-dishes: the eggs of swans and those of land-ostriches and of geese. Now in other respects I do not blame him; but as for swans, which are servants of Apollo and most tuneful, as the report that goes about says, to plot against their offspring and destroy their eggs, dear Indians — no more of that.

The haemorrhois (this would be a kind of viper) has its haunts and dwellings chiefly in rocky hollows. It is a foot in length, and from a broad head it goes down tapering to the tail; and in part it is fiery to see, in part terribly black; and it bristles its head as it were with certain horns. It crawls slowly, pressing the scales of its belly, and goes forward on a slanting course. So it makes a faint sound, so that one would judge it sluggish and of no account. But when it bites it makes a puncture, and this at once is seen to be blue, and the one struck suffers most pitiably at the heart, and his belly discharges streams. The first night comes, and blood flows out through the nostrils and the neck and indeed through the ears, with a bilious venom, and the bladder lets out bloody urine. And if there are any old scars about the body, these too burst open. And if a female haemorrhois strikes, it lets out from the very tips of the nails, and the venom runs up into the gums, and blood pours out in plenty, and the teeth are squeezed out of the gums. They say that the helmsman of Menelaus, Canobus, fell in with this beast in Egypt when Thonis was king, and that Helen, perceiving the strength of the biting creature, broke its spine and took out the venom. But for what use she was eager to take this treasure, I do not know.

The following too are peculiar to the fishes of India. There are rays among them, each no smaller than an Argolic shield, and the shrimps of India are larger than crayfish. Those that run up out of the sea through the river Ganges have very large claws, rough to the touch; but those that fall from the Red Sea into the Indus have smooth spines, as I have learned, though the coiled appendages that hang from them are rather long and curling. These have no claws.

The following too, it seems, was a gift of the plover, which it is by no means right to dishonour. If anyone whose body has been filled with jaundice then looks keenly at it, it looks back, and that quite unflinchingly, as though contending against him in honour; and such a returning of the look heals the man of the aforesaid affliction.

The home and haunts of the sea-blackbird are the rocks and the cavernous recesses. Each of these takes many wives and lodges his brides apart, as it were, in chambers in the hollows. And this luxurious way of marriage, and the dividing of his impulse among many, you might call the manner of barbarians who are voluptuous in love, and — if one may jest while being in earnest — the Median and Persian life. It is the most jealous of fishes, both in general and not least when its brides are bearing young to it. And if this is told too wantonly, by a misuse of words, what is done by nature gives us licence for such language. For the females, when already in the throes of labour, keep quiet and remain within, while the male, like a husband, hovers about the doors and watches against plots from outside, fearing for his young. For he seems to love even the offspring not yet born, and with a father's fear,

The chameleon is by nature not to be seen or recognized in a single colour, but steals itself away, both confusing and turning aside the sight of those who look. For if you should meet it black in appearance, it changes its form to green, as though it had changed its dress; then again it appeared different, having put on

A helmsman, seeing in the midst of the open sea cranes turning back and flying the other way, understood that they had given up going forward at the assault of a contrary wind; and becoming, as one might say, a pupil of the birds, he sailed back and saved his ship. And this, having happened first, was handed down to men by these birds as at once a lesson and a teaching.

The weasel is a wicked beast, and so is the snake. So when a weasel is about to fight a snake, it first chews rue and then comes to the fight as though fenced and armed. The reason is that rue is most hateful to the snake.

In the island of Gyaros, Aristotle says, there are mice, and indeed they eat the iron ore of the earth. And Amyntas says that those in Teredon (this is a land of Babylonia) feed on the same. In Latmus in Caria, I hear, there are scorpions which sting their own citizens to death, but the strangers only gently and just enough to cause an itch—Zeus the protector of strangers, it seems to me, having assigned this gift to those who come there.

The hyena, as Aristotle says, has in its left hand a sleep-producing power, and by merely touching it induces torpor. At any rate it often comes into the steadings, and when it meets someone sleeping, approaching it lays its, so to speak, sleep-producing hand upon the nose, and the man is choked and oppressed. And it digs out the earth beneath his head so far that it bends him back into the hole and makes his throat lie bare and exposed; and then the hyena fastens on and throttles him and carries him off to its den. And it attacks dogs in that manner too. When

The goat too, it seems, was good at curing the dimness of the eyes which the sons of the Asclepiads call cataract, and men are said to have learned this remedy from her. It is of this kind. When a goat perceives that her eye has grown clouded, she goes to a bramble and brings her eye against the thorn. The thorn pricks it, and the fluid flows out, but the pupil remains unharmed, and she sees again, and needs not a whit of human skill or surgery.
Wolves, if they happen upon an ox that has fallen into a deep marsh, harass it from outside and frighten it,

That if one touches the torpedo-fish the affliction named after it seizes his hand—this too I heard, when I was a child, my mother often saying. And from wise men I learned that even if one touches the net in which it has been caught, he is wholly numbed. And if one should put it alive into a vessel and pour in seawater, then, if it is pregnant and the time of its labour has come, it gives birth. And if one pours the water in the vessel over a man's hand or foot, the hand or the foot must be numbed.

The Egyptians seem to honour the hawk to Apollo, and they call the god Horus in their own tongue, and they hold the birds in wonder, and rightly say that they belong to the god aforesaid. For of all birds the hawks alone look easily and without strain straight at the rays of the sun, and least dazzled, they travel the highest course, and the divine flame does not trouble them at all. And those who have seen it say that the hawk also flies upside down, as though swimming on its back. From this too the same bird looks toward heaven and toward the all-seeing Sun very freely and unwaveringly. It is the greatest enemy of serpents and biting creatures. Neither serpent, then, nor scorpion, nor any other offspring of evil stock could escape its notice. Of fruits and seeds it does not taste, but it delights in eating flesh, and it drinks blood, and rears its young on the same, and it is most fierce in lust. If a bone of its leg be set beside gold, it draws the gold and by some secret spell leads it to itself and charms it to follow, just as men sing that the Heraclean stone somehow bewitches iron. The Egyptians say that the hawk lives even to five hundred years; and they have not yet persuaded me of it; but what I hear, I tell. Homer too seems somehow to hint that the hawk is dear to the son of Zeus and Leto, when he says:
Various and manifold things about the peculiar nature

The catfish is found about the Maeander and the Lycus, the Asian rivers, and in Europe about the Strymon, and it is like the sheatfish in form. And it is by nature the most loving of its young of fish. At any rate, whenever the female has spawned, she is released from care for the young, as a woman in childbed; but the male, appointing himself to the guarding of the offspring, remains, warding off everything that plots against them. And it is able even to swallow a hook, as Aristotle says.

The hare, when pursued by hounds and horsemen, runs — if it comes from level ground — more swiftly than mountain hares, being small of body and slender; and on this account it is not unlikely that it should be light. At first it skips up from the ground and leaps, and slips easily and smoothly through bushes and through every marshy place; and if the grass anywhere is deep, it passes through that too with ease. And just as they say the lion's tail can rouse and spur him on, so for the hare its ears serve as signals of speed and rousers of its course. It lays them back along its shoulders, and uses them, like spurs, to keep from idling and shrinking. It does not run a single straight course, but swerves this way and that, and twists here and there, confounding the hounds and deceiving them. Wherever it sets out and wishes to turn aside, in that direction of swerving it inclines one of its ears, as though steering its course by it. Nor does it spend its strength without stint, but watches the onset of its pursuer; and if the hound is sluggish, it does not let loose its whole speed, but holds something back, so as to run ahead of the hound, yet not to give out from the strain of the running itself. For it knows it is the better, and sees that it is the moment not to over-tax itself. But if the hound is very swift, then —

As for the Libyan gazelles and the young deer there, my heart bids me speak of them now. The gazelles are swiftest, and yet they do not escape the Libyan horses. They are taken also with nets. They are grey in the belly, and this colour goes up into the flanks; and along either side of the belly black bands run down. For the rest of their body they are tawny, long in the legs, black in the eye, their heads adorned with horns, and their ears are very long. The creature called

The Indians bring to their king tamed tigers and gentle panthers and four-horned oryxes, and two kinds of oxen, racers and others terribly wild. From these oxen they make fly-whisks; and in the rest of their body these are wholly black, but they have tails very white. They bring also pale doves, which they say are neither tamed nor ever made gentle, and birds which they like to call cercorones, and noble dogs, of which I have spoken above, and white apes and others very black; for the red ones, as woman-mad, they do not bring into the cities, but, springing upon them from somewhere, they kill them, hating them as adulterers.

The river-tortoise in India has a shell no smaller than a full-sized boat. At any rate each one holds ten medimni of pulse. There are also land-tortoises, and they would be the size of the largest clods which rise up in deep tillage, when the soil is yielding and the plough goes down deep and cuts the furrow most easily and lifts the clods on high. These, they say, even shed their shells. So the ploughmen and all who labour about the fields drag them up with mattocks, and pull them out as one pulls maggots out of worm-eaten plants. They are sweet of flesh and fat, not bitter like the sea-tortoises.

I, for my part, have not believed it; but if another trusts Eudoxus, let him believe what Eudoxus says — that, having passed the Pillars of Heracles, he saw in certain lakes some birds even larger than oxen. And that he who says this does not persuade me, I have already said; but what I heard, I did not pass over in silence.

once caught, he is now afraid, and spends the whole day on guard, tasting nothing, and his anxiety feeds him; but when late evening comes he is released from this constraint, and seeks his food, and does not fail to find it. And each of the females within, whether she is still in labour or already a mother, finds plenty of seaweed in the hollows and about the rocks, which is her dinner. A fisherman cunning at plotting against the sea-blackbird fits a heavy lead to a hook, strings a large prawn on the hook, and lets the bait down. He keeps moving the line, rousing and whetting his quarry toward the food, and the prawn, as it moves, gives some impression that it is about to enter the holes of the blackbird. To him this is most hateful; and so, perceiving it, in the fury of his anger he rushes to destroy his enemy — for he cares nothing then for his belly — and having crushed her, he goes off, judging it of higher worth and more important than food not to let his guard fall asleep. But of the other things that fall in his way, when he is about to eat one, he first crushes it and then leaves it lying; and when he sees it dead, he then feeds on it. The female blackbirds, so long as they see the male standing on guard, as one might say, remain within and keep the appearance of housekeeping; but when he has disappeared, they are at a loss, and despondency leads them out and brings them forth, and there they are caught. What do the poets say to this, who so famously sing to us of Evadne the daughter of Iphis and Alcestis the daughter of Pelias?

a grey hue, like another mask or another robe an actor puts on. Since, then, this is so, one might say that nature too is a sorceress, even though she does not boil or smear on drugs, like a Medea or a Circe. The pilot-fish one must know to delight in the open sea and the deep more than any of the fish we know by hearsay; and either it hates the land, or the land that fish. As ships cleave the midst of the passage, these pilot-fish, swimming up like lovers, escort them, and go round here and there, both dancing and leaping. Now the passengers cannot at all know how far off the land they are; but the sailors — yet even from them the truth is wont to be hidden. But the pilot-fish perceive it from afar, like a keen-scented dog that catches its quarry most swiftly, and no longer does so great a love of the ship hold them as to make them stay, but as though at a signal they gather in throngs and depart. And from this the masters of the ship know that they must look about for land, not judging by beacons but instructed by the creatures aforesaid.

Doves in the cities herd together with men, and are most gentle, and crowd about their feet; but in desolate places they run away, and do not endure men. For they take courage in their numbers, and know very well that they will suffer nothing harsh. But where there are fowlers and nets and plots against them, they no longer dwell fearlessly, to use what was said of those very birds by Euripides.

When the wolf has filled itself to satiety, it will not taste even the smallest morsel thereafter; for its belly is stretched, its tongue swells, and its mouth is blocked, and it is most gentle to meet, like a lamb, and it would not plot against either man or beast, not even if it walked through the middle of the flock. But its tongue diminishes quietly and little by little, then returns to its original shape, and it becomes a wolf again.

Wasps too, then, are ruled by a king, but not tyrannized as men are. And the proof is that these also are stingless. And the subjects have it for a law to mould the works, while the rulers are double the size, but gentle and such as can harm neither willingly nor unwillingly. Who then would not hate the Dionysii in Sicily, and Clearchus in Heraclea, and Apollodorus the butcher of the people of Cassandrea, and Nabis the ruiner of the Lacedaemonians, if indeed those took heart in the sword, while the kings of the wasps took heart in stinglessness and gentleness?

the circle of the moon is full, it takes the light behind it, and casts its own shadow upon the dogs, and at once silences them, and having bewitched them like the sorceresses it then leads them off in silence, and uses them thereafter for whatever it wishes. The love of a dolphin at Iasus for a beautiful boy, long since sung of, I do not think right to leave without mention from me, and for that reason it shall be told. The gymnasium of the Iasians lies by the sea, and the youths, after their runs and the wrestling-grounds, going down there, wash themselves according to an ancient custom. So as they were swimming, a dolphin fell into a most ardent love with one of them, the most outstanding in beauty. And at first, coming near, it frightened and astonished him, but then by familiarity it drew from the boy a strong friendship and goodwill toward itself. At any rate they began to play with each other, and now they would contest, swimming alongside and racing, now the boy mounting like a rider on a colt would be carried proudly, the lover swimming beneath. And to the Iasians and the strangers what happened was a thing to envy. For the dolphin carried its beloved far out to sea, as far as the boy could be borne in comfort; then it turned back and brought him near the shore, and parting from each other, the one went off to the deep, the other returned home. And the dolphin came to meet him at the time the gymnasium was dismissed, and the boy delighted in the expectation of his friend and in the play with him, and besides his natural beauty he was admired, since he seemed most lovely not only to men but also to the irrational creatures. Yet not long after, this counter-love too was overcome by envy. For it happened that the boy, having exercised more than usual, and being tired, threw himself upon the one that carried him, belly-down, and it chanced that the creature's spine along its back was upright, and it pricked the lovely boy's navel. Then some veins burst beneath, and there followed much flowing of blood, and there the boy died. Now the dolphin, perceiving this from the weight (for he lay upon it not light as usual, since he no longer lightened himself by his breathing), and seeing the sea purple with blood, understood what had been done, and did not dare to outlive its beloved. Using great force, then, like a surging skiff, it cast itself willingly upon the shores, and brought out the corpse along with it, and both lay there, the one dead, the other breathing its last. But Laius, for Chrysippus, O noble Euripides, did not do this, although he was the very first of the Greeks to begin the love of males, as you yourself say and as report teaches. And the Iasians, requiting that strong friendship of theirs, made a common tomb for the lovely youth and the loving dolphin, and set up a monument over it. There was a beautiful boy riding upon a dolphin. And they struck coins of silver and bronze, and stamped on them the figure of the fate of both, and handed it down to memory, honouring the work of so great a god, the people there. And I learn that in the city of Alexander, in the time of the second Ptolemy, a dolphin loved with a love much the same, and at Dicaearchia in Italy. And if Herodotus had known these things, he would, I think, have marvelled less at the tale of Arion of Methymna.

Elephants cross a river—the young still swimming across; but those already full-grown, even if they are covered by the current, hold their trunks up above the water, while the mothers carry the newborn calves upon their tusks. The young take the lead in dangers and toils, but yield place at drink and food to their elders, showing them respect; and these need no laws of Lycurgus at all. An elephant enfeebled by age or seized by sickness those of its herd would never abandon, but they remain faithfully by it, and are eager to restore it to strength both in other ways and if it is pursued; and they fight in its defence, and are wounded as they stand by it, though they could flee. The mothers too would never betray their young calves, but they too stay faithfully by them, even when the hunters press hard, and would sooner lose their own life than their offspring. But I knew, when I was a youth, an old woman named Laenilla, and she was pointed out by everyone, and a tale was told about her, and the tale was this. My elders told me that this woman, falling passionately in love with a slave, slept with him, and so fastened a stain upon her own sons. They were noble, and belonged to the senate of the Romans by descent from their fathers and from the higher members of their family. The sons, then, ashamed, were grieved that their mother did such things, and gently admonished her, and quietly reminded her of the disgrace of her conduct. But she, surging with desire and setting her passion before her sons, denounced them to the magistrate, and said that they were plotting against him. He, having an ear ready for slanders, and being suspicious and cowardly—these are the afflictions of an ignoble mind—believed her. And they, though guilty of no wrong, were put to death, while she carried off as the prize of her denunciation the freedom to sleep with a slave without restraint. O gods of our fathers, and Artemis of childbirth, and the Eileithyiae, daughters of Hera, why should we still speak of Medea the Colchian or Procne the Attic woman, when we recall the sufferings that have happened of late and in our own time?

not allowing it to swim across and set foot on the land, but in time they compel it, writhing and twisting, to be choked to death. Then one of them, the most accomplished, leaping into the water and bending toward it, takes hold of the ox's tail and drags it outward; and another, taking hold of that one, drags him; and the third the second, and the fourth this one, and the thing described is done down to the last, who stands outside the water. And in this manner, having drawn out the ox, they make a meal of it. And if they catch in ambush a calf that has strayed, they leap upon it, and taking hold of its muzzle they drag it; and it pulls against them, and there is much contest over it, the wolves trying to force it, and the calf making it a struggle not to yield. But when they see it straining hard against them in this way, they let go; and the calf, by the force of its own backward pull, is overturned, and the wolves fall upon it and tear open its belly and eat it. When elephants are unable to cross a trench, one of them, the largest, throws himself into it, and stands across it, and bridges the gap, and walking over him the rest go to the far side and escape—first, however, rescuing him too. And the manner of his rescue is this.
