One from above stretches out his foot, and offers that one his trunk to wind around; and the others throw in brushwood and logs as quickly as possible, on which, climbing and having his foot held very firmly and carefully, he is pulled up most easily. There is in India a tract of land, and it is called Phalacra, the Bald Place. The cause of the name is that whoever tastes of the grass that grows there loses both his hair and his horns. The elephants, therefore, of their own will do not approach this tract, but turn away when they come near it, fleeing all that is harmful, like prudent men—the elephants.

Animals do not always have the same power in their blows or in their bites, but it is often heightened by some cause. The wasp, at any rate, when it has tasted a viper, is harsher in its sting; and the fly that has come upon some such thing is bitterer to bite and gives pain; and indeed the bite of the asp becomes wholly incurable if it has eaten a frog. And the dog, if it bites while healthy, makes a wound and kindles pain; but if it bites while rabid, it destroys. A seamstress mending a little tunic torn by a rabid dog, having somehow bitten the tunic with her mouth to stretch it, contracted the madness and died. And the bite of a fasting man is grievous and hard to cure. The Scythians are said, besides the poison with which they smear their arrows, to mix in human serum as well in their poisoning, the part that somehow floats upon the blood, which they know to be a secretion of it. Theophrastus too is sufficient to attest this.

He went down from the mountains of Ida, like a swift hawk, the slayer of doves. The beetle is a creature without a female sex; it sows its seed into the ball which it rolls, and having done this for twenty-eight days and warmed it, on the day after these it brings forth its young. The warriors of the Egyptians used to wear engraved upon their rings a beetle, the lawgiver hinting that those who fight for their country must be in every way wholly male, since the beetle too has no share in the female sex.

of elephants I have related above; but now it shall be told that this animal is good of memory, and knows how to keep commands and not to falsify in any way the expectation and hope of those who entrust anything to it. When, at any rate, Antigonus was besieging the people of Megara, with one of the war-elephants there was reared also a female, named Nicaea. To her, then, the wife of the man who reared the elephant entrusted a child whom she had chanced to bear thirty days before, addressing it in the tongue of the Indians, which the elephants understand. And it both loved the child and guarded it, and was pleased when it lay near, and looked toward it when it whimpered, and as it slept it kept off the flies with its trunk, with a reed-branch of the kind thrown to it for food; and if the infant was not present, then it would refuse food too. The nurse, then, had to fill it with milk and set it beside its guardian, or Nicaea was plainly indignant and enraged and intending some dreadful thing. And often, when the child had wept itself out, it would then shake the cradle in which it lay, soothing the infant with the rocking, just as nurses and wet-nurses are wont to do — doing this, O men, was the elephant. Of jealousy among various animals, most active in its season, I know I have spoken — of the purple coot and the dog and indeed, in the third place, by Zeus, the stork; but now I am about to tell of an elephant's anger at being wronged in his marriage. For catching in the very act the wife of the man who trained and reared him committing adultery, it ran one of its two horns through both of them and killed both the adulterer and the adulteress, and let them lie upon the outraged bedclothes and the trampled couch, so that the trainer, when he came, both condemned the wrong and recognized the avenger for him. And this was an Indian deed, but it spread abroad even here; and I hear that in the time of Titus, a good and noble man, the same thing happened in Rome. They add that the elephant there killed both, and covered them with a cloak, and when the keeper came, casting off the cloak, showed them lying near one another, and the horn too, with which it had pierced them, this also was seen stained with blood.

The frog hates the water-snake and fears it strongly. So by its loud croaking it tries to terrify it in return and frighten it back. And there is the malice of the crocodile in hunting man and other animals. The path by which it knows men come down to the river, either for drawing water or for watering a horse or a camel, or, by Zeus, even to board a boat — this path it sprinkles by night with much water, and filling its mouth it pours often over the path, wishing to make it slippery and rendering its prey easier for itself; for those that slip do not keep their footing on the bank, but they are carried down, and it darts up and, catching them, dines. And I shall say a little about crocodiles now too. This beast is not at peace with the whole tribe of trochilus-birds (many are their kinds and names, harsh and grating to hear, and for this reason I leave them out); but only the so-called slack-beak does it have as comrade and friend; for this one can without pain pick out the leeches for it.

— the hare runs at the full stretch of its legs. Indeed, when it has got a long way ahead and left hunters and hounds and horses far behind, it leaps up onto some high hill and, raising itself upon its hind legs, looks out as from a watchtower at the contest of its pursuers, and seems to me to laugh at them as the weaker. Then, taking courage from this as having the advantage, and gladly seizing as it were a moment of peace and calm, it settles down and lies sleeping. The mountain hare is not so swift as those that dwell on the plains — unless indeed those mountain hares too have a plain lying below them, on which they come down and range; for they dwell on the mountain, but exercise there, often running together with those from the plains. In the plains, then, they are wont to be hunted, and some are stirred up while others lie hidden; and then, when from the customary chase the hidden ones are roused, not one escapes. But when they are on the point of being caught, turning a little aside from the plain track they leap up into the steep and mountainous ground, hastening as toward their own native and accustomed haunts; and going off in this way they are gone, having met with unexpected safety. For climbing the heights is by nature hostile to horses and hounds, since their feet fail them and are easily worn away. The hounds suffer this still more; for their feet are fleshy and have nothing resistant against the rock, as horses have their hoof. But the hare is the opposite: its feet are shaggy by nature, and so it endures rough ground. But hares whose haunts are in thickets and brush are sluggish in running and slow to flee; for such are fattened and, through idleness, not practised in running, and least of all do they stray far from the brush. The hunting of these is as follows. At first they slip through the small bushes, where the covert is not continuous; but the denser ones, since they cannot pass beneath, they naturally leap over. Some bushes are continuous and woven through one another; where these are, the hare — being often forced to do this, and not being given to leaping because of the weight of its body — soon tires and gives out. The hounds at first stumble and miss it; for they do not see it through the thickness of the wood, but they too leap over the bushes, led by the scent; yet at last they catch sight of it and pursue and give no quarter, while the hare, from the unbroken leaping, tires and gives out and is thereupon caught. Hares run up steep heights with ease, for their hind legs are longer than their front; but they do not run down so well, for the contrary disposition of their legs hinders them. There is also another hare, small by nature, that never grows large: its name is the coney. I am no coiner of names, and so in this treatise too I keep the name given it from the first, which the western Iberians bestowed upon it, among whom it is both bred and found in great abundance. Its colour, compared with the others, is dark, and it has a short tail; in other respects it is like in appearance to those described. It differs also in the size of its head, for its head is more slender, exceedingly fleshless, and shorter. It is whiter than the rest. They have year-round irritants in their nature, by which they are stung and driven wild when they rush upon the females. There is a bone in its heart, and to know what that bone is good for shall be another's concern.

by the poets the "young deer" is swiftest to run, like a storm, but to look upon it is red-haired and very shaggy, and it has a white tail. Its eyes are likened to a dye of blue. Its ears are full of the thickest hairs. Its horns are facing each other and fair, so that, fair as it is, it both meets the hunt and at the same time both frightens and is harmed. This young deer displays the swiftness of its feet not on land alone, but, falling into a river's current, rowing as it were with the hooves of its feet, it then cuts through the stream. It delights also to swim in a lake, and there too it gets its food, dining ever on flourishing reed and galingale. So at the beginning of spring it lightens its filled belly, and lets down its udders, and indeed the young deer rears its own offspring. The murry, I learn, is a fish. From what it drew that name I cannot say; but it has been called so. They say it is a sea-snake. Whichever of its eyes is taken out and made into an amulet rids a man of dry ophthalmia; and they say another eye grows again for this murry. But one must let the fish go alive, or you keep the eye in vain.

The great king of the Indians sets up, on one day in each year, contests for all those others I have spoken of elsewhere, and among them also for irrational creatures — but for those that have horns. These butt one another, and by some marvellous nature strive to the point of victory, like athletes contending either for the greatest prizes or for august glory and some good report. These irrational contestants are wild bulls and tame rams and the so-called "middle ones" and one-horned asses and hyenas. They say this creature is smaller than a gazelle, but far bolder than a deer and quick to anger with its horn. Then, after all, the elephant contestants come in; and these go even to death, wounding one another with their tusks, and often the one prevails and kills its adversary, but often they die together.

There are quick-witted creatures among us too, not indeed as many as in India, but a few. There the elephant is of this kind, and the parrot, and the sphinges, and the so-called satyrs; and wise too, it seems, was the Indian ant. Now our own ants dig their burrows and runs under the earth, and make certain hidden lairs by burrowing, and wear themselves out in mining-work, so to speak, secret and unseen; but the Indian ants build for themselves heaped-up dwellings, and these not in flat and smooth and easily flooded places, but in lofty and high ones. In these they bore certain passages and, so to speak, Egyptian conduits or Cretan labyrinths, with a secret skill, and so make habitations for themselves, not straight and easy to pass through, but slanting with windings and borings; and they leave on the surface a single opening, through which they themselves go in and out and bring in whatever seeds they gather, and then carry them into their storehouses. They contrive their lofty dwellings in order to escape the overflowings and floodings from the rivers. And by this skill it comes about that they live as it were on look-out points or islands, when the ground all round those little hillocks is flooded. Yet those mounds, heaped up though they are, are so far from being dissolved and broken up by the flooding all about that they are even made firm by it: first by the morning dew, for from this they are clothed, so to speak, with a thin but strong coat of frost; and then they are bound together below by a mossy crust of the river-mud. About the Indian ants Juba wrote of old; let what I have said suffice for now.

Aristotle says that the female partridge, when she gets to windward of the male, becomes pregnant by some secret nature. This bird weaves its nest in seven days, and in seven lays its eggs, and in as many rears its young. Timaeus and Heracleides and Neocles the physician say that toads have two livers, and that the one kills, while the other is its opposite by nature; for it saves.

The hake is such a father among fishes. He guards strongly the young born from his mate, that they may be safe from plots and unharmed. And as long as they swim about cheerful and free from fear, he does not abandon his watch, but now follows behind, now does not, swimming now on this side, now on that; and if any of his little ones is afraid, he opens his mouth and takes the infant in; then, when the fear has passed, he spits out again the one that fled to him, just as he received it, and the little one swims off once more.

If a redness ever rises and a paleness on bare skin stripped of hair, it is no wonder; but the tarand is a creature that changes itself with the very hairs, and produces a countless variety of colours, so as to astonish the sight. It is a Scythian, and in its back and size resembles a bull. And the Scythians, knowing its hide to be a good defence against the spear, stretch it over their own shields.

When partridges are about to lay, they prepare for themselves out of certain twigs what is called the threshing-floor. It is a hollow plaited thing, very suitable to sit in. And pouring in dust, and making, as it were, a soft bed, and creeping in, then covering themselves above with twigs so as to escape the notice both of the rapacious birds and of the hunters among men, in great peace they lay; then they do not entrust the eggs to the same place, but to another, as though removing house; for they fear lest they be detected. And in their nesting they warm the tender young and keep them warm with their own feathers, wrapping them as in swaddling-clothes with their plumage; they do not wash them, but make them brighter by dusting. And if a partridge sees someone approaching and plotting against both itself and its young, then it rolls itself before the feet of the hunter, and gives him hope of being able to catch it as it tumbles. And he stoops to the prey, while the partridge unrolls itself; and it escapes, and the young get on their way. And when the partridge perceives this, taking courage now it relieves the fowler of his vain occupation by flying up, and leaves the man gaping. Then the mother, being in safety and standing in a good place, calls her young. And they fly to her, recognizing the cry. The partridge, when about to be delivered of her eggs, tries to escape her mate's notice, lest he break the eggs; for being lustful, he does not let the mother have leisure for rearing the young. So unbridled is the race of partridges. When the females have left them and are brooding, the males deliberately kindle one another to anger, and strike and are struck most bitterly; and the one defeated is mounted like a hen, and the victor does this without restraint, until he too, defeated by another, then falls into the same holds.

Cocks in a flock all mount the newcomer. And tame partridges do the same to the one that has just arrived and is not yet subdued. And in return for those who rear them, the partridges themselves lure the free and wild ones, doing this just as the pigeons do. Now the decoy partridge attracts and holds out its siren-song to draw the others on in this way. It stands singing, and its song is a challenge, goading the wild bird to battle; and it stands in ambush by the snare. The leader of the wild birds, answering the song, comes forward to fight in front of the flock. Then the tame one retreats step by step, pretending to be afraid; but the other advances proudly, as if already victorious, and is caught fast in the snare. Now if the one that has fallen into the trap is a male, his companions try to come to the rescue of the captive; but if it is a female, they strike at the one caught, one from one side and one from another, as having fallen into slavery through lust. And I shall not pass over this, since it too is worth hearing. If the decoy is female, then, so that the male may not fall in, the females outside sound an answering song and rescue the one who would have fallen into the snare, since he gladly stays beside his many mates, as though drawn by some erotic spell, by Zeus indeed.

The wasps that have stings are said to do this too. Whenever they see a dead viper, they fall upon it and poison their sting. Whence men too seem to me to have learned a lesson, and that not a good one. And indeed Homer bears witness in the Odyssey, saying, "seeking a man-slaying drug, that he might have wherewith to anoint his bronze-tipped arrows"; or, by Zeus, if one must give any heed to the tale about Heracles—that he dipped his arrows in the poison of the hydra—so those too whet their stings with the dipping.

When a famine is about to visit, dogs and oxen and pigs and goats and snakes and other animals perceive it, and when a plague is to come they understand it first of all, and earthquake too. And they foreknow also the healthiness of the air and the abundance of crops. And though they have not received the reason that has power both to save and to destroy, yet of the aforesaid things they are not deceived.

Eagles seize land tortoises and then dash them down from above upon the rocks, and having shattered the shell, so extract the flesh and eat it. In this very way too, I hear, Aeschylus the Eleusinian, the tragic poet, met the end of his life. Aeschylus was sitting upon a rock, philosophizing and writing, as was his wont; and his head was bald and bare of hair. An eagle, then, supposing his head to be a rock, let fall upon it the tortoise it was holding, and the missile struck the man aforesaid and killed him.

The sponge is steered by a small creature, not like a crab in form, but rather like a spider. For the sponge is no soulless thing, nor without a share of blood—it is an offspring of the sea, and clings to the rocks, just as other things do, but has a certain motion of its own, and needs, as one might say, something to remind it that it is alive. For when it lies still, through a kind of natural porousness, and is quiet, then, when something falls into its openings, it is pricked by the spider-like creature, and seizes what has fallen in, and gets its food. And when a man approaches to cut it off, being stung by its companion creature it bristles and contracts itself, and becomes the cause of much labour and toil, by Zeus, to the gatherer.

When the snake casts off its old age—it does this at the beginning of spring—then too it cleanses the mist of its eyes and the dimness of its sight, this also being as it were an old age of the eyes; and rubbing and stroking each eye against fennel, it then becomes free of this affliction. For it grows dim-sighted through hibernating in winter in a recess and in darkness. So the fennel, gently warming the creature's sight, numbed by the cold, clears it, and makes it keener of vision.

The sow, out of gluttony, spares not even her own young, and indeed, if she comes upon a human body, she does not refrain but eats it. For this reason the Egyptians hated the animal as foul and all-devouring. But the prudent love to honour, even among the brute beasts, the gentler ones that have a share of frugality and of piety. The Egyptians, accordingly, even worship the storks, since these care for their fathers in old age and hold them in honour. The same Egyptians honour also the fox-goose and the hoopoe, since the one is loving to its young, and the other dutiful toward its parents. And I hear too that Manetho the Egyptian, a man who had advanced to the summit of wisdom, said that whoever tastes sow's milk is filled with leprous and scaly disease; and all the people of Asia hate these afflictions. The Egyptians have believed the sow to be most hateful to the sun and the moon. Whenever, therefore, they hold a festival of the moon, they sacrifice sows to her once a year, but at no other time will they sacrifice this animal either to her or to any other of the gods. But the Athenians sacrifice sows at the Mysteries, and very justly; for they ruin the crops, and often, leaping in among them, they break off the young ears not yet ripe, and dig others up. Eudoxus says that the Egyptians, sparing the sows, do not sacrifice them, since, when the grain has been sown, they drive their herds over it; and the sows trample it and push it down into the moist earth, so that it may remain alive and not be consumed by the birds.

Prophecy too, it seems, was peculiar to serpents. In Lavinium, at any rate, the small town that is of the land of the Latins (it has been named after Lavinia the daughter of Latinus, when Latinus fought as ally with Aeneas against the people called Rutulians and then conquered them; and Aeneas the Trojan, son of Anchises, founded the city aforesaid, which would be, as one might say, the grandmother of Rome on the mother's side; for setting out from there Ascanius the son of Aeneas and Creusa the Trojan woman founded Alba, and of the Albans Rome is a colony) — in Lavinium, then, a great and thick grove is honoured, and it has near it a temple of Argive Hera. And in the grove there is a great and deep den, and it is the lair of a serpent. And sacred virgins on appointed days go into the grove carrying in their two hands a barley-cake, and with their eyes bound up by fillets. A divine breath leads them straight to the lair of the serpent, and they go forward without stumbling, step by step and quietly, as though seeing with uncovered eyes. And if they are virgins, the serpent accepts the food as pure and befitting a god-beloved animal; but if not, the food remains untouched, since he foreknows and has divined the corruption. And ants, crumbling into small pieces the cake of the woman who has lost her virginity, so that it may be easy for them to carry, then bear it out of the grove, cleansing the place. And the deed is recognized by the natives, and those who went in are tested, and she who has shamed her virginity is punished with the penalties of the law. Thus I would demonstrate the prophetic power of serpents.

Democritus says that the sow and the dog are prolific, and he adds the reason, saying that they have many wombs and the parts receptive of the seed. The semen, then, does not fill them all from a single impulse, but these animals couple twice and three times, so that the continuity may fill the parts receptive of the offspring. And he says that mules do not bear young; for they do not have wombs like those of other animals, but of a different shape, least able to receive the seed; for the mule, he says, is not a work of nature, but a contrivance and theft, as one might say, of human ingenuity and an adulterous daring. "It seems to me," he says, "that an ass forced a mare by chance, and that men, having become learners of this violence, then went on to the habit of breeding them." And especially the asses of the Libyans, being very large, mount mares not maned but shorn; for a mare that has its own splendour through its mane would not, the wise in these matings say, endure such a mate.

The Italians and Sicilians like to call the hunting of tunny the "monster-fishery"; and the places where they store their great nets and the rest of their hunting gear are called "monster-hunting stations," since they wish to distinguish the tunny's size as belonging among the sea-monsters. I am told that the Celts and Massaliotes and all the Ligurian folk hunt tunny with hooks; these are made of iron, and are very large and thick to look upon. And let what I have now said about tunny, in addition to what was said before, be enough for me.

The wild goats that tread the Libyan heights are in size like oxen to look upon, but their thighs and breasts and necks bristle with the thickest hairs, and with these their chin too. Their foreheads are curved and rounded, their eyes flashing, but their legs are stunted. Their horns, after the first joining together, stand apart from each other and slantwise; for they are not at all upright like those of the other mountain goats, but go down crosswise and reach toward the shoulders. So very long are they. From the topmost ridges, which both herdsmen and the sons of poets like to call "crags," they leap easily to another peak; for these are the best leapers of all goats. And even if one should fall farther than where there is anything to receive it, so as to be beyond its reach, yet such strength resides in its limbs that it remains unharmed when it has come down. At any rate it breaks nothing, even if it falls upon a cleft rock, neither horn nor skull; for these are strong and like the resistance of the rock. Most of them, then, are taken on the very heights with nets and javelins and foot-traps, by the cunning that is in huntsmen generally and in goat-hunting especially; but they are hunted also in the plains, and there they are too weak to flee. So even one who is slow of foot will catch them. Both the hide and the horns are useful; for the hide, in the fiercest winters, keeps the cold from coming near herdsmen and woodcutters; and those horns are good for drawing up and drinking from a river flowing by, or some spring rising in the summer season, and serviceable for quenching thirst; for it lets you drink at a draught no less than the largest cups, until you have cooled your breath and quenched all that smoulders and inflames within. So if the inside be cleaned out by one skilled in scraping horns, one of the two would easily hold three measures.

Theophrastus says that the young of the viper do not eat through their mother's belly, knocking at the door, as it were (to add a jest), and breaking out a barred exit, but that, the female being squeezed and her belly straitened (I speak in Homer's way), she does not hold out but bursts asunder. And he persuades me by what he says, since the sea-needles too, being without a pocket and slender, suffer the same things from their own young, as I have said somewhere above. But I beg Herodotus not to be wroth with me if I set down among tales all that he sings about the birth-pang of vipers.

Among the Indian Arianians there is a chasm of Pluto, and below it certain secret conduits and hidden ways and runs, unseen by men but deep and reaching to a vast length; how they came to be, and in what manner they were dug, neither do the Indians say, nor do I busy myself to learn. Now the Indians drive thither more than thirty thousand beasts — sheep and goats and oxen and horses; and each of those who suspect a dream, or some omen, or a rumour, or an ill-boding bird, casts in, in place of his own life, according to the means he has at home, ransoming himself and giving the life of the beast in exchange for his own soul. And the beasts are led, neither dragged by bonds nor otherwise driven, but of their own will they accomplish this journey, drawn by some secret attraction and spell. Then, standing at the mouth, they leap in of their own accord, and to human sight they are no longer to be seen, once they have fallen into the secret and yawning chasm of the earth; but from above are heard the lowings of oxen and the bleating of sheep, the neighing of horses and the bleating of goats. And if anyone walks along the surface and goes forward, putting his ear to the ground, he will hear the sounds I have mentioned for a very long way. Nor does the mingled noise ever fail, since they send down the beasts in their stead every day. Whether only the recent ones are heard, or some of the first as well, I do not know; but heard they are. And let this too be reckoned among the things peculiar to the creatures there.

Theopompus says that the Heneti who dwell about the Adriatic, when it is the season of ploughing and sowing, send gifts to the jackdaws; and the gifts would be certain cakes and barley-loaves nicely and well kneaded. The purpose of the setting out of these gifts is that they may be soothing offerings to the jackdaws and agreements of truce, that those birds may not dig up the corn of Demeter when it has been cast into the earth, nor pick it out. Lycus agrees to these things, and adds besides the following: that there are also thongs purple in colour, and that those who set these out then withdraw. And the clouds of jackdaws remain outside the boundaries, while two or three, chosen like ambassadors from the cities, are sent to inspect the abundance of the hospitable gifts; and these, having looked, come back and call the rest, in the way in which the one kind are wont to call, the other to obey. So they come in clouds; and if they taste of the aforesaid gifts, the Heneti know that they are under truce with the said birds; but if they overlook them and, dishonouring them as cheap, do not taste, the natives are persuaded that the price of that contempt is famine for them. For the said birds, remaining untasting, fly down so to speak untithed upon the fields and plunder most of what has been sown, and that most bitterly, with anger both digging it up and tracking it out.

The dogfish, when she has given birth, has her pups swimming with her at once and without delay. And if any of them is afraid, it slips back into the mother through her opening; then, when the fear has passed, it comes forth, as though being born again.

A fish of the open sea by lot, black in appearance, in length like a measured eel, taking its name from what it does, fastening on a running ship and that with a fair wind, and biting the tip of the stern, just as one most violently reins in a disobedient and rough horse by the mouth with a hard bit, checks it from its course and holds it fettered; and in vain are the sails filled out in the midst, and to no purpose do the winds blow, and grief holds the sailors. And the sailors understand, and recognize the ship's affliction. And from this it got its name; for those who have experience call it the ship-holder.

Euripides says that envy bears an ill name; and this, it seems, dwells also in some of the animals. The gecko, for instance, as Theophrastus says, when it has cast off its old age, turning round then swallows it and makes it disappear; for it seems that the old skin of this creature is a remedy against epilepsy. And the deer too knows that its right horn is good for many things, and indeed buries it and hides it out of grudging that anyone should enjoy so great a benefit. And the mare knows the love-charms she brings forth with her foal; and so, as soon as the young is born, she bites off the bit of flesh on its forehead. Men call it the horse-frenzy. And the sorcerers say that such things provide and kindle certain impulses that draw toward uncontrollable union and an amorous frenzy. So the mare is not willing that men should share in this charm, grudging it as a very great good. Is it not so?

The land-hedgehog too is believed to be one of the envious, malign creatures. At any rate, whenever it is caught, it at once wets its own skin with urine and renders it useless—though the skin seems serviceable for many purposes. The lynx too hides its urine; for when it congeals it becomes a stone, and is suited for engraving, and serves, they say, as an ornament for women.

Let the fly too have from us the honour of not being left without mention here; for it also is a creation of nature. The flies of Pisa, at the festival of the Olympic games, make, as one might say, a truce both with the visitors and the natives. At any rate, when so many victims are sacrificed and blood is shed and meats are hung up, the flies vanish of their own accord, and cross the Alpheus to the bank opposite. And they seem to differ not at all from the women of the country, save perhaps that those flies are admitted to be somewhat more self-controlled than the women in their conduct; for the women are driven out by the law of the contest and of the temperance belonging to it, but the flies withdraw of their own accord from the sacred things, and during the rites and throughout the appointed time of the games they depart. The contest is dissolved, and they return, as though exiles who have obtained a recall by decree; then the flies flow back into Elis again.

In the land of the so-called Jews or Idumaeans the natives sang, in the time of King Herod, that a snake of the very greatest size fell in love with a beautiful girl, and visiting her would sleep with the aforesaid girl most amorously. So the girl did not take courage at her lover, though it crept up as gently and tamely as possible. She withdrew, then, and stayed away a month, expecting, of course, that the snake would forget her during the absence of his beloved. But for him the solitude intensified his passion, and he came daily and by night; yet not meeting her as he wished, like a lover unfortunate in his longing, he too grieved. But when the woman returned again, the snake came, and embracing her with the rest of its body, with its tail struck the legs of his beloved sparingly, as one slighted and indeed angry. So He who rules over Zeus himself and the other gods does not overlook even the irrational creatures, but shows by these and by others how he is disposed toward them.

The cerylus and the halcyon share the same way of life and live together. And when they are enfeebled by age, the halcyons take them up and carry them about upon what are called their mid-wings. But men despise their fellow men as they grow old, and look toward the young; and those who have married flutter about the young women, setting no store by their older wives, and the gifted speakers among them are not ashamed to live more irrationally than the irrational animals.

We have spoken, then, of elephants separately, and shall speak of them more. Just as they are masters of their way of life, so, in what manner they have a share of self-control, it is most fitting to say. For they do not come to union with the female as though in wantonness or lust, but like those who need a continuation of their race and beget offspring, that the line of descent from one another may not fail them, but that they may leave seed behind. Once, at any rate, in their lifetime they call to mind love, when the female too submits; then, each having filled his mate, he thereafter knows her no more. And they do not couple openly, nor in the sight of the others, but having withdrawn; and they set before themselves either dense trees or some thick wood or a hollow and deep place that affords them abundant concealment. That they are just, I said above, and their courage too has already been told; and now this present matter has demonstrated their self-control. But their hatred of wickedness too, whoever has leisure to learn it, let him incline his ears and hear. A tame elephant had a keeper, and he had a wife older than himself, but rich. So, being in love with another woman, and eager that his wife's property should become that other's, this hot-headed man strangled her and buried her near the elephant's stall, and married the other. There, then, the elephant, taking hold with its trunk of the newly arrived woman, led her near the dead one, and digging her up with its tusks and laying the body bare, showed by the very deeds those things which it could not say, teaching the woman the character of the man who had married her—the elephant that hated wickedness.

When the halcyon perceives that she is pregnant, then she makes a nest for the reception of her chicks, neither needing mud and a roof and houses, as the swallow does, and entering uninvited as a stranger, and troubling the early morning with her chatter and cutting short the sweetest of sleep; nor again does she hold to the aforesaid task with her body alone in open places, but weaving and gathering together the spines of the needlefish, with a kind of secret bond of orderliness she encompasses her work. For some of them she binds straight, and others crosswise—you would say it was a woman skilled in weaving interlacing the woof with the warp—and she makes the work gently rounded and hollow, fashioning it like the weave of a fish-trap. And when she has woven the thing described, she carries it to the sea, where, as the wave breaks gently upon it, the lapping that comes upon it proves the halcyon's work; for the part that is not watertight she mends again against the water that falls in. But the parts that are fitted together, even if you strike them with a stone, you could not pierce. And if you should wish to cut through them with iron, they would not yield, being so well and finely woven together, no less than the linen corselet which they sing that Amasis dedicated to Athena of Lindus. And the mouth of this trap is to no other creature either passable or even very visible, but it admits her alone. Nor would even any of the sea flow in through it; so watertight is it. There, then, the halcyon rears her chicks too, borne upon the waves, as they say.

When elephants are torn from their accustomed land, even if they are tamed, first by bonds and hunger, then by food and its variety, still the love of the country that reared them never grows faint in them. Most of them, indeed, are destroyed by grief, and some, weeping in floods and with measureless tears, have been blinded in their sight. They are led into the ships across a bridge, on either side of which boughs in full leaf and foliage are set fast, and other green vegetation is shaken, to deceive the beasts; for if the elephants see these, they think even then that they are still going across the land, nor do these things let the sea be seen. The waters before the country from which they must sail are shallow and not deep close in, and the merchant ships stand off at a distance; and for this reason there is need of the bridge and of the device and the contrivance by means of the boughs and the vegetation aforesaid.

Homer, then, says: "Hard are the gods to look upon when they appear manifest." So the serpent, too, that is held in the most sacred honours has something the more divine about it, and it is not profitable to look upon it. And what I say is this. In Melite of Egypt there is a sacred serpent in a tower, and it is honoured and has attendants and ministers, and there is set for it a table and a mixing-bowl. Into this, then, each day, they steep barley-groats in honey-water and then go away; and on the next day, returning, they find the bowl empty. So the eldest of these ministers conceived a very keen longing to behold the serpent, and going in alone and doing the customary things he withdrew; and the serpent, climbing up onto the table, was feasting. And the busybody, opening the doors (for he had chanced to shut them as was customary), made a loud noise. The serpent grew indignant and withdrew; and the man, having seen what he longed for to his own hurt, became out of his mind, and having told all he had seen and confessed that he had committed sacrilege, was speechless, and then not long after, falling down, died.

Democritus says that embryos are aborted more in southern weather than in northern, and reasonably; for the bodies of pregnant women are made loose by the south wind and gape apart. So, the frame being relaxed and not knit together, the embryos, warmed and heated, slip this way and that and are aborted more easily; but if there be frost and the north wind blows, the embryo is compacted, but is hard to move and is not troubled as by a swell, and being unbuffeted and in calm it is strong and firm and lasts to the natural time of bearing. So in cold, the Abderite says, it holds together, but in warmth for the most part it is cast out. And he says it is a necessity, when the heat abounds, that both the veins and the joints gape apart.

About the islands called Tyrrhenian those engaged in fishing hunt the monstrous fish of those waters, which they call the aulopias; and it is no bad thing to describe its peculiar features. In size the largest aulopias is inferior to the largest tunny, but in strength and fighting power it would bear off the first prize when set against them. For the tunny too is a valiant tribe of fishes, but to one who faces it and contends with it eagerly it yields the mastery after its first onset, its blood congealing within it, and being spent it is very swiftly caught. But the aulopias holds out for a long while when one sets upon it with force, and stands against the fisherman as against an adversary, and prevails for the most part, pressing itself harder down and bending its head and thrusting toward the deep; for it is strong in the jaw and powerful in the neck, and has excellent vigour. When it is taken, it is most beautiful to see, with its eyes open and round and large, such as Homer sings of in oxen; and its jaw, though strong as I said, yet also lends to its beauty. Its back imitates the colour of the deepest blue, but it is girt with a white belly; and a line of golden colour begins from its head and, running down to the tail-end, finishes in a circle. I am willing to tell the crafty way they hunt them, which I know from hearsay. Choosing out in advance the spots where they suppose the aulopiae to gather, they then catch with their bait-nets many small crows-fish; and mooring their boat upon anchors and continually making a certain noise underwater, they stretch out the crows-fish, fastening them tight with cords. These, hearing the noise and seeing the bait, swim up from this side and that, gather, and circle round the fishing-boat, and grow so tame at the din and the abundance of food that they remain even when men stretch out their hands. They endure a human touch — in my judgement, enslaved by the feeding, but, as the hunters say, also trusting in their strength. Among them there are tame ones too, which the fishermen recognize as benefactors and companions, and have a truce with them. Other strangers follow these as leaders, and these newcomers, as one might call them, they both hunt and kill; but toward the tame ones, which are like decoy doves, there is for them no hunting and a truce. Nor would so great a want ever come upon a skilled fisherman that he should take a tame aulopias by treachery; for if it is caught by chance, for certain reasons, it even causes grief. It is caught either by being pierced upon a hook or by being wounded to death. We see that fowlers too will not kill any of the decoy birds, either for sale or for dinner. And there are other ways of hunting these fishes as well.
There are also tortoises bred in Libya, the most curly-shelled to look upon, and these are mountain tortoises, and they have a shell good for lyres.

There was, then, a certain natural fellowship and secret kinship between the lion and the dolphin. For it is not enough that the one is king of land creatures and the other of sea creatures; but indeed, even when they waste away advancing into old age, the one has the land-ape as a remedy, while the other seeks out its kindred ape. For that there is an ape in the sea too, I have said somewhere; and this is good for the dolphin, as that one for the lion.

In what is called the Great Sea they tell also of a very large island, and its name, I hear, is Taprobane; I learn that the island is very long and high, that it has a length of seven thousand stades and a breadth of five thousand, and that it has no cities, but seven hundred and fifty villages; and the dwellings in which the natives lodge are made of wood, and indeed of reeds. There are bred in this sea tortoises of the greatest size, whose shells become roofs; for a single shell is even fifteen cubits, so that not a few may dwell beneath it; and it keeps off the most burning suns, and gives welcome shade, and against the downpours of rain it is a defence, stronger than any tile, and shakes off the onsets of the showers; and those dwelling beneath hear it drummed upon, as when waters fall on a roof. Yet they have no need to replace it as they would a cracked tile; for the shell is hard, and is like a rock hollowed out, with a cave and a self-made roof.

Amyntas, in his work entitled by him the Stages, says that in the Caspian land there are many herds of cattle and of horses, too many to count. He adds also this: that in certain turns of the seasons there come migrations of mice, an unmatched multitude, and he brings forward as proof, saying, that when the ever-flowing rivers come down with much roaring, the mice quite unflinchingly swim upon them, and biting one another's tails hold this as ballast, and make this a most strong bond for crossing the channel. And having swum across to the fields, he says, they crop the corn, and creep up through the trees, and make the ripe fruit their meal, and even break through the branches, not being unable to gnaw even these to pieces. So the Caspians, to ward off the inroad and the ruin from the mice, spare the crook-taloned birds, which, themselves flying in clouds, snatch up the mice, and by a peculiar nature stay off famine from the Caspians. As for the Caspian foxes, their multitude is so great that they not only frequent the steadings in the fields, but now even come into the cities. And a fox will appear in a house, not, by Zeus, for ruin or plunder, but as though tame; and they fawn and cajole like the lapdogs among us. The mice that are an epidemic evil to the Caspians are in size to be seen like the Egyptian ichneumons; and they are wild and terrible and strong of tooth, and able to cut through and gnaw through even iron. Such too are the mice in Teredon of Babylonia, whose skins their dealers bring to the Persians as merchandise. They are soft, and being sewn together they become at once tunics and keep the people warm. These are called kandytanes, as is dear to them. And the following too is worth marvelling at in these mice. If a pregnant mouse is caught, and then the embryo is taken out, and that one too, when cut open, is in turn laid open, that one also has a young one within.

Men marvel at women as exceedingly fond of their children; yet I observe that mothers have gone on living after the death of their sons or daughters, and in time have come to forget their suffering, their grief withering away. But the female dolphin is the fondest of her offspring of all creatures to the very last degree. She bears two; and when a fisherman either wounds her young with his trident or strikes it with a barb — the barb is pierced at its upper end, and a long cord is fastened to it, and the prongs, sinking in, hold fast to the beast — then, so long as the wounded dolphin still has its strength, the hunter slackens the cord, lest by its violence it should break it and he suffer two evils, the dolphin departing with the barb in it and he himself meeting with an empty catch; but when he perceives it grown weary and somewhat enfeebled by the wound, he gently brings his boat alongside and has his prey. The mother does not shrink from what is done, nor draw back in fear, but by an unspeakable instinct she follows in her longing for her child; and bring on as many terrors as you please, she is not dismayed, since she cannot bear to abandon her young while it is amid the slaughter, but one may strike her even from one's hand — so does she come to grips with those who strike, as though to defend it. And by this she is caught along with her young, when she might be saved and depart. But if both her offspring are with her, and she perceives that one has been wounded and is being led off, as I said before, she drives the unhurt one away, lashing it with her tail and biting it with her mouth, and blows a kind of inarticulate snort, as best she can, giving the signal of flight for its safety. And that one departs, but she herself remains until she is taken, and dies together with the one that was caught.

The art concerning the wounded and those needing a drug rises in Homer even to a third generation of teaching. For Patroclus, son of Menoetius, is taught medicine by Achilles, and Achilles, son of Peleus, by Chiron, son of Cronus. And among heroes and the children of gods the lessons were: to know the nature of roots, the use of various herbs, the mixing of drugs, and incantations against inflammation, to stanch blood, and all the rest those men knew; and indeed those of later time too have tracked out some things. But of these contrivances nature had no need; and the elephant proves it. So when many spears and arrows come into him, he eats the flower of the olive, or the oil itself, and then shakes out all that fell into him, and is whole again.

In the Red Sea Leonides of Byzantium says there is a fish, no smaller at all than a full-grown goby; but it has neither eyes nor a mouth in the manner of fish. There are attached to it gills and the shape of a head, as one might guess, yet it is not formed into a clear shape; and below, under its belly, there is impressed a gently hollowed mark, and it sends out the colour of an emerald. This, he says, is its eye and its mouth too. And whoever tastes it has hunted it to his own hurt. And the manner of the destruction: the one who has tasted it swells, then his belly bursts, and the man perishes. And the fish too, when caught, pays its penalty. First, on being out of the wave, it swells; and if anyone touches it, it is inflamed still more. And if one continues handling it, it becomes, by putrefaction, wholly transparent, like a man with dropsy; then at last it bursts. And if one should wish to let it back into the sea while still alive, it floats like a bladder lifted by air. And he says that from this affliction they called it the puffer.
A lion that has eaten of the "lion-killer" dies. Insects are destroyed if one smears them with oil. Perfume is the death of vultures. And you will destroy a beetle if you throw roses upon it.

The orphus is a sea creature, and if you catch and cut it open, you would not see it die at once, but it lingers in motion, and that for no short time. Through the winter it likes to keep house in its holes; and its haunts are dearer to it nearer the land.

Snakes, conscious that they have a thin and long gullet, yet being gluttonous and most omnivorous, as Aristotle says, rise upright and stand on the tip of their tail, and the food slips down for them and passes into the bulk of the body; and being footless they then creep most swiftly. There is one that even shoots itself like a javelin and rushes on, and it has its name from what it does; for it is called the dart-snake.

The Egyptians say that around the place called Coptos only two ravens are to be seen. But the Romans too who guard the mountain region on account of the emerald mine assert—these men also—that just so many birds of this kind dwell there. A temple is honoured to Apollo in that place, of which they say the ravens are sacred.

Anchovies—some call them encrasicholi, but I have heard a third name for them too, for there are those who call them "wolf-mouths." They are little fishes, prolific by nature, and very white to look at. The fishes that go in shoals eat them most of all. So, when frightened, they run together, and each holding to its neighbour, by that close packing it escapes being easily plotted against. So great, indeed, does their union become when they have run together, that not even passing ferry-boats split them; and indeed, if anyone should wish to pass an oar or a pole through them, they are not torn apart, but hold to one another as if woven together. And if you put down your hand, you may, as from a heap of grain or beans, draw them out by force, so that they are often even torn apart, and half of the little fishes are taken while the rest are left. For you will hold the tail-part, while the head remains with the others; or you will carry a head home, while the rest remains in the sea. Their dense and continuous shoal is called a "haul," and one haul has often filled fifty fishing-boats, as the seafarers say.

Near the Nile there grows a plant, and it is called wolf's-bane, and it is not falsely named, and reasonably so; for when a wolf treads upon it, it dies in convulsions. For this reason those Egyptians who revere this animal forbid this plant to be brought into their country.

I hear that the ram, for the six most wintry months, lies and sleeps upon his left side whenever sleep takes and enfolds him, but from the spring equinox he rests the other way and lies upon his right. So at each equinox the ram changes the side on which he lies.

Peculiar to animals are these things too. The peacock, that it may not be bewitched, seeks out the root of flax as a kind of natural amulet, and stuffing it under one of its wings carries it about. And it is said too that if a horse's urine be retained, a virgin loosing the girdle she wears and striking it across the face with the girdle, the horse straightway urinates copiously and ceases from its pain. And a mare maddened very violently for mating one can easily stop, as Aristotle says, if one shear off the hairs along its neck; for it is ashamed, and is not unruly, and ceases from its insolence and its much frisking, downcast at the shame. This too Sophocles hints at in his play Tyro; she is made to say, and what she says is this: "I suffer grief for my hair like a filly, who, seized by the cowherds in the horse-pastures with a savage hand, has the yellow harvest of her neck reaped off, and going to drink in the meadow of the river waters, sees in a shadow the image of herself outraged by the shearing, her mane plucked off without honour. Alas, even one without pity would pity her, cowering for shame, how she rages, mourning and weeping for her former mane."

The same man says that the cause of the growth of horns in deer is this. Their belly, he agrees, is very hot, and he says that their veins, which run through the whole body, are very loose, and that the bone enclosing the brain is very thin and membranous and porous, and that veins, very thick, rise up from there even to the top of the head. So the food, and the most fruitful part of it, is distributed very swiftly. And the fat, he says, is poured round them on the outside, but the strength of the food leaps up to the head through the veins. From there, then, the horns grow forth, watered by much moisture. So the moisture, being continuous and flowing on, pushes out the earlier matter. And the part that projects, the moisture outside the body, becomes hard, the air fixing and horn-forming it, but the part still shut up within is soft. And the one hardens by the chill from outside, but the soft part remains so by the warmth within. So the growth of the new horn pushes out the older as something alien, the part within pressing and wishing to thrust this up and swelling and throbbing, as though hastening to be born and come forth. For the moisture, fixing and rising up, is unable to keep still, but itself becomes hard and is thrust upon the earlier matter. And most of the horns are pressed out by the strength within; but some, caught by branches and hindering the swift course, the beast, driven by its rush, has knocked off. And some slip out, and others nature brings forward ready to peep out.

In the royal palace of the Indians, where the greatest of their kings dwells, there are many other things worthy of wonder, so that one should set against them neither the Memnonian Susa and its sumptuousness, nor the magnificence at Ecbatana; for those would seem mere Persian boasting if compared with these. To go round the rest in my account does not belong to this treatise; but in the parks there are reared tame peacocks and pheasants made gentle to the hand, and these have their place among the trees that have been cultivated, which the royal keepers think worthy of the needful care. For there are shady groves and pasture grown together, and branches woven into one another by a certain art of arboriculture. And the most august thing about the beauty there is that the trees themselves are of the evergreen kind, and never grow old or shed their leaves; some are native, others brought from elsewhere with great care, which adorn the place and give it splendour — except the olive; for the land of the Indians does not bear it, neither produces it of itself, nor rears it when it comes from elsewhere. Other birds too come there, free and unenslaved, and arriving of their own accord they have their roosts and resting-places among the trees. There too the parrots are reared and throng about the king. No Indian eats a parrot, though they are very many in number; the reason is that the Brahmans believe them sacred, and indeed they honour them above all birds. And they add that they do this with good reason; for the parrot alone most eloquently imitates the human voice. There are also in this palace beautiful artificial lakes, and they hold fish of the greatest size and gentle; and no one hunts them except the king's sons while they are still children, fishing and playing in the calm and least dangerous water, and at the same time learning to swim.

When a mare gives birth, a piece of flesh, not large but small, grown out of the foal, hangs attached — some say to its forehead, some to its loins, others to its genitals. This the mare bites off and makes away with, and this little piece of flesh is called the "horse-frenzy." It is done out of pity and mercy of nature toward horses. For if, they say, that piece were always and right through attached, the males and females among them would be kindled to a frenzy of unrestrained mating. Let it be, if you please, a gift given to horses by Poseidon the Horse-god or by Athena the Horse-goddess, that their race may endure and not be destroyed by a madness of lust. Horse-keepers know this well and rightly, and if ever they need the said piece of flesh for some plot against a person, to kindle love in him, they keep watch over the pregnant mare, and when she gives birth they at once snatch away the foal and cut off the said flesh, and put it into the hoof of a mare; for there alone could it be well kept and stored up. The foal they sacrifice at sunrise; for the mother no longer suckles it, the token having been taken away and it having lost the ground of her affection; for it is from biting off that flesh that the mother begins to love her young strongly. And whoever, by some plot, tastes that little piece of flesh is held by a love most unrestrained, and is parched and cries out, and rushes uncontrollably even upon the basest favourites and upon a woman past her prime and ugly, and bears witness to his disease, and tells those he meets how he is goaded. And his body wastes and pines, while his soul is driven by erotic madness. I am told, then, that even at Olympia the bronze mare, with which horses fall in love and go mad and wish to mount, and neigh an erotic neigh when they see it, has within it, in the bewitched bronze, a plot derived from this horse-frenzy lying hidden, and that by some secret device of the craftsman the bronze plots against living creatures; for there could not be such accuracy that horses seeing it should be thus deceived and goaded by the work itself. And perhaps those who say this say something, and perhaps they say nothing; but what I heard about these matters too I have told.

There is, among the things past telling and beyond number, also the sepedon, an evil reptile; Nicander says that this too is of the same colour as the haemorrhois, and its sister in shape. And this he says; it seems also to be swifter, and it gives some appearance of smallness; for it goes forward on a curved and winding course, and chiefly in this it deceives those who see it as to how great it is in size. The wound from it is dreadful; for it spreads and rots beneath, and proves the said beast true to its name. The venom is thrust over the whole body with irresistible speed, and indeed the hair too, rotting, disappears, and the eyebrows and eyelashes run off, and a mist holds the eyes, and they become blotched.

The island in the Great Sea, then, which they call Taprobane, has palm-groves wonderfully planted in rows, just as in luxurious parks their keepers plant the shade-bearing trees; and it has also pastures of many elephants of the greatest size. And the island elephants are mightier in strength than the mainland ones and larger to look upon, and would in every way be judged quicker-witted. So men build great ships and carry them across to the mainland opposite — for the island has forests too — and on crossing over sell them to the king in the country of the Calingae. And because of the size of the island, those who dwell in its midst do not even know the sea, but pass a mainlander's life, though they learn by report that a sea goes round and encircles them. Those who live by the sea know nothing of the hunting of elephants, but know it by hearsay only; about the catching of fish and of sea-monsters, however, they busy themselves. For they say that the sea which goes round the circle of the island nourishes an irresistible multitude of fish and sea-monsters, and that these have heads of lions and leopards and wolves and rams too; and, what is a still greater wonder, some of the monsters carry about the shapes of satyrs and the look of women, to whom, in place of tresses, spines are attached. They tell too of other monstrous shapes which the monsters have, the forms of which not even men skilled at painting and at compounding bodies into monstrous spectacles could ever exactly represent and set forth by skill of drawing; they have long, coiling tails, and for feet either claws or fins. I learn too that they are amphibious, and by night graze on the fields; for they eat grass like cattle and seed-gathering birds, and delight also in the ripe palm-dates, shaking the trees by throwing about them their coils, which are moist and able to twine. So this palm, falling down from the violent shaking, they feed upon. But night wanes, and there is not yet clear day, when those creatures vanish, plunging into the deep, just as the dawn is about to shine forth. There are also, they say, many whales, but these do not come on to the land, lying in wait for the tunnies. And of dolphins, they say, there are two kinds: one wild and jagged-toothed and most ruthless toward fishermen and utterly merciless; the other gentle and tame by nature. It leaps and swims about, and is like a fawning lapdog, and you may stroke it, and it will submit; and if you throw it food, it will gladly take it.

The following too I have further heard as peculiar to the sea-ray. On the fishing-boat someone dances, when he sees it swimming up below, and indeed makes some mocking jest, and besides this, if he be skilled with the pipe, he carries the pipe as a bait and plays an accompaniment; and the ray is over-delighted (for it has ears, they say, that take in music, and eyes that understand dancing), and then, enchanted, it swims up quietly. And while the one waves the said charms most effectively, another sets the basket-net, and brings up the fish; and — this, I suppose, the strangest thing of all — being enchanted, it has then unawares been caught.

The sea-ox is born in the mud, and from birth it is very small, but from being very small it becomes very large. Its underbelly is white, but its back and face and sides are intensely black; its mouth is small, and you would not see its teeth when its mouth is closed; it is very long and very broad. It feeds on many of the fishes, but most of all it delights to eat human flesh. It is conscious that it has very little strength, and relies on its size alone. And for this reason, when it sees someone either swimming or labouring at his fishing, it raises and arches itself and swims over him, lying heavy above, pressing down and hanging over him as a thing of terror, spreading its whole body over the wretched man like a roof, and preventing him from coming up and breathing. So, when his breath has been cut off, the man, as is likely, dies, and the sea-ox, falling upon him, has for the reward of its patience the dinner it most craves.

And this wonder too is peculiar to this creature. The bear does not know how to bear a formed cub, nor would anyone, seeing the offspring from her labour, agree that she brings forth a living thing; but she has given birth, and it is a shapeless lump of flesh, unmarked and unformed and without shape. Yet she loves and recognizes the young, and warms it under her thighs, and smooths it with her tongue, and shapes it into limbs, and indeed little by little forms it, and on seeing it you will say, This is a bear's cub.
The seal, as I hear, vomits out its own rennet,

Indian dogs—these too are wild beasts, mighty in strength, most spirited in soul, and the largest of dogs anywhere. They look down on all other animals; but the Indian dog goes to meet the lion, and endures its onset, and barks back when it roars, and bites in return when bitten; and having greatly distressed and wounded it, in the end the dog is overcome. Yet a lion might also be overcome by an Indian dog, and indeed once the dog has bitten it holds on most firmly. Even if you come and cut off the dog's leg with a knife, it has no leisure in its pain to relax its bite, but the leg is cut off first and only as a corpse does it let go its mouth, and it lies there, forced to release its hold by

The wolf is least apt to go to meet a bull and come at it face to face, but it fears the horns and swerves from their points. And as though it would fight in a straight line it threatens; yet it does not do this, but only makes a show as if about to attack, and then when the bull charges, it twists itself aside and leaps onto its back, and the rival beast holds the beast firmly, and overpowers it, the wolf making up by natural cunning for what it lacks.

Of the birds that excel in song and music not one has escaped notice, but we know swallows and blackbirds and the race of cicadas, and the chattering jay and the buzzing locust and the murmuring grasshopper, and the

In this respect too it is not amiss to speak of the peculiarities of animals. The sheep and the ass seem somewhat sluggish; timorous are the fawns and roe-deer and gazelles and pygargs and hares, which the poets call "cowerers." But among the winged creatures too the sparrows are timorous, and among the water creatures the grey mullet. Lewd are the dog-headed apes and the he-goats, and they say these even consort with women, and Pindar seems to wonder at it. Dogs too have been said to make bold against women, and indeed a woman at Rome is said to have been brought to trial for adultery by her husband, and the adulterer was said in the suit to be a dog. I have heard too that dog-headed apes go mad for maidens, and indeed violate them, beyond the petty lewdnesses of Menander's youths at the all-night festivals. Most lustful too and adulterous is the partridge. At any rate they are said to go to the females secretly and somehow noiselessly. But the sharing of food

The sow recognizes the voice of the swineherd, and obeys when he calls, even if it has strayed; and the proof of this is near at hand. Off the Tyrrhenian coast some malefactors brought to land a pirate ship, and coming up they happened upon a steading, and the steading was a swineherds', and it had many sows. These, then, they seized and threw into the ship, and casting off the cables they set about their voyage. The swineherds, while the pirates were present, kept quiet; but when the men had got out to sea, as far as the carry of a shout, then the swineherds called the sows back to themselves with their accustomed cry. And the sows, when they heard, crowding themselves to one side of the ship, overturned it. And the malefactors were at once destroyed, while the sows swam back to their own masters.

If a domestic fowl falls into wine and is drowned, they say it does no harm either to the wine or to those within the house; but if it falls into water, it makes the water foul-smelling and works a bad odour about the air. But if a gecko slips into wine and is then drowned, it does no harm at all; whereas if it falls into oil and dies, it makes the oil foul-smelling, and whoever tastes of it breaks out swarming with lice.

The fish called phagri the people of Syene consider sacred, but those who inhabit the island called Elephantine hold sacred the maeotae; and this too is a tribe of fish. The honour paid by both peoples to either kind has its origin from this. When the Nile is about to rise and flow up, these fish run ahead and swim, as though messengers of the new water, and the

When a house is about to fall down, the mice in it, and indeed the weasels too, have a sense of it, and they anticipate the collapse and move out of house. This too, they say, happened at Helice. For when the people of Helice committed impiety against the Ionians who had come to them, and slaughtered them at the altar, then surely (this is the Homeric saying) "to them the gods showed forth portents"; for five days before Helice disappeared, all the mice in it, and weasels and snakes and centipedes and beetles and the rest of such creatures, withdrew in a body by the road that leads to Cerynia. And the people of Helice, seeing what was being done, marvelled indeed, but could not conjecture the cause. But when the aforesaid animals had departed, an earthquake came by night, and the city subsided, and a great wave overwhelming it, Helice disappeared, and by chance ten Lacedaemonian ships
The gelded oxen (Democritus says) grow crooked and thin and long horns, but the entire ones thick at the root and straight and less

In the Ionian Sea, off Leucas and the sea by Actium — where they call the region Epirus — there are, one might say, countless schools of grey mullet and very great numbers of them. They are hunted in a most astonishing way; and the manner of the hunting is this. The fishermen there, watching for a moonless night, after supper put out two to a boat, when there is no swell but the sea is calm and unbroken; then quietly and little by little they row forward. One man works the boat with his oar, bringing the skiff along at a walking pace, as one might say; the other, reclining on his elbow, weighs down his own side of the skiff and tilts it so far that its rim comes near the water. The grey mullet and the striped mullet of like kind, whether delighting in the night or rejoicing in the calm, leave their hollows and burrows and swim up, showing the tips of their faces above the water, taking so much of their upward swim that they come near the shore. The hunters, seeing them, row on, and the wash of the skiff begins gently to ripple. So the fish, fleeing the land and turning back, push themselves into the tilted side of the boat, and passing within are caught.

It is said that in Libya there is a lake of boiling water, and in this water, they say, fish live and swim, and when food is thrown in they leap up toward the food. But if one should throw them into cold water, they die; this too I have heard besides.
The land-tortoise is a most lustful creature — the male, that is; the female mates against her will. And Demostratus, a man, as I say this too, of the Roman

The sea-hare (of the Great Sea, that is; for I have spoken of the other one, of the other sea) — this one resembles the land-hare in every way except its hairs. For the down of the land creature seems soft and not resistant to the touch; but this one has prickly, upright hairs, and if anyone touches it, he is scratched. They say that it swims on the very surface-ripple of the sea and does not sink into the deep, and that it is swiftest in swimming. Alive, it would not easily be caught. The reason is that it never falls into a net, nor

The Galatians of the East, Eudoxus says, do such things; and if they seem credible to anyone, let him believe, but if they seem otherwise, let him pay no heed. When clouds of locusts come upon their land and then injure the crops, the people make certain prayers and offer sacrifices of birds, that charm the locusts; and the birds obey, and come in a common host, and make the locusts vanish. But if a Galatian hunts one of these birds, the penalty for him by the local laws is death. And if he meets with pardon and is let go, the people throw the birds into wrath, and avenging the captured one they refuse to obey, even if they be called again.

Most other song-birds have a fine voice and sing with their tongue, like a man; but the cicadas are most talkative from the loins. They feed on dew, and from dawn until the market-place is full they are silent, but when the sun begins its full strength they let loose their din, industrious choristers, as one might say, singing over the heads of the shepherds and the travellers and the reapers. This love of music nature has given to the males; but the female cicada is voiceless, and seems to keep silent like a modest bride.
Horns stand unbending and upright on all bulls, and for this reason, as a man is roused to his weapon, so the bull is roused to his horn. But Erythraean cattle move their horns like ears.

that it may not be a cure for those subject to epilepsy. A spiteful creature, then, the seal, indeed by Heaven. The pelicans in the rivers gape round the mussels and then swallow them, and warming them within in the recess of the belly, vomit them up; and the shells have parted by the heat, like those of boiled things, and the birds dig out the flesh and have their dinner. And indeed the gulls too, as Eudemus says, raising the snails on high and lifting them up, dash them most violently against the rocks.

death. What is fitting I shall tell elsewhere. Of man alone and of the dog does the food rise up again when they are full. And in man the heart is attached to the left breast, but in other animals it is set in the middle of the chest. No crook-taloned bird drinks or makes water or herds together with others.
The sea-ass has its heart placed in its belly, as those skilled in such matters agree with us and teach.

cricket that does not keep silent, and besides these the halcyons and the parrots; and of the water-creatures the green tree-frog does not keep silent. And of these some utter mournful and womanish cries, others shrill and piercing; and some, running from branch to branch, sing, as though changing house to house, while others sing in the meadows, as if keeping festival, and living, as one might say, a flowery and delicate life, they hymn, I would say, the coming of spring with their melodies. About swans, and whose servants among the gods they are, I have spoken above. The jay, then, is most imitative of other sounds too, and of the human voice most of all. But the bird called the anthus and the trumpet-bird and the wryneck and the raven are peculiar in such imitations. And the anthus imitates the neighing of a horse, the trumpet-bird the trumpet that shares its name, and the wryneck the slanting flute; and the raven likes to imitate the dropping of rain. Of scorpions the male is most harsh, but the female seems gentler. And I hear that there is a white one, and again a tawny one, and another smoky, and a black one besides; and I have learned of a green and a pot-bellied one, and another crab-like; but the most harsh they sing of as flame-coloured. And I have received by report that there are winged ones too, and some with double stings; and somewhere one was seen with seven joints. The scorpion brings forth not eggs but living young. And it must be known that some say the offspring of these creatures comes not from intercourse with one another, but that scorpions breed amid excessive heat. And what each of them does by smearing its sting, and in what way it kills, you will learn elsewhere.

dogs least of all admit. Often, indeed, they tear one another to pieces even over a bone, as did Menelaus and Paris over Helen. Only the Memphite dogs, I hear, lay down what they have seized in the midst and eat in common. Implacable and merciless is the boar; for they eat one another's dead bodies. Most fishes too do this. Most impious is the river horse, the hippopotamus; for it tastes even of its own father. Shameless, and not easily turned aside, are flies and dogs. Most savage are wolves. The Egyptians say that they even eat one another, and they describe the manner of the plot thus. Having brought themselves into a circle, they run; and when one of them, dizzied by the whirling of the running, grows giddy and is overturned, the rest fall upon him as he lies and tear him to pieces and eat him. They do this when they have fallen into a lack of prey. For, against being hungry, they reckon everything mere nonsense, just as wicked men reckon everything nonsense against silver.

They say that the stork too is jealous. At Crannon in Thessaly a man who had married a beautiful woman named Alcinoe, leaving her at home, set out on a journey abroad. Now Alcinoe consorted with one of the servants. The household stork, perceiving this, did not endure it, but avenged his master. Leaping upon her, it blinded the woman's eyes. Earlier I made mention of the jealousy of a purple coot, then of such a dog; and now of a stork doing the same as they against a marriage gone sick.

That the horn of a deer, when burned as incense, drives away snakes is clear. And Aristotle says that the stone that occurs in the river Pontus—this river is in the country of the Sinti and the Maedi—when burned as incense drives away the same creatures, and indeed he describes the nature of the stone as follows. If one pours water upon it, it kindles into flame; and if you should wish to fan the burning stone with a fan to make it blaze higher, it is quenched. And burned as incense it gives off, they say, a smell heavier than bitumen. With these things Nicander too agrees.

expectant minds of the Egyptians they gladden beforehand with fair hopes, being the first to perceive the coming of the stream and by some marvellous nature foretelling it. And the people aforesaid love to add this too, for the honour they pay these fish: they say that the two kinds never taste of one another. Now in the Red Sea there are also other shellfish, not smooth in their shells, but having certain notches and hollows. These have sharp edges, and when they come together they close upon one another, fitting their projections alternately, so that they seem like the canine teeth of two saws meeting together. So if they seize any swimmer among the fishermen and bite whatever part it may be, they cut it off, even if there be a bone beneath the part bitten; and biting at a joint, they cut even this off, and naturally; for their bite is most keen.

lying at anchor perished together with the aforesaid city. And Justice uses, for the punishment of impious men, the animals as ministers. And here is the proof: Pantacles the Lacedaemonian, having forbidden the artists of Dionysus who were departing to Cythera to pass through Sparta, then, as he sat in the ephors' office, was torn apart by dogs. In Sicily there is a city, Adranus, as Nymphodorus says, and in this city a temple of Adranus, a local god; and he says this god is very manifest.
