And the other things he says about him, and how he is conspicuous and to those who pray gracious and propitious, we shall learn another time; but now these things shall be told. There are sacred dogs, attendants of his and ministering to him, surpassing the Molossian dogs in beauty and along with this in size too, not fewer than a thousand in number. So these, by day, fawn upon and wag their tails at those who pass into the temple and the grove, whether they be strangers or natives; but by night they lead, like escorts and guides, very kindly, those who are by now drunk and stumbling along the road, going before each to his own home, and from the drunken and disorderly they exact a sufficient penalty; for they leap upon them and tear their clothing, and so far chasten them; but those who attempt to steal cloaks they tear most bitterly apart.

drawn out to length. And he says these are broad-browed much more than the others; for the veins being many there, the bones are widened by them. And the growth of the horns, being thicker, leads this same part of the animal toward breadth too; but the geldings, having a small circle at the seat of the horns, are less broadened, he says. And the hornless bulls, not having the honeycomb-like part (so Democritus names it) on the crown (he would mean the spongy part), the whole bone being resistant and not receiving the confluences of the humours, become bare and without a share of their weapons of defence. And the veins along this bone, being less nourished, become thinner and weaker. And the neck of the hornless ones too must be drier; for its veins too are thinner. And so they are less robust. But all the Arabian cattle that are female in kind, yet well grown in their horns, in these the great influx of humours, he says, is the nourishment of the noble growth for the horns. And those too are hornless which have the bone receptive of the moisture more solid and least receptive of the humours. And to speak in sum, the influx is the cause of growth to the horns; and this the veins channel, being very many and very thick and pregnant with as much moisture as they can hold.

Of the sea-monsters, those that are exceedingly huge and prodigious in size swim in the midst of the open sea, and are even struck by thunderbolts. Besides these there are certain other rare creatures of the kind, and their name is "wheels." These swim in schools, chiefly on the right of Thracian Athos, in the gulfs as one sails from Sigeum; one may also meet them along the mainland opposite, by what is called the tomb of Artachaees and the Acanthian isthmus, where the Persian's cutting is to be seen, by which he cut through Athos. These monsters, which they call wheels, are said not to be valiant; but they show a crest and exceedingly long spines, so that these are often seen above the water. On hearing the noise of oars they wheel about and coil up, thrusting themselves as far down as possible; and from this they have got their name. They come up again unrolled and rolling the other way.

Men skilled in fishing say that if one should melt down the belly of a sea-horse in wine by boiling, and give this to someone to drink, the wine is a poison strange when set against other poisons. For the one who drinks of it is first seized by the most violent hiccup, then coughs a dry cough, and is racked, yet nothing comes up; and his upper belly swells and grows distended, and hot fluxes rise to his head, and through his nose phlegm runs down and strikes with a fishy smell; and his eyes become bloodshot and fiery, and his eyelids swell. Desires for vomiting are kindled, they say, yet nothing comes up. And if nature prevails, the man passes through what is perilous to the point of death, but slips into forgetfulness and madness. But if it slips down into the lower belly, there is nothing more to be done, and the man taken so dies altogether. Those who survive, run aground upon madness, are seized with a great longing for water, and thirst to see water and to hear it flowing; and this lulls and soothes them to sleep. And they like to spend their time either by ever-flowing rivers or near shores or by springs or certain lakes, and they are not very eager to drink, but they love to swim and to wet their feet or wash their hands. But some say that it is not the belly of the sea-horse itself that is the cause of these things, but that the creature feeds on a certain seaweed exceedingly bitter, whose quality passes into its belly. The sea-horse was found also serviceable for saving life, by the shrewdness of an old fisherman, wise in matters of the sea. There was an old Cretan fisherman, and he had young sons who were also fishermen. Now it chanced that the old man caught sea-horses along with other fish, and that the young men were bitten by a mad dog — the others having come to the aid of the first bitten and fallen into the same misfortune. So they lay near the shores of Rhithymna in Crete (this is a village, as they say), and the onlookers shared in grief at the misfortune, and bade them kill the dog and give its liver to the young men to eat as a remedy of the evil; while others bade them take them to the Artemis called Rhoccaea and ask healing from the goddess. But the old man, very fearlessly and unshaken, let those who gave such advice be praised, but he cleaned out the bellies of the sea-horses, and roasted some and gave them to the young men to take, and others he crushed into vinegar and honey, and plastered with these the wounds of the bite; and then he overcame the young men's madness by the longing for water which the sea-horses kindled in them. And in this way he healed his sons, late though it was.

senate (and not, indeed, for this reason already qualified to bear witness, but it seems to me he drove the science of fishing to its height and told most beautifully all that he knew; and if some other, more weighty matter was also his study, and he touched besides on wisdom concerning the soul, I should not wonder) — this man says that for what other reason the female refuses union he cannot clearly know, but he conjectures this. The female does not mate except looking toward the male; and he satisfies his desire and then goes off, but she is least able to turn herself over, both by the bulk of her shell and being propped against the ground. So a ready dinner is left by her mate for the other creatures and indeed for the eagles. The females, then, dread this, as he says; but the males cannot persuade them, prudent as they are and setting safety before pleasure. So the males, by some secret nature, shake at them an erotic charm that makes them forget all fear. Now these charms of the amorous tortoise were not songs, by Zeus, such as Theocritus, the composer of pastoral trifles, prattles, but a secret herb, of which neither he says he knows the name, nor admits that any other has known it; and they seem to deck themselves out with the herb and certain secret amulets. So if they hold that herb in their mouth, the opposite of the aforesaid happens; for the male is coy, and the female, who hitherto fled, now runs after, inflamed, and is goaded and longs for union; and fear is gone from them, and they have no dread at all for themselves. Near Thessalonica of Macedonia there is a place called Nibas. Now the cocks there have no share in their natural song and are silent wholly and everywhere. And there is current a proverbial saying, used of things impossible, which goes: "Then you may have this thing, when Nibas crows."

does it approach the rod with hook and bait. But when this hare falls sick, and being then least able to swim is cast ashore, anyone who touches it with his hand perishes, abandoned. Indeed, if one touches this hare even with a staff, he suffers the same thing through the staff itself, just as those do who touch the basilisk. There is a root, they say, that grows in the island in the Great Sea, well known to all, which is a remedy against faintness. Brought to the nose of one who is fainting, it brings the man back to life. But if it is neglected, the suffering goes on even to death for the man; so great is the strength this hare has for harm. In the regions of India — I mean the innermost — there are mountains, they say, hard to climb and full of game, and they have all the creatures that our own land nourishes, but wild; for they say that even the sheep there are wild beasts, and the dogs and goats and oxen wander free and unowned, released from any herdsman's rule. The numbers of them are beyond counting, say the learned men of the Indians; and among these the Brahmans too deserve to be counted, for they agree to the same about these things. There is said to be a single-horned creature among them, called by them the cartazon. In size it is like a full-grown horse, and it has a mane, and tawny down, and is excellently endowed in the feet. Its feet are unjointed and like an elephant's, and it has a boar's tail; in the middle of its brows it has a horn growing, not smooth but with certain spirals and quite natural, and black in colour; and that horn is said to be exceedingly sharp. I hear that this beast has a voice harsher and louder than that of any other. When other animals approach it, it is forbearing and gentle; but toward its own kind it is somewhat quarrelsome. They say that not only do the males have a natural impulse to butt and fight one another, but that they feel the same passion toward the females, and pressing the rivalry even to death of the loser, they fight it out. The whole of its body is sturdy, but the strength of its horn is irresistible. It loves deserted pastures and wanders alone; but at its season of mating, having paired with the female, it grows gentle, and indeed the two graze together. Then, when that time has passed and the female is pregnant, it grows savage again, and this Indian cartazon becomes a solitary. The young, while very tender, are brought, they say, to the king of the Prasii, and show their strength against one another at the festal spectacles. But no one remembers a full-grown one ever being caught.

Aristotle says that in Samos there is a white swallow; and that if anyone pricks out its eyes, it becomes at once blind, but afterward its eyes are restored and its pupils made bright, and it sees from the first again, as he says.

Men say that the goddess Ergane invented weaving and spinning; but the spider nature made wise in the art of the loom. And it works with skill, not by imitation, nor does it take its thread from outside, but drawing the threads from its own belly, it makes snares for the light birds, as though spreading out nets. And by the same threads with which it weaves, taken from its belly, it nourishes that same belly, working most industriously, so that not even those of women who are most deft of hand and clever at producing finished thread can be set against it; for it has surpassed even a hair in fineness.

The Ethiopian land — a neighbour, and a very good and enviable one, is the bath of the gods, which Homer sings to us as Ocean — this land, then, is the mother of serpents greatest in size; for they reach even thirty fathoms, and they are not called by the name belonging to their kind, but men say they are slayers of elephants, and these serpents strive to the utmost length of old age. Here my Ethiopian accounts come to a halt. But Phrygian accounts say that serpents are born in Phrygia too, and that they reach ten fathoms, and that in midsummer daily, after the market-place is full, they creep out of their dens. And by the river called Rhyndacus they rested part of their coil on the ground, raising up all the rest of their body, and quietly and gently stretching up their throat and opening their mouth, then they draw the birds as with a spell by their breath. And the birds fall into their bellies, dragged by the inhalation from them, feathers and all. And this they do by themselves toward sunset; then the serpents, having hidden themselves, ambush the flocks as they come from pasture toward the folds, and take them, and having wrought much slaughter, have often destroyed the herdsmen too along with them, and have an abundant and ample dinner.

Eudemus says that on Thracian Pangaeum a bear, finding a lion's lair empty of its guard, destroyed the lion's cubs, because they were still small and unable to defend themselves. And when the father and the mother came back from some hunt, and saw their young amid the slaughter, they grieved, as was likely, and rushed at the bear; but it, in fear, ran up into a tree as fast as its feet could carry it, and sat there trying to avoid the plot from them. And when they seemed to come there to avenge themselves on the ravager, then the lioness did not leave the watch, but sat under the trunk lying in wait and looking up with bloodshot eyes, while the lion, distressed and wandering in his grief, roamed in the mountains and met a woodcutter. The man was afraid and dropped his axe, but the lion fawned on the beast and, raising himself, embraced him, as best he could, and brightened the man's face with his tongue. And the man took courage, and the lion, throwing his tail about him, led him on, and would not let him leave the axe behind, but signalled with his foot to take it up. And as the man did not understand, the lion took it with his mouth and held it out to him, and the man followed, and the lion led him to the lair. And the lioness, when she saw him, herself coming up fawned too, and looked piteous, and gazed up at the bear. So the man, perceiving and inferring that these had been wronged in some way by the bear, with all his strength and the work of his hands cut down the tree. And it was overturned, and the bear was brought down; and the beasts tore it to pieces. But the man the lion led back unharmed and unhurt to the place where he had first met him, and restored him to his original woodcutting.

There is an Indian beast violent in strength, in size like the largest lion, red in colour so as to seem like cinnabar, and shaggy like dogs, named in the Indian tongue the martichoras. Its face is such as to seem to belong not to a beast but to a man. It has three rows of teeth set in above and three rows below, exceedingly sharp at the point, larger than the teeth of dogs. Its ears resemble a man's, but are larger and shaggy. Its eyes are grey, and these too resemble a man's. Imagine its feet and claws to be like a lion's. To the tip of its tail is attached a scorpion's sting, and this would be more than a cubit long, and on either side the tail is set with stings. The tip of the tail stings whomever it meets to death, and destroys him at once. If anyone pursues it, it shoots its stings sideways like arrows, and the creature is a far-darter. When it discharges its stings forward, it bends back its tail; but when backward, after the manner of the Sacae, it stretches it out straight. Whatever the missile strikes it kills—the elephant alone it does not destroy. The stings it hurls are a foot in length and the thickness of a rush. Ctesias says, and affirms that the Indians agree with him, that in the places where those stings are discharged others grow up beneath, so that there is a whole crop of this evil. It delights, as the same author says, above all in eating men, and it kills many men, and lies in wait not for one alone, but would attack two or even three, and overpowers so many single-handed. It masters the rest of the animals too, but could never bring down a lion. That this animal takes the greatest delight in glutting itself with human flesh, its very name proclaims; for in the Greek tongue it means "man-eater," and from this deed it is named. In speed it is like the deer. The Indians hunt the young of these beasts while their tails are still without stings, and they crush the tails with a stone so that they cannot grow stings. Its voice it sends forth as nearly as possible like a trumpet. Ctesias says he has also seen this animal among the Persians, brought as a gift from the Indians to the king of the Persians—if indeed Ctesias is a sufficient witness in such matters. At any rate, having heard the peculiar features of this animal, let one then give heed to the writer of Cnidus.

The peacock knows that it is the most beautiful of birds, and where its beauty resides, this too it knows, and on it it prides itself and is haughty, and takes confidence in its feathers, which both lend it adornment and send forth fear upon outsiders, and in the summer season provide it with shade from its own resources, not begged nor borrowed. At any rate, if it wishes to frighten anyone, it raises its tail-feathers and then shakes them and sends forth a sound, and the bystanders are afraid, as though frightened by the clang of a soldier from his armour. It lifts its head and nods most haughtily, as though shaking a triple crest. And when it needs to cool itself, it raises its feathers, and inclining them forward displays a kind of natural shade of its own body, screening off the keen point of the sunbeam. And if there is also a wind behind, it quietly parts its feathers; and the breath that flows through, blowing soft and most pleasant breezes upon it, gives the bird refreshment. And when praised it perceives it, and just as a beautiful boy or a lovely woman displays the most advantageous part of the body, so too the peacock raises its feathers in order and in rows, and resembles a flowery meadow or a picture variegated with the many hues of paints; and the labour lies before painters to liken the peculiar work of nature. And it shows how it stands in abundance for display; for it allows the bystanders to take their fill of the sight, and turns itself about, showing diligently the many-formed splendour of its plumage, displaying its own robe above the dress of the Medes and the embroideries of the Persians, and that most haughtily. It is said to have been brought from the barbarians to the Greeks. And being long rare it was then shown for a fee to those who loved beauty, and at Athens at the new moons they received both men and women to view them, and made the spectacle a source of revenue. They valued the male and the female at ten thousand drachmas, as Antiphon says in his speech against Erasistratus. And a double house is needed for their keeping, and guards and attendants too. Hortensius the Roman was judged the first to sacrifice a peacock for a banquet. But Alexander of Macedon, seeing these birds among the Indians, was astonished, and marvelling at their beauty he threatened the heaviest threats against anyone who should sacrifice a peacock.

Among the Indians, as I hear, the elephant and the snake are bitterest enemies. So the elephants, tearing off the branches of the trees, feed on them. And the snakes, knowing this, creep up onto them, and wind the lower half of their bodies, the tail part, around the foliage of the trees, while the half that goes toward the head they let down, hanging like a rope. And when the elephant comes to pluck the boughs, the snake leaps at its eyes and gouges them out, then creeping around its neck, drawing with its tail part and tightening with the other, throttles the beast with an unaccustomed and strange noose.

The most malicious of animals is the ape, and the more so in those things in which it tries to imitate man. For example, having seen from a distance a nurse bathing a child in a basin—first loosing its swaddling-bands, then, after the bath, wrapping it up again—it watched where she laid the infant to rest, and when it saw the place deserted, it leaped in through an open window, from which everything was visible to it, and lifting the child from its bed, and stripping it as it had seen done, and bringing the basin into the middle, it poured boiling water—for there was water being heated upon some coals—over the unhappy child, and indeed killed it most pitiably.

Sheep change their colours through the change in their drink, according to the peculiar nature of the rivers; and the season of the year at which this befalls them is the time of their mating. So they turn from white to black, and again change the colour the other way. This is wont somehow to happen about the river in Antandria and the one in Thrace, whose name the Thracians who dwell beside it will tell. But the Scamander at Troy, since it makes the ewes that drink of it yellow, has had set upon it, alongside its original name Scamander, another name, Xanthus, from the acquired colour of the sheep.

The island of Pharos long ago—the Egyptians say what I am about to say—was filled with snakes many and various. But when Thonis, the king of the Egyptians, had received as a trust Helen, the daughter of Zeus—for Menelaus, wandering about upper Egypt and Ethiopia, had entrusted her to him—then Thonis fell in love with her, and when he was offering violence to Helen to compel her to amorous union, the daughter of Zeus, the story says, told each of these things to the wife of Thonis, who was called Polydamna; and she, fearing lest the stranger should surpass her in beauty, secretly removed Helen to Pharos, and gave her a plant hostile to the snakes there, of which the snakes, when they perceived it, sank down into the ground. And Helen planted it, and in time it grew up and gave off seed hostile to snakes; and indeed in Pharos no such creature any longer came to be. And those skilled in such matters say that the plant was called helenion.

As for the crocodiles, some of the Egyptians revere them, as the people of Ombos; and just as we hold the Olympian gods in wonder, so do they hold these. And when their children are often snatched away, they rejoice exceedingly, and the mothers of the wretched victims are glad and go about proud, as though they had borne food and a feast for a god. But the people of Apollonopolis, a portion of the Tentyrites, catch the crocodiles in nets, and hanging them aloft from persea trees (these are plants native to the place), they scourge them with many lashes and flay them as they whimper and weep, and then cut them up and eat them. This animal is pregnant for sixty days, and lays sixty eggs, and broods over them for as many days; it has as many vertebrae upon its spine, and is girt, they say, with as many sinews; its delivery proceeds to so great a number, and it lives sixty years (I say these things as Egyptian reports and beliefs); one may also count sixty teeth in this animal, and lying hidden each year for sixty days it stays still and takes no food. To the people of Ombos the crocodiles are even familiar, and indeed those reared in the lakes made by them obey when they call. They bring to them the heads of the animals sacrificed (for they themselves would not taste of this part) and throw them in, and the crocodiles leap about for these. The people of Apollonopolis, however, hate the crocodile, saying that Typhon slipped into its form. But others give not this reason, but say that a crocodile carried off the daughter of Psammyntis, a king good and just to the utmost; and that then, in memory of that misfortune, they hate the whole tribe of them, even those born long after in time.

The sea-snail that is found in the Red Sea was very fair to look at and very great. For its shell is of purple, and it has also a spiral, finely wrought and varied by Nature. You would say you were looking at a garland woven of some many-coloured flowers, green and gold-like and vermilion, the colours scattered alternately at equal intervals.

Peculiar to animals is kindness toward man too. An eagle, at any rate, reared an infant. And I wish to tell the whole story, that it may be a witness of what I have proposed. When Seuechorus was king of the Babylonians, the Chaldeans said that the child born of his daughter would take away the kingdom from his grandfather. He shuddered at this, and, to put it with a touch of play, he became an Acrisius toward the girl; for he guarded her most bitterly. But secretly the girl (for fate was wiser than the Babylonian) conceived by some obscure man and bore a child. So those guarding her, in fear of the king, threw it from the citadel; for there the aforesaid girl was shut up. The eagle, then, with very keen sight, seeing the child's fall while it was still in the air, before the infant was dashed against the earth, came beneath it and put its back under it, and carries it to a certain garden, and sets it down very carefully. So the keeper of the place, beholding the beautiful little child, loves it and rears it; and it is called Gilgamos, and becomes king of the Babylonians. And if anyone thinks this a myth, I agree, having examined it to the best of my power and found it so; yet Achaemenes the Persian, from whom the nobility of the Persians descends, was, I hear, a nursling of an eagle.

About Tritons the fishermen say they cannot give a clear account or strong proof; yet a report widely current says — yes, by Zeus, much is told — that there come to be in the sea certain monsters of human shape, in all that reaches from the head down to the waist. Demostratus, in his discourses on fishing, says that at Tanagra he saw a salted Triton. In all else, he says, it was like the figures sculptors fashion and painters draw; but its head, ruined by time, was not very clear, nor such as one could easily make out and recognize. "And when I touched it," he says, "rough scales fell off, and very resistant ones at that." One of the magistrates assigned by lot to govern Greece and entrusted with the office for a single year, wishing to test and prove the nature of what was seen, took off a little of the skin and consigned it to fire; and a heavy smell from the burning thing struck the nostrils of those present. Yet, he says, we could not determine whether the creature was by nature a land or a sea animal. But the trial did not pay him a good wage. For not long after he ended his life, crossing a narrow strait in a small skiff. And the Tanagraeans said, as Demostratus tells, that he suffered this in requital for the impiety he had committed against the Triton, alleging as proof that, while it was breathing out its last, it was taken from the sea and gave off an ichor like in smell to that of the Triton's skin when he burned and set fire to it. From where this Triton wandered, and how it was cast up here, let the Tanagraeans and Demostratus tell. As for these matters, I reverence the god, and it is right to believe so great a witness; and the Apollo at Didyma would be sufficient to prove it to anyone whose mind is sound and whose understanding is strong. He says, then, that the Triton is a sea-creature, and what he says is this: "A nursling of Poseidon, a watery monster, loud-voiced Triton, swimming, met the rush of a hollow ship." If, then, he who knows all things says that Tritons exist, we need not be perplexed about it.

About sea-dogs we have spoken at length; but the river-dogs are to look upon like the small land-dogs, and they are shaggy in the tail too. They are said to soothe swelling sinews in men with their blood, if you pour it on mixed with water and vinegar; and their hide gives good shoes, and these good for the sinews, as they say.

When Alexander was shaking some of the land of the Indians and taking other parts, he met with many other creatures, and among them a dragon, which the Indians, holding it sacred in a certain cave, used with much religious awe to worship. So the Indians became urgent in begging Alexander that no one should attack the creature; and he consented. So when the army was passing the cave and a din arose, then the dragon perceived it; for it is the keenest of hearing of creatures and the keenest of sight. It let out a most loud hiss and snort, so as to astound and confound all. It was said to be seventy cubits long, though it did not appear wholly; for only its head peeped out. And its eyes are sung to be the size of a Macedonian shield.

To one who has crossed the mountains bordering the Indians on their innermost side there appear, they say, very thickly wooded glens, and the place is called by the Indians Colounda. In these glens, they say, there wander creatures resembling satyrs in shape, shaggy over their whole body, and they have a horse's tail along the loins. By themselves, when undisturbed, they spend their time in the thickets feeding on wood; but when they perceive the noise of hunters and hear the barking of hounds, they run up to the very peaks with unmatched speed; for they are practised in mountain-climbing. And they fight off their pursuers by rolling certain rocks down upon them, and many of those who overtake them are destroyed. By this means they are hard to catch, and only with difficulty and after long time, they say, are a few of them brought to the Prasii. And of these the sick ones were brought, or some pregnant females; and it came about that the former were caught through their sluggishness, the latter through the burden of the belly.

The cinnamon, I hear, is a bird, and indeed it carries twigs of the plant of the same name from the ends of the earth, and weaves its nests where Herodotus and others tell, and these birds somehow love to weave their own beds and lodgings. So those who care for these twigs shoot heavy arrows with most violent rush and a strong drawing of the bowstring against the nests; and the nests break, and the twigs slip down, and indeed the much-celebrated cinnamon is just this.

Writers sing of the Babylonians and Chaldaeans as wise in the things of heaven; but the ants, though they neither look up to heaven nor can count the days of the month on their fingers, yet have received from nature a marvellous gift; for on the new day of the month they keep within their own house, not passing over the entrance but staying still.

Mud is the begetting of the small fry; they do not breed through one another nor are descended one from another, but when the mud in the sea, and very slimy mud, has set and grown black, it is warmed by some unspeakable and life-giving nature and changes and turns into very many creatures. And the small fry are these, born like worms in the filth and foulness. And when the small fry have come to be, they are a most swimming thing, and do what they are by nature fit to do, then are led by some wonderful cause to safe places, where they shall have shelter and a barrier, by which life may be possible for them. The refuge would be either a rock standing up great and high, or what are called ovens; these would be hollowed rocks eaten away by the waves in time and become caverns. These nature has shown them as refuges, so that they may not be beaten by the surge and made to disappear; for they are weak and least able to resist its assaults. And they need no food; it is enough for them to lick one another. The catch of them is made with very fine threads, and with garments of loose warp sewn to these. And this would be a contrivance quite sufficient for their taking and capture, but least of all for the hunting of other fish.

The battle of the Egyptian beasts, the asp and the ichneumon. And the ichneumon comes to the contest against its adversary not without plan nor in panic, but as a man arms himself with full armour, so that creature, rolling itself in the mud and filling itself with what has caked on, seems to have a sufficient and water-tight defence. And if there is a lack of mud, washing itself in water and throwing itself, still wet, into deep sand, from this device drawing a means of defence out of difficult straits, it goes to the battle. And it will keep guard over the tip of its nose, somewhat exposed to the asp's bite, by bending back its tail and stopping the nose up with it. And if the asp succeeds in striking this, it has brought down its antagonist; but if not, it wears out its teeth in vain on the mud, and again the ichneumon, creeping up unexpectedly and seizing it by the neck, throttles
The sea-scolopendra, they say, bursts asunder when a man spits upon it.

When mice fall into wine-coolers, being unable to swim up and climb out, they bite each other's tails, and so the first draws up the second, and the second the third. Thus indeed most wise Nature taught even these to ally with and help one another.

Bitterest foes to the lion are fire and the cock, the hyena to the leopard, and the gecko to the scorpion; at any rate, numbness seizes the scorpion when the aforesaid creature is brought near it. The elephant dreads the snake; every beast of burden fears the shrew-mouse; the lobster the octopus. And indeed dogs, when pushed off the roofs, you could not throw down; for they dread the greatness of the danger.

Malicious too is the hyena and what they call the corocotta. The hyena, then, comes by night to the farmsteads and imitates men vomiting. The dogs, hearing it, approach as though toward a man; and it seizes and eats them. And the cunning of the corocotta, which I too have heard of, I think I shall now tell. Hiding itself in the thickets, it then hears the woodcutters calling one another by name, and indeed talking of various things. Then it imitates their voices and speaks—even though what is said sounds like a fable—in a human voice, at any rate, and calls the name it has heard. The man called approaches; the beast withdraws and calls again; and the man comes still more after the voice. But when it has drawn him away from his fellow workers and made him solitary, it seizes and kills him and makes him its food, having lured him on by its voice.

Animals are good at remembering a kindness in this respect too. At Tarentum there was a woman in other respects worthy of esteem, and chaste, moreover, toward her husband; Heracleïs was her name. While her husband lived she tended him most carefully; but when he ended his life, the woman aforesaid came to hate the haunts of the city and the house in which she had seen her husband dead, and as her grief moved her she moved her dwelling to the tombs, and remained, enduring hardship, by the grave of her one-time husband, showing herself faithful to him who was beneath the earth. And once it was summertime, and as young storks were making their first trial of their own flight, one, the youngest, still not in command of his wings, slipped down and broke one of his two legs. So Heracleïs, seeing the fall and learning of the injury to the foot, pitied the nestling, and taking it up with much care she bound up the hurt, and treated it with fomentations and plasters, and brought it food and offered it drink, and in due time, when it had grown strong and grown its swift wings, she let it go free. And it, knowing by some natural and wonderful sense that it owed a ransom for its life, went away. Then, when a year had passed, she happened to be warming herself in the sun as spring was dawning, and the stork that had been healed by her, seeing its benefactress, slackened the rush of its wings, and bringing itself down in a lower flight came near, and gaping disgorged a stone into the lap of Heracleïs, and spreading its wings settled itself upon the roof. At first, as was natural, she wondered, and being disturbed was at a loss, unable to make out what had happened; but she put the stone away somewhere within, and then, waking by night, she sees it giving off a kind of light and gleam, and the house was lit up as though a torch had been brought in—so great was the radiance that rose and was born from the stone. And taking up the stork and stroking it she observed the scar from the wound, and recognized that this was the very one that had met with her pity and her care.

Starfish are a sea creature, and they too are soft-shelled, and are enemies to oysters; for they dine on them. And the manner of their plot against them is this. The oysters often gape, needing coolness, and besides to be fed by anything that may fall into them; so the starfish insert one of their own limbs into the middle of the shells, each of them, and fill themselves with the flesh, the shells being kept from closing together again. Let this be told by us as peculiar also to starfish.

The Vaccaei (this is a Western people), abusing the bodies of those who die of disease as men who have died unmanly and soft deaths, bury them by fire; but those who have ended their lives in war, as good and noble men who have had a share of virtue, they cast out to the vultures, believing the bird to be sacred. Romulus, having taken omens on the Palatine hill from twelve vultures, and obtaining a favourable prophecy, in imitation of the number of the birds ordained that as many rods, equal in number to the birds then seen, should be carried before the magistrates of the Romans in procession. The Egyptians have believed the vulture to be a bird sacred to Hera, and they adorn the head of Isis with vulture feathers, and they have carved vulture wings on the roofs of their temple-gateways. I have said many other things about this animal above also.

Nature, they say, made the dolphin ever in motion, and the limit of this motion is also that of its life. When, at any rate, it needs sleep, it raises its body and floats up to the surface of the water, so that the whole of it is seen, and then it falls asleep; yet it too is not sleepless and without a share of this god. While it sleeps, then, it is pushed down into the depth, until it touches the earth below. And when it draws near to it, it is awakened by being struck against the bottom, then it rises again. And again drawn into sleep and overcome by the god, it slips down, and once more awakened by the same striking it floats up again. And it does this many times, being between rest and activity, yet never falling into complete motionlessness.

In Crete there is a temple of Artemis so called, "of Rhoccaea." There the dogs go raging mad violently. So whenever they fall into this disease, they then throw themselves headlong from the height into the sea.

When the king of the Indians goes forth to give judgement, the elephant is the first to do obeisance to him, having been taught this, and performing it both mindfully and obediently. There stands beside it the man who gives it the reminder of its lesson by a stroke of the goad and by a certain native call, which elephants are appointed by some secret nature to understand — a thing very peculiar to this creature. Moreover it sets in motion a certain warlike movement, as though showing that it preserves this lesson too. Twenty-four elephants attend the king as guards, by relief, like the rest of his sentinels, and the keeping of the watch is a lesson to them, and they do not nod off; for they are taught this too by a certain Indian art. Hecataeus of Miletus says that Amphiaraus the son of Oicles lulled the watch to sleep and suffered what he relates. But these elephants are wakeful and not overcome by sleep, and are the most trustworthy of the guards there after men.

The fish called the grayling is bred by the Ticinus (this is the name of an Italian river), and in size it reaches even to a cubit, and to look upon it is between a bass and a grey mullet. When it is caught, its smell is worthy of wonder; for it does not at all strike a fishy air like the rest, but you would say you held in your hands a grayling freshly gathered, and indeed it is sweet-smelling, and one who has not seen the creature will think there is within a herb that is above all the nurse of bees, whence indeed it has its name. So it would be most easily taken with a net; but with bait and hook you will not catch it — not with pig's fat, not with a gnat-grub, not with a cockle, not with the gut of another fish, not with the sinew of a whelk. With the mosquito alone it is caught — a wicked creature, hostile to men by day and by night both to bite and to buzz, yet it catches the said grayling; for the fish delights in it alone.

It is the crows' work to provoke the eagles. But the eagles despise them, and leave to them the lower flight, while they themselves cut the higher air with swiftest wings — not, surely, from fear (for how could one say that, who well knows the strength of eagles?), but by some peculiar magnanimity they let the crows go beneath.

There is also a people beyond the Indians called the Sciratae, and they are flat-nosed, whether because they have remained so from soft infancy through the crushing of the nose, or because they are even born in this manner. There are bred among them snakes of the greatest size, of which some seize the flocks and devour them, while others suck out their blood, just as among the Greeks do the goat-suckers, of which I know I have made very timely mention above.

Let us give a place to Cleitarchus too. Cleitarchus says that in India there is a bird, and that it is exceedingly amorous, and he says that its name is the orion. Come, let us describe it too in words, as he teaches. In size this orion is like the birds called herons, and its legs too, like theirs, are red; but it has dark eyes (this is not as theirs are), and it has been taught by nature to make music, such songs as are sung at weddings, sweet, and rivalling the Sirens.

The home of the sargue-fish is the rocks and caverns, having, however, small clefts, so that the sun's beam may come down and fill these spaces with light; for the sargues delight in light of every kind, and thirst still more for the sun's ray. Many of them dwell in the same place; their abodes and haunts are the shallows of the sea, and they are very glad to be near the land. And somehow they are strongly fond of goats. If, when goats are grazing near the shore, the shadow of one or two appears in the sea, the sargues gladly swim up and leap, as if delighting, and long to touch the goats, jumping out — though otherwise they are not at all good leapers; yet, swimming even beneath the waves, they have a perception of the goats' smell, and from pleasure they hasten to come forth to them. So, since they are sick with love, they are caught by the very things they desire. For a fisherman wraps himself in a goat's skin, flayed together with the very horns; and the hunter, plotting against his prey, takes the sun at his back, then scatters into the sea, beneath which the aforesaid fish dwell, barley-meal soaked in goat-broth. And the sargues, drawn as by some spell by the aforesaid smell, come up and feed on the barley-meal, and are bewitched by the skin. He takes many of them with a strong hook and a line of white flax; and it is fastened not to a reed but to a rod of cornel-wood, for the one that is caught must be pulled up most easily, lest it alarm the others. They are also caught by hand, if one gently draws down, from the head to the lower part, the spines which they raise to defend themselves, and then bends and presses them and pulls them out of the rocks into which they thrust themselves to hide.

The lizard, if you should strike and cut it through the middle with a rod, whether on purpose or by chance, neither of its parts has died, but separately and by itself each half-section goes forward and lives, dragged along on two feet, this one and that. Then when they come together — for the one part often comes together to the part that is wanting — being paired, the two have come together out of the division; and the lizard, made one again, has the scar to betray the trace of its experience, but running about and keeping its former life, it seems like one that has not undergone the things aforesaid.

the asp. And the one that strikes first wins. To feed their fathers grown old storks both wish and have made their practice; and no human law bids them do this, but the cause of it is nature. And these same birds love their own offspring too; and the proof: when the full-grown bird is in want of food to set before its still unfledged and tender nestlings in the nest, a scarcity having come upon it by chance, it vomits up its own food of the day before and feeds them. And I hear that herons do the same, and pelicans too. I learn besides that the storks themselves flee together with the cranes and run away from the winter; and when the frosty season is over, when both these and those return to their own homes, each recognizes its own nest, as men recognize their house. And Alexander of Myndus says that when they come to old age, passing to the islands of the Ocean they change their shapes into a human form, and have this as a prize of their piety toward their parents — and besides, if I understand anything, the gods wishing thereby to suggest that at least the race of men there is pious and holy, since it was not possible for such a one to live out his life in the rest of the world under the sun. And it does not seem to me a fable. For with what end in view would Alexander have invented this marvel, gaining nothing at all? And besides, it would not befit a sensible man to set falsehood before truth, not even for the greatest gain, much less when about to fall into holds most profitless concerning such matters.

If one were to give the crushed fruit of the willow to drink to dumb animals, they are not harmed at all, but rather are even nourished by it; but a man who drinks it destroys his power to beget children and bear fruit. And it seems to me that Homer, having tracked out even the secrets of nature, then said in his verses "and willows that lose their fruit," hinting at this. And a man who drinks hemlock dies through the congealing and chilling of his blood, but a pig gluts itself on hemlock and stays healthy.

Crocodiles lie in wait for those who draw water from the Nile in the following way. They throw brushwood over themselves, and looking out through it they swim beneath the brushwood. The people come bringing jars or pitchers or water-pots. Then, as they are drawing water, the crocodiles slip out from the brushwood and spring up onto the bank, and seizing them with a most violent snatch they have their dinner. These present remarks of mine have been about the inborn wickedness and cunning of crocodiles.

What devices, then, nature seems to have given to scorpions too, peculiar to them. The Libyans, suspecting their numbers and their contrivances, devise countless devices against them: wearing hollow boots, and sleeping high up and aloft, and pulling the bed-cords away from the walls, and setting the feet of their beds in jars full of water, and they think they shall thereafter sleep in much safety and peace. But see what the scorpions contrive. If a scorpion can find anywhere to hang itself from the ceiling, it clings there with its claws most firmly and lets down its sting. So the second comes down from the roof, and creeps down by way of the first, and clings to that one's sting with its own claws, and leaves its own sting hanging; and the third clings from there, and the fourth from the third, and the fifth in a row, and those after them creeping down by way of the first. Then the last one strikes the sleeper and creeps up by way of those above, and the one after it, and the third from below, and the rest, until they have all loosed themselves from one another as though undoing a chain.

The lion knows how to avenge itself on one who has first wronged it, and if it does not take vengeance at once, yet afterward it keeps its wrath in its breast until it may accomplish it. And a witness of this is Juba the Mauretanian, the father of him who was a hostage among the Romans. He was once marching through the desert against certain peoples that had revolted, and one of the youths running beside him—a youth of noble birth and already handsome, and now too a hunter—threw a javelin at a lion that appeared somehow beside the road, and hit the mark and wounded it, though he did not kill it. Since the march was urgent, the beast withdrew, and the man who had wounded it ran on, with the rest. But when a whole year had passed, Juba, having succeeded in the purpose for which he had been sent, returned by the same road and came to the place where the lion happened to have been wounded. And though the company was very great, that beast came up, and held off from all the others, but seized the man who had wounded it the year before, and pouring out all at once the anger which it had kept through the time aforesaid, it tore the youth to pieces, having recognized him. And no one took vengeance, fearing the strong and dreadfully terrifying anger of the lion; and besides, the journey was pressing.

A lobster, if you should take it and carry it very far away, leaving a mark from where you caught it, you will find again in the same place from which it was taken. I mean, if you carry it along the seaside and then set it down somewhere near, so that it can creep into the sea.

The Lernaean hydra, Heracles' labour, let the poets sing of, and the compilers of ancient myths, among whom is Hecataeus the chronicler; and let Homer too sing of the nature of the Chimaera with three heads, that Lycian monster of Amisodarus, king of the Lycians, a creature reared for the destruction of many, varied and unconquerable, by Zeus. And these things seem to have been set apart for the realm of myth; but the amphisbaena is a two-headed snake, both above and at the tail-end; and as it goes forward, however the need of its progress draws it to its course, it leaves the one part to be tail, and makes the other its head. And again, if it needs to go backward, it uses its heads in the opposite way to that in which it used them before.

In Coptos of Egypt the Egyptians revere Isis, both with their other rites and indeed with the service and worship rendered by women mourning either their husbands or their children or their brothers. There are scorpions there, very great in size, very swift in their sting, and most dangerous in experience (for they kill at once when they strike); and though the Egyptians devise countless contrivances for protection against them, yet the women mourning beside the goddess, sleeping on the ground and walking barefoot and all but treading upon the scorpions aforesaid, remain unharmed. The same people of Coptos revere also the female gazelles and deify them, but they sacrifice the males. They say the females are a plaything of Isis.

In the Red Sea there is a fish flat in shape like the sole, as they say. And in its scales it is not very rough to the touch, but in colour it is golden, and it is marked with black lines from the top of the head to the tail. One might say these were strings stretched taut; from this the fish itself is called "the harper." Its mouth is set close together and is intensely black, but it is girdled with a saffron-coloured band; and its crown is variegated with the gold-like gleam and indeed with certain black outlines. And it has gold-like fins, but its tail is black except at the tips; these are intensely white. And other harpers too are sung of as being born. And they are purple over the whole body, having golden lines at intervals; and they have on the head bands like violet flowers, the one creeping before the eyes as far as the gills, the other passing after the eyes to the middle of the head, and another running round the neck like a necklace.

In the land of Elymais there is a temple of Anaitis, and there are tame lions there, and they greet and fawn upon those who pass into the temple. And if you call them while you eat, they come like invited banqueters, and taking whatever you hold out, they then depart modestly and orderly.

As for me, with all the eagerness I had, examining and tracking these matters and what bears on them to the farthest point, I have learned that the centipede also is a kind of sea-monster, this too the greatest of monsters; and one cast up on shore no one would be bold enough to look upon. Those who know sea-creatures precisely say that these are seen afloat, and that the whole of what is the head juts out above the surface, and that they show hairs projecting from their nostrils, very tall ones, and a broad tail like that of a crayfish. The rest of its body too is seen floating on the waves, of such size as to be set against a full-sized trireme in bulk. They swim with many feet, ranged in a row on this side and on that, like oar-blades hung along (if it is somewhat harsh to hear), rowing themselves along. Those skilled in these things say that the wash sounds gently beneath them, and they persuade by what they say.

At the foot of the Alpine mountains, toward the north wind, under the Bear, are men so called. These are a race of horsemen. From there comes forth the greatest of the European rivers, the Ister, from no many springs, but facing the first assaults of the sun. Then, as it were a bodyguard about it, as about the king of the local streams, many rivers rise along with it, and their stream is ever-flowing, and those who dwell around them know the name of each. But when they fall into the Ister, their name from birth ceases, and they give up their name to it, and are all called from it, and pour out together into the Euxine. There are various kinds of fish there: corvina and mullet and antacaei and carp (these are dark), and "swine-fish" and blackbird-fish (white to look upon), and besides these perch and swordfish. These fishes suit their name, and the proof is this: in all the rest of their body they are soft and harmless to one who touches them, and their teeth are not at all crooked or cruel to see, no upright spine grows on their backs, none at the tail; but — a wonder both to hear and to see — beneath the very snout, through which it breathes and the stream flows into its gills and passes out, its jaw runs out to a point, and it is straight and grows little by little in length and thickness, and as the fish grows monstrous it grows along with it, and resembles the beak of a trireme. And the swordfish, falling in a straight line upon other fish and killing them, then feasts, and with this same weapon defends itself against the greatest of the sea-monsters. And this unforged weapon has grown upon it, and is sharpened by nature. So these swordfish, advancing to great size, go even against a ship. And some men boldly tell that they saw a Bithynian ship hauled up, that its keel, worn by age, might get the needful care; and that they saw the head of a swordfish nailed into it: for the beast having driven its natural point into the hull, and trying to draw itself out, by the violence of its rush its whole body was split from the neck, while the point remained fixed as it fell in at the first. This fish is hunted both in the sea and in the Ister, and it delights in both salt water and a sweet stream.

The fish called the pilot-fish they say is not only sacred to Poseidon, but also dear to the gods in Samothrace. A certain fisherman, in times long ago, paid a penalty to this fish. The fisherman's name, as the story goes, was Epopeus, and he was from the island of Icarus, and he had a son. Once, when there was a dearth of fish, he hauled up a catch that had taken pilot-fish alone, which Epopeus made into a dinner along with his son. But not long after, avenging justice came upon him; for a sea-monster, coming upon his fishing-boat, swallowed Epopeus in his son's sight. They say too that dolphins are enemies of the pilot-fish, yet that even they do not come off well when they taste of it; for they at once writhe and go mad, and unable to keep still they are carried up onto the shores, and once cast up by the wave they become a dinner for sea-crows and gulls. And Apollonius of Rhodes, or of Naucratis, says that this too was once a man, and was a ferryman. Apollo loved a girl and tried to lie with her; but she, fleeing, came to Miletus and asked a certain Pompilus, a man of the sea, to carry her across the strait; and he consented. But Apollo, appearing, snatched away the girl, made the ship a stone, and changed Pompilus into this fish.

The teachableness of the horse too, it seems, was one of its peculiar traits, and of this the following is a proof. The Sybarites in Italy, I hear, took an excess of thought for luxury, and were ignorant of all other works and pursuits, and passed their whole life in idleness and extravagance, taking their ease. To describe each of the things at Sybaris would now be a long task; but the following at least admits an irresistible luxury. Their horses had been trained to dance to the pipe at the time of their banqueting. The Crotoniates, then, knowing this — for they were at war with them — silenced the trumpet and its strenuous note that summons to arms, and taking pipes and pipers, when they were near and an arrow now reached its mark, struck up the dancing-tune; and the horses of the Sybarites, hearing it, as though they were in the midst of their banquets, shook off their riders and leaped and danced. And so they threw the line into confusion and danced the war away.

There is a bird, Indian by race, called the katreus, which Cleitarchus says is by nature surpassing in beauty; for in size it would be like the peacock, and the tips of its wings resemble the emerald. And while it looks elsewhere, you do not know what kind of eyes it has; but if it should look at you, you will say its eye is vermilion, except for the pupil; that is likened in colour to the apple, and looks keenly. What in all other eyes is white is, in this katreus, pale yellow. The feathers of the head are blue-grey, and have drops as it were likened to saffron, scattered one here, another there. Its feet are red-orange. It has also a tuneful voice, clear like the nightingale's. The Indians, it seems, had the rearing of birds, so that those who looked on them might feast their eyes. At any rate it is possible for them to see birds wholly purple and resembling the purest flame; and the flights of these are in such numbers that one might think them clouds; others again are variegated and not very easy to describe in form, but in melody and sweetness of mouth and grace of tongue unmatched, so that they are — if it is not too rough to say it — a kind of Sirens. For that the maidens of the myth were winged, the poets sing and the painters show.

The viper, twined about the female, mates with her; and she endures her bridegroom and grieves him not at all. But when they are near the end of their union, the bride pays a wicked return of affection to the bridegroom for their intercourse; for fastening on his neck, she bites him through, head and all. And he is dead, but she has a fruitful union and conceives. She bears not eggs but living young, and they are already active according to their own most evil nature. They eat through the maternal womb and come forth at once, avenging their father. What then have

The venom of reptiles is terrible, and that of the asp still more so. And against these one would not easily find counter-remedies and defences, even if one were most wise at charming away and removing pains. But there was, it seems, a certain secret venom in a man too, and it has been detected in the following way. If you take a viper, and very cautiously and firmly hold it by the neck, and force its mouth apart, and then spit into it,

The swallow, when it has plenty of mud, carries it with its claws and builds up the nest; but if there is a lack, as Aristotle says, it wets itself, and falling into dust mingles it with its feathers, and when the mud has caked on, then scraping it off with its beak it works the building it has in hand. And knowing well that, the nestlings being tender and bare of plumage, they will be hurt and pained if they rest on bare twigs, it perches on the backs of sheep, and tears off some of the wool, and from this strews a soft bed for its young.

The Indians cannot easily capture a full-grown elephant, but going to the marshes that border the river they take the young of them. For the elephant loves dewy and soft places, and is fond of water, and wishes to live in such haunts,

The hare fears dogs, and so too the fox. And these same, by their barking, even rouse a boar from the thicket, and turn a lion, and pursue a deer; but no bird makes any account of a dog, and there is a truce between them. The bustard alone shudders at dogs. The reason is that they are heavy and carry a mass of flesh. So their wings do not lift and lighten them easily, and for this reason they fly low and near the ground, the mass weighing them down. And they are often caught by the dogs. Being conscious of this, whenever they hear barking, they run down into the thickets and marshes, putting these before themselves as a defence, and so rescue themselves from the present danger most readily.

The fox is a crafty thing. At any rate it plots against the land-hedgehogs in this way. It cannot overcome them while they are upright. The reason is that the spines fend it off. But quietly and sparingly using its mouth it turns them over and lays them on their backs, and ripping them open eats easily those that were until then formidable. And the bustards in Pontus they hunt thus. Turning themselves about and ducking their heads to the ground, the foxes raise their tails like a bird's neck; and the bustards, deceived, approach as toward a bird of their own kind, and then, coming near, are caught most easily by the fox, which turns about and attacks by main force. And the little fish it hunts most cleverly. It comes along the bank of the river and lets down its tail into the water; and the fish swimming up are caught and entangled in the thickness of the hairs. And the foxes, perceiving this, withdraw from the water, and coming to the dry places shake their tails, and the little fish fall out, and they have a most delicate dinner. And the Thracians make this hunting a sure index of the firmness of the freezing of the rivers. And if the fox runs across the ice, it not yielding nor giving way under her steps, they take courage and follow. And she makes trial of the safe passage in this way. She lays her ear to the ice; and if she perceives

There are, I hear, different kinds of crabs and varied tribes. For there are rock crabs; but mud also breeds crabs, and seaweed and sand. Their forms and their names are many. Those called runners—for so it is most fitting to call them—wander here and there; for they neither wish nor are by nature able to remain quiet and still in the same place, but they roam about the shores from which they were born; and already too they set out farther afield, like those men who are fond of travel. The cause of all this wandering is their wish to enjoy something more. In the Thracian Bosporus, when the current rushes violently down from the Pontus, the crabs wish to walk against the opposing stream, but, as is likely, the current breaks more violently around the headlands. The stream, therefore, would certainly push the crabs back and overturn them, if they were to go straight against the flow. But they know this beforehand, and when they come near the headland, each one waits in some bay-like spot and awaits the rest. Then, gathered together in one place, they creep up onto the land, and clamber up the cliffs, and on foot they cross the most rushing and violent part of the sea. Then, having got beyond the headland and passed it by, they go down again into the sea. And the fishermen spare them, because of their own accord they creep up onto the land, asking to be saved together with them. The fishermen, therefore, do not endure to seem more savage than the surge—

Agreus is its name, a winged creature by nature, of the clan of blackbirds, black in colour, musical in voice. It is called Agreus, "the hunter," and rightly; for by its song it catches the tender young of other birds as they fly to it, charmed by its fine music. Knowing, then, the advantage that is bred in it, it seems to use the gift of Nature for pleasure and for food at once; for in hearing itself it is gladdened, and in hunting what comes to it it fills itself. If anyone should catch this bird and shut it up in a little cage, his pains profit him nothing; for he has a voiceless bird, which avenges itself upon its captor for its slavery by silence.

There was, it seems, a kind of frog, and it is called the angler, and it takes its name from what it does. It has, above its eyes, baits—long, as one might say, eyelashes—and to the end of each a little ball is attached. It is aware, then, that it has been equipped by Nature, and besides whetted, with these lures against the other fish. So, hiding itself in the muddier and more silt-filled places, it lies quiet, holding out the aforesaid hairs. The smallest of the fish, then, swim toward these eyelashes, thinking the spherical orbs at the tips to be bait; and the angler, lying in wait, keeps still, and when they have come near, it draws the hairs into itself—and they are drawn in by certain hidden and unseen ways—and the little fish, having come close in their gluttony, are a meal for the frog aforesaid.

The crocodile (and this too I have heard about the animal, in addition to what has already been related) is by nature cowardly, and moreover spiteful and terribly cunning; it snatches and plots very keenly, but it shudders at all loud noises, and fears even the more violent shout of a man, and indeed it dreads strongly those who attack it more boldly. The people of Egypt called the Tentyrites know also from what point the beast is easily mastered; it would be wounded best of all if struck in the eyes or the armpits or the belly. Its back and tail are by nature unbreakable; for they are fenced and, as one might say, armed with scales and plates, and resemble strong shells or shellfish. The aforesaid people, then, are so industrious in hunting the crocodiles that the river there enjoys the deepest peace from them. There, indeed, men swim with confidence and sport as they swim. But among the people of Ombos or Coptos or Arsinoe it is not even

A leopard-fish grows in the Red Sea, as those who have seen it say, and it resembles in colour and in its round spots the mountain leopard. And the oxyrhynchus that is found there has a long mouth, but its eyes are golden, and its eyelids are white; on its back are sprinkled pale markings, and its fins, those on either side, are black, but those on the back are white; and its tail is long in shape, but in colour green, and a golden line divides it down the middle.
In the Red Sea there is a fish, they say, and its name is the watery palm, and it has black lines, and between them it is dotted with dark-blue drops.

Xenophon says this too about hounds. One ought often to lead them into the mountains, but less into cultivated land; for the beaten paths from the worked fields trouble them and throw them off. It is better, he says, to lead them onto rough ground, and he teaches this further gain besides — that they become good of foot and better leapers by training their bodies. He says that the tracks of a hare are seen long in winter because of the length of the nights, but not so in summer, for the contrary reason. And it is plain from what has been said what the contrary reason means.

When the fiercest summer is at its height, the sea-dogs and the other creatures that have boldness bred in them come up to the shores and go straight to the cliffs, and run beneath the headlands where currents flow, and swim into the narrow and deep straits. They flee the haunts of the open sea, and

The Indians take pains also about their racing oxen. And both the king himself and many of the nobles contend over their swiftness, and make wagers on much gold and silver, and do not think it shameful to dispute over these creatures; and they yoke them and gamble over the victory. Now the horses run as the yoke-pair, and the oxen as the trace-team, and the one grazes the turning-post, and they must run thirty stades. The oxen run a match for the horses, and you could not tell which is swifter, ox or horse. And if ever the king makes a wager with someone over his own oxen, he goes to such a pitch of rivalry that he himself follows on a chariot and urges on the driver. And the driver draws blood from the horses with the goad, but holds back his hand from the oxen; for these run without the goad. So great is the eagerness about the ox-race that not only the
About the horses called wolf-torn I have spoken above; and now too shall be told what peculiar things I have further heard. They have a face compact and

The haunts and resorts of the swan are lakes and marshes and pools and ever-flowing rivers that run gently and quietly. They are peaceful, and come to an old age that is light to them. They are valiant too in strength, and confident in it, yet not so as to begin injustice, but to ward off the aggressor. So they easily get the better even of eagles, when those dare to set upon them. And I have told above the manner of the fight.

the Orestes and the Alcmaeons to say to this, O my friends the tragedians? The hyena, if you should see it male this year, you will see the same one female next year; and if female now, afterwards male: they share in both kinds of love, and both wed and are wedded, changing their sex every year. So this creature has proved Caeneus and Tiresias to be old tales, not by boasting but by the deeds themselves.

the spittle slips down into its belly, and so great an evil arises for it that it rots the viper. Whence indeed the bite of a man is foul and dangerous to a man, no less than that of any beast. In the summer season, when harvest has come and the ears of corn are threshed on the floor, the ants gather in troops, going one by one and two by two, and even into a third row, leaving behind their own homes and accustomed dwellings; then they pick out from the wheat and the barley, and travel the same path. And some go off to the gathering of the aforesaid grain, while others carry the load, and they yield the road to one another very respectfully and sparingly, the unladen rather to the burden-bearers; and when they have come down to their own dwellings and filled the pits in their inmost recess, having bored through the middle of each seed, the part that falls out becomes for the time the ant's dinner, but the rest is barren. Now these noble stewards and guards contrive this, lest, when the rains flow round, the seeds, being whole, should take some sprouting and shoot up, and if this happened they should fall into want of food and famine through the winter, and their pains should miscarry. So ants too have had the good fortune to receive nature's gifts, even as others.

The swallow as a mother makes her nestlings just, keeping equality among them through equal feeding; she does not bring one thing for all, since indeed she cannot; but the things she brings are small and few, and she feeds the first hatched first, the second the one after it, and feeds third the one of the third birth, and so proceeds up to the fifth in this manner; for the swallow neither conceives nor bears more. And she herself takes down only so much of the food as she can gain in the nest from what slips by her. And her young see late, as do the pups of dogs; she brings and applies a certain herb, and they look up, and then, having kept still a little, being now able to fly, they leave the nest for pasture. To get possession of this herb men thirst, and have not yet attained their desire.

and is, as one might say, a marsh-dweller. So having taken them tender and tractable, they rear them with flattery of the belly and tending of the body and a coaxing voice (for elephants understand even the human speech of the country), and, to put it briefly, they rear them as children and bestow upon them care and various kinds of training. And they obey. When it is threshing-time and the oxen turn about the threshing-floor, and the floor is full of the sheaves, to keep the oxen from tasting the ears they smear their nostrils with dung, having devised this stratagem most aptly. For this animal, loathing the aforesaid smearing, would not taste anything, not even if it were pressed by the heaviest hunger.

Late does a man begin to recognize his parents, being taught and in a way compelled to look upon his father and greet his mother and smile upon his kin; but lambs leap about their mothers from birth, and know both the strange and the familiar, and need to learn nothing at all from the herdsmen.

that the stream does not echo beneath nor make any quiet noise down in the depth, then she takes courage in the ice as standing firm, and runs across unflinching; but if not, she would not set foot on it. The poets reverence the daughter of Iphis, and the theatres are filled by them hymning that heroine, since she surpassed all others in temperance, having preferred her own husband to life; but the animals have left no excess of affection unmatched. For the dog of Erigone died upon its mistress, and the dog of Silanion likewise upon its master, and neither by force nor by coaxing departed from the tomb. And for Darius, the last king of the Persians, when in the battle against Alexander he had been struck down by Bessus and lay there, all having abandoned the corpse, the dog reared by him alone stayed faithful, not betraying the one who could no longer feed it, as though it were still alive. Something of the sort Xenophon the son of Gryllus plainly tells, with youthful spirit, about the friends of the younger Cyrus: that his messmates alone stayed by him and perished with him, and that the eunuch who was his sceptre-bearer in honour, Artapates by name, killed himself upon the corpse, scorning a life that would be bereft of Cyrus for him. And to King Lysimachus too a dog willingly shared in the common end, though it could have been saved.

men do not. I know that somewhere above I have spoken of the jealousy of a most prudent and indeed most chaste animal—the purple coot was the animal, if my memory is at all sound—and now too I have learned of a little Sicilian dog, an enemy and most hostile to the tribe of adulterers. The adulterer was hidden within, since the wanton wife had learned that her husband had come home from abroad, and, as she supposed, was nicely concealed; for the household slaves, having been bribed—at least those who helped their mistress hide the mischief, and there were such, both the keepers of mirrors and perfumes, as Euripides says, and the doorkeepers too—made the thief of the marriage bed take courage. But it did not turn out so for her, far from it; for the little dog both barked and beat its paws against the doors, so as to astonish the master and make him infer from what was happening that some evil was lurking hidden. And, as was likely, having broken down the doors, he caught the adulterer. And that man had a sword, and was waiting for night, that he might kill the master of the house and afterward take the woman aforesaid to wife.

Above I told of the kindness that the trochilus-birds render to the crocodiles, which Herodotus too mentions in his Egyptian account; but what I did not say, though I knew it, shall now be told, that another too may learn. The trochilus is one of the marsh birds, and roams along the banks of rivers and feeds, picking up whatever it chances upon; and the crocodile too feeds it in the way I have said. And the bird repays it by looking out for it when it sleeps and keeping watch over it; for when it lies and slumbers the ichneumon plots against it, and fastening on its throat has often choked it; but the trochilus cries out and strikes it on the nose and rouses it and sets it on against its enemy. Whether, then, one ought to praise the bird for being so thoughtful of a beast omnivorous and gluttonous, we shall consider; but I have told what is peculiar to these creatures.

The crayfish is an enemy to the octopus. The reason is that, when the octopus throws its tentacles about it, it pays no heed to the stings that grow upon its back, but pouring itself around it, throttles it to suffocation. The crayfish knows this clearly, and flees from it. And the nature of the crayfish is this. When it is without fear, this fish goes forward, slanting its horns this way and that, so that the water, coming against its swimming, may not check its horns and hinder it from going forward; but if it flees, going backward it lets them down entirely. The reason is that, rowing as with oars and stirring like a ferryboat, it draws far away. And if there should be a battle of crayfish with one another, raising their horns and then falling upon each other like rams, they dash their foreheads together. The contest of the lamprey and the crayfish I have told above.

easy to wash one's feet, nor convenient to draw water; nor is it possible to walk along the banks of the river freely and unguardedly. The Tentyrites revere hawks. Accordingly, those who dwell in Coptos, choosing to vex them as enemies of the crocodiles, often crucify hawks. The one people liken the crocodile to water, and therefore revere it; the other liken the hawk to fire, and therefore worship it; and they bring as evidence that fire and water are unmixable, saying that the two are kept apart. Such marvels the Egyptians tell. When one has crossed the Egyptian Oasis, there meets one a deep desert of seven whole days. After this, men called the Dog-faced dwell along the road that leads to Ethiopia. These live by hunting gazelles and antelopes; to look at they are black, and they have the head and teeth of a dog. Since, then, they resemble this animal, it is very fittingly that I have made mention of them here. They are without voice, but they utter a sharp gibbering; a beard hangs down beneath their chin, so that one might liken it to that of serpents. Their hands are armed with strong and very sharp nails; their whole body is shaggy, in this too like the dogs. They are very swift, and they know the difficult places in those regions. From this they seem also hard to capture.

To Ptolemy the Second, whom they also call Philadelphus, an elephant calf was given as a gift, and it was reared in the Greek tongue, and understood those who spoke it. It had been believed before this animal that elephants gave ear to the tongue of the Indians alone.

The horse-mackerel there is equal in length to the one found in our sea, and bands resembling gold run round it, descending from the gills to the tail, and through the middle of them a band resembling silver divides them. Its mouth gapes, and the lower jaw is bent toward the upper; it has green eyes, and gold-like eyelids run round them. And the so-called charax is a nursling of the same sea. It has fins, and as far as the eye can see those on either side resemble gold, and those on the back it has gold-like too. Lower down there are bands purple in colour, and conceive the tail-part of it as gold-like too, and purple spots mark the middle of its eyes to beauty. And the toxotes that is found in the same sea is like the sea-urchin in form, but it has spines firm and long.

Horses and elephants the Indians honour as creatures useful both in arms and in war, and very greatly so. To the king, then, they bring sheaves which they cast into the mangers, and fodder, and they display it fresh and unspoiled. And if it is such, the king commends them; but if not, he punishes most severely the keepers of the elephants and the grooms of the horses. Nor does he dishonour the other creatures, but he accepts these too when they are brought to him as gifts. For the Indians despise no creature, neither tame nor wild. At any rate the subjects who are held in honour bring as gifts cranes and geese, fowls and ducks, turtle-doves and besides francolins, partridges and "spindali" (this last is like the francolin), and besides these, smaller than the aforesaid, "boccalides" and fig-peckers and the so-called millet-birds.
