They display them spread open, testing the depth of their fatness. And they bring a wealth of fattened deer and antelopes and gazelles and oryxes and the asses that have a single horn, of which I made mention somewhere above; and various kinds of fish too they bring.

at that season scorn the pasture there. Now there grows on the deep reefs a certain seaweed, in size like the tamarisk, and it bears a fruit like the poppy. For the rest of the year it is shut, and is resistant and hard by nature, like an oyster's shell; but after the summer solstice it opens, just like the buds in rose-gardens. The casing that surrounds it guards what is within, and goes round it like a fence, and it is most tawny to see. But what is beneath this tunic is blue in colour and loose, like a swollen bladder, and exceedingly translucent, and there drips from it a baleful poison. By night it sends out a gleam like fire, and gives off certain flashes; and as the Dog-star rises, the malignancy of the poison grows still stronger. And from this those who hunt in the water, giving it the name "all-dog," then think that the rising of the star brings it to birth. So the sea-dogs, falling upon the fiery appearance of the flower by night — as it were upon this sea-tamarisk on a reef — some of the poison soaking them, some swallowed, and yet other slipping in through their gills, then die and at once float up. So those skilled in tracking such things gather this poison from the said monsters, partly from the rest of their limbs, partly from the mouth of the beast. The second such evil is that of the land-plant called the aglaophotis. They have given it also the name "dog-torn"; and what the reason is, if I remember to tell, you shall learn it. The Mysians — not those who dwell about Telephus's Pergamum, but think of those lower ones by the Pontus, who dwell next to the Scythian land, keeping back the Scythians' raids and guarding the said whole region for Rome — I mean those near Heraclea and the streams of the Axius. There too the natives celebrate that Medea daughter of Aeetes dared that deed against her brother Apsyrtus with wicked hands — yes, by Zeus, the Mysians sing this unhappy report of the Colchian sorceress, besides those others among the Greeks. But these men hunt that kind of fish. A man, an Istrian by birth, a fisherman by trade, drives a yoke of oxen near the bank of the Ister, by no means needing to plough; for as the saying goes, an ox has nothing in common with a dolphin, so whence could friendship come between the hands of fishermen and a plough? So if he has a yoke of horses at hand, he uses the horses. The man carries the yoke upon his shoulders, and goes where it seems good to him to seat himself and where he is persuaded he is in a good place for the catch. The cord being firm and very strong to drag, he ties one end of it to the middle of the yoke, and sets food in plenty before either the oxen or the horses, and they fill themselves. And he attaches to the other end of the cord a hook, strong and exceedingly sharpened, and threading on it a bull's lung, he lets it down as food for the Istrian sheatfish, food most delicious, having hung upon the line that holds the hook a sufficient weight of lead, to serve as ballast for the hauling. So the fish, when it perceives the bull's flesh, at once rushes to the catch; then, meeting all at once with what it craves, and gaping wide and ungovernably, it draws into itself the evil banquet that has fallen to it. Then, writhing with pleasure, the glutton has unwittingly impaled itself upon the said hook, and thirsting to escape the evil that has befallen it, it disturbs and shakes the cord as best it can. So the hunter perceives it and is filled to overflowing with pleasure, and then springs up from his seat and gives himself over from river-works and watery huntings, and like an actor in a play changing his mask, he drives the two oxen or the two horses. And the strength of the monster and that of the draught-beasts are matched. For the beast bred in the Ister drags down with all the might it has within it, while the team pulling the other way stretches the cord. But it avails nothing more; for in the pull on both sides the fish is beaten, and giving out is dragged to the shore. A son of Homer would say that certain mules were dragging trunks of oaks, as Homer sings of those celebrated things at the funeral of Patroclus.

rich strive over them for much money, nor only the owners, but also the spectators, just as Idomeneus the Cretan and Locrian Ajax in Homer are shown striving. There are also other oxen among them, to look upon like the largest he-goats; and these too are yoked by themselves, and run very swiftly, and are not more sluggish than the Getic horses. There is a story that the horses which drink from the river Cossinitus (this is in Thrace) become terribly wild; and this river empties into the land of the Abderites and is spent in the Bistonian lake. There too were once the palaces of Diomedes the Thracian, whose those untamed mares were, the Labour of Heracles. They say the same befalls the horses that drink from the spring of Potniae. Potniae, the place where the spring is, is not far from Thebes. They say that the Oreitae and Gedrosii set fish as fodder before their horses. And I am told that the Celts give fish as a dinner to both their oxen and their horses. There too they say that the horses, fleeing the breath that comes from men, are carried off to the more southerly parts of Europe, especially when the south winds blow. And some agree that the Macedonians and Lydians too feed their own horses on fish, and that the Lydian and Macedonian sheep are fattened on the same. Among the Mysians, when the mares were being mounted, certain men piped, singing as it were a wedding-song over the horses' marriages; and the mares, charmed by the melody, very quickly became pregnant, and indeed bore beautiful foals. And this too I have heard about horses. They say the older ones, now advanced in age, beget weak offspring; for among other things their feet are ignoble. They reckon the life of horses at so many years: of the males up to thirty-five, but Aristotle the son of Nicomachus says that a horse has lived seventy-five years.

short, and besides flat-nosed. They are said to be lovers of the Greeks too, and to have a certain secret understanding of this race, and to keep a connatural friendship toward them; and when men approach and touch them and clap them gently with the hollow of the hand, they are not vexed nor do they leap away, but spend the day with them as though bound, and when the men sleep, they sleep beside them. But if a barbarian approaches, then — just as the scent-tracking hounds know the wild beasts from their tracks — so those mares too recognize the race, and neigh and flee, as though in dread of a wild beast. To the men they are used to, who throw them fodder and bestow the rest of their care upon them, they are very much attached, and they wish to appear beautiful, and still more to their own charioteers. And the proof is that, when they swim, they go further into the lake or the sea or the spring, wishing to brighten their faces, lest anything ugly or unsightly that has fallen on them from the manger or from the road should then sully their beauty. To a wolf-torn mare fragrant ointments are dear, as to a bride, and the scent of perfumes. And Homer too admits that all horses by nature delight in unguents, when he says: "For they have lost the good strength of their gentle charioteer, who full often poured liquid oil over their manes, when he had washed them in clear water." And Simonides, when he says that women were begotten and moulded from all manner of beasts, says that in some of them, those made from horses, the love of adornment and of perfumes was also born by nature. And what he says is this: "Another a horse, dainty and long-maned, bore — she who turns aside servile tasks and toil; she would not touch the mill, nor lift the sieve, nor cast the dung out of the house, nor sit by the oven, shunning the soot. She makes a man her friend by force. Every day she washes off the dirt twice, sometimes thrice, and anoints herself with perfumes. Always she wears her hair combed out, deep, shaded with flowers. A fair sight, indeed, is such a woman to others, but to him who has her she becomes an evil — unless he be some tyrant or sceptred king, who glories his heart in such things." The following too, I suppose, are peculiar to horses. The Persians, so that their horses may not be easily startled, accustom them to noises and to clashings of bronze, and ring bells at them, so that they may never in war be afraid of the clatter of full armour and the din of swords upon shields. And images of corpses stuffed with chaff they lay beneath them, that they may grow used to treading on corpses in war, and may not, dreading something terrifying, then be useless in the works of arms. Nor did this escape Homer, as he himself shows. For that the Thracian Rhesus was slain, and his companions with him, we hear in the Iliad from boyhood; and what we hear is this. The son of Tydeus slaughters the Thracians, and the son of Laertes drags away the slain by the feet, so that the Thracian horses, being newcomers, might not be startled at becoming entangled with the corpses, and, treading on them unfamiliarly as though on terrors, leap away. But once they have learned, no forgetting of the lesson would seize them; so good are horses at learning whatever is useful. As for how they are capable of loving, and to what degree, I have spoken in earlier books.

Cleitarchus says that there are kinds of apes in India variegated in colour, and the greatest in size. In the mountainous regions their multitude is so great that Alexander son of Philip, he says, was quite dismayed, even with his own force at hand, supposing, when he saw them in throngs, that he beheld an army gathered together and lying in wait for him. The apes happened to be standing upright when they appeared. They are hunted neither with nets nor by the cunning of scent-tracking hounds skilled in the chase. The creature is fond of dancing, if it sees dancing; and it wishes also to play the pipe, if it learns to blow. Besides this, if it sees someone putting shoes on his feet, it imitates the shoeing; and when a man paints his eyes round with black, it wishes to do this too. So, with a view to what has been said, men set out hollow and heavy shoes made of lead, having laid nooses beneath them, so that the apes thrust in their feet but are held by the trap, and that an inescapable one; and as a bait for their eyes is set out birdlime in place of the black. The Indian, using a mirror while they watch, then takes the mirrors away, and sets out others in their stead; and to these they fasten strong weights beneath; and indeed they are such. So the apes come, and nobly do as they saw done in imitation; but a sticky strength leaps out upon their eyelids from the resistance against the brightness, when they look intently; then, no longer seeing, they are caught most easily; for they are now least able to flee. Other things too have been said about apes, both Indian and not Indian; and these things have something not unworthy of effort, by Zeus, for one who understands.

He-goats fight he-goats over the females, as over lovely women, and bulls bulls, and rams fight their rivals over the ewes; and the sea-beetles too are roused over their females. They are found in the places called rough grounds, and they are jealous, and you may see a fierce battle over the females; and the contest is not over many, as with the sargues, but over each one's own mate, as Menelaus' was with Paris over his wife.

Never does the eagle need a spring nor crave a dust-bath, but it is superior to thirst, and does not wait for a remedy for weariness procured from outside, but despising both waters and rest, it cleaves the airy vault, and sees most keenly from the great and lofty air. And the serpent, that most unyielding of beasts, on merely hearing the whirr of the eagle's wings, at once dives down and gladly disappears. And this is its test of its true-born young: it sets them, while still moist and unfledged, facing the sun's beam; and if any blink, dazzled by the keenness of the ray, it is thrust out of the nest and rejected from this hearth; but if it looks back most unflinchingly, it is above suspicion and is enrolled among the true-born, since the heavenly fire is the unbribed and truly unbought registration of its lineage.

Hoopoes are the most harsh of birds, and they seem to me, in memory and also in hatred of the former wrongs of mankind toward the race of women, to weave their nests in deserts and on the high crags; and so that men may not come near their young, they smear their nests instead of with mud, casting around human dung, warding off and checking by the stench and foul smell the creature hostile to them. And once this bird, having raised young in a more deserted part of a wall, in a cleft of stone parted by time — so the keeper of the wall, seeing the young within, smeared over the hole with mud. And the hoopoe, returning, when it saw itself shut out, brought a herb and applied it to the mud; and the mud flowed off, and it came to its own young, then went to pasture. So again the same man smeared it over, and the bird with the same herb opened the hole; and a third time the same things were done. Then the guardian of the wall, seeing what was being done, took up the herb and used it, not for the same purpose, but to open up treasures that in no way belonged to him.

The Indians hunt hares and foxes in the following way. They have no need of dogs for the hunt, but taking the nestlings of eagles and ravens and kites besides, they rear them and train them in hunting. And the lesson is this: they fasten meat to a tame hare and a domesticated fox, and let them run, and sending the birds after them at their heels they allow them to snatch away the meat. The birds pursue with all their might, and having caught the one or the other they hold it as the prize of their capture, the meat. And this is a bait for them, and a most enticing one. So when they have perfected the hunting skill, they let them loose upon the mountain hares and the wild foxes. And the birds, in hope of their accustomed meal, whenever one of these appears, give chase and seize it most swiftly, and carry it back to their masters, as Ctesias relates. And that in place of the meat formerly fastened to them the entrails of the captured prey serve them as dinner, this too we learn from him.

The monkey is a most imitative creature, and whatever you teach it of the things done with the body, it will learn exactly, so as to display it. At any rate it dances, if it learns, and plays the flute, if you teach it. And I myself have seen one holding the reins and laying on the whip and driving. And learning one thing and another it would not disappoint its teacher; so varied and versatile is nature.

The monkey is by some called a mountain-climber, by others, as I hear, a wood-runner, and it is born in the trees and has hair; it is called by some also the flea. Its belly is cut in gently, so to say, as though severed with a thread. It gives most dangerous bites, and trembling follows for the one bitten, and a strong pain comes upon the heart, and the urine is blocked, and the other passage too becomes impassable. And the river-crab, when eaten, seems to be the antidote to the aforesaid.

Wise too are these things in goats. They know well that human spittle is deadly to another animal, and they guard against it, just as we too try to flee whatever is an evil to a man, if he should taste of it. Indeed a man has before now, in ignorance and unawares, swallowed something harmful; but the goats—the thing aforesaid would never escape them. This same spittle is most deadly for killing even the sea-scolopendras. A goat that is about to be slaughtered knows it clearly. The proof: it would no longer touch food. And it does not deign to follow at the rear of the sheep, but agrees, even by its manner of walking, that it ought to lead. At any rate it runs before them; and the he-goat runs before the she-goats too, taking pride in its beard and, by some wonderful natural instinct, preferring the male to the female.

The stingray—I do not now mean the one of the air, but the one in the sea—when it wishes, swims, and again, rising up, flies. It has a sting, of which I made mention above too, that brings death. Now that it stings both irrational animals and men and destroys them at once is not yet a marvel; but what is worthy of astonishment shall be told. If you bring the sting to the largest tree, very flourishing and well-grown and exceedingly luxuriant in its foliage, and prick the tree, not long after it casts off its leaves; and as these fall to the ground the whole trunk withers, and looks as if it had been struck by the sun.

The dewy and moist calamint, they say, drives away snakes strongly, and so does the chaste-tree. This too the Attic women spread beneath them in their bedding at the Thesmophoria. And the chaste-tree seems both to be an enemy to venomous creatures, and is besides a check upon amorous impulse, and seems to have got its name from this. The same venomous creatures fear too the plant called rosemary.

The wolf's neck is drawn together into a short space. It is therefore not able to turn round, but always looks straight ahead; and if it should ever wish to look behind, it turns its whole body. It is the sharpest-sighted of animals, and indeed it sees even by night, and when there is no moon. From this too that hour of the night is called "wolf-light," in which it alone, having received light by gift of nature, possesses it. Homer too, it seems to me, speaks of the "wolf-twilight" night, during which wolves walk about, seeing. They say the wolf is dear to the Sun, and on this account some say that the year too is called lykabas, in honour of the animal. There is a story that Apollo too delights in it, and the reason of this has reached even me as it has been current. For they say that this god was born when Leto changed her form into that of a she-wolf. For this reason Homer too says "wolf-born, famed for the bow"; and for this reason, too, I learn that a bronze wolf is set up at Delphi, hinting at the travail of Leto. But others say it is not for this reason, but because, when offerings had been stolen from the temple and buried by the temple-robbers, a wolf revealed it. For coming into the temple and seizing with its mouth the sacred robe of one of the prophets, and leading him as far as the place in which the offerings were hidden, it then dug it up with its forefeet.

It seems that even among the brute beasts the male is honoured by Nature. At any rate, the male serpent has the crest and the beard, the cock too has the comb and the wattles, the stag the horns, the lion the mane, the cicada the voice.
The Libyan porcupines prick those who touch them bitterly, and indeed work grievous pains. And even of the dead the wounds from their spines prove troublesome, they say.

There is also a sea-cicada. The largest of them resembles a small crayfish, but it has not large horns like those, nor stings. To look upon, the cicada is darker than the crayfish, and when it is caught it is like one chirping. A few small wings have grown beneath its eyes, and these too would be like those of the land cicadas. Most people do not eat it, holding it sacred. I am told that the Seriphians even bury one when it is caught dead; but if it falls alive into their net they do not keep it, but give it back to the sea. They make lament over them when they die, and they say that they are the plaything of Perseus son of Zeus.

The Ister has also a gulf of the deepest kind, and resembles the sea in much of its compass. And that this gulf reaches a good depth, this too is enough to prove. The merchant ships that cross the sea sail into the gulf here too, and they dread this also as a sea, when it grows wild under the winds that blow down, kindling it into waves and driving it mad. There are islands in it, and indeed certain harbours of refuge along the bank into which one may flee. There are beaches too, and headlands that jut out, and a wild swell breaks upon them and is split about them, whenever, filling itself to the full, it is then thrust out as it were into a narrow space toward the sea. And it is wont to do this when the autumn season has now run past and the wintry is beginning, and at its height it advances flooding. As it swells, the north wind drives it back and kindles it to come down wild. And the river bears down upon itself its own ice, as a cargo for sailing, while the north wind falls upon it, blowing hard and most frosty. So it does not allow the river to cast its birth-pang, as one might say, out into the sea, but holding it in check and thrusting it back it stops it. So the ice, kept back and held in, goes to the depth and grows thick to a great extent; and from this the genuine water of the Ister flows beneath by hidden ways, as one might say, while the added and bastard part lies upon it like a plain, and over this, at that season, the men there journey in yokes and single horsemen. Now how the wicked and crafty beast the fox tests and proves the freezing of this river and of Thracian Strymon, I have said above. But the ice on the Ister, growing thick about a cargo-ship borne along the stream, then fetters it, and there is no more need of spread sails, nor does the lookout man see ahead, nor does the captain of the ship turn the rudders; for they are frozen fast, since the whole hull is gripped by the encircling bond, and it is no longer, by Zeus, like a ship — for it is no longer beaten by the waves — but like a hill rising in a great plain, or, by Zeus, a watchtower or a headland. So the passengers and sailors leap out and run upon the river, and bring wagons and shift the cargo over what was lately water. And again after the wintry season, when the river runs strongly, they bear and carry the loads. The ship remains until the frost relaxes and the ice melts and is loosed, and the merchantman is set free from its strange cable. At that moment the fishermen too, taking pickaxes, cut through the freezing of the water where their heart leads them, and make a circular trench going down to the water; you would say it was the mouth of a well or of a very large and big-bellied jar. So many fish, wishing to escape the ice that lies over them like a roof, and longing for the light, swim gladly into the opened mouth, and become an irresistible multitude, and thrust against one another, and are easily caught, as in a narrow pit. And one may take carp and corvina in plenty, and perch, and swordfish — but not yet large, and still without the snout-spine — and antacaeus, this too soft, since the great ones advanced in age might grow as big as the largest tunny. This is fattest in the flanks and belly, and you would say it was the udders of a sow suckling her young. It has a rough hide, and indeed spear-makers smooth their spears with it. Beneath the marrow of this creature there runs a moist and narrow membrane, beginning from the middle of the head and reaching to the tail. If you dry this in the sun, you will have, if you wish, a whip for driving a yoke of horses; for it differs little or nothing from leather. But when it has now advanced to great size, one would not see it slip out from beneath the ice and fall into the pit, but either it goes beneath a much-sheltering rock, or, hiding itself in deep sand, it then warms itself most contentedly. At that season it needs neither grass nor another fish for food, but in the frost it wishes to be idle, and delights in its leisure, and eats its own fat; and just as octopuses, in the season when there is no hunting, gnaw their own tentacles and feed themselves, so does it. But when winter is ending and spring beginning and the Ister runs free, it hates its idleness, and swimming up it fills itself with the foam upon the water; and there is much of this when the stream murmurs and is thrust along most strongly. There too it is easily caught, the fishermen lying in wait for it and letting the hook down into the foam along with the line. And the hook is hidden by the whiteness, and the gleam of the bronze is not easy for it to see, and on this account, gaping and greedily drawing in the said food, it swallows the trick, and perishes from the very source whence it was first fed.

Going from Susa of the Persians to Media, at the second stage there is said to be so vast a multitude of scorpions that the king of the Persians, whenever he passes through, three days beforehand commands all to hunt them, and gives gifts to whoever catches the most. For if this were not done, the place is impassable; for under every stone and every clod there is a scorpion. They say too that the Rhoetians were driven from their homes by centipedes, so great a multitude of these came upon them. And they say that in Cyrene there are various kinds of mice, differing not only in colours but in shapes; for some of them are broad-faced like martens, and again others are hedgehog-like, which the natives call echineae. In Egypt I am told there are two-footed mice, and that they grow to a very great size, and use their forefeet as hands; for these are shorter than the hind. They walk upright on their two feet; but when pursued, they leap. Theophrastus says this.

In frosty places, when the snow lies thick and the cold is at its height, the sheep are free of gall (being shut in, and not partaking of fresh fodder, they are then found to be such); but at the beginning of spring, when they go out to pasture, they fill up with gall. This, they say, is still more wont to attend the Scythian sheep.

That lions grow to the greatest size in India I do not doubt; the reason is that this land is a good mother of the other creatures too. They are most savage and most beast-like. The mane of those lions is black to look at, and bristling it stands erect and sends out a kind of terror that strikes dismay. If they can be caught, they are tamed — but not the largest; and they are made gentle and very easily domesticated, so as to be led on a leash to the hunting of fawns and deer and boars and bulls and wild asses. For they are clever, I hear, even at scent-tracking.

The octopus feasts on one food after another; for it is both a fearsome eater and very cunning at laying plots — the reason being that it is the most omnivorous of sea-creatures. And the proof: if ever it meets with no prey, it bites off some of its own tentacles, and having filled its belly, it remedies the scarcity of the catch; then it grows again what it lacks, as though nature prepared for it in its hunger a ready dinner.

The great bird the ostrich is feathered with shaggy plumage, but has not the nature to be lifted up and raised into the deep air. But it runs most swiftly, and unfolds the wings on either side, and the wind, striking them, fills them out like sails.

The Peloponnese is barren of lions; and Homer, as was likely, perceiving this with an instructed mind, said, when he sang of Artemis hunting there, that she ranges over Taygetus and Erymanthus delighting in boars and swift deer. And since these mountains are empty of lions, very reasonably he did not mention them.

I am told that the griffin, the Indian animal, is four-footed like the lions, and has claws of the greatest strength, and these very like a lion's; and that it is winged, and the feathers of its back they sing of as black in colour, those of its front they say are red, but the wings themselves no longer such, but white. Ctesias records that its neck is variegated with dark-blue feathers, and that it has an eagle-like beak and a head such as artists draw and model. Its eyes, he says, are fiery. It makes its nest upon the mountains, and to take a full-grown one is impossible, but they catch the young. And the Bactrians, who are neighbours of the Indians, say that the griffins are guardians of the gold in those parts, and that they dig it up and weave it into their nests, and the Indians take what flows off. But the Indians deny that they are guardians of the aforesaid gold—for the griffins have no need of gold (and if they say this, they seem to me to speak credibly); rather the Indians themselves come to gather the gold, while the griffins, in fear for their young, fight with those who approach. And they contend with the other animals and overpower them most easily, but do not withstand the lion or the elephant. So the natives, dreading the strength of these beasts, do not set out for the gold by day, but come by night; for at that hour they seem more likely to escape notice. This region, where the griffins live and the gold is found, is dreadfully desolate. The seekers of the aforesaid wealth come a thousand and twice as many strong, armed, and they bring mattocks and sacks, and they dig, watching for a moonless night. Now if they escape the notice of the griffins, they gain a double profit; for they are saved and they carry their freight home, and those who have learned to refine gold, by a certain skill of their own, have very great wealth in return for the aforesaid dangers; but if they are caught in the act, they perish. And they return home, as I learn, every third or fourth year.

There are also these peculiar and various natures of animals. Theopompus says that the hares among the Bisaltae have double livers. Ister says that the Meleagrides in Leros are harmed by none of the crook-taloned birds. Aristotle says that the oxen among the Neuri have their horns on their shoulders, and Agatharchides that the pigs in Ethiopia have horns. Sostratus says that the blackbirds in Cyllene are all white. Alexander of Myndus says that the sheep in Pontus are fattened by the most bitter wormwood. The same author says that the goats born on Mimas do not drink for six months, but only look toward the sea and gape and receive the breezes from there. And I hear that Illyrian goats have a solid hoof, not a cloven one. And Theophrastus tells the most marvellous thing: that in the Babylonian land the fish often come up out of the river and then graze on the dry land.

Of cats the male is most lustful, but the female loves her young, and shuns intercourse with the male; for he discharges his seed most hot and resembling fire, and burns the female's parts. Knowing this, then, the male makes away with the offspring they have in common, and she, out of longing for other young, offers herself to him when he is eager to come together. And they say that cats hate and loathe everything that is foul-smelling. For this reason they discharge their own excrement only after digging a hole, in order to make it disappear by throwing earth upon it.

The most obedient of animals are sheep, taught by nature to be ruled. At any rate they obey both the shepherd and the dogs, and indeed they follow the goats. They love one another strongly too, and are less plotted against by the wolves; for they do not each wander on their own, nor split off from the flock, as goats do. The Arabs say that among them the flocks are fattened by music more than by fodder. They eat salty things with more pleasure; for they make such food a relish for their drink. Sheep know this too, that the north and the south wind help them to breed no less than the rams that mount them; and they know this also, that the north wind is the maker of males, while the south wind is by nature the begetter of females; and if the ewe needs this offspring or that when she is mounted, she looks toward this wind or that. Achilles, that his friend lying on the pyre might be consumed, had need of prayer, and Iris summoned the winds for him, O noble Homer, and promised them a sacrifice, like a wage, when they should come; and the son of Neocles taught the Athenians to sacrifice to the winds; but the ewes have the winds, without all this trouble, as ready and unsummoned servants of their own travail. And the shepherds too are good observers of these things. At any rate, when the south wind blows, then they lead the rams to the ewes, so that their offspring may rather be female.

The elephant is born coming out head first, and the size of the newborn is that of the largest piglet. To one mother several little elephants follow, they say. And if you should wish to touch the calves when they are newly born, the mothers are not at all vexed but allow it; for they understand that no one touches them to harm or to punish them, but that all do so caressing and fondling them. For who would injure so small a creature? But when, being hunted, they fall into the trench, and see that escape is now impossible for them, they take forgetfulness of their former spirit that went with freedom, and when men hold out food they readily accept it, and when they offer water they drink, and when men pour wine into their trunks they do not refuse the pledge of friendship.

From Theophrastus I have heard these things too. This man records a certain plant, and calls it by the name "woman-slayer," which, if one should place it upon a scorpion's back and leave it there, the scorpion is at once withered. And the same man says that the same scorpion will revive, if you should sprinkle white hellebore upon it. But I praise the woman-slayer, and the white hellebore least of all. The reason is that I hate scorpions, but love men. And Callimachus sings that in the land of Trachis there grows a tree, and it is called smilos, which the creeping things, when they come near and merely touch it, then die.

There is an Egyptian village named Chusae (it belongs to the Hermopolite nome, and seems small but is charming); in it they revere Aphrodite, calling her Urania. They honour also the female cow, and they give this reason. They have believed that cows belong to this goddess; for the female cow has a strong frenzy for love, and is more on heat than the male. At any rate, when she has heard the bellowing, she is most ardently inflamed and kindled for the union. And those skilled in observing such things say that even from thirty stades away a cow hears the bull bellow his amorous and lustful signal. And the Egyptians both mould and paint Isis herself with the horns of a cow.

The cause of the war for the Achaeans and the Trojans, they say, was Helen the daughter of Zeus, and for the Persians against the Greeks Atossa the wife of Darius, who longed to possess Attic handmaids; and the cause of the long war for the Greeks was the tablet against the Megarians. The Magnesians and the Ephesians a locust set at war, a dove the Chaonians and the Illyrians; and the Thebans in Egypt are said to have warred against the Romans over a dog.

There is in the Red Sea also an "ape," not a fish, but a cartilaginous creature, and this too not large. In colour the sea-ape resembles the land one, and its face too is ape-like. Over the rest of its body is thrown a shell, not fish-like, but such as is the tortoise's. It too is somewhat snub-nosed, as indeed is the land one. The rest of the body is flat in shape like the torpedo, so as to be, one might say, a bird with its wings spread; and as it swims it resembles one flying. It differs from the land ape in this too. It is spotted, and the broad parts along the nape are tawny, like gills. And it has a long mouth at the tip of its face, the fish being likened in this too, fittingly, to the form of the land ape.

The "hyena" is a fish that shares its name with the land hyena. If you place its right fin beneath a sleeping man, you will throw him into great disturbance; for he will see certain fearful sights and apparitions and phantoms, and other dreams in no way kindly or friendly. Again, if you cut off the tail of a horse-mackerel while it is alive, and then let the horse-mackerel go free again into the sea, but hang the said tail upon a pregnant mare, before long the embryo will be cast and the mare will miscarry. Again, when a youth, longing for the hairs of his chin, is at a loss for the longest time, the blood of a tunny smeared on makes the youth smooth before his time. The torpedo-fish and the "lung" do the same; for the flesh of these, rotted in vinegar and smeared on the chin, works, they say, the banishment of the hairs. What against this can those mischievous sophists of Tarentum and Tyrrhenia say, who tracked down and tried out that cunning pitch, to mark off men from women?

The name of a plant is "dog-torn" (the same is also called aglaophotis; for I wish to pay a debt now that I have been reminded). By day it is hidden among the others and is not at all visible, but by night it shows itself and shines forth like a star; for it is fiery and resembles fire. So men fix some mark beside its roots and go away, having no means by day of remembering its colour, unless they do this, nor its shape. When the night is past they come, and seeing the mark they left, and recognizing it, they can infer that this is the very plant they need, since it is wholly like those standing by and differs not even a little from them. But they do not pull up this plant themselves, or they will surely come to no good. So no one digs about it or pulls it up, since, they say, the very first man who touched it, in ignorance of its nature, it destroyed before long. So they bring a young dog that has been starved for days and is fiercely famished, and fasten to it a very strong cord, and to the lower stem of the aglaophotis they attach a knot hard to loose, from as far off as they can; then they set before the dog much roasted meat giving off savour; and the dog, inflamed by hunger and racked by the savour, darts at the meat set before it, and by its rush pulls up the plant roots and all. And as soon as the sun sees the roots, the dog dies on the spot. They bury it in that very place, and after performing certain secret rites and honouring the dog's corpse as having died on their behalf, they then dare to touch the said plant, and carry it home. And they make use of it, they say, for many useful purposes; and among others they say it heals the disease said to be sent upon men by the moon, and the affliction of the eyes which, when fluid floods over and freezes, takes away their sight.

There is a story that the birds called francolins, brought over to Egypt from Lydia and let loose in the woods, at first uttered a quail's cry; but later, when the river ran low and a famine came, and many throughout the country were perishing, these birds did not cease uttering, far more clearly and articulately than a child, and saying: "Threefold to the wicked their wickedness." The same story says that, when caught and snared, not only are they not tamed, but they no longer utter even the cry they uttered before; for slavery condemns them to silence. But if they are let go and spread their wing free, and come again to their own haunts, they become vocal, recovering at once both their cry and their freedom of speech.

Agatharchides says that there is a race of certain men in Libya, and that they are called Psylli. In all the rest of their manner of life they differ in nothing from other men, but they have a body strange and marvellous when compared with that of other peoples; for the biting and stinging creatures, many as they are, do no harm to them alone. They feel nothing when a snake bites, nor when a venomous spider stings to death the rest of mankind, nor when a scorpion drives in its sting. But when any of these comes near and brushes against the body and at the same time draws in the scent of these men, then, as though it had tasted a drug producing a drowsiness that draws toward insensibility, it grows weak and slack, until the man has passed by. And how they test their own infants, whether they are true-born or bastards, proving them among the reptiles as craftsmen prove gold in the fire, I have told above.

In the land of the Libyans there was, they say, a people called the Nomaeans. And in all else they prospered, with a portion most well-ordered and happy, by Zeus; and then they were utterly destroyed, when lions came upon them in vast multitude and of the greatest size and unmatched in daring, by whom they were destroyed, all the people and all the race together, and then perished utterly. For an invasion of lions in throngs is an irresistible thing.
A horse cast out becomes the breeding-place of wasps. For it rots, and from its marrow fly out these creatures, the winged offspring of the swiftest of animals — wasps from a horse.

The bustard is, I hear, the most horse-loving of birds. And the proof: it despises the other creatures grazing in meadows and pastures; but when it sees a horse, it most gladly flies up and draws near, like men who are lovers of horses.

There is a fish born in the Red Sea, and, as far as I know, the natives gave it the name Perseus. And the Greeks call it so, and the Arabs likewise with the Greeks; for they too sing of Perseus as the son of Zeus, and they celebrate the fish as named after him. In size it is like the largest anthias, and to look at it is like a sea-bass; it is slightly hook-nosed, and is variegated with bands likened to gold; the bands begin from the head, slanting, and end at the belly. It is fenced with large and close-set teeth. And it is said to surpass fishes in strength of body and force; nor does it lack daring. Its hunting and catching I have told elsewhere.

The severed head of a sea-tortoise sees and closes its eyes when a hand is brought near; and it would even bite if you brought your hand nearer. And for a long time it keeps its eyes shining; for its pupils are very white and very conspicuous, and when taken out they are set in gold and necklaces. Hence indeed they seem marvellous to women. These tortoises, as I learn, are found in the sea that men call the Red Sea.

The purple coot, besides being most jealous, possesses this peculiarity too. They say it is a lover of its own kind and cherishes the companionship of its mates. At any rate I have heard of a purple coot and a cock reared in a house, feeding on the same food, taking the same walks, and bathing together in the dust. And from this a wondrous friendship grew up between them. And once, when a festival came round, the master of both, having sacrificed the cock, feasted with his household; but the purple coot, having lost its mate and unable to bear the loneliness, destroyed itself by refusing food.

They say that the most licentious of fish is the octopus, and that it indulges in lust to such a degree that all the strength of its body flows out and is rendered weak, and it is least able to swim and unable to seek food, and for this reason it feeds others. The little fish, at any rate, and what are called the hermit-crabs and the crabs come upon it and devour it. And they say this is the reason why the octopus cannot live longer than a year's time. And the female octopus too is easily consumed, since it gives birth often.

When the kinsmen of those who first drank wine and fell asleep killed Icarius—not knowing yet that what had befallen them was not death but a wine-heavy stupor—the people of Attica fell sick, as it seems to me because Dionysus was avenging the first and eldest tiller of his own plants. The Pythian god, then, gave an oracle that, if they wished to obtain deliverance, they must sacrifice to Icarius and to Erigone his daughter and to the celebrated dog, because, through excess of goodwill toward its mistress, it had resolved not to live after her. Euripides jests when he says, "To good slaves the misfortunes of their masters, falling out ill, lay hold even upon their hearts." For where has a man died for his master, when a slave dog has done so?

The fish called ellops men hold to have been called by the poet "the sacred fish." A certain account says that it is rare, and is caught in the sea off Pamphylia, though there too only scantily. And if it is caught, the fishermen adorn themselves with garlands over their good fortune, and they garland the boats too, and put in to shore with clapping and pipes, bearing witness to their catch. But others hold not this, but the anthias, to be sacred. The reason is that, wherever this fish appears in the sea, that place must surely be free of beasts, and there is a truce for the fishes against everything that hunts in the water, and the fishes themselves, taking courage, spawn. But to scrutinize the secrets of Nature is not for me, and reasonably so, since a lion fears even a cock, and the basilisk fears the same, and the elephant a pig; and as for the causes, those who have much leisure, in seeking them, will despise the time spent, yet will not come at last to the end of their search.

That the sow has flesh more pleasant than other flesh has long been believed. And experience teaches this too, very clearly. Whenever it eats a salamander, it itself is unharmed, but it kills those who taste of it.

The sound of the trumpet the people of Busiris and Egyptian Abydos and Lyconpolis abhor, since it somehow resembles a braying ass. And indeed all who are concerned with the worship of Sarapis hate the ass. Knowing this, Ochus the Persian killed the Apis bull but deified the ass, wishing to grieve the Egyptians to the utmost. But he too paid the sacred bull a penalty not to be despised, and no less than that of Cambyses, who first dared this sacrilege. The same worshippers of the Zeus aforesaid hate also the oryx. The reason is, they say, that the Egyptians say it turns away toward the rising of the sun and voids the surplus of its own food. The Pythagoreans say of the ass this too: that it alone of animals was not born according to harmony; and for this reason it is most deaf to the sound of the lyre. And some have said that it was dear to Typhon. They say men attach also this reason to the ass, besides those mentioned. Everything fruitful is honoured; but this animal is by nature contrary to such things. At any rate, no account easily recalls an ass that has borne twins.

A certain account says that Pythochares the flute-player checked an onset of wolves by playing an intense and noble strain on the flute. A multitude of flies drove out the Megarians, wasps the people of Phaselis, and centipedes the Rhoetians.

The nightingale through the summer changes its colour to a different form, and alters its voice; for it does not sing in many tones and variously, but otherwise than through the spring. The blackbird sings in summer, but in winter it chatters and utters a confused sound, and having changed its colour like a garment, from its former black it is somewhat yellow. The thrush in winter is more starling-coloured to look at, but in summer shows a variegated neck. And these fish too change their colour: thrushes and blackbirds and wrasses and sprats. And jackals, as Aristotle says, are bare through the summer, but shaggy through the winter.

The gilthead is the most cowardly of all fishes. In the ebbings of the sea, when the season runs with Arcturus, the sea retreats about the headland, and bare sand is left behind, and ships often stand upon the land widowed of water. So the natives, sharpening green and leafy shoots of poplar like stakes and fixing them in the sand, withdraw; then the returning wave drags along an irresistible multitude of the said fish, and ebbs again, and many gilthead are left behind in shallow water, wherever a low hollow place is found. Then, cowering beneath the branches, they keep still; for being shaken and stirred by the wind that strikes them they take fright, and neither gasp nor leap up. So one may seize them like captives and strike them — a populace of cowardly fish, one might call it — with whatever comes to hand. At any rate not only experts catch them, but even a layman who chances to be by, and children and women too.

There is a sea-snail, small in size but most beautiful to see, and it is bred in the purest sea and on the underwater rocks and on what are called the reefs. Its name is the nerites, and a double story runs about this creature, and both stories have come down to me; and indeed to relate at some length certain small matters in a long treatise is nothing other than to give the ear a rest and to sweeten the discourse. To Nereus of the sea — whom we ever hear to be true and without falsehood — Hesiod sings that Doris daughter of Ocean bore fifty daughters; and Homer too mentions them in his verses. But that a single son was born to him besides so many daughters, those poets do not say, though sea-stories celebrate it. They say he was called Nerites and became the most beautiful of men and of gods, and that Aphrodite, while she dwelt in the sea, took delight in this Nerites and held him dear. But when the appointed time came, and she had to be enrolled among the Olympians, her father calling her up, I am told that as she went up she wished to bring with her her companion and playmate. But he, the story has it, would not obey, preferring to dwell with his sisters and his parents rather than Olympus. And it was open to him to grow wings, and this, I suppose, was the gift Aphrodite gave; but he set even this favour at naught. So the daughter of Zeus grew angry, and turned his form into this snail, while she herself chose as attendant and servant, in his stead, Eros, who was also young and beautiful, and gave him the other's wings. The other story proclaims that Poseidon loved Nerites, and that Nerites loved Poseidon in return, and that from this came the birth of Anteros who is celebrated. So I am told that in all else the beloved spent his time with his lover, and that when Poseidon drove his chariot over the waves, the other monsters and the dolphins and besides the Tritons leapt up from the depths and danced about the chariot and circled round it, but were left behind by the speed of the horses altogether and everywhere; only the favourite kept pace alongside, very close, and the wave was smoothed for them and the sea parted in reverence for Poseidon; for the god wished his beautiful beloved to be esteemed in all things and especially to excel in swimming. But the Sun, the tale says, grudged the boy his speed, and changed his body into the snail it now is, angered for some cause I cannot tell; for the tale does not say. But if one must guess about things past finding out, it might be said that Poseidon and the Sun were rivals in love. And perhaps the Sun was vexed that the boy moved in the sea, and wished him to be numbered not among the sea-monsters but to be borne among the stars. And there let the two tales end; but for me, let the things from the gods be gracious, and let what comes from me toward them be reverent. And if anything too bold has been said in the tales, theirs be the blame.

They say too that the scops-owls (which Homer too mentions in the Odyssey, saying that many of them roosted about the cave of Calypso) are caught by dancing. Men skilled in dancing say that a kind of dance has even been named from them, and, if one must believe them, this dance is called the "scops." And to mimic someone in a ludicrous way and to make fun seems most pleasant to these birds; whence indeed the word has been turned, and we too call mocking thus. This scops is said to be smaller than the little owl, and to have a colour like the deepest lead, and they say its wings have whitish spots. It shows two feathers from the brows, one at each temple. But Callimachus says there are two kinds of scops, and that some utter sound, while others are allotted silence; and that some of them are called scopes, others aei-scopes ("ever-scopes"). Aristotle says that those in Homer are not spelled with a sigma, but are simply named copes; so that those who put in the sigma err from the truth of the name and from Homer's judgement and knowledge about the bird. And in the other seasons of the year they are not eaten, but in autumn, on two days or one, those caught are even edible. The scopes differ from the aei-scopes in fatness, but they are similar in appearance to the turtle-dove and the wood-pigeon.

Callias, in the tenth of his books about Agathocles of Syracuse, says that the horned snakes are terrible in their bite; for they kill both irrational beasts and men, unless a Libyan man be present, of the Psyllian race. This man, then, whether he comes when summoned or chances to be present, if he sees the victim still gently suffering, by merely spitting on the wound soothes the pain and charms away the danger with his saliva. But if he finds the man distressed and bearing it ill, he draws a great draught of water within his teeth, uses it as a rinse for his mouth, and then, pouring it into a cup, gives it to the wounded man to drink. And if the evil prevails even beyond this remedy, he lies down naked beside the sick man, naked himself, and rubbing against him the connatural strength of his own skin, makes the man free of the harm. A sufficient witness to this might be Nicander of Colophon, when he says: "I have heard how the race of the Libyan Psylli neither themselves suffer at all from beasts with their festering wounds — they whom the dune-nursing Syrtis feeds — and how they have well warded off from other men too the wounds that grieved them, not by watering roots, but from their own bodies," and what follows.

Euphorion, in his Memoirs, says that Samos in the most ancient times became desert; for there appeared in it beasts of the greatest size, wild, and terrible to come near to, called the neades. These by their mere cry split the earth. So there is a proverb current in Samos that says, "He shouts louder than the neades." And their bones, the same writer says, are shown even now, great ones.

The owl is a wily creature, like the witches. And first it captures the fowlers who have caught it. So they carry it about like a darling, or, by Zeus, like an amulet, on their shoulders. By night it keeps watch for them and with its voice, as though by some incantation

A fly that has fallen into water, though it is the boldest of creatures, yet neither runs over it nor is it a swimmer, and for this reason it is drowned. But if you take out its corpse and sprinkle ash on it and set it in the sun, you will bring the fly back to life.

The pinna is a sea-creature, and is of the shellfish. It gapes by the parting of the shells that lie about it, and holds out a bit of flesh from itself like a bait to the fish swimming by. And a crab stays with it, reared together and feeding together. So when one of the fish swims up, the crab gently pricks it; and the pinna opens itself wider, and receives within the head of the approaching fish — for it lets it down as if for food — and eats it.

The cock, when the moon rises, is filled with rapture, they say, and frolics. And the rising sun could never escape its notice, and at that hour it is most musical of all. I am told too that the cock is a bird dear to Leto. The reason is that they say it stood by her when she was in the double and blessed throes of childbirth. Hence even now the cock attends women in labour, and seems somehow to make their delivery easy. And when the hen has died, the cock himself broods upon the eggs, and hatches out his own chicks in silence; for he does not sing then, from some wondrous and secret cause—no, by heaven; for he seems to me to be conscious that he is then doing the work of a female and not of a male. And a cock defeated in battle and in the contest against another will not sing; for his spirit is cast down, and he sinks away in shame. But the victor is proud and holds his neck high, and

At Aegium in Achaea a goose loved a beautiful boy, Amphilochus by name, an Olenian by descent. Theophrastus tells this. The boy was being kept under guard at Aegium together with the Olenian exiles. So the goose brought him gifts. And in Chios, since Glauce the lyre-player was very beautiful—if men loved her, that is nothing strange; but a ram and a goose too, as I hear, loved her. The geese, in crossing Mount Taurus, fear

Phylarchus relates that a boy who strongly loved birds received an eaglet as a gift and reared it with varied food and bestowed every care upon it; for he did not rear the bird as a plaything for amusement, but like a beloved or a younger brother—so providently did the boy treat the eagle. And as time went on it kindled them to a strong friendship for each other. It happened that the boy fell ill in body. And the eagle stayed and nursed its rearer, and while he slept kept quiet, and while he was awake stood by him, and while he fasted would not take food. But when

The peculiar goodwill of dogs toward those who rear them this too bears witness. A man of Colophon came to Teos to buy something in partnership; for he was a merchant, and had as his livelihood the trafficking and exchange of wares. He brought along money and a slave and a dog, and the slave carried the money. When they were on their way, the slave turned aside; for some natural need pressed him, and the dog followed too. The young man set down the purse, and did not think to take it up again, but went off; while the dog, laying itself down upon the money, remained quiet. When the master and the slave came to Teos and then returned empty-handed, having nothing to buy, they turned aside again by the same road where the slave had left the purse, and they found their dog lying upon it and scarcely breathing for hunger. When it saw its master and its fellow slave, it leaned itself off the purse, and at the same moment let go both its watch and its life. So not even Argus the dog was a fiction of yours, divine Homer, nor a poetic boast, if indeed

The Euphrates, which flows between the Parthians and the Syrians—what else it has beyond other rivers, remarkable, I shall tell at another time; but what the Parthians and the Syrians know of it, and what is in tune with these accounts, shall be told. At the first sources of this river there are born certain snakes, and very hostile to men—but not to the natives and those reared among them, while to strangers and foreigners they are in no way hostile. And they are honoured by causing death to these.

In Egyptian lore I have heard this too of the ibis. Whenever it hides its neck and head beneath the feathers under its breast, it traces the shape of a heart. Moreover, that it is most hostile to the creatures born for the harm of both men and crops, I have said already above. They mate with their mouths, and beget their young in this manner. The Egyptians say (and they do not easily find me believing) — they say, then, that those set over the embalming of animals, and skilled in this wisdom, agree that the intestine of the ibis is ninety-six cubits long. I have also heard that it walks measuring out a cubit at each stride. When the moon is eclipsed, it shuts its eyes until the goddess shines forth again. And they say it is dear to Hermes, the father of speech, since its
They say that sheep in Pontus have no gall, and in the island of Naxos a double gall.

In Bubastus of Egypt there is a lake, and it nourishes a very great multitude of sheatfish, and these are tame and the gentlest of fish. And men throw to them fragments of bread, and the fish frisk up and leaping, one before another, pick out the food thrown to them. This fish is found in rivers too, as in the Cydnus of Cilicia; but this one is small in size. The reason is that a transparent and clear stream, and cold besides (such is the Cydnus), does not nourish it abundantly, but it delights more in a turbid one full of mud, and there it grows fat. The Pyramus and the Sarus nourish fatter ones, and these too are Cilician. The same would be reared in the Orontes of the Syrians too, and indeed the river Ptolemaeus nourishes very great ones, and the lake of Apamea.

Where the river Tanarus and the Eridanus meet (the latter going about in glory and renown, the former not very well known), there are, by Zeus, hunts of fish peculiar to the place, which have come down to me in the verses of a man of Mytilene, whom I myself knew; let these too not go unrewarded by me in this account. When their streams are fettered by ice, all who dwell about them, in the winter season, both plough and sow; for somehow they have been allotted a fertile region. Then at the beginning of spring, the said streams still standing for the reason I have given, the farmers — for the time being now fishermen — choose out a certain bay-like spot, and cut around it with well-sharpened axes, and the water appears in a circle like a pool; yet they do not cut close to the bank, but leave the ice as it was bred from the first. So they throw about the bared spot a wide net, and indeed throw around it a stout rope. And this net men standing on the bank draw in, both fishermen and others; and many who know nothing of the craft watch the taking of the fish, and a certain delight steals over them. But when the fish, drawn in, come near the bank, then too —
But the nation of the Pygmies, I am told, this too

Empedocles the natural philosopher says — speaking also, no doubt, about the peculiarities of animals — that there come into being certain creatures grown together and mixed, differing in form but woven together in unity of body. And what he says is this: "Many things were born with double faces and double breasts, ox-natured with the prow of a man; and on the other hand there sprang up man-natured things with ox-heads, mingled, here from men, there with the nature of women, fitted out with shadowy limbs."

When the king of the Indians marches against his enemies, a hundred thousand war-elephants lead the way. Another three thousand, I hear, the greatest and strongest, follow, which have been trained to overthrow the walls of the enemy, falling upon them when the king bids; and they overthrow them with their breasts. Ctesias says these things, writing what he heard. But in Babylon, the same writer says, he himself saw the palm-trees overthrown root and all by the elephants in the same manner, the beasts falling upon them most violently; and they do this if the Indian who breaks them in bids them do it to the trees.

of wily and bewitching enchantment scattered abroad, it draws the birds and makes them settle near it; and even by day it offers other lures to the birds, mimicking and at one time and another twisting its face into a different shape, by which all the birds are charmed and stay rooted, held by a very strong fear at the grimaces it makes. The sea-bass is overcome by the prawn, and would be — to put it with a touch of jest — the most gluttonous gourmet of fishes. So, being marsh-dwellers themselves, the prawns ambush the marsh-bass. For there are three kinds of them: some are such as I said before, others come from seaweed, and the third are rock-prawns. Being unable to defend themselves against the bass, they choose to die along with him. And I will not hesitate to tell their stratagem. When they perceive that they are being seized, the projecting part of the head — it resembles the ram of a trireme and is very sharp, and besides has notches like a saw — this the noble creatures cleverly turn round, and they leap and spring up lightly and nimbly. The bass gapes wide, and the parts of its throat are soft. So while it thinks, having seized the prawn now worn out, that it will have a dinner, the prawn in the freedom and open space leaps about, dancing, as one might say, all over its throat; then it fixes its spines into the wretched hunter, ulcerates his inner parts, and they, swelling up, pour out much blood and choke him; and so, in the strangest of ways, having killed him, it is destroyed.

A cock, whether you buy it or receive it as a gift, if you wish to count it among your own flock and your accustomed birds, you must not let it go and release it carelessly and at random; otherwise it will at once depart as a runaway to its own kin and fellows, even if these are very far off. You must throw about it a guard and invisible bonds beyond the Homeric chains of Hephaestus. And what I mean is this. Setting in the middle the table on which you eat, and taking the bird, and leading it three times round the said scene, then let it go from there to wander free with your household birds; and it will not depart, as though it were fettered.

These things too, it seems, were proper for the educated man to know. The cuckoo is most wise and most clever at weaving easy contrivances out of difficult straits. For it is conscious of itself that it cannot brood and hatch, on account of the coldness of the constitution in its body, as they say. So when it lays, it neither weaves a nest itself nor tends the young, but watches for the owners of the nests being away and wandering, and slipping into a stranger's lodging lays its eggs there. And it does not pounce on the nests of all birds, but of the lark, the wood-pigeon, the greenfinch, and the pappus; for it knows these lay eggs like its own. And when the nests are empty, it would not enter; but when there are eggs within, then it mingles in its own. And if those are many, it rolls some out and makes them disappear, and leaves its own, which cannot be discerned and detected because of the likeness. And the aforesaid birds hatch what in no way belongs to them, but those young, as they set firm, being conscious to themselves of their spurious birth, fly off and go to the parent that bore them; for when the feathers have grown about them they are recognized as alien, and are most bitterly maltreated. The cuckoo is seen one season of the year, the best; for at the beginning of spring it appears, until the rising of Sirius, and then withdraws from the sight of the many.

is like one exulting. And this too is surely worthy of wonder in the creature: when going under a doorway, even a very high one, it stoops, performing this most boastfully; for it seems to do so out of regard for its comb. Jackdaws love their own kind dreadfully. This is just what often destroys them, and the thing done is as follows. Whoever has a mind to hunt jackdaws contrives thus. Where he knows their feeding-grounds and pastures and sees them gathering in flocks, there he sets out basins full of oil. Now the oil is clear, and the bird is curious, and it comes and sits on the rim of the vessel, and bends down and sees its own reflection, and thinks it sees another jackdaw, and is eager to come down to it. So it descends and flaps its wings and covers itself with oil, and is least able to flutter up again, and without nets or snare or cords the creature remains, as one might say, fettered.

the eagles, and each of them, biting a stone so as not to scream, as though putting a bit in their own mouth, fly over in silence, and for the most part thus escape the eagles' notice. Now the goose, being most hot and fiery in nature, loves bathing and delights in swimming and most of all in the moistest foods—plants and lettuces and the rest, whatever produces coolness within them; and even if it should be wasting with hunger, it would not eat a laurel leaf, nor would it taste oleander, either willingly or unwillingly; for it knows that it will die if it eats any of these. But men through profligacy are plotted against both in food and in drink. Countless ones, at any rate, have swallowed something deadly while drinking, like Alexander, and while eating, like Claudius the Roman and Britannicus his son; and having lain down to sleep they did not rise again, by the use of poison, some having drunk it willingly, others by treachery. As for the fox-goose, its name has been woven from the peculiar and inborn traits of each animal. For it has the form of the goose, but in cunning it might most justly be matched against the fox. And it is smaller than a goose, but braver, and formidable at coming to close quarters. At any rate it defends itself against eagle and cat and the rest, whatever are its adversaries.

the boy died, the eagle followed even to the tomb; and when the body was being burned, it threw itself into the pyre. The fish called the hake has all its other internal organs not very different from those of others, but it is solitary and cannot endure to live with others. And of fish this one alone has its heart in its belly and stones in its brain, which resemble millstones in shape. And at the rising of Sirius it alone goes into its hole, while the others are accustomed to go into theirs in the most frosty seasons.

that befell the man of Teos which I have told. There is a kind of crab, and they are named mud crabs. They are whiter to look at than the others, and are born in the mud. When frightened, these even fly; for they have little wings, which gently lift and lighten them. So when walking they have no need of these at all, but when frightened they have a certain not very strong defence; for they are caught neither flying high nor able to travel aloft. These crabs some people eat; and they say too that they are good for pain in the hip, if one in pain should eat them.

The lion, when it walks, does not go straight forward, nor does it let the marks of its tracks be simple, but now it goes forward, now it goes back, and again it holds to its forward course, and indeed it darts in the opposite direction. Then it confounds its road, and makes it impossible for the hunters to go along its trail and easily to find the lair where it rests and dwells with its cubs. And these too are the lions' peculiar gifts of Nature.

form resembles the nature of speech. For the black wing-feathers might be compared to speech kept silent and turned over within, while the white might be compared to speech now uttered and heard, the servant and messenger, as one might say, of the speech within. That the creature is very long-lived I have already said; but Apion says, and brings forward as witnesses the priests of Hermopolis, that they showed him an immortal ibis. This seems, even to him, to stand very far from the truth, and to me it would surely appear false. The ibis is by nature very hot; at any rate it is a great eater and eats foul things, since it feeds on serpents and scorpions. But some of these it digests easily, and others it most readily voids. One would very rarely see a sick ibis. Though the ibis everywhere thrusts in its beak, despising filth and stepping into it in order to track down something even from there, yet when it turns to roost it first washes and cleanses itself. It nests in the palm trees, fleeing the cats; for that animal cannot easily climb up and creep up the palm, being often struck against and thrown off by the projections on the trunk. These things too about baboons have now come to my mind. If a baboon gets things that are to be cracked, together with their shells (I mean almonds and acorns and nuts), it shells and cleans them, first cracking them very intelligently, and it knows that the inside is edible, but the outside must be thrown away. It drinks wine, and when boiled and roasted meats are set before it, it fills itself, and it delights in seasoned dishes, but is much vexed at meats carelessly boiled. It is sparing too of clothing when it has put it on, and does the other things I have mentioned above. If you bring a baby still at the breast to a woman's nipple, it will draw the milk like an infant.
The bee-eater bird seems in this respect more righteous than the storks; for it does not wait to feed its parents when they have grown old, but does this as soon as it has grown its wing-feathers.

Tame fish, obedient to a call and gladly receiving food, both are and are reared in many places, as in Epirus, in the city that still stands, which they called of old Stephanepolis, in the temple of Fortune, in the cisterns on either side as one goes up; and in Helorus of Sicily, which was of old a fort of the Syracusans; and in the temple of Labrandean Zeus, in a spring of transparent water, and they have little gold necklaces and earrings, golden too. The temple of this Zeus is seventy stades distant from the city of the Mylasians. The statue has a sword hanging at its side, and he is honoured under the names Carian and Stratian; for the Carians first devised a market of war, and served for silver, and fastened handles to their shields, and fixed crests on their helmets. And they were called by this name from Car the son of Crete and Zeus; and Zeus Labrandeus got this title from raining "labros" and abundant. And in Chios too, in the so-called Harbour of the Old Men, there is a multitude of tame fish, which the Chians rear for the consolation of old age for their elders. And in the land between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris a spring is celebrated as being transparent to the depth and casting up water white to look at, and there comes from it a river named Aborrhas. And the natives sing over the name a sacred story too, and the story is this: Hera, after her marriage to Zeus, bathed there, as the Syrians say, and to this day the place breathes fragrance, and all the air round about is blended with it there. And there frisk shoals of tame fish.

the water-hunters outside cut the ice there; for they are engaged in the hunt, and check the way out for the fish. And when this has been done, that net, full of fish, thrusts and brings along with it the cut-out rock of ice, and the fishermen standing upon it seem to be borne along on a floating island. These too are things peculiar to the fish there, and not to be likened to other hunts. And Homer will grant me to say that these men receive a double wage, one from the river, one from the land, so that the same men are both sailors and farmers.

is ruled by itself, and indeed there was among them, when the male king failed, a certain queen who ruled the Pygmies, named Gerana, whom the Pygmies, deifying her, honoured with honours more august than befit a human being. From this, they say, her mind was carried away by the wind, and she set the goddesses at naught. Hera especially and Athena and Artemis and Aphrodite she said did not come even near to her beauty. So she was not to escape harm, sick with such things; for, by the anger of Hera, she changed from her original form into a most shameful bird, and she is the bird now called the crane, and she makes war on the Pygmies, because they drove her mad with excessive honour and destroyed her.

In Lycia, Callisthenes of Olynthus says, the goats too are sheared, just as everywhere the sheep are; for they grow exceedingly shaggy and thick-haired, so that, one might say, curls or coils of hair hang from them, and indeed the craftsmen who build ships use them, plaiting them into ropes.

Zenothemis says that a certain Paeonian lake bears fish which, if one casts them gasping to the cattle, the cattle eat very gladly, as the rest do the grass. But of the fish when dead the cattle would no longer partake, that writer says.

Bears and wolves and leopards and lions are confident in the sharpness of their claws and the cutting edge of their teeth; but the porcupine, I hear, has neither of these, yet is not left destitute of defensive weapons by nature. For against those who come to harm it, it shoots out the hairs on its back like arrows, and often hits the mark accurately, bristling its back; and those hairs leap forth as though shot from some bowstring.

The salamander is not one of the offspring of fire, like the so-called fire-born, but it takes courage and goes to grips with the flame, and strives to overcome it as an adversary. And the proof: it haunts the workmen and craftsmen who work with fire. Now so long as the fire is at its height for them, and they have it as a helper to their craft and a partner in their skill, they take no thought at all about this creature; but when the fire is quenched and dies down, and the bellows blow in vain, then indeed they know well that the said creature is working against them. So having tracked the beast out and punished it, the fire is thenceforth kindled for them, and is obedient, and is not quenched, being fed by their habitual use.

A lion fears a cock. And the basilisk too dreads the same bird, as they say, and trembles on seeing it, and hearing it crow is convulsed and dies. For this reason those who travel through Libya, the nurse of such creatures, in fear of the aforesaid basilisk take with them as a fellow-traveller and companion of the road a cock, which will rid them of so great an evil.

The elephant—some say it has tusks projecting, others horns. It has on each foot five toes, showing the beginnings of separation, but not divided. Hence indeed it is least able to swim. Its hind legs are shorter than its front ones; its breasts are by the armpits; it possesses a trunk more all-useful than a hand, and a short tongue; its gall, they say, is not by the liver but by the intestine. I learn that the elephant is pregnant for two years. Others say not so long, but agree it is eighteen months. It brings forth one as large as a yearling calf, and the calf draws the teat with its mouth. When inflamed to mating and burning with frenzy, it falls upon a wall and overturns it, and bends palm-trees, dashing its forehead against them after the manner of rams. It drinks water neither clear nor pure, but when it has muddied and stirred it. It sleeps standing upright; for to lie down and rise up again is laborious for it. The prime of an elephant is sixty years. It is least able to bear frost. It prolongs its life even to two hundred years.

These too are peculiar to the snake. Its heart is placed at the throat, its gall in the intestines; it has its testicles by the tail; it lays its eggs long and soft; and it carries its venom in its teeth.

Those who hunt crabs have contrived music as a bait against them. With a little pipe (this is the name of an instrument) they catch them. For some of the crabs have sunk into their holes, and others begin to come at the sound of the tune. And the crabs, hearing it, are persuaded as though by some spell to come forth from their chamber, then, drawn by the pleasure, they advance even outside the sea, and the pipers retreat step by step. And the crabs follow and are caught upon the land.

The hermit crabs are born naked, but they choose for themselves a shell to inhabit as the best of houses. They slip into the shell of a purple-fish, lighting upon an empty one, or of a whelk. And as long as it covers her, she rejoices in her lodging; but if she grows in flesh, she moves into another house. And she meets with many of those aforesaid.

Imagine for me a good herdsman, skilled in pasturing. Now the herdsman loves the sheep, and loves the goats too, but hates the hiccup. This is a disease that often befalls a man, and repletion brings the hiccup upon these animals too. So the herdsmen plant near the folds of the aforesaid animals a certain plant hostile to this affliction, and this plant wards off the evil from them. And those who have tried it say that this plant is good for men too against the same affliction.

The thermouthis asp, to which the Egyptians gave this name, they say is sacred, and the people there revere it, and they bind it about the statues of Isis as a kind of royal diadem. They say that it was born not for the harm and hurt of men; and they tell this marvel, that it spares the good but kills the impious. If this is so, Justice would value this asp at the highest price, since it punishes on her behalf and sees most keenly.
