Others add that Isis sends it against those who have committed the greatest offences. The Egyptians say that it alone of asps is immortal, reckoning sixteen kinds and varieties of this animal. And in the temples, as they themselves say, building in each corner certain chambers and crypt-like burrows, they then settled thermouthides there, setting calf's fat before them as food at intervals.

This too, it seems, is a peculiar good thing of animals. The gods take forethought for them, and neither despise them nor hold them in slight regard. For even if a creature has no share of reason, yet at least it is not unfortunate in understanding and the wisdom proper to itself. How, then, the animals too are loved by the gods I shall tell, and if not many examples out of many, yet enough. A horseman, Lenaeus by name, had a horse fair to look at, very swift to run, and most brave in spirit; and it was good in the displays at running through the cavalry-drill it had been taught, and steadfast in war itself, and very noble both at pursuing where there was need and at retreating where the occasion called him. So from all these things it was a good possession, and he seemed most renowned among his fellow-cavalrymen. This horse, then, of such a kind, was unable to see with one of its eyes, the right, owing to a blow that had fallen upon it. So Lenaeus, seeing all his hope tottering in the affliction of that noble horse — since indeed the cavalry shield also covered for him the left eye, the only one that saw — comes to the temple of Sarapis, bringing the horse as a most unusual patient, and Lenaeus beseeches the god, as on behalf of some brother or son, to pity the suppliant the horse, and that too one who had wronged him in nothing. For men, he said, are causes of evil to themselves, either by doing some impious thing or by saying something forbidden; "but of a horse," he said, "what sacrilege, what murder, what blasphemy, or how or whence?" And he himself called the god to witness that he had never wronged anyone in anything, and for this reason he begged him to deliver his fellow-soldier and friend from the eye-disease. And the god did not despise nor make light of healing the speechless and reasonless creature, great a god though he is, and for this reason he pitied both the sick one and the one who prayed on its behalf, and gave a cure: not to drench the eye, but to warm it with fomentations at midday in the precinct of the temple. And these things were done, and the horse's eye was made strong. And Lenaeus offered thank-offerings and life-ransoms, but the horse frisked and snorted and seemed greater and fairer, and was bright and ran to the altar and gloried, and indeed was seen rolling at the foot of the steps, paying thank-offerings to the god its saviour, as far as it had strength.

The peculiarities of animals not even the gods disdain to know. I hear, at any rate, that Eurysthenes and Procles, the sons of Aristodemus the son of Aristomachus the son of Cleodaeus the son of Hyllus the son of Heracles, wishing to take wives, came to Delphi and asked the god with whom of Greeks or barbarians they might form an alliance and then seem to have married well and prudently; and the god answered them to go back to Lacedaemon, and to return by that road by which they had come. And in whatever country there should meet them the most savage animal carrying the gentlest, there they should arrange their marriages; for thus it would be better for them. And they obeyed, and they come to the land of the Cleonaeans, and a wolf meets them carrying a lamb that it had snatched from some flock. They conjectured, then, that these animals were what the oracle meant, and they married the daughters of Thersander the son of Cleonymus, a man of repute. And if the gods know the gentlest animal and the most savage, it is not unfitting for us either to know their natures.

Ctesias says, in his Indian accounts, that the people called the Cynamolgi keep many dogs the size of Hyrcanian hounds, and that they are mighty keepers of dogs. And the Cnidian gives these reasons. From the summer solstice to mid-winter there come upon them herds of oxen, like a swarm of bees or a stirred-up wasps' nest, the oxen too many to count; and they are wild and insolent, and rage terribly with their horns. So, having no other way to drive them off, the people loose upon them their bred dogs, reared for this very purpose, which overcome and destroy the oxen with ease. Then of the flesh they take out what seems to them fit for eating, and the rest they set apart for the dogs, very gladly sharing with them, as though making first-offerings to benefactors. And in the season when the oxen no longer come, they keep the dogs as fellow-hunters against the other creatures. And of the females they milk the milk, and from this they get their name; for they drink it, just as we drink that of sheep and goats.

Among the Armenians, I hear, there is a high rock, and this casts out very much water. Beneath the rock, I learn, there lies a spring four-square on every side, and each side is half a stade long, and the depth is three fathoms. There fall out together with the aforesaid water, I further hear, fish often a cubit in length, and even larger, and indeed smaller ones too, but not by much. And some of them slide down half-dead, while others gasp and, struggling violently, die. Rumour says that they are exceedingly black and unsightly to look upon. And if either man or beast tastes of them, it perishes at once. The Armenians, then, because their land is full of game and abounding in beasts, gather these fish and dry them under the sun's heat, then pound them, having bound something over their nostrils and their mouth, so that they may not, drawing in with their breath the air from the pounded fish, then die. So, having made the fish into flour, they sow it in the regions most full of beasts, and they are wont to mix figs in with the flour. In this way there perish the wild boars and the gazelles and the deer and the bears and the wild asses and the goats — wild ones too, these; for these creatures eat figs and barley-meal. But lions and leopards and wolves, being flesh-eaters, they kill otherwise. For having cut open the side of tame sheep and goats, far enough to let the hand down, they stuff in the same flour, so that there lies, by Zeus, an evil bait for the aforesaid. So when a lion or a leopard or a wolf or any other such beast meets it and tastes it, it dies at once. And the whole of Armenia is at once nurse and mother of wild beasts, and the plain country still more, and that by the river most of all.

A terrible evil and a savage disease is enmity and inborn hatred, if indeed it is fixed even in the irrational creatures and is hard for them too to wash out. The moray hates the octopus, the octopus is at war with the crayfish, and the crayfish is most hostile to the moray. For the moray cuts through the octopus's tentacles with the sharpness of its teeth, and then, slipping even into its belly, does the same things, and reasonably; for she is a swimmer, while the octopus is like a crawling thing; and even if it changes its colour to match the rocks, this stratagem seems to profit it not at all, for she is clever at seeing through the creature's trick. The crayfish, however — they seize and crush to death, and when they have made corpses of them, they suck out their flesh. But the crayfish, raising up its own horns and growing angry with them, challenges the moray. So she, not considering the spikes which the crayfish holds out as a defence, bites at them; but he, stretching out his claws like hands, holds her firmly on either side of the neck and does not let go. And she frets and coils herself and presses against the points of the shell, which, fixing into her, numb her and make her give up; and at last she lies slackened, and he makes the adversary his dinner.

The swan, which poets and many accounts free of metre have given as a servant to Apollo — how it stands in other respects with regard to music and song, I cannot say; but it has been believed by men of older time that, having sung what is called the swan-song, it then dies. And nature honours it more than even fine and good men, and reasonably; if indeed such men are both praised and lamented by others, while those swans, whichever you please of these, perform for themselves.

Crete is most hostile both to wolves and to creeping beasts. And I hear Theophrastus saying that on Macedonian Olympus too there are places impassable to wolves. The Cephallenian goats, it seems, do not drink for six months. And the sheep of Budinum you will not see white, as they say, but all black. A difference too and peculiarity of animals would lie in this: some of them are biters and inject poison from their tooth, while those are strikers which, having struck, then likewise inject such an evil.

The sheep-rearing of the Indians is worth learning what it is like. I am told that their goats and sheep are larger than the largest asses, and that each bears four; indeed an Indian goat or sheep would never bear fewer than three. The tails of the sheep reach to the foot, but the goats have very long ones, so as almost to touch the ground. Now from the sheep that are good at bearing the herdsmen cut off the tails, so that they may be mounted, and from their fat they press out oil too; but of the males they cut through the tails and take out the fat and sew them up again, and the cut grows together once more, and the traces of it disappear.

To the peacock, the aforesaid bird, these traits too are natural and peculiar, which are worth learning. At three years old it begins to conceive and brings forth, and then begins the many-coloured beauty of its feathers. It broods not on successive days, but leaving an interval of two days. The peacock too might lay wind-eggs, as other birds also do.

Those who dwell by the lake Mareia hunt the shad there with the clearest of songs and a clapping of shells keeping time with the tune; and the fish, as though dancing to the music, leap up, and fall into the nets, which are spread out for them, and the Egyptians take a fine catch of fish with dancing and play.

The whelks even have a king, and are ruled very obediently. And this king is the greatest in size and the most beautiful in beauty. If it is better to sink down, he does this first; if to rise up, of this too he leads the way; and as he shifts his place, the rest follow. And whoever takes this king knows well that he will fare the better for it. And indeed, if anyone should see it caught, he goes away in better spirits, as though he too would have some good fortune. At Byzantium too a prize is set for the man who has caught the whelk aforesaid; the fellow fishermen each give an Attic drachma to the one who has taken it, and this is the prize.

Those whose business it is to gather henbane and its juice dig pits round about and loosen the roots, but they do not pull them up with their own hands, but having caught or bought some winged creature, they tie one of its two feet to the plant. And it, writhing, then pulls the plant up. And both are profitable for the uses men have of them. But if one should not pull it up in this way, he gets in another fashion what he thinks a fair and useful treasure he has taken.

The bird Acanthus took its name, the experts in birds say, from the thistles that nourish it. It utters a tuneful and wonderfully musical song. Aristotle says that if one mixes the blood of this Acanthus and of the so-called aegithus into the same vessel and wishes to blend them, they will not come together nor unite into a single mixture. They say the Acanthus is sacred to the spirits that escort men along the road and guide them.

In a vineyard a farmer was digging a trench, that he might plant a fair and noble vine-shoot; then, bringing down his mattock, he unawares cut through the middle a sacred asp that was lurking there, an asp least hostile to men. And carding the earth, seeing the tail-part held fast in the sand, but the half from the belly up to the neck still creeping and full of the gore from the cut, he is struck with terror, and becoming out of his mind he passes into downright madness and as strong as could be. And by day he was without mastery of himself and of his reason, and by night too he was raving, and would start up from his couch and say he was pursuing the asp, and as though he were all but at the very biting, he would cry out most terrifyingly and call for allies, and indeed he said he saw the image of the creature slain by him, raging and threatening, and he confessed at times even to have been bitten, and that he was in pain was plain from his groanings. When, however, the disease was far advanced in time, his kinsmen lead the man as a suppliant to the temple of Sarapis, and begged the god to check and make disappear the phantom of the aforesaid creature. The god, then, pities the man and heals him; but that the asp did not remain unavenged has been said, and quite sufficiently.

The land of the Indians bears many and various things. And some are evidences of a happy and wondrous productiveness, but others are not enviable nor such as to be worthy of praise or longing. And concerning the profitable or the luxurious and costly things I have said some, and others shall be told, with the help of the gods; but for the present I am set to tell how the land displays a brood of serpents. It bears many and various ones, and what is left over is past counting for the inexperienced. These serpents, then, harm both men and the other animals. But the same land bears also herbs that ward off the bites, and the natives have experience and wisdom of them, and have learned what drug is the antidote to which serpent, and they help one another as quickly as possible, trying to cut short the spreading of the venom over the body, which is very sharp and swift. And these things the country sends up to them for their necessary aid very readily and abundantly. But a serpent that kills a man, as the Indians say (and they bring forward as witnesses many of the Libyans and those of the Egyptians who dwell about Thebes), can no longer go down and creep into its own home, the earth not receiving it, but casting it out of its own bosom, as one might say, an exile. And from then on it goes about a wanderer and a vagabond, and is wretched in the open air both through summer and through winter, and neither does its mate any longer come near it, nor do its own offspring recognize their father. Such a punishment, then, for the slaying of man was shown by nature even to the brute beasts, by the forethought of the divine, according to my recollection; and it has been told for the instruction of him who understands.

Aeschylides, in his work on farming, says that in the land of the Ceans few sheep are bred by each of the farmers. The reason is that Ceos is exceedingly thin-soiled and has no pastures; so they give them tree-medick and fig-leaves, and the fallen leaves of the olive, and indeed the chaff of various pulses, and they sow thistles besides, and these things are a good meal for them. From these is got milk, and this, when worked, makes most excellent cheese; it is called Cythnian, says the same writer, and indeed a talent of it sells for ninety drachmas. There are bred also lambs splendid in their season, and they sell not like the others, but at a haughtier price.

In the Caspian land, I hear, there is a very great lake, and great fishes are bred in it, called sturgeon. So the Caspians hunt them, and sprinkling them with salt and making them into salt-fish and drying them, they load them on camels and carry them to Ecbatana. And they make an unguent from these fishes, taking off the fat, and they anoint themselves with the fish-oil, very greasy and not ill-smelling; and they draw out the entrails of the fish and boil them, and from these they make a glue able to be very useful; for it holds everything strongly, and clings to whatever it is joined to, and is most bright to look upon. And it so holds together whatever it binds and fastens, that even when soaked ten days it is neither loosened nor comes apart. Indeed, those who work ivory use it too, and finish their works most excellently.

The open sea feeds the moray-fish. When the net surrounds her, she swims about and seeks very cleverly either a wide mesh or a tear in the net; and finding one of these and slipping through, she swims free again. And if one of them chances on this good fortune, all the rest of the same kind that have been caught with her get out by her escape, as though they had taken a path from a guide.

How great a crocodile is, both the full-grown and the one first hatched, and indeed how its tongue is, and whether it moves its jaw, and which one it brings against the other, many tell. And some have noted of this creature that it lays as many eggs as the days in which, after brooding, it hatches its young. And I myself have heard that when the crocodile dies, a scorpion is born from it, and they say it has a tail-sting filled with venom.
The Libyan asp, I hear, blinds the sight of one who looks back against its breath; but the other kind does not blind, but kills most easily.

Alexander of Myndus says that the chameleon harasses snakes and brings them to starvation in the following way. Biting on a broad, firm twig, it turns itself about and comes face to face against the enemy. The snake is unable to lay hold of it, having no way to gape wide enough to take in the breadth of the twig. So the snake remains, as far as the chameleon is concerned, without its dinner; for biting the rest of its limbs it accomplishes nothing, since the chameleon has a firm hide, and feels nothing at all of the snake's teeth.

The duck, when it lays, lays on dry ground, but near a lake or marsh or some other watery and dewy place. And the duckling by a certain peculiar and secret instinct knows that it has no share either in flight aloft or in life on dry land. And from these it leaps into the water, and is a swimmer from birth, and needs no teaching, but dives and rises most cleverly, as though it had long been trained in this. But the eagle which they call the duck-killer leaps upon the swimming duck as if to seize it; and the duck, diving, makes itself disappear, then swimming under, peeps out elsewhere. And the eagle is there too, and again the duck dives, and again this happens, and again. And one of two things: either it is drowned in diving, or the eagle withdraws to another prey, while the duck, having safety, swims on the surface again.

I learn that the Egyptians by a certain native magic bring down the birds from the sky; and the snakes, having bewitched them from their holes with certain incantations, they then lead out most easily.

The surge, rolling the sea urchins outward and dashing them against the dry land, casts them out most violently. Fearing this, then, whenever they perceive the wave bristling and about to rise up larger, they take up with their spines little stones, such as are easy for them to carry, and they have ballast, and are not easily rolled over, nor do they suffer what they fear.

As for southernwood, what good things it does, and how it gives passages to the breath, and indeed is a cleanser of the lung, this is not the time to tell; but at any rate it is an enemy to a noxious creature, and destroys the tapeworm, which, when it goes on further, becomes a beast engendered in the entrails, but reckoned among human diseases—and that among those most incurable and impossible to be brought to a cure by a mortal hand. To attest this Hippys too is sufficient. And what the writer of Rhegium says is of this kind. A woman had a tapeworm, and the most skilled of the physicians despaired of curing her. So she came to Epidaurus, and begged the god that she might be freed of the affliction that dwelt with her. The god was not present; the sacristans, however, laid the woman down where the god was wont to heal those who needed it. And the woman lay quiet, as she had been bidden, while those who served the god did what was needful for her cure, and they took her head off from her neck, and one of them put in his hand and drew out the tapeworm, a great thing of a beast. But to fit and restore the head to its former joining they were no longer able. So the god arrives, and was angry with them, that they had attempted a task too great for their own skill; but he himself, by some irresistible and divine power, restored the head to the body, and raised up the stranger. And not at all, O lord Asclepius, most humane of the gods, do I set southernwood against your skill—may I never go so mad—but it came to my mind, and I made mention of your beneficence and your astonishing cure. And that this plant too is your gift one must not even doubt.

That the turtle-dove is chaste, and would never, apart from her mate to whom she joined herself from the first, consort and welcome a strange and alien bed, I have said above. But I hear from those exact in the inquiry about such matters that white turtle-doves have often appeared. They say these are sacred to Aphrodite and Demeter, but the others to the Fates and the Furies.

The king of the Egyptians, having received as an Indian gift a peacock, the greatest and fairest of peacocks to look at, does not think fit to rear it with the common ones, as though it were a household plaything or for the belly's sake, but dedicates it to Zeus the Guardian of the City, judging the bird aforesaid a worthy offering to the god. A profligate young man, and very rich too, longs to seize it and make a dinner of it; for always and on every occasion this profligate gratified his belly, accounting the variety of food, and what was procured with danger, and what was bought with many toils, gain toward pleasure, in his excess of gluttony and loathsomeness. So he holds out a generous wage for the sacrilege to one of the god's attendants, and promises another besides. And he, lightened by an empty hope, went where he knew the bird roosted and attempted to seize it and bring it to the rich man. And he does not see it, but saw a very great asp upright and enraged against him. And at first he was afraid and went off, but as the profligate pressed and urged him on, the servant went after the peacock, but it, darting higher and raising itself on its wings and lifted light, settled neither on any of the sacred trees nor on any other high and lofty place, but on the middle of the temple, and looked at them unflinchingly, as though hinting that it was by nature superior to the plot from them, and that it was not theirs to take it. So when nothing had been accomplished, the profligate demanded back the silver he had paid in advance, but the other would not give it back, saying that he had done all that was his, but was unable to steal a possession of the gods. As was natural, then, there was strife about these things and by now an outcry, and many heard; then the priest set over all comes up, and asks the ground of the quarrel in the temple, and they accuse one another. And the rich man, abused with threats and blasphemies and revilings, departs, and swallowing the bone of another bird and in pain ended his life most painfully, and the wicked servant, as a temple-robber, the governor of the city punished, but the bird they beheld neither living nor dead, but, having lived loud and famous a hundred years, as the story goes, it then disappeared.

Dogs, it seems, are more useless than geese at guarding, and the Romans detected this. The Celts were warring against them, and having very strongly pushed them back, they were in the city itself, and Rome had been taken by them except the Capitoline hill; for it was not easily accessible to them. The places that seemed able to receive an assailant with a plot were fortified. And it was the time when Marcus Mallius, being consul, was guarding the aforesaid hill committed to him. This is the man who both crowned his son with a garland for valour, and yet killed him because he had left his own post. When the Celts saw that all sides were impassable for them, they resolved, in the dead of night, lying in ambush, then to fall upon men sleeping most deeply, and they hoped it would be accessible to them by the unguarded part, where there was quiet, the Romans having believed that the Gauls would not attack from there. And indeed by this both he himself and the citadel of Zeus would have been most ingloriously taken, had not geese chanced to be present; for the dogs kept silent before the food that was thrown them, but it is peculiar to geese to cry out at things thrown to them for food and not to keep still. So they roused Mallius, screaming, and the guard about him. For this the dogs pay penalties among the Romans even now, every year, in memory of that ancient betrayal, but a goose is honoured on appointed days, and goes forth in a litter very ceremoniously.

Phoenician accounts say that the native cattle there are so great in size that the milkers, even the very tallest, stand, or need a stool, that climbing up they may reach the udders. Among the Libyans bordering on the Indians, I hear, there are certain herds of backward-grazing oxen. The reason is that Nature, having at first erred or been careless, set the horns before their eyes, and does not let them see what is before their feet; and she turns their walk toward the rear, and so, stooping down, they crop the grass. Aristotle, however, says that in the cattle of the Neuri the horns and the ears grow from the same outgrowth, and are woven together. The same writer says that in a certain region of the Libyans the goats have their teats hanging from the breast. The following too might be the son of Nicomachus's: among the Budini who dwell about Cariscus, he says, no white sheep is born, but all are black.

A certain account says that among the Caspians there is bred a bird the size of the largest cocks, variegated and flowered with many colours. It flies, I hear, on its back, having stretched its legs out beneath its neck and as it were holding itself up by them. It gives out a cry like a puppy's. It makes its flight not in the deep air but near the ground, being unable to lighten itself to a height. This bird too is Caspian, or rather Indian (for it is said to be of that breed there as well), and it would be the size of a goose. And it has a head broad but thin, and long legs. Its colour is blended and mixed; for its back is adorned with purple, and the parts under the belly are likened to the most genuine and most beautiful scarlet, and the head and neck are both white. It cries like a goat.

When the good hunters of the cuttlefish are about to take her, she, perceiving it, releases her own dark juice and pours it over herself, and conceals and hides herself entirely, and steals away the fisherman's sight; and she is before his eyes, but he does not see her. Some such thing Poseidon did when, casting a cloud about Aeneas, he deceived Achilles, as Homer says.

If these things are clear and not disputed, let the accounts of the Indians convince. What I shall now tell, the report from there carrying it across, is this. I myself heard from the son of Nicomachus that there is a bird with the same name as the plant cinnamon, and that the bird brings this plant of like name to the Indians, but that men know nothing at all of where or how it grows.

Epirote cows are said to be milked in very great abundance, and Scyrian goats to give the most plentiful milk, as much as no other goats. And some Egyptian goats bear five at a birth, and most bear twins. And the Nile is said to be the cause, providing water most productive of offspring. Whence indeed the herdsmen who are very fond of fine beasts and careful of their own flock bring water from the Nile to their own herds by every possible device, and to the barren ones still more. To Ptolemy the Second, they say, a horn was brought from the Indians, and it held three amphorae. What sort of ox, then, that one was, to have grown so great a horn!

The lion's neck is composed of a single bone, not of many vertebrae. And if anyone cleaves the lion's bones, fire leaps out from them. They have no marrow; for they are not hollow after the manner of pipes. No season of the year holds it back from mating. It is pregnant for two months. It bears five times: at the first birth five, at the second four, three at the next, two at the one after, and one at all the last. The newborn cubs are small and blind like puppies; they begin to walk when they have lived two months from birth. The story that says they tear apart the womb is a myth. A hungry lion is hard to meet, but a sated one is most gentle; and they say it is then fond of play. A lion would never flee turning its back, but quietly retreats step by step, looking the foe in the face. When old age begins, it comes to the steadings and the huts and the cave-dwellings of the herdsmen, and with reason; for it can no longer take heart for the hunts on the mountains. It dreads fire. Now whichever of them is rounder and more compact and shaggier in mane seems more faint-hearted and less daring; but the one well-grown in length and straight-haired is believed more manly and more spirited. Being a glutton, it would, they say, swallow whole limbs by gulping. So when filled with these it often does not eat for three days, until what it first took has been consumed and digested. It drinks little.

The swan surpasses men in the greatest matters; for it knows when the end of life comes to it, and moreover, having received from nature this most beautiful gift, it bears its approach with good cheer; for it is convinced that there is nothing painful or grievous in death. But men dread what they do not know, and consider it the greatest of evils. So great is the cheerfulness that abounds in the swan, that even at the close of its life it sings and strikes up, as it were, a funeral song for itself. Such a one, prepared for death heroically and greatly, does Euripides hymn in Bellerophon. At any rate he has made him say to his own soul, "You were ever pious toward the gods, while you lived, and you helped strangers, and never wearied for your friends," and what follows upon this. So the swan too sings a kind of funeral music for itself, giving as provision for its journey either hymns of the gods or some praise of its own. And Socrates too bears witness to it, that it sings not grieving but rather rejoicing; for one who has anything grievous and painful against his soul would never have leisure for song and music. And the swan is brave not only toward death, but also toward battles. It does not begin unjust acts, like a temperate and well-bred man, but from one who has begun it neither withdraws nor yields. Now the other birds are at peace and at truce with one another, but the eagle has often rushed upon this one too, as Aristotle says, and yet never once overcame it, but was always beaten, the swan fighting not only with strength but defending itself also with justice.

The beaver is an amphibious animal, and by day it lives sunk in the rivers, but by night it roams on the land, feeding on whatever it meets. So it knows the reason why the hunters come against it with all eagerness and onset, and stooping and biting it cuts off its own testicles and throws them to them, like a prudent man who, falling among robbers, lays down all that he is carrying for the sake of his own safety, exchanging these, of course, as a ransom. And if it has previously cut them off and been saved, and is then pursued again, it raises itself up and shows that it has not the object of their zeal, and so frees the hunters from further toil; for they have less concern for its flesh. And often, even while still entire, having run off as far as possible, then drawing up the part that is sought for, most cleverly and craftily they deceive, as though they had not what they kept hidden.

The purple-fish is exceedingly greedy, and has a rather long tongue, and inserts it through everything that it can, and through this it draws in whatever it eats, and through this too it is caught. And the manner of the hunt is this. A small but close-woven wicker trap is plaited; and within it has a whelk, and this is fastened in the middle of the trap. It is a struggle, then, for the purple-fish to stretch out its tongue and reach the whelk; and it must thrust out its whole tongue, if it is not to miss what it longs for. And having inserted its tongue, it sucks; then its tongue swells with fullness, and it is unable to draw it out again. So it remains caught, and the purple-fisher, perceiving it, has caught, in second place, the creature that its own greed first chose.

The nautilus is itself also an octopus, and has a single shell. So it swims up, turning the shell about the lower part, that it may not draw in the brine and so push itself down again; but when it is on the waves, when there is calm and a peace of the winds, it turns the shell on its back—and it floats like a ferryboat—and putting out two tentacles on this side and that, and stirring them gently, it rows and pushes forward its connatural ship. But if there is a wind, having first stretched out the oars it makes them longer rudders, and raising up other tentacles, between which is a very thin membrane, it spreads this and makes it a sail. So it sails in this manner when it is without fear; but if it is frightened by any of the larger creatures, sinking the shell it fills it, and slips down by the weight, and having hidden itself it escapes its enemy. Then, when it is at peace, it springs up and sails again. And from these things it has its name.

White swallows too have sometimes been seen, as Alexander of Myndus says. In the tent of Alexander the son of Pyrrhus a swallow built her nest, and then signified to him that the enterprise on which he was setting out would be left unfulfilled, being not at all good. And to Antiochus too a swallow nesting in his quarters hinted at what was to befall him; for going up to the Medes he then did not return to the Syrians, but threw himself down from a certain cliff. And he too had set out upon an enterprise that was not good. When Dionysius first left the citadel, the swallows nesting there went up together with him, and prophesied his return. The swallow is honoured by the gods of the inner chamber, and by Aphrodite, of the inner chamber too in this case.

This too resembles and agrees with that. A man named Cissus, who served Sarapis devotedly, having been plotted against by her who was first his beloved and afterward his wife, and having eaten serpent's eggs, was in pain and ill, and was expected to die. He beseeches the god, and the god bade him buy a living moray and put his hand into the live-tank. And Cissus obeys and puts it in, and the moray, fastening on, held to it, and being drawn off, drew off together with itself the disease in the young man. This moray, then, having become a minister of the god's healing, has come to our hearing.

And these things too about animals are not beside the Muse to tell. The Scythians, from lack of wood, boil whatever they sacrifice with the bones of the animals themselves. And the Phrygians, if anyone among them kills a plough-ox, the penalty for him is death. The Sagaraeans hold a contest of camels for Athena every year with reverence for the goddess, and these camels among them are very fleet and swift. The Saracori have their asses neither as burden-bearers nor as grinders, but as warriors, and on them they endure the dangers of battle, just as the Greeks do on horses. And whichever of their asses seems to be the most braying, this one they bring as a sacred offering to Ares. Clearchus of the Peripatetic school says that the Argives alone of the Peloponnesians do not kill a serpent; and on the days which the same people call "lamb-days," if a dog comes into the marketplace, they kill it. In Thessaly the man about to marry, sacrificing the marriage-feast, brings in a war-horse wearing its bridle and the whole panoply of war; then, when he has finished the rite and poured libation, leading the horse by the rein he hands it over to the bride. What this means, let the Thessalians tell. The people of Tenedos rear a pregnant cow for Dionysus the man-render, and when she has calved they tend her like a woman in childbed. But the new-born calf they sacrifice, having put buskins on it. And the one who has struck it with the axe is pelted with stones by the people, and flees as far as the sea. The Eretrians sacrifice mutilated victims to Artemis at Amarynthus.

Nymphodorus says that Sardinia is a good mother of flocks. And it is worth marvelling at the creature this land breeds — the goats. For the natives wear the skins, and these are a covering; in winter they keep warm, and in summer they cool, by some secret nature; and the hair, a cubit long, grows fast to the skins. This garment, it seems, must in the cold have the hairs turned toward the skin, and in the summer outward, if the wearer is to be warmed in the cold and not stifled in the summer.

The Caspian goats are exceedingly white, without horns, and small in size and flat-nosed. The camels are too many to count, the greatest of them the size of the greatest horses, and very fine-haired. For their hair is exceedingly soft, so that in softness it rivals the Milesian wool. So from this the priests, and the richest and most powerful of the Caspians, clothe themselves in garments.

Even the irrational animals guard against the eyes of the envious and of sorcerers, by some secret and wonderful instinct. I hear, at any rate, that as a defence against the evil eye the wood-pigeons bite off little sprigs of laurel and then put them in their nests for the protection of their nestlings; the kites use buckthorn, the hawks sow-thistle, the turtle-doves the fruit of the iris, the ravens chaste-tree, the hoopoes maidenhair — which some call beautiful-hair — the crow vervain, the hen-harrier ivy, the heron crab, the partridge a tuft of reed, and the thrushes a spray of myrtle. The lark too sets dog's-tooth grass before it, and the eagles the stone which from them is called eagle-stone. This stone is said to be good also for pregnant women, being an enemy to miscarriages.

The Egyptians say that they learned clysters and purging of the belly from no human invention, but they sing that the ibis is their teacher of this cure. And how it taught those who first saw it, let another tell; that it knows the waxing and waning of the moon, this too I have heard. And that it takes away and adds to its own food according to the goddess's diminishing and increase, I will not deny having learned somewhere.

You would never hear one single cry from all partridges, but they are different. And at Athens those beyond the deme of the Corydallians sound one note, and those on this side another. And what the names of these cries are, Theophrastus will tell. But in Boeotia and the Euboea opposite they are of like voice and, as one might say, of like tongue. Wholly voiceless are the frogs in Cyrene, and the swine in Macedonia. And there is a kind of cicada, these too voiceless.

The gentle ox would never forget the one who strikes and chastises it, but remembering, it takes vengeance even after an interval of time. For while under the yoke and in a way penned up, it is like a prisoner and keeps quiet; but when released, often it has struck with its leg and crushed some limb of the herdsman, and often, growing angry, has fallen upon him with its horn and killed him. Yet toward the others it is gentle, and comes into the stall quietly; for it is not savage toward those against whom it has no cause for anger.

The heron is clever at eating oysters, and swallows them closed, just as the pelicans do the cockles. And in what is called its crop the heron warms the oysters and keeps them; and they gape open from the heat, and it, perceiving this, vomits up the shells but keeps the flesh, and has its food, consuming whole, by the power of digestion, what has passed within.
The buprestis is a creature which, if an ox swallows it, the ox is inflamed and bursting dies not long after.

The scolopendra is a sea creature, and to look at is most like the land creature; and if human flesh touches it, it is at once stung and itches, and suffers such things as it does from the plant which they call the nettle. Sea nettles too cause itching, but not yet so much. They are more fit for eating after the equinox is past.

To three hundred fathoms, they say, the things in the sea are visible to men, but no further. Whether fishes swim still below this, or beasts too, or whether these regions are untrodden even by them, and the sea gods and the spirits of the deep have been allotted the place, and indeed the lord of the watery element—neither do I busy myself to inquire, nor does anyone else tell.

When partridges are brooding upon their eggs, they set before them certain bushes and other thickets, to keep off dews and rains and everything moist. For if the eggs become wet, unless the mother comes quickly again and warms them beneath her, they become barren. She lays as many as fifteen eggs together. Theophrastus says somewhere that the partridges of Paphlagonia are seen to have a double heart. Others say that the partridge is a plaything of the son of Zeus and Leto.

Chrysermus too, in the time of Nero, vomiting blood and already wasting away, this same god healed by his drinking bull's blood. And I say these things because animals are so beloved of the gods that they are even saved by the gods, and save others when those gods will it. Moreover this god made Basilis the Cretan, who had fallen into a wasting disease, free of so great an evil by tasting the flesh of an ass. And it fell out that this happened to him according to the name of the animal; for the god said this treatment and cure would be "profit-bringing" to him. And concerning these matters these things too are enough.

I have learned, besides what I have already related, that there were dogs loving their master, those of Xanthippus the son of Ariphron. For when the Athenians were removing to the ships, at the time when the Persian kindled the great war against Greece, and the oracles said it was better for the Athenians to abandon their fatherland and embark on the triremes, the dogs of the aforesaid man were not left behind either, but removed together with Xanthippus, and swimming across to Salamis they expired. And Aristotle and Philochorus tell these things.

What then? Shall we leave Orthagoras without mention? He says, in his Indian accounts, that there is a village called Coytha, taking its name in this way, and that to the native goats, within their pens, the herdsmen throw dried fish for fodder.

In his Cretan accounts, Antenor says that upon the city of the people called the Raucii there came, by some divine visitation, a swarm of bees, which are sung of as bronze-coloured, and that, driving their stings into the people, they grieved them most bitterly. The people, unable to bear the assault, rose up from their fatherland and came to another place, and out of love for their mother-city — to speak in the Cretan way — founded Raucus, since, even though the deity drove them from the place, they would not endure to be wholly torn away from the name. Antenor says that still upon Cretan Ida there are likenesses of that breed of bees, not many, but there are some, and bitter to encounter, as those were.

The fish called the torpedo, whatever it touches, gives it its own name and makes it numb. The ship-holder holds back ships, and from what it does we call it so. When the halcyon is breeding the seas stand still, and the winds keep peace and friendship. It breeds in the middle of winter, and yet the calm of the air gives fine weather, and at that season we have what we call halcyon days. A horse by chance treads on a wolf's track, and a numbness seizes it. And if you throw a wolf's knuckle-bone under a four-horse team as it runs, it will stand as though fixed, the horses having trodden on the knuckle-bone. The lion sets the leaves of the holm-oak on his footprint, and goes numb; and the wolf too, if he only comes near the leaves of the squill. For this reason the foxes throw these into the lairs of wolves, and reasonably; for because of the wolves' plots against them they regard them as their bitterest enemies.

The most bitter sting, and bringing danger more than all, the stingray from the sea has. And the proof: if you should fix it into a flourishing tree running well up with growth, neither after delay nor later in time but at once the tree is withered; and if you should scratch any of the creatures, you have killed it.

There is, they say, a kind of venomous spider, and they call the spider rhax, either because it is black and truly resembles a grape-berry and somehow looks round too, or for another reason. It is found in Libya, and has small feet; and it has been allotted a mouth in the middle of its belly, and it is very swift to kill.

The land of the Indians—the historians say it is rich in drugs and dreadfully prolific of such growths. Some of them preserve and rescue from danger those who, through bites, are at death's door (and there are many such things there), while others destroy and kill most swiftly—among which would be that produced from the purple snake. Now this snake is about a span long to look at, and in colour resembles the deepest purple. They describe its head as white and no longer purple, and white not, so to speak, ordinarily, but beyond snow and milk. This snake is toothless. It is found in the most fiery regions of India. It is least apt to bite, and in this respect you would say it is tame and gentle; but whomever it vomits upon, as I hear, whether man or beast, that limb must wholly rot away. So when it has been caught they hang it up by the tail, and as is natural it has its head down and looks toward the ground; and beneath its very mouth they place a vessel made of bronze. And through the mouth drops trickle from it into this, and what flows down sets and congeals, and on seeing it you would say it was the gum of an almond. And the snake dies, and they take away the vessel and set another in its place, of bronze too; and from the dead snake there flows again a watery ichor, and it resembles water. They leave it three days, and this too sets. And there would be a difference between the two in colour; for the one is dreadfully black, while the other is like amber. Now of this, if you gave to anyone as much as a sesame seed mixed into wine or food, first a convulsion will seize him, and a very strong one, then his eyes are distorted, and his brain slips out, trickling through his nostrils, and he dies most pitiably; but if he takes less of the drug, from then on his case is hopeless, yet he perishes only in time. And if you offer the black, which flowed from the dead snake, this too the size of a sesame seed, the man who takes it grows full of pus, and consumption seizes him, and within a year he is wasted away in decay; but many have gone on even to two years, dying little by little.

There is a bird named the asterias, and it is tamed in Egypt, and understands human speech. If anyone, reproaching it, calls it a slave, it grows angry; and if anyone calls it lazy, it bristles and is indignant, as though mocked for baseness and rebuked for idleness.
Caterpillars feed on the vegetables, and indeed destroy them. But these are killed if a woman undergoing her monthly purgation passes through the midst of the vegetables.

When elephants are routed by the hunters, like soldiers in war, and rush into flight, they do not flee scattered nor one by one, but in common, and they press close together, holding to their fellows. And in a ring are the young, so to speak, the most warlike part, and in the middle the aged and the mothers, and under these the calves, each one hiding her own; and these little ones are very rarely seen. But if even lions see them in a mass, either they flee headlong or one here and one there cower down like fawns—the lions, who till then were dreadful and terrifying, now dreading the elephants. An elephant does not stand against its pursuers, except perhaps in defence of its young and of the sick. There it is unconquerable.

There was, it seems, a fish accustomed to the rocks and feeding among them, of the mullet kind, and yellow to look at. A double name is current about it; for some call it adonis, and others exocoetus, the "out-sleeper." For when the wave is calmed in fair and gentle weather, then it runs itself aground, riding upon the impulse of the wave, and spreads itself out upon the rocks, and sleeps a deep and most peaceful sleep. And it knows well that from all the rest it is under truce, but it dreads those birds that are and are reckoned bred of the sea. So if one of these appears, it leaps up and springs by some natural dance and, as one might say, a most secret caper, until, leaping off the rock and then falling among the waves, it is saved. And they like to call it adonis, since it has both land and sea for friends, the first who, it seems to me, gave it the name hinting at the life of the son of Cinyras, which was divided between two divinities, the one beneath the earth and the one above the earth being in love with him.

I have spoken above also about swans, but now too let me say what I did not say before. Aristotle says that in the sea of the Libyans a flock of swans once appeared, and that a certain song of theirs was heard, as from a chorus singing in unison, very sweet indeed, yet mournful, and such as to break the hearers into pity. And he says that some of them appeared dead at the song. The swan was dear to springs and shallows and lakes and to all the natural confluences and abundances of waters. There, at any rate, the wise in these matters say that it pursues its own muses in love of wisdom.

Peculiar to animals are these things too. Mares are believed to be most suited for chariot-driving. And I learn that the men who train them say that horses delight in bathing and anointing. And that horses were anointed with perfume too, Simonides says in his iambics. The Persians, after the battle of Cyrus in Lydia, rear camels along with their horses, trying to cast out, by the rearing-together, the fear of the horses that is kindled in them by the camels.

The Crathis sends forth water that makes white. At any rate, the sheep that drink of it, and the cattle and all the four-footed herd, as Theophrastus says, become white from black or tawny. And in Euboea too the cattle are born white almost all, from which the poets called Euboea "Argiboeon," land of white cattle.

That the elephant fears the pig I have said above; but I wish to tell what happened at Megara when the Megarians were besieged by Antipater, and what is to be told is this. When the Macedonians were pressing hard, the Megarians smeared pigs with liquid pitch and set them on fire and let them loose against the enemy. And the pigs, falling among the squadrons of elephants, frenzied and squealing as they burned, drove the beasts mad and threw them into dreadful confusion. So the elephants neither kept their ranks nor were any longer tame, although they had been broken in from infancy — whether because elephants by some peculiar nature hate and loathe pigs, or because they shudder at the shrill and harsh sound of their cries. The keepers of the elephants, perceiving this, rear pigs alongside them, they say, so that from familiarity they may dread them less.

The lion delights to eat camel's flesh. And the proof is that Herodotus says lions attacked the camels of Xerxes that carried the corn. But the rest they did not harm, neither beast of burden nor man, he says. Herodotus knew but little when he examined the food of Thracian lions; the Arabs too know these things, and all who have a land that is at once mother and nurse of lions and camels. I should not, then, marvel if by some secret nature a lion delights in camel's flesh and would eat it even without having seen it, if ever he met with it; for natural desire kindles even those who have not seen toward the desire for that food.

The storks defend themselves very cleverly against the bats that ruin their eggs; for the bats, by merely touching them, make them addled and barren. So the remedy against these is this: they bring plane-tree leaves to their nests; and when the bats come near them they grow numb and become unable to do harm. Nature gave the swallows too such a gift. The cockroaches damage their eggs as well. So the mothers set a sprig of celery before their young, and to the cockroaches from then on it is impassable. And if one casts rue upon octopuses, they remain motionless, as a certain account says. And if you strike a serpent with a reed, after the first blow it keeps still and, fettered by numbness, lies quiet; but if you give it a second or third blow, you have revived it. And the moray, struck once with a fennel-stalk, keeps still; but if more often, it is kindled to rage. The fishermen say that octopuses too come out onto the land when a spray of olive lies on the shore. And the fat of the elephant was, it seems, an antidote against all beasts: if one were to smear oneself with it and go to grips, even naked, with the fiercest creatures, he would come off unharmed.

The shrew-mouse, as far as it goes about its ordinary way, has life, and nature has made a truce with it, unless it should be caught by some other chance and perish; but whenever it falls into a chariot-rut, it is caught as by a fetter, and a very unseen one, and is dead. And for one bitten by a shrew-mouse there is this remedy: the sand raised by the running of the wheels, sprinkled on the bite, has saved at once.

In Seriphus there are frogs, of which you would not at all hear any utterance; but if you carry them elsewhere, they sound piercing and most harsh. And in Pierus of Thessaly there is a lake, not ever-flowing, but in winter it is formed from the waters that run together into it. So if one throws frogs into it, they keep silent, though they utter their voice elsewhere. And concerning the Seriphian frogs the Seriphians boast that Perseus, coming from his contest against the Gorgon, after going round much land, and being weary, as was likely, rested near the lake and lay down needing sleep. And the frogs cried out and mocked the hero and broke his sleep; and Perseus prayed to his father to silence the frogs. And he listened, and to please his son condemned the frogs of that place to everlasting silence. But Theophrastus, throwing out the fable and freeing the Seriphians from their boasting, says that the coldness of the water is the cause of the silence of the aforesaid frogs.

The ostrich lays many eggs, but does not hatch them all; rather it sets aside the infertile ones, and broods upon the fruitful. And from these it hatches out its chicks, while those that have been rejected it sets before them as food. If anyone pursues it, it does not venture upon flight, but runs with its wings spread; and if it is about to be caught, it slings with its feet the stones that lie in its way back at the pursuer.

If one holds Cyrenaic juice and takes hold of the torpedo-fish, there indeed he has escaped the effect that comes from it. But if you wish to pull up a sea-dragon with your right hand, it will not follow, but will fight with all its might; if you draw it up with your left, it yields and is caught.

Bitterest foes to oxen would be the gadfly and the horsefly. And the gadfly is like the largest flies, and has a firm and large sting, and gives off a buzzing and harsh sound; the horsefly resembles the dog-fly, but buzzes more than the gadfly, though it has a smaller sting.

The elephant of Porus, king of the Indians, in the battle against Alexander, when his master had been wounded many times, gently and carefully drew out the javelins with its trunk; and indeed, though it too was wounded many times, it did not yield before it understood that its master, through the great flow of his blood, was sinking and dying. So it lowered itself, and knelt and remained so, that Porus, falling from above, might not have his body further harmed.

The branch of one plant grows upon the trunk of another, often belonging to it not at all. The cause Theophrastus tells, having traced it out most naturally: that the little birds, feeding on the bloom of the trees and then perching upon the plants, void their droppings. So the seed, falling into the hollows and openings and clefts of them, and watered by the rains from heaven, then makes grow again those things from which it sprang. Thus you will observe a fig-tree growing in an olive, and in another tree another.

The owl, accompanying a man set out upon some enterprise and settling upon him, is no good sign, they say. Here is the proof: Pyrrhus of Epirus was going by night straight to Argos, and this bird met him as he sat upon his horse, carrying his spear upright. Then it settled upon this, and did not depart, escorting with no good escort the man aforesaid. Pyrrhus, at any rate, went on into Argos, and died most ingloriously of men. From this, it seems to me, Homer too, knowing well the bird's never-favourable omen, says that Athena sent a heron from the rivers to the company of Diomedes, when they went off to spy out the affairs of the Trojans, but not the owl, even though it seems to be dear to her. And that the land of Ilium is dewy and well-watered, Homer is able to attest in the passages before the battle at the walls.

Those creatures are called cartilaginous which have no scales; these would be the moray, the conger, the torpedo, the sting-ray, the ox-ray, the dogfish; the dolphin, the whale, the seal. These alone of water-creatures bear their young alive. Those are called soft-bodied which have no bone; these would be the octopus, the cuttlefish, the squid, the sea-nettle. These too are without blood and entrails. The soft-shelled are the lobsters, shrimps, crabs, sea-crabs; and these too cast off their old shell. The hard-shelled are oysters, purple-shells, trumpet-shells, conches, sea-urchins, crayfish. Saw-toothed are the wolf, the dog, the lion, the leopard; these too eat flesh. With teeth in both jaws are man, horse, ass, which also have fat. With teeth meeting in front are the ox, the sheep, the goat. With tusks are the wild boar, the mole; for the elephant I say has not teeth but horns. Insects are the wasp, the bee; and they say these have not even lungs. Amphibious are the river-horse, the otter, the beaver, the crocodile. Scaly are the lizard, the salamander, the tortoise, the crocodile, the snake; and these too cast off their old skin except the crocodile and the tortoise. Solid-hoofed are the horse, the ass. Cloven-hoofed are the ox, the deer, the goat, the sheep, the pig. With many divisions of the foot are man and dog. Web-footed and flat-clawed are the swan and the goose. With curved talons are hawks and eagles. The peculiar nature of the other animals I have told elsewhere.

A cock fell in love with a royal cupbearer (and the king was Nicomedes of the Bithynians), and the cock's name was Centaur, and Philo tells this. And a jackdaw too fell in love with a beautiful boy. And I have learned that certain bees are amorous, even if most are chaste.

Among the Indians called Psylli (for there are also Libyan Psylli, different from these) the horses grow no bigger than rams, and the sheep are seen to be small, like lambs, and the asses too are of this size, and the mules and the oxen and every other beast whatever. They say that no pig is bred in India, neither tame nor wild; and the Indians loathe even to eat this creature, and would never taste swine's flesh, just as the same people would not taste human flesh.

Reaping men, sixteen in number, oppressed by thirst as the sun blazed down, sent one of themselves to bring water from a neighbouring spring. So the one who went held in his hand the reaping-sickle, and carried the drawing-vessel on his shoulder. And coming, he finds an eagle firmly and warily wrapped about by a snake. The eagle had happened to swoop down upon it, but had not got the mastery of its design, nor (this is the Homeric phrase) carried the feast to its own young; but falling among that creature's coils it was about to — not, by Zeus, to destroy, but to be destroyed. So the farmer, knowing that the one was the messenger and servant of Zeus, and knowing too that the snake was an evil beast, cuts the beast through with the aforesaid sickle, and indeed frees the eagle from those inescapable prisons and bonds. These things had been done by the man as a by-work of his journey; and having drawn the water he came, and mixing it with the wine handed it to all, and they drank at a draught, and many draughts after their meal. And he too was about to drink after them; for he happened to be at that moment a servant and not a fellow-drinker. But when he was bringing the cup to his lips, the eagle that had been saved, paying him the ransom of his life and by good fortune still lingering about the place, falls upon the cup and overturns it and spills the drink. He was angered (for he happened to be thirsty), and says, "So you are that one" (for he recognized the bird), "is this how you render thanks to your saviours? But how are such things any longer good? And how would another wish to do anyone a kindness, out of reverence for Zeus the overseer and watcher of kindnesses?" So he had spoken, and was vexed; but turning round he sees those who had drunk gasping and dying. The snake, it seems, as one may infer, had vomited into the spring and mixed it with its venom. So the eagle paid to the one who saved it a recompense equal to the saving. And Crates of Pergamum says that Stesichorus too sings of these things in a certain poem not widely circulated, bringing it in as venerable and ancient, so far as I can judge as a witness.

The elephant dreads a horned ram and the squeal of a pig. So it was, they say, that the Romans routed the elephants that were with Pyrrhus the Epirote, and the victory fell brilliantly to the Romans. By a beautiful woman this creature is overcome and loses its rage, deafened by her beauty. And they say that in the Egyptian city of Alexandria an elephant was a rival in love, against Aristophanes of Byzantium, for a woman who plaited garlands. The same creature loves every sweet scent, being charmed by the smell of perfumes and flowers. Whoever, being a thief or a robber, wishes to silence very savage dogs and put them to flight, takes a brand from a man's funeral pyre and goes to grips with them, they say, and the dogs are afraid. I have also heard this account: if one shears a sheep that has been mauled by a wolf, works the wool, and makes a tunic of it, he troubles the wearer; for it produces itching, as the story goes. And if one wishes to make strife and quarrelling at a banquet, he casts into the wine a stone that has been bitten by a dog and so troubles the drinkers, driving them mad. And if one sprinkles perfume on beetles, those evil-smelling creatures, they cannot bear the fragrance but die. So they say that tanners too, reared in foul air, loathe perfume. The Egyptians say also that all serpents fear the feathers of ibises.

These things too I have heard about the Egyptian ibis. The bird is sacred to the moon. So it hatches its eggs in as many days as the goddess waxes and wanes. And it never leaves Egypt. The reason: Egypt is the most southerly of all lands, and the moon is believed to be the most southerly of the wandering stars. Willingly, then, the ibis would not go abroad; but if anyone attacks it and by force takes it out, it avenges itself on the plotter, bringing his pains to nothing; for it kills itself by starvation, and shows the aforesaid man's eagerness profitless. It walks quietly and like a maiden, and one would not see it going faster than at a walk. And the black ones of these birds do not let the winged serpents pass from Arabia into Egypt, fighting in defence of the land they love; while the others meet and destroy those that come from Ethiopia at the inundation of the Nile. Else what would have hindered the Egyptians from perishing through the visitation of these serpents?

In moist places, and where the air is exceedingly damp, cocks do not crow, says Theophrastus. And the lake in Pheneus is barren of fish. And cicadas, being cold in their constitution, then, being heated by the sun, sing — so he says.

The small sparrows, conscious of their weakness because of the smallness of their bodies, build their nests upon the slender tips of the branches that can bear them, and thus for the most part escape the plots of the hunters, who cannot climb out upon the twig; for it does not bear them, owing to its thinness.

I hear Charmis the Massaliote saying that the nightingale loves music, and indeed loves glory too. At any rate, in the solitudes, when it sings to itself, the bird sings a simple song without elaboration; but when it is caught and does not miss its hearers, it sings varied strains and winds out the song softly. And Homer too seems to me to hint at this when he says, "As when the daughter of Pandareus, the pale-green nightingale, sings beautifully when spring is newly come, sitting amid the thick leaves of the trees, and pouring forth, with frequent turns, her many-toned voice." Indeed some write "many-modulated voice" for that which is varied in its imitations, as "unsweet" for that which is not turned to imitation at all.

Of those bitten by an asp not one is recorded to have escaped the evil. Hence indeed I hear that the kings of the Egyptians wore embroidered asps upon their diadems, hinting at the invincibility of their rule by the form of the aforesaid creature. There are asps even five cubits long. And most are black or ash-coloured, but you might see a tawny asp too. Those bitten by an asp do not live beyond the fourth hour, but choking and convulsion and hiccupping pursue them, they say. And I hear that the ichneumon destroys the eggs of the asp, as though removing for its own young the future adversaries. And a certain tale says that the Libyan asp even makes men blind by its blast.

The Hyrcanians and the Magnesians took dogs to war with them, and this too was a good ally and aid to them. And a certain Athenian brought a dog as a fellow soldier to the battle of Marathon, and both are depicted in a painting in the Painted Stoa, the dog not being dishonoured but, having received its reward for the danger, being shown together with Cynegirus and Epizelus and Callimachus. These figures, and the dog, are the work of Micon. But some say they are not his, but the work of Polygnotus of Thasos.

The "sheep" lurks in the recesses of the sea, and the so-called hepatoi, and those which the fishermen like to call the "fitting ones." And they are the greatest in nature to look at, but sluggish in swimming, and they coil about their lurking-places, whence indeed they do not leave their own retreat. And they lie in wait for those of the weaker fishes that swim past. Among these too the "ass-fish" would be reckoned; and this ass-fish fears most of fishes the rising of Sirius.

The octopus is fearful to the crayfish. At any rate, if ever they are caught in one net, the crayfish die at once. There is a river named Lusias in Thurii, which has the whitest of waters and flows most clear, but breeds intensely black fish.

The fox-goose too, it seems, is a creature loving to its young, and does the same things as the partridges. For it too rolls itself before its young, and gives hope to the one who comes upon it that he will catch it; and they, meanwhile, escape. And when they have got well on their way, it too, lightening itself with its wings, departs.

They paint and mould the sphinx winged, with all the diligence and labour about the handiwork. And I hear too that at Clazomenae there was a winged sow, which ravaged the land of Clazomenae; and Artemon tells this in his Annals of the Clazomenians. From this a place there is called and celebrated as "of the winged sow." And if this seems to anyone a myth, let it so seem; but for my part what was said about an animal and not left unnoticed has not grieved me by being told.

At Metropolis in the Ephesian land, I hear, there is a lake, and near it a cave; and the cavern has an unmatched multitude of snakes, and these are said to be of the greatest size and terrible in the bite. They come forth from the cavern, the story goes, far enough to crawl out into the neighbouring lake and swim; but trying to advance further than the water, they cannot, for as they are about to set foot on land, great crabs lie in wait, which, raising their claws, seize them in a stranglehold and kill them. So the snakes, in dread of their enemies, keep quiet, and the land is impassable to them; for they shudder at the guard and the punishment from the crabs. And surely all those about the place would have perished long ago, had not the said crabs, by some secret nature, encompassed the edges of the lake and, keeping the snakes out, made everything in that place peaceful.

In the Caspian sea there are islands, they say, and there are bred in them birds various indeed, but one that has obtained the following peculiarity. They say it is the size of geese, but has feet like a crane's. Its back is scarlet-dyed and very pure, and the parts under the belly green; its neck is white, and it has certain drops as it were of saffron-colour scattered over it. It is no less than two cubits long, and its head is at once thin and long, its beak black; and it gives out a voice like the frogs'.

Those who are skilled in the snares for turtle-doves hunt them, and they very rarely fail in the attempt, in the following way. They stand dancing and singing most musically; and the doves, charmed by the sound and bewitched by the sight of the dancing, come nearer. And the men retire quietly and step by step to where the trap is set for the poor creatures, the spread nets; then they fall into them and are caught, taken first by dance and song.

I hear also of a kind of eagle, and they have given it the name golden eagle, while others call the same one the starred; and it is not often seen. Aristotle says that it hunts fawns and hares and cranes and geese from the yard. It is believed to be the largest of eagles, and they say that it attacks even bulls by force, and they describe the deed thus. The bull grazes stooping downward; and the eagle, seating itself on the creature's neck, strikes with its beak with continuous and strong blows; and the bull, as though stung to frenzy, is kindled, and begins to flee as fast as its feet can carry it. And so long as the ground is easy to run over, the eagle is quiet and flies along watching; but when it sees the bull come near a precipice, wheeling its wings and stretching them over its eyes, it makes the bull, not seeing what is before its feet, fall down most violently. Then, falling upon it and tearing open its belly, it uses the prey easily, as long as it wishes. But it does not touch another's prey lying ready, but delights in its own toils, and least of all admits partnership with another. And when sated, it then breathes over the rest an evil and most foul-smelling breath, and leaves the remains uneatable to the others. Moreover, eagles dwell in nests set apart from one another, so as not to quarrel over prey and often, being grieved, to grieve one another.

The boldest of creatures, it seems, was the goatsucker; for it despises the small birds, but attacks the goats by force, and indeed, flying onto their udders, sucks out the milk, and does not fear the punishment from the goatherd, though it pays them a most wicked wage for its fill; for it blinds the teat and quenches the flow from there.

Foxes, having reached the height of cunning and crafty ways, whenever they see a thriving wasps' nest, themselves turn aside from the hollow, swerving away and guarding against the wounds of the stings; but they let down their tail, which is very thick and long, and shake the wasps with it. The wasps cling to the thickness of the hairs. And when they have become entangled in it, the foxes dash the tail against a tree or wall or stone fence; and the wasps, being struck, die. Then the foxes come again to the same spot, and having gathered up and killed the rest just as they did the first, when at last they perceive that there is peace and freedom from the stings, they put down their mouth and eat the wasp-grubs, neither disturbed nor any longer wary of the stings.

Democritus says that of all animals the lion alone is born with its eyes open, being already in a way enraged and eager from birth for some noble deed. And others have observed that even while sleeping it moves its tail, showing, as is likely, that it is not wholly at rest, nor has sleep encircled and overcome it, as it has the other animals. The Egyptians, having observed something of the sort about it, are said to boast, saying that the lion is stronger than sleep, being ever wakeful. For this reason too, I learn, they assign it to the sun; for the sun, being the most industrious of the gods, is either seen above the earth or goes its lower course without resting. And the Egyptians bring Homer as witness, who says "the unwearying sun." But besides its strength the lion is also intelligent. At any rate it plots against the cattle, going by night to the steadings. And Homer knew this too, saying, "As cattle which a lion has frightened, coming in the dead of night." And it strikes them all with terror by its might, but snatching one it devours it. And when it has filled itself to satiety, it wishes to store some up for another time, but shame holds it from remaining to keep guard, as though it feared hunger from lack of food. So gaping over it, it breathes its own breath upon it, and to this entrusts the guard, while it itself departs; and the other animals, coming and perceiving whose leavings the carcass is, do not dare to touch it, but depart in fear of seeming to rob and cut off anything of their own king's. Now if good hunting and success come to it, it forgets the first kill and, scorning it as stale, departs; but if not, it comes to it as to its own treasure. And when it is over-full, it empties itself by rest and fasting, or again, meeting a monkey and eating it, it empties its belly, purging it with that creature's flesh. The lion, then, was just, and such as to defend a man when someone first does him wrong. At any rate it stands against the one who attacks, lashing its tail and curling it against its sides, then rousing itself as though whetting itself with a goad. But the one who has shot at it and missed it punishes with an equal measure, frightening but harming not at all. When tamed from young, it is most gentle and pleasant to meet, and is fond of play, and endures everything gently to gratify its keeper. Hanno, at any rate, had a lion as a baggage-carrier, and a tame lion accompanied Berenice, differing nothing from her hairdressers. At any rate it brightened her face with its tongue, and smoothed her wrinkles, and shared her table, eating gently and orderly and in human fashion. And Onomarchus the tyrant of Catana, and the son of Cleomenes, had lions as messmates.

Must one not then marvel at nature in this respect too, among others? The fathers of the males destroy most of the fawns, lest they multiply and then mount their mothers; for this seems a defilement even among the irrational creatures, and a polluted deed, no doubt. But to Cyrus and Parysatis, O Persians, these things seemed both noble and just; and Cyrus loved his mother wickedly, and was loved by his mother with a like love. And these things, indeed, were done by them—but men, desiring everything and sparing nothing.

Those who say that the female deer does not grow horns are not ashamed before the witnesses to the contrary: Sophocles, who said, "And a horned deer crept down from the steep crags to the pastures"; and again, "And raising her nostrils and her horned antlers she went on at her ease." These verses are by the son of Sophillus in the Aleadae. And Euripides in the Iphigenia says, "I will set in the dear hands of the Achaeans a horned deer, which as they slay it they will boast that they slay your daughter." And in the Temenidae the same Euripides says that the labour of Heracles had horns, singing thus: "He came after the golden-horned deer, undertaking one dreadful labour of the great labours, over the trackless mountain glens and the meadows and the wooded groves of the flocks." And the Theban poet, in one of his victory odes, celebrates it, saying: "By the compulsion of Eurystheus he was to bring the golden-horned female deer from her sire." And Anacreon speaks of a female: "Like a newly weaned suckling fawn, which, left in the wood by its horned mother, took fright." Against those who would corrupt the saying, and indeed assert that one ought to write "wooded" instead of "horned," Aristophanes of Byzantium argues with all his force, and for my part he wins me by his counter-argument.

There is born in the cornfields of wheat and in the poplars and in the fig-trees besides the tribe of the cantharid-beetles, as Aristotle says; in the chickpeas the tribe of caterpillars; in the vetch certain spiders; in the leeks the so-called leek-cutter. There is born too in the cabbage a kind of grub, and its name is from the haunts in which it lives; it is called the cabbage-grub. The apple-tree too breeds something; and this often destroys the fruit of that plant, but for those still of an age to bear it might even be good for fruitfulness. And the manner another will tell.

A leopard, named "ampelos" after the plant of the same name, they say is so called as having a nature peculiar beyond the rest, and I hear that it has no tail. If it is seen by women, it casts them into an unexpected disease.

The Egyptians say that the hawk, while living and still surviving, is a god-beloved bird, but when it has departed from life, it both prophesies and sends dreams, having put off its body and become a naked soul. And the Egyptians say too that a three-footed hawk once appeared among them, and they seem to those who believe them to speak soundly.

To Halia, as she passed by Sybaris into a grove of Artemis (the grove was in Phrygia), a divine serpent appeared, very great to look upon, and consorted with her. And from this the so-called Ophiogeneis, the Serpent-born, sprang of the first stock.

Onesicritus of Astypalaea says that in India, in the time of the expedition of Alexander son of Philip, there were two serpents, which Abisares the Indian kept, of which the one was a hundred and forty cubits long, the other eighty; and he says that Alexander earnestly desired to see them. Egyptian accounts say too that in the time of Philadelphus two living serpents were brought from Ethiopia to the city of Alexander, and that one of them was fourteen cubits, the other thirteen; and that in the time of Euergetes three were brought, and one was nine cubits, the other seven, and the third fell short by one; and the Egyptians say that they were reared in the temple of Asclepius with much care. And the same people say that asps four cubits long are often produced.
