I have made mention of these things, since, in going through the peculiar nature of the creatures, I wished also to show to what length they naturally grow. So those too who have written the histories about Chios say that on the island, beside the mountain called Pelinnaeus, in a glen thickly wooded and full of tall trees, there was a serpent of the greatest size, at whose very hiss the inhabitants of Chios used to shudder. None therefore of the farmers or herdsmen dared, coming near, to judge its size, but from the hiss alone believed the beast to be monstrous and terrifying; and yet it was learned how great it was in size, by a divine and marvellous device, by Zeus. For when a violent and harsh wind fell upon them, the trees in the glen were thrown against one another, and the branches, violently dashed, give birth to fire, and a great flame rises up, and embraces the whole place and encircles the beast; and it, cut off and unable to crawl away, is burned up. So when the place was laid bare, all became visible; and the Chians, freed from their fear, came to see, and find the bones of the greatest size and a terrifying head, so that from these it could be guessed how great and of what kind that creature was while still alive.

In the Prasiacan country (this is part of India) Megasthenes says that there are apes no smaller than the largest dogs, and that they have tails five cubits long; and that there grow on them forelocks and beards let down and deep; and their whole face is white, but their body is black to look at, and they are tame and most kindly to men, and do not have the malice that is connatural with the apes elsewhere.

The fish called the orcynus, a whale-like fish, is not without cunning for what is most to its own advantage, having received this as a gift by nature, not by art. So when it is pierced by the hook, it dives down into the deep and pushes and dashes itself against the bottom, and strikes its mouth, wishing to throw out the hook; and if this is impossible, it widens the wound and spits out what pains it and leaps free. But often it fails in the attempt, and the hunter, drawing it up against its will, has his catch.

There was, it seems, a kind of eagle affectionate even toward those who reared it, like the one of Pyrrhus. This one, they say, died upon its master, refusing food. And once too the pet eagle of a private man, when its master was being burned, threw itself into the pyre; though some say it was a woman's, not a man's, nursling. And the eagle was, it seems, a most jealous creature toward its young. So if it sees anyone approaching, it does not let him go off unpunished; for it strikes him with its wings and tears at him with its talons, and inflicts the penalty on him sparingly, for it does not use its beak.

Metrodidactus, the son of Arete, the sister of Aristippus, the many celebrate; but Aristotle says that he himself saw the nestlings of the nightingale being taught to sing by their mother. The nightingale was, it seems, of birds a strong lover of freedom; and for this reason the full-grown one, when caught and shut up in a little cage, refrains from song, and avenges itself on the fowler for its slavery by silence. Of this men, having experience, let the older ones go, but are eager to hunt the nestlings.

A dog's skull has no suture. And one that has run a great deal becomes more lustful, they say. As a dog grows old its teeth grow blunt and turn black. It is so keen of scent that it would never taste roast dog's flesh, not even if it were bewitched with the most varied and crafty sauce. Three diseases, and no more, are allotted to the dog: quinsy, madness, and gout; but to men there are countless ones. Everything that is bitten by a mad dog dies. And a dog that has gout you will rarely see recover. The longest life of a dog is fourteen years. Argus, the dog of Odysseus, and the tale about him, seem to be a fancy of Homer's.

They say the leopard has obtained a certain wondrous fragrance, hidden from us, but it knows its own advantage, and indeed the other animals know it along with the leopard, and it is caught in the following way. The leopard, when it needs food, hides itself either in thick brush or in deep foliage, and is invisible to meet, and only breathes. So the fawns and gazelles and wild goats and such animals are drawn, as by some spell of the fragrance, and come near; and it leaps out and has its prey.

An island in Pontus named after Heracles is held in honour. So all the mice there revere the god, and whatever is dedicated to him they believe to be dedicated as pleasing to the god, and they would not touch it. So a vine flourishes for the god, and is honoured as an offering to him alone, and the ministers of the deity keep the clusters for the sacrifices. So when the grapes come to ripeness, the mice leave the island, lest by remaining they should at least unwillingly touch what it is better not to handle; then when the season is past, they return to their own haunts. And these are good acts of the Pontic mice; but as for Diagoras and Herostratus and the rest of the catalogue of those hateful to the gods, how would they have spared the clusters or other offerings, men who had chosen somehow to plunder even the names and works of the gods?

Peculiar to dogs too are these things, which surpass every excess of goodwill. To Polus the tragic actor his foster-dog, when he was dead and was being burned, gave itself to be burned with him, leaping into the pyre. And to Mentor, as he burned, Eretrian puppies gave themselves to be burned with him willingly, sharing in his end. Theodorus, a man good at the harp—his kinsmen laid him in the coffin, and a little Maltese dog threw itself into the tomb of the dead man and was buried with him. I have learned too that there is a people of the Ethiopians among whom a dog is king, and they obey its impulse; and they know, when it whines, that it is not angry, and when it barks, they understand its wrath. If Hermippus is sufficient for anyone to prove this, let him persuade by bringing Aristocreon forward as a witness of the account; but it did not escape me, and so came opportunely into my memory.

Each of the animals knows in what part it possesses its strength, and in this it takes courage, and when plotting uses it as a weapon, and when in danger as a means of defence. The swordfish, at any rate, defends itself with its snout as with a sword, whence indeed it has its name; the stingray with its sting; the lamprey with its teeth, and very reasonably; for it has a double row of them.

In the land of Scythia there are horned asses, and those horns hold the Arcadian water called the water of the Styx; but all other vessels it breaks through, even if they are made of iron. One of these horns, they say, was brought by Sopater to Alexander the Macedonian, and I learn that he, marvelling at it, dedicated the horn at Delphi as an offering to the Pythian god, and inscribed these lines: "To you, O Healer, Alexander the Macedonian dedicated this horn of a Scythian ass, a thing divine, which was not subdued by the unstained stream of Lusian Styx, but bore up the manhood of the water." Demeter, then, sent up this water near Pheneus, and I have told the reason elsewhere.

The partridges of Paphlagonia are double-hearted, as indeed Theophrastus says. And Theopompus says that the hares in Bisaltia each have a double liver. And Apion says, if he is not playing the wonder-monger, that deer too in certain places have four kidneys. And the same man says that in the time of Oenis the son of Menis a two-headed crane appeared, and Egypt flourished; and in the reign of another king a four-headed bird, and the Nile flooded as never before, and there was abundance of crops and a wondrous prosperity of harvests. And Nicocreon the Cyprian had a four-horned deer, and dedicated it at Delphi and inscribed beneath it: "For your sake, child of Leto mighty with the bow, Nicocreon conceived this design and took this four-horned deer." And indeed there were four-horned and three-horned sheep in the temple of Zeus the Guardian of the City. And I myself have beheld a five-footed sacred ox, an offering to this god in the great city of the Alexandrians, in the celebrated grove of the god, where persea trees growing together showed forth a most beautiful shade and coolness. And there was a calf there, in colour like wax, and it had on its shoulder a foot hanging down, superfluous indeed for treading upon, but complete in its formation. And these things do not seem to agree very well with nature, but I have told what came to my sight and hearing.

The Delphians honour the wolf, the Samians the sheep, and the Ambraciots the lioness; and the reasons for each honour it is not beside this study to tell. For the Delphians a wolf tracked out sacred gold that had been stolen and buried on Parnassus; for the Samians too a sheep found such gold that had been stolen, and from this Mandrobulus the Samian dedicated a sheep as an offering to Hera; and the former Polemon tells, the latter Aristotle. The Ambraciots, since a lioness tore in pieces their tyrant Phaylus, honour the creature as having become for them the cause of freedom. And Miltiades buried in the Ceramicus the mares that thrice won at Olympia, and Euagoras the Laconian too buried magnificently his Olympic-victor horses.

There is a snake named the seps, and it has the following marvel worth noting. It changes its own colour, and is like the places through which it goes. It bears four hollow teeth in the lower jaw, on which lie membranous sheaths, covering the hollows. From these, when the beast has struck, it then sends forth its venom; and it makes putrefy at once and kills most swiftly.

In India there is a country about the river Astaborras, in the land of the so-called Rhizophagi. At the rising of the Dog-star there appeared certain dreadful clouds of gnats, such as to fill the air, and then they did much harm. And about the lake called Aoratia (this too is Indian, and is near the aforesaid river) this same beast, the gnat, swarms; and the place is desert and is so called. The reason the Indians who dwell round about give is this: that the aforesaid place was not desert of men from above or from the beginning, but that scorpions swarmed there in an unmatched multitude, and a certain horde of venomous spiders came upon it, spiders such as they call four-jawed. These evils, they say, were bred by the corruption of the air. And for a while the people there endured the assault of the evil patiently and bore it with toil; but when it was utterly irresistible, and every age was perishing, then at last, in their helplessness to ward off the onset of the aforesaid visitation, they left the country, and abandoned to desolation that land which was before dear, and the best of fatherlands; nor shall I err, perhaps, if I call the same a mother-land.

The blacktail is the most cowardly of fishes, and has the fishermen as witnesses of its cowardice. They are not taken in basket-traps, nor do they go near them; but if a seine ever surrounds them, they are caught unawares. And when the sea is calm and smooth, they rest somewhere below by the rocks or the seaweed, and put up every defence they can, hiding their body. But when it is stormy, seeing the other fishes dive into the deep from the assault of the waves, they take courage, and draw near the land, and swim up to the rocks, and reckon the foam swimming over them to be sufficient cover, hiding and shading them. And they understand most secretly that in such weather, by day or by night, the sea is impassable for the fishermen, the sea being savage and the waves rising high and fearful. They have food too in the storm, the surge tearing some things from the rocks and dragging others from the land; and the blacktails feed on the dirtier things, such as no other fish would readily eat unless very hard pressed by hunger. In calm they hover over the bare sand alone, and feed from there. How they are caught, another shall tell.

Of sea-creatures the red mullet is the greediest, and beyond dispute the most unsparing in tasting everything that comes its way. And some of them are called scabby, drawing the name from the places which have for their bound scabby and porous ground, with thick seaweed among them, and somewhere mud or sand lying beneath. The red mullet would eat both a man's corpse and a fish's; and they delight rather in the defiled and foul-smelling.

The land of India bears one-horned horses, they say, and the same land rears one-horned asses, and from these horns drinking-cups are made. And if one should put into them a deadly poison, the man who drinks will suffer no harm from the plot; for the horn, both of the horse and of the ass, seems to be a defence against the evil.

There is also a kind of very small Indian birds. It nests on the high crags and on the rocks called "leprous," and the little birds are in size about as big as a partridge's egg; imagine their colour to be that of realgar. The Indians in their own tongue like to call it dikairon, and the Greeks, as I hear, dikaion. If one were to take of its droppings as much as a millet seed dissolved in drink, he is dead by evening. And the death resembles sleep, and a most sweet and painless one, such as the poets like to call "limb-loosing" or "gentle"; for it too would be free of pain and therefore most pleasant to those who need it. The Indians set the highest value on obtaining it; for they consider it truly a remedy that brings forgetfulness of evils; and so among the most precious gifts to the king of the Persians the king of the Indians sends this too. And he, receiving it, prizes it above all the rest and lays it up in store as an adversary and defence against incurable evils, should necessity overtake him. So no one else among the Persians has it, save the king himself and the king's mother. And so let us, comparing them, examine of the two drugs, the Indian and the Egyptian, which was the more to be prized; since the Egyptian held back and checked the tears for a day, but the Indian provided eternal forgetfulness of evils; and the one was a woman's gift, the other a bird's, or rather of a mysterious nature that releases one from the truly heaviest of bonds through the aforesaid servant. And the Indians have had the good fortune to possess it, so as to be released from their watch here whenever they wish.

I learn that the ruminant animals have three stomachs, and I hear their names are the reticulum, the omasum, and the abomasum. And cuttlefish and squids feed by two proboscises—for it is no worse so to name them, taking the hint both from their use and from their shape. And when it is stormy and the surge is troubled, they lay hold of the rocks with these same projections, and cling as with anchors most firmly, and remain unshaken and unwashed by the waves; then if it becomes calm, they release and free themselves, and swim again, knowing a lesson not to be despised—flight from the storm and safety from danger.

This is an Egyptian custom. When it rains in Egypt (it rains in fine drops), mice are at once bred. So wandering through the fields these harm the crops, cutting under and shearing off the ears, and indeed by ravaging the heaps of sheaves they grieve the Egyptians. And for this reason they trap them with snares and check them with walls and fend them off with trenches and burn fire in these. But the mice do not even approach the snares from the start, but let them stand idle; and the walls, though smoothed with plaster, they climb, being most apt at leaping, and then leap over the trenches. So when the Egyptians, having given up their devices and contrivances as useless, abandon them and turn instead to prayer and supplications to the gods, then indeed the mice dread the wrath from the gods, and withdraw to some mountain, keeping the order of a square. The youngest go first, and the largest bring up the rear, and turning back they then force the laggards to follow them. And if the youngest, growing weary, hold back, the whole following halts, as is wont to happen in a military force. And when the movement of the foremost begins, then the rest follow too. And those who dwell in Pontus say that the mice do the same there too. And it is believed that from every house which is about to fall they all move out as fast as their feet can carry them. And this too is a peculiarity of mice. When they hear a weasel squeaking or a viper hissing, from the one mouse-hole they move their young, one here, one there.

Lacydes the Peripatetic had a remarkable creature, a goose. It loved its keeper strongly, and walked beside him as he walked, and rested when he sat, and was never for a moment parted from him. When it died, Lacydes buried it most lovingly, as one might bury a son or a brother. And Pyrrhus of Epirus had an elephant which so loved its own keeper that, when Pyrrhus had died at Argos, and the man who drove it had fallen, it would not be still and quiet until it had rescued him from the enemy and brought him back to friendly ground.

The mice in the house are a timid and weak creature, and they fear a noise, and shudder at a weasel's squeak; and the field-mice too are timid. But of the domestic ones the sea-mice are bolder. Small is their body, but their daring is irresistible; and they take courage in two weapons, a tough hide and the strength of their teeth; and they fight even with the larger fishes and with the fishermen most skilled at hunting them.

To Eupolis the comic poet, Augeas of Eleusis gave as a gift a puppy fair to look at, of Molossian breed, and Eupolis called it Augeas, after the giver. Coaxed by its food, and won over by long familiarity, Augeas the dog loved its master. And once a young fellow-slave of his, named Ephialtes, stole certain plays of Eupolis, and did not escape notice in his theft, but the dog saw him, and falling upon him and biting most unsparingly, killed him. Some time later Eupolis ended his life in Aegina, and was buried there; and the dog, howling and lamenting the lament of dogs, then, wasting itself away with grief and hunger, died upon its keeper and master, hating life. And the place is called, in memory of that event, "The Dog's Lament."

The Ganges that flows among the Indians, taking its beginning from its springs, is twenty fathoms deep and eighty stades broad; for it still goes forward with its native water unmixed with another; but as it goes on, the others falling into it and sharing their water with it, its water reaches a depth of sixty fathoms, and it widens and overflows to four hundred stades. And it has islands greater than Lesbos and Cyrnus, and it nourishes sea-monsters, and from their fat they make an unguent. And there are tortoises in it too, and the shell of these is not less than a cask holding even twenty amphorae. And it breeds two kinds of crocodiles. And some of them harm not at all, but others most voraciously eat flesh and most unsparingly, and they have on the tip of the snout a projection like a horn. These men use as ministers for the punishment of evildoers too; for those convicted of the greatest crimes they throw to them, and they have very little need of an executioner.

Megasthenes says that in India there are winged scorpions of the greatest size, and that they drive in their sting much as the European ones do. There are also snakes there, and these too winged; they come not by day but by night, and discharge from themselves a urine which, if it drips upon any body, works putrefaction at once. So much for what Megasthenes says. Polyclitus, however, says that in the same land there are lizards of the greatest size and of many colours, with their skins exceedingly variegated with certain bright dyes, and that they are also very soft to the touch. Lizards, Aristotle says, are bred in the land of the Arabs, and these are two cubits long.

An incursion and host of field-mice, no good thing, by the gods, drove some of the people in Italy from their ancestral land, and made them exiles, like droughts or frosts or some other unseasonable weather, shearing the crops and cutting through the roots. A horde of sparrows that came upon Media drove out those inhabitants too, destroying the seed and making it vanish. And half-formed frogs, falling in numbers from the air, made the Autariatae migrate to another place. And a certain Libyan people, of whom I made mention above, when lions came upon them, then were forced to rise up from their ancestral land.

The eagle is the keenest-sighted of birds. Homer too knows this of it and bears witness in the Patrocleia, likening Menelaus to the bird when he sought out Antilochus to send him as a messenger to Achilles — a bitter message, but a necessary one, concerning the fate of his comrade, whom he had sent out but had not received back, though that man longed for it. And the eagle is said to be useful not only to itself but also good for men's eyes. If anyone, dissolving its gall in Attic honey, anoints his dimming eyes, he will see, and will have very keen eyes for seeing.

Hawks too are quite able hunters, and no less than eagles, but they are the gentlest of birds by nature and the most man-loving, being in size not smaller than eagles. And I hear that in Thrace they are fellow-hunters with men in the marsh-fowling. And the manner is this: the men spread their nets and keep still, while the hawks, flying over, frighten the birds and drive them together into the encircling nets. So of those taken the Thracians set apart a portion for them too, and have them as faithful friends; but if they did not do this, they would deprive themselves of their allies. And the full-grown hawk fights both the fox and the eagle, and often fights the vulture. But a hawk would never eat a heart, doing this, I suppose, as something ritual and mystic. And a hawk, on seeing a dead man, the story goes, always casts earth upon the unburied — and this Solon does not bid it do — nor will it touch the body. And it remains untasting even of drink, if one man is channelling water into a furrow; for it believes it injures him in his toil by taking away water from his use; but if more than one are irrigating, seeing the abundance of the stream, as of some loving-cup, it takes a share from them and drinks with pleasure.

The purple coot is at once the most beautiful and the most aptly named of creatures, and it delights in dusting itself, and now too it takes the bath of doves; but it does not give itself to the dust-baths and the washings before it has walked a certain number of paces sufficient for it. And eating before witnesses it dislikes, and for this reason withdraws, and eats secretly. It is strongly jealous, and watches the married women, and if it judges the mistress of the house to be committing adultery, it strangles itself. It does not fly high. Men delight in it, and rear it sparingly and carefully. And it seems either to be a plaything of a stately and very rich house, or a temple receives it, and it wanders free within the enclosure. The peacock, being beautiful, the prodigal both slaughter and eat; for of that bird the feathers are an adornment, but the body is little or nothing. But I do not know of anyone who has slaughtered a purple coot for dinner — not Callias nor Ctesippus the Athenians, not Lucullus nor Hortensius the Romans; and I have named a few out of many prodigal and most intemperate men, both otherwise and indeed about the belly.

The bird called the attagas (Aristophanes too mentions it in his play the Birds) utters and sings out its own name with such voice as it has. They say that the birds called Meleagrides do the same, and that they are most fittingly attested to be related by descent to Meleager, the son of Oeneus. The myth says that all the women who were kin to the young son of Oeneus fell into uncontrollable weeping and unbearable grief and lamentation, admitting no remedy for their sorrow, and that through the pity of the gods they were changed in form into these creatures. And there is in them an image and a seed of that ancient grief, fixed deep within, and even now they sing of Meleager, and they sing too that they are his kin. And whoever reveres the divine would never touch these birds for food. And what the reason is, both the inhabitants of the island of Leros know, and it may be learned elsewhere.

If you wish to learn the names of bees, I would not grudge to tell what I have learned. Some are called leaders, and others sirens, and some water-carriers, and others moulders. Nicander says that the drones are the water-carriers. About the land of the Cappadocians they say that the bees make honey without combs, and tradition holds that this is thick like oil. In Trapezus on the Black Sea I learn that honey is made from the box-tree, and that this is heavy in smell, and makes the healthy go out of their minds, but brings epileptics back to health again. In Media I hear that honey drips from the trees, as Euripides says in his Cithaeron that sweet drops flow from the branches. And I have heard that in Thrace too honey comes from the plants. But in Myconos no bee is bred, and even one brought from outside dies.

There is an Italian tale, recalling a deed that flourished along with the city of the Sybarites, and which has come to me, that it is no worse to tell. A boy barely past childhood, a goatherd by occupation, Crathis by name, falling into amorous desire, mingled with the most beautiful to look upon of the she-goats, and took pleasure in the union, and whenever he needed love he went to her, and had her as his beloved. And indeed such gifts as he could obtain, such did the goatherd lover bring to the aforesaid beloved, and sometimes he offered her the loveliest sprays of clover, and often gave her smilax and mastich to browse, making his own mouth fragrant for her, should he need to kiss her. And he prepared too a bed for her to sleep in, as for a bride, most delicate and soft. But the leader of the herd, the he-goat, did not behold these things heedlessly, but jealousy stirred him. And he hid his anger for a time, but once, while the boy was sitting and even sleeping, he lay in wait for him; and the boy had buried his face in his lap. So with all his force the he-goat dashed his head against him, and crushed his skull. The deed, then, spread among the natives, and they raised over the boy a tomb not without renown, and from him named the river Crathis. And from the union with the goat a child was born, with the legs of a goat and the face of a man. This one too, the story says, was deified, and the same was held to be a god of the woodland and the glen. So the he-goat teaches that the animals partake of jealousy too.

The malice of a mule Thales of Miletus countered, having detected it very secretly. A mule was carrying a load of salt, and once, going through a river, it chanced to slip and was overturned. The salt, then, being soaked, melted away, and the mule, having become light, was pleased; and perceiving how great the difference was between toil and ease, it made fortune its teacher for the future, and what it had at first suffered unwillingly, it then did willingly. To drive it by another route, out of the river, was impossible for the muleteer. When Thales learned of this, as it was related to him, he thought he ought by wisdom to counter the mule's malice, and ordered that, instead of salt, it be loaded with sponges and wool. The mule, not knowing the plot, slipped as usual, and having filled with water the load upon it, perceived how its trick had turned to its own harm, and from then on it crossed quietly, keeping control of its legs, and preserved the salt unharmed.

Tunny perceive the change of the seasons, and know the turnings of the sun most keenly, and have no need at all of those skilled in the heavens. For wherever the beginning of winter overtakes them, there they stay quiet and remain content, and abide until the coming of the equinox. And Aristotle attests this. And that they see with one of their eyes, but no longer with the other, Aeschylus too agrees, saying, "casting his left eye aside, like a tunny." And they go into the Pontus, and take the land on their right side, the side with which they also see; and going out again they swim along the land on the opposite side, taking, most providently, the guard of their body on the side of the eye that sees.
They say there is a kind of deadly ant, and that this ant has the name "laertes." And they used to call certain wasps "laertes" too. Telephus the critic, from Pergamum in Mysia, says these things.

The wise in things of the sea let down as bait for the parrot-fish, as Leonides says, coriander and especially leeks, and these are good catching and easiest to take; for the parrot-fish swims toward them, bewitched as by seasonings. And the leaves of beet take the red mullet; for the creature delights in this vegetable, and by it is caught and most easily enslaved.

Pammenes, in his work on beasts, says that in Egypt there are scorpions winged and double-stinged (and he says he does not speak by hearsay, but acknowledges this account as his own), and snakes with two heads, which have two feet at the tail. Ctesias of Cnidos says that about the Persian Sittace there is a river named the Argades. Many snakes are bred in it, black in the body except for the head; that is white. These snakes extend to a fathom in length. By day they are not seen, but swim under water; by night they kill either those who draw water or those who clean their clothes. And many, it seems, suffer this, either through need when the water fails, or because, being busy by day, they could not wash their clothes.
In the land of Babylonia there are bred ants, and they have the procreative body turned to the rear, opposite to the others and the reverse.

The nightingale is the clearest-voiced and most musical of birds, and sings over the desolate places most sweetly and piercingly of all birds. They say that its flesh is good against sleeplessness. Wretched, then, and terribly ignorant are those who feast on such food; for wretched is the gift of that food — the flight of sleep, the king of both gods and men, as Homer says.

There is a tribe of hawks, and it is called the kestrel, and it needs no drink at all. And another kind of them is the mountain-hawk; and each is terribly fond of the female, and follows like men sick with love, nor is left behind. And if the female goes off somewhere unseen, he grieves exceedingly and cries out, and seems like one most amorously distressed. And hawks, when sick in their sight, go straight to the stone walls, and pull up the wild lettuce, and hold its juice, bitter and sharp as it is, over their own eyes, and receive it as it drips, and this brings them health. And they say that physicians too use this drug for the need of those ailing in their sight, and the cure is named after the birds; and men do not deny that they are pupils, listening to birds, but agree to it. And a hawk is said once to have convicted a temple-robber at Delphi, falling upon him and striking his head. And there are believed to be bastard hawks too, set in contrast with the tribes of eagles. And at the beginning of spring those in Egypt choose two out of all, and send them to scout out certain desert islands which lie off Libya. Then these return, and lead the flight for the others. And those that arrive provide a festival, by their coming, for the creatures in Libya; for they do no harm at all. And going to the islands which those first scouts judged more suitable for themselves than the others, there in great calm and quiet they lay and hatch, and hunt sparrows and pigeons, and rear their young in abundance; then, when these have set firm and become able to fly, they take them and lead them off to Egypt, as to their ancestral home, their haunts in the regions where they were reared.

The raven, when now grown old and unable to feed its young, offers itself to them as food; and they eat their father. And from this, they say, the proverb took its origin which says, "Of a bad raven a bad egg."

I have learned this too about ants. So present in them is the love of toil and the willingness to labour, without any excuse and without any malingering pretext and pretence behind which sloth lurks, that even at the full moon they do not even by night grow idle or rest, but cling to their work. O men, who devise countless excuses and pretexts for taking your ease! And what need is there to recount and pour forth so great a crowd of them? For Dionysia have been proclaimed, and Lenaea, and Chytri, and Gephyrismi, and when one passes to Sparta there are other festivals, and to Thebes others, and in every city countless ones, some barbarian, some Greek.
Aristotle says that about the river Hypanis is bred the creature so called, the "one-day" creature, being born at nightfall and dying as the sun turns to its setting.

The historians sing of Egyptian galleries, and they too, and the tribe of poets, sing of certain Cretan labyrinths; but the varied paths and windings and circuits of ants in their burrowing they do not yet know. By wisdom they fashion this underground household most winding, rendering the passage difficult or even wholly impassable for the beasts that plot against them. And the earth they dig out, this they throw up around the mouth and make, as it were, walls and bulwarks, so that the water rushing down from heaven may not then easily flood and destroy them all or at least most of them. And they wall off with certain partition-walls the chambers that divide the burrows from one another, and that most skillfully, and there would be three areas, as in a stately house. And one they make a men's quarter, in which dwell the males and such females as are with them; the second, where the pregnant ants give birth, a kind of women's quarter; and a third, another, they set apart as a treasury and granary for the gathered seeds. And neither Ischomachus there nor Socrates, zealous for enviable household management, teaches them these things. And the ants going forth, as if to gather provisions, follow the largest, who lead like generals. And coming to the cornfields, the still young ones wait below at the stalk, while the leaders creep up, and biting through what are called the tail-ends of the grain throw them down to the people below; and they, going round, cut off the beards and shell out the little husks that cover and enwrap the wheat. And needing neither threshing nor men able to winnow nor winds urged on to separate and divide the chaff and the grain, the ants have food without men ploughing and sowing. And this too I have heard as wise: that the kinsfolk bury their dead ants in the husks of the wheat, as men bury their fathers or all that is dear to them in coffins.

I learn that in the city of Antioch in Syria there was a gentle elephant, and that as it went to its pasture it looked with pleasure upon a woman who sold garlands, and stood beside her, and with its trunk wiped the woman's face. And she would let down to it, as a bait of love, a garland woven from the flowers of the season; and it was his daily business to take it, and hers to give it. But in time the woman ended her life, and the elephant, missing its accustomed ways and not seeing the woman it had longed for, like a lover unlucky in his beloved, grew wild; and the one till then most gentle was kindled to anger, just as those among men who, being overwhelmed by grief, have been driven out of their senses.

For the rock-crabs the first shell breaks, and just as the snakes their old age, so indeed do these too cast off their shell. And when they perceive it parting from their flesh, they go everywhere maddened and seek more food, that, when bulk has been added to them, they may swell and break their shell off themselves. And when they have slipped out of it and become free, they lie relaxed upon the sand, like dead things; for they are afraid for the hide that is growing upon them, which is still wet and tender. But little by little, gathering themselves and in a way coming back to life, they first taste the sand. And to such a degree are they without daring and least courageous as long as a membrane covers them as an outer shelter; but when it begins to harden and to pass into the nature of a shell, then they cast off their cowardice, taking courage as in a weapon, in the shelter of their covering and, as one might say, in full armour.

Through the most fiery summer the Nile floods the plains of the Egyptians and gives them the appearance of a sea spread out and smooth, and the Egyptians fish over what was lately ploughland, and sail in boats made for this season and this visitation of the river. Then the river recedes and returns to its own measures, those appointed for it by nature, and fish are left behind, orphaned of their father and bereft of the water that flowed up, fed in thick mud as a dinner for the farmers. And though it will be put rather strongly, this is the Egyptian harvest of fish.

Of the hunting of water-creatures there are four kinds, they say: net-fishing, harpooning, weel-fishing, and hook-fishing besides. And net-fishing is wealth-bringing, and resembles the taking of an army and the capture of certain prisoners, and it needs varied equipment, such as broom-cord and white flax and another black, and galingale and cork and lead and pine and thongs and sumac and stone and papyrus and horns and a six-oared ship and an axle and pegs and a windlass and a drum and iron and wood and pitch. And various kinds of fish fall into it, and shoals various and many. Harpooning is the most manly of the rest, and needs the most robust hunter. There must be present a straight fir-pole and broom-cord ropes and torches of the most resinous pine; and it needs a small boat and vigorous rowers and good arms. Weel-fishing is the most deceitful hunting and terribly treacherous, and seems least fitting for free men. It needs dry rushes and withy and a stone and bedding-weights and sea-weed and rushes and cypress foliage and corks and wood and bait and a small boat. Hook-fishing is the cleverest and most becoming to free men. It needs horsehair, of colours both white and black and tawny and grizzled; and of the dyed they approve the grey-green and the sea-purple; for all the others are bad, they say. They use also the stiff bristles of wild boars and turpentine, and very much bronze and lead and broom-cord and feathers, especially white and black and variegated. And the fishermen use also crimson and purple wools and corks and wood; and they need iron and other things, among them well-grown and dry reeds and soaked rushes and a polished fennel-stalk and a rod of cornel-wood and goat's horns and hide. And one fish is taken by one of these, another by another, and I have already told their hunting.

The Carian and Lycian leopard is not high-spirited, nor very ready to spring, but long in body; and when wounded with spears and points it is resistant, and does not easily yield to the iron, doing that Homeric thing, "And truly, pierced through by the spear, it does not give up."
The cries of cranes summon rains, as they say; and the brain has for women some love-charms toward amorous favour, if those who first observed these things are sufficient to bear witness.

The rainbow-wrasses are fish bred among rocks, and they have their mouth full of venom, and whatever fish they taste they make uneatable. And fishermen too, meeting with a half-eaten prawn, and judging the catch unsaleable, if they taste of it out of poverty, are convulsed in the belly and twisted. And they trouble those who dive and swim in the sea-fishing, falling on them in numbers and biting, just like flies on land; and one must shoo them off or be punished by being eaten; but to one shooing them off the work is ruined by the distraction.

The wood-pigeons are sung as the most chaste of birds. For the male and the female, having paired and, as it were, breathed together into marriage, cling to one another and are chaste, and neither of these birds would touch a stranger's bed. And if they cast amorous eyes on others, the rest go round upon them, and the male the males of its kind tear to pieces, the females the female. This law of chastity reaches also to the turtle-doves and remains unchanging, except that each bird is not put to death; for the male they kill, but the female they pity and leave unharmed, and it goes about widowed.

As evidence of the nature of animals—that they are not altogether hard to manage, but, when well treated, are good at remembering the kindness—there are in Egypt the cats and the ichneumons and the crocodiles and still the race of hawks. Each is taken by flattery of the belly, and being thence tamed remains thereafter most gentle; and it would never attack its own benefactors, once the anger inborn and kindred to it has been loosed. But a man—a creature endowed with reason and deemed worthy of intelligence and granted a sense of shame and entrusted with the power to blush—becomes a grievous enemy to his friend, and the secrets entrusted to him, for the slightest and most casual cause, he spits out to the ruin of the one who trusted him.

The cuttlefish has a venomous bite and teeth strongly concealed. The osmylus too and the octopus were biting creatures; and the octopus would bite more violently than the cuttlefish, but discharges less venom.

A horse, if it meets with care, requites its benefactor with goodwill and friendship. And what kind of horse Bucephalas was to Alexander runs everywhere as a tale, and it is no more pleasant for me to tell it. And the horse of Antiochus that avenged its master and killed the Galatian who had cut down Antiochus in the battle (the Galatian's name was Centoarates)—this one too I pass by. But Socles (for I do not think many know this man) was an Athenian, and was both reputed and by nature beautiful. He, then, bought a horse, lovely too, but strongly amorous and somehow wiser than other horses. So it fell most ardently in love with its master, and as he approached it neighed, and as he patted it it whinnied, and as he mounted it offered itself obedient, and as he stood by facing it, it gazed at him with melting eyes. And these things, being amorous, yet seemed pleasant; but when it was as though too forward, eager to do something to the youth, and a tale more outrageous spread about them both, Socles, not bearing the slander, hating it as a licentious lover, sold the horse. And it, not enduring the deprivation of the beautiful one, freed itself from life by a most violent starving.

Elephants worship the rising sun, stretching their trunks straight toward the ray like hands, and for this reason they are beloved of the god. Let Ptolemy Philopator be a good witness for us. The victory over Antiochus was won with the help of the sun, and Ptolemy, sacrificing thank-offerings and propitiating Helios, sacrificed magnificently in other ways, and presented four elephants of the greatest size as victims, as he supposed, honouring the divinity with this sacrifice. But a dream troubled him, as though the god were threatening him for the strange and unwonted sacrifice; and in fear he made four bronze elephants and dedicated them to the god in place of those he had killed, propitiating and appeasing him. Elephants, then, worship the gods; but as for men, whether they are gods, and whether, being gods, they care for us, is a matter of doubt.

The Troglodytes are a celebrated race of men, and they have taken their name from their way of life. The snakes fear them. The reason is that the men eat them. And the snakes, when they mate with one another, give off a most heavy smell.

There are not a few kinds of cicada, and those skilled in knowing such things count them and sing their names. One is named "ashy" from its colour, another is the "membrax," from where I do not know, and "laketas" was a cicada's name too, and I have received by hearsay the "kerkope" and a certain "acheta" and "acanthias." For my part, having heard of so many kinds of cicada, I remember these; but whoever has come to know more than those mentioned, let him speak.

By these two accounts an Indian and a Libyan, differing in race, shall speak: the Indian will tell the things of his country, and the Libyan as much as he too knows; and what both accounts sing is this. Among the Indians, if a full-grown elephant is caught, it is hard to tame, and longing for freedom it thirsts for slaughter. And if you grip it with bonds too, it is kindled still more to anger, and will not endure to be a slave and a prisoner. But the Indians coax it with food too, and try to tame it with varied and enticing baits, setting before it whatever fills the belly and charms the spirit. But it is vexed with them and disdains them. What, then, do they devise? They bring against it a native music, and sing over it with a certain instrument familiar too; and the instrument is called the skindapsos. And it lends its ears and is charmed, and its anger is softened, and its spirit draws back and is calmed, and little by little it looks toward the food too. Then it is released from its bonds, but remains bound by the music, and dines eagerly, a dainty banqueter; for from longing for the strain it would no longer stand off. And the mares of the Libyans (for one must hear the other account too) — the flute-playing takes them so far. They are softened and tamed, and cease from their insolence and frisking, and they follow the herdsman wherever the strain leads them away, and when he stops they too stop; and if he raises the strain higher, tears are shed from them for pleasure. The cowherds of the horses, hollowing out a branch of oleander and making a flute and breathing into it, then thus pipe to the aforesaid mares. And Euripides too speaks of certain "shepherd hymenaeals"; and this is a strain which casts the mares into love and amorous frenzy, and maddens the males to mate with them. So horse-marriages are accomplished in this manner, and the strain seems to sing a wedding-hymn.

To describe the form of the rhinoceros is to tell a thrice-stale tale; for many of the Greeks and Romans know it from having seen it. But to tell its peculiar traits in its way of life is no worse a thing. At the tip of its nose it bears the horn, whence indeed it has its name; and it is exceedingly sharp at the point, and the hard part of it is likened to iron. Rubbing it against the rocks, it then will set upon the elephant, coming to close quarters, being otherwise no match for it, both because of the other's height and because of so great a strength of the beast. So it gets beneath its legs, and cuts and rips up the belly with its horn; and the elephant, not long after, when its blood has flowed out, slips down. The fight of the rhinoceros against the elephant is over pasture, and one may meet with many elephants dead in this way. But if the rhinoceros does not first do this, but, running somehow beneath, is pressed down when the elephant falls upon it, the elephant, throwing about its trunk, holds it and draws it to itself, and falling upon it with its tusks cuts it up as with axes. For even if the rhinoceros has a hide hard and hard to pierce, yet the force of the one that falls upon it is very strong.

If one burns vultures' feathers, as I hear, he will most easily draw serpents out of their holes and dens. The bird the woodpecker is named from what it does. For it has a curved beak, and with this it pecks at the oaks, and there, as into a nest, it puts its young, needing no straws nor any weaving and building from them at all. So if one inserts a stone and blocks the entrance of the aforesaid bird, it, perceiving the plot, brings a herb hostile to the stone; and the stone, as though weighed down and unable to bear it, leaps out, and the dear retreat opens again for the aforesaid bird.
The sea-hare, when eaten, has often brought death, and in any case pains the belly. It is born in mud, and is not seldom caught together with the small fry; in shape it would be like the naked snail.

Aristotle says that of doves the males share the labour of the females in giving birth, and when these wander outside the nest thrust and drive them back, and when they have laid force them to brood. And the same author says that the males too warm the young and rear them together with the females, and that, so the young may not be ill-fed, the parents give the infants as their first food salty earth, which when they have tasted, then they readily feed on the rest. And doves seem somehow to be at truce with the other rapacious birds, but to dread, they say, the sea-eagles and the hawks. And what they contrive against the falcons is worth hearing. When the one that is high up and made to fly aloft pursues them, they slip down and draw themselves lower and try to press in their wing; but when the one that has by nature its flight lower pursues, they rise and travel aloft, and flying above it take courage, since it cannot lead higher.

Eudemus says there is a tale worthy of wonder, and this is the man's tale. A young hunter, able to live among the wildest of animals—reared, that is, from young and from cubs—had as his fellow-nurslings and messmates a dog and a bear and a lion that had grown up together. And these, Eudemus says, kept peace with one another for a time and were friendly in their feelings; but one day it happened that the dog, playing with the bear and fawning upon it and teasing it, the bear was contrary to custom turned savage and fell upon the dog, and tore the belly of the poor creature with its claws and rent it apart. The same author says that the lion was indignant at what had happened, and as it were hated the implacable and unfriendly act of the bear, and longed for the dog as a comrade, and came to a just anger, and laid upon the bear its punishment, and did to it the very things that it had done to the dog. Now Homer says that it is good that even a son of one who has perished should be left behind; but nature seems to show that to leave behind a friend to avenge oneself, dear Homer, is also a gain. Something of the like we think too about Zeno and Cleanthes, if we hear aright.

They say that the wild boar does not charge anyone before it has whetted its tusks; and Homer indeed bears witness to this, saying, "having whetted his white tusk in his curved jaws." And I hear that the boar fattens most when it does not bathe, but spends its time in the mire and wallows and drinks muddied water, and delights in quiet and a darker shelter, and in foods that are most flatulent and able to fill it up. And Homer seems to hint at these things. About their wallowing and delighting in the filthier sloughs . . . saying "swine that bed on the ground"; that they fatten on troubled water . . . he says "drinking black water, which nourishes in swine their thriving fat." That they delight in darkness he proves by these words: "beneath a hollow rock they slept, in the shelter from Boreas." And he hints at the flatulence of their food when he says they eat "the heart-cheering acorn." And Homer, knowing that the boar wastes away and ruins its flesh at the sight of the sow, has made the males sleep apart and the females apart. And in Salamis, if a sow falling upon green corn and a flourishing crop crops it, it is a law of the Salaminians to grind out its teeth. And this they say is what is meant by Homer's "corn-wasting sow." But others think otherwise, and say that the sow that has tasted green corn has weak teeth.

There is bitterest enmity between the francolin and the cock, and again the cock against the francolin, and the hawk against the crow and it against him, and the raven against the sea-hawk and he against the raven, and the raven and the hawk against the turtledove, and indeed the turtledove against each. And I learn that the stork hates the bat, and it hates back in return as an enemy, and that the pelican is not friendly to the quail. And the hatred, I hear, is mutual.

The priests in Egypt sprinkle themselves not with any water, nor with whatever is at hand, but with that from which they have been persuaded the ibis has drunk. For they know very well that it would never drink water that is foul or polluted by any harmful substances; for they believe that the creature has within itself something of prophecy too, inasmuch as it is sacred. And I hear that elephants which are unwounded gently draw out from the wounded the lances and javelins, like men skilled in surgery and trained in the wisdom of such matters. So even the irrational creatures were objects of earnest concern to the men of former times. The Eagle—Pyrrhus of Epirus—rejoiced to hear himself so called, and so did the one called the Hawk—Antiochus. These various and gathered things have been told, worth learning for the man who understands.

When a field borders on the sea and fruitful plants stand beside it, the farmers often catch, in the summer season, octopuses and squids that have come out of the waves and crept up through the trunks and fallen upon the branches and are gathering the fruit, and they arrest them and bring a charge against the thieves. And in return for what the aforesaid creatures gathered, the masters of the plundered fruit feast on them in turn.

These things too I have heard about dogs. Puppies are born blind, and do not see when they have come forth from the mother's womb. For the first thirteen days they are held by this affliction, as many days as the moon also does not shine by night; but then the dog becomes the sharpest-sighted of animals. The Egyptians honour it, and named a nome after it, and they say there is a twofold reason for the honour: one which says that, when Isis was seeking Osiris everywhere, dogs went before her and partly tried to help her track the child, partly to keep off the wild beasts; and the other, that the star called the Dog, which report says was Orion's, now rises, and together with it in a way rises also the Nile, coming to water the land of Egypt and pouring over the fields. So, as bringing and summoning this fruitful water, the Egyptians honour it.

That the tribe of dolphins is fond of song and of the flute, Arion of Methymna is a sufficient witness, both from the statue at Taenarum and from the epigram written upon it. And the epigram is: "By the escort of the immortals, this conveyance saved Arion the son of Cycleus from the Sicilian sea." And a hymn of thanksgiving to Poseidon, witness to the dolphins' love of music, Arion wrote, paying these too, as it were, a ransom for his life. And this is the hymn: "Highest of gods, lord of the sea, gold-tridented Poseidon, earth-holder, through the teeming brine; round you the swimming beasts dance in a ring with their fins, with light tossings of their feet lightly leaping, snub-nosed, bristle-necked, swift-running whelps, the music-loving dolphins, sea-nurslings of the maiden Nereid goddesses, whom Amphitrite bore; you who brought me to the land of Pelops, to the Taenarian shore, as I wandered in the Sicilian sea, carrying me on your arched backs, cleaving the furrow of the Nereid plain, an untrodden path, when treacherous men cast me from their hollow sea-faring ship into the sea-purple swell of the deep." Peculiar to dolphins, surely, in addition to what has been said above, is their love of music too.

Most savage of creatures, it seems, were the bulls of the Ethiopians called the flesh-eaters. They are twice the size of those among the Greeks, and swiftest of speed. They are red-haired, grey-eyed, and these surpass the lions. Their horns at other times they move as they do their ears, but in their fights they raise them and, having set them up firmly, then fight thus; and the horns, once raised, are not bent down by their rage, by a nature, by Zeus, that is marvellous. They are unwoundable by spears and by every weapon; for the iron does not pierce in; for the bull, bristling, casts it off when it has fallen on him in vain. It attacks even herds of horses and other beasts. So the herdsmen, wishing to help their own herds, make deep hidden trenches and lie in wait for them with these; and the bulls, when they fall in, are choked by their own rage. And this creature has justly been judged the best among the Troglodytes; for it has the valour of a lion, the swiftness of a horse, the strength of a bull, and is stronger than iron.

The dentex-fish are not solitary, nor do they endure separation and division from one another. They love to gather in shoals according to age. The younger swim in troops, the more mature again in common; and, as the saying goes, age delights age, the present delighting the present, as comrades and friends from the same pursuits and ways of life. And they contrive thus against the hunters. When a fisherman lets down the bait for them, they all go round and form a circle and look at one another, each giving, as it were, a signal to each, neither to approach nor to touch the bait let down. And those drawn up in this array keep still; but from another shoal a dentex comes and swallows the hook, taking capture as the reward of his solitude. And he is drawn up, and the others now take courage, thinking they will not be caught, and so, growing contemptuous, they are caught.

The vulture is hostile to the corpse. So it falls on it and eats it as an enemy, and watches one about to die. And indeed vultures follow armies marching abroad, knowing very prophetically that they are going to war, and knowing too that every battle makes corpses. And they say a male vulture is never born, but all are females; and the creatures, knowing this and fearing a barrenness of offspring, do such things for the sake of progeny. They fly facing the south wind; and if there is no south wind, they gape toward the east wind, and the breath flowing in fills them, and they conceive for three years. And they say a vulture does not weave a nest. But the lammergeiers, being on the borderline between vultures and eagles, are both male and black in colour. And of these I hear that nests too are shown; but vultures, I have learned, do not lay eggs, but bring forth nestlings. And that from birth these are feathered, this too I have heard.

An Indian horse-trainer met with a white elephant-foal, and taking it reared it while still young, and little by little made it tame, and rode upon it, and loved the possession and was loved in return, receiving from it the recompense for having reared it. So the king of the Indians, learning of it, asked to take the elephant. But the man, as a lover jealous, and indeed greatly grieved if another were to be master of it, said he would not give it, and went off into the desert, mounting the elephant. The king was angered, and sent men against him to take it away and at the same time to bring the Indian to justice. And when they came, they tried to use force. So the man too pelted them from above, and the beast, as though wronged, joined in defending him. And at first it was so; but when the Indian, being struck, slipped down, the elephant bestrode his foster-father, like a man shielding him in arms, and killed many of the assailants, and put the rest to flight; then, throwing its trunk about its foster-father, it lifted him up and carried him to the lair, and stayed by him as a faithful friend by a friend, and showed its goodwill. O wicked men, ever about the table and the clatter of the frying-pan, and dancing toward your dinner, but in dangers traitors, and to no purpose and to no end gaping with the name of friendship!

Among the Indians there are creatures as large as beetles might grow, and they are red; you would liken them to cinnabar, if you first beheld them. These have very long legs, and are soft to the touch. They grow upon the trees that bear amber, and feed on the fruit of these plants. The Indians hunt them and press them out, and from them dye their scarlet cloaks and the tunics beneath them and whatever else they wish to turn and dye to this colour. And such clothing is brought also to the king of the Persians. And the beauty of the clothing seems marvellous to the Persians, and when set beside the native Persian dyes it far surpasses and astonishes them, as Ctesias says; since it is keener and more brilliant than the famous Sardian dyes. There are produced too, in that part of India where the beetles are, the so-called Cynocephali, "Dog-heads," to whom the appearance and nature of their body gave the name; for in all else they have the features of men, and they walk clad in the skins of wild beasts. And they are just, and harm no man, and they utter no speech, but howl, yet they understand the language of the Indians. Their food is wild animals; and they catch these most easily, for they are very swift, and having caught them they kill them, and roast them not with fire, but tear them into pieces and dry them in the heat of the sun. They also rear goats and sheep. And they make the wild animals their food, but drink the milk of the flocks they rear. I have made mention of them among the irrational creatures, and with reason; for they have no articulate, distinct, and human voice.

Nature gave to dogs a herb that counteracts wounds. And if worms trouble them, by eating what is called the green corn they expel them. They are said too, when they need to empty either belly, to eat a certain herb, and to vomit up the part of the food that floats on top, while the surplus is excreted below them, they say. From this the Egyptians too are said to have learned the practice of purging. And partridges and storks when wounded, and ringdoves, gnaw, as the story goes, marjoram, then putting it in their wounds they heal their bodies, and indeed need nothing at all of human medicine.

The eagle is killed by what is called comfrey, the ibis by the gall of a hyena, the starling by garlic-seed, the plover by asphalt, and the hedgehog by what is called pondweed. The hedgehog cannot endure the gall of the shearwater. The hawk and the gull and the turtledove and the blackbird and the tribe of vultures, if they gnaw a pomegranate that has been cut, perish. Cedar leaves destroy the reed-warbler, the flower of the chaste-tree the blackcap, and rocket-seed the raven. By perfume the beetle dies, and by the fat of a gazelle the hoopoe. The crow, coming upon the remnant of flesh devoured by a wolf, dies. The lark dies by mustard-seed, and the crane, having sucked the sap of a vine, perishes.

Mithridates of Pontus, when he slept, trusted less to arms and bodyguards, and for this reason he kept as tamed guards a bull and a horse and a deer. These beasts, then, kept guard over him as he slept, perceiving most swiftly from the breath if anyone approached. And the one by its bellowing, another by its neighing, and another by its bleating would wake him.

Rhyades is the name of a sea creature wise at discerning the passage of the seasons. At the beginning of winter, at any rate, they stay quiet, fleeing the frosts, and gladly warming themselves by remaining together in brotherly equal shares; then in spring these begin to swim and to take longer journeys, and they feed not only on what falls in their way, but also on what they seek out and trace.

The fish called oxyrhynchus is so named, and seems to have taken its name from its face and from the shape of it. The Nile nourishes this fish, and indeed a nome is named after it, where this same fish has honours. A fish caught with a hook these men would never eat, fearing that perhaps their sacred and wonderful fish, of which I spoke, had chanced to be pierced upon it. And if ever fish are caught in nets, they search through them, lest that one had slipped in unnoticed, and they prefer a catch of nothing to the very best catch with that fish taken. The people round about say it was born from the wounds of Osiris; and they hold that Osiris is the same as the Nile.

A certain Tyrrhenian account is current that says the wild boars and the deer among them are caught by nets and dogs, as is the law of hunting, but with music fighting on the hunters' side, and the more so. And how, I will now tell. They throw round the nets and the rest of the hunting-gear, all that lies in wait for the animals; and a man stands by skilled in the flute, and tries as much as possible to relax the strain, and lets be whatever is intense in the music, but whatever is sweetest in flute-song, this he plays. Stillness and quiet easily carry it across, and to the heights and the glens and the thickets and, to speak in sum, to all the lairs and beds of the beasts the strain flows in. And at first, as the sound passes into their ears, they are struck and somewhere too filled with fear; then a pure and irresistible pleasure of the music takes hold of them, and enchanted they have forgetfulness even of offspring and homes. And yet the beasts love not to wander from their accustomed places. But the Tyrrhenian creatures, little by little, as though by some persuading spell, are drawn, and as the strain bewitches them they come and fall into the snares, mastered by the music.

Mnaseas says that in Europe there is a temple of Heracles and of his wife, whom the poets sing to be the daughter of Hera. So within the precinct of the shrine, he says, many tame birds are reared, and this too, that these birds are cocks and hens. They graze and herd together by kind, and have public feeding, and are votive offerings of the aforesaid gods. The hens, then, graze in the temple of Hebe, and their mates in that of Heracles. And a channel of ever-flowing and pure water runs through the midst. No female at all comes in to the temple of Heracles; but the males, when it is the season for mating, fly over the channel, and then, having consorted with the females, go back again to their own quarters beside the god whom they serve, having purified themselves with the water that divides the kinds of the birds. So there are born, as is natural, first from the consorting eggs; then, when the mothers have warmed them and hatched the young, the males take their sons to themselves and rear them; and as for the female birds, it is their task to rear the daughters.

epilogue. All, then, that my own zeal and care and toil, and my mind advancing toward learning yet more even in these matters, has tracked out and discovered — things which approved men and philosophers made a contest of, setting up experience in them as a prize — has now been told by me, as well as it was possible to tell it, neither passing over what I knew nor playing the sluggard, as though I had despised and dishonoured a herd irrational and voiceless; but here too the love of wisdom that dwells with me and is connatural to me kindled me. I am not unaware that some of those whose eyes are keen upon money, and who are whetted toward honours and powers and all that loves glory, will hold it against me that I laid out my own leisure upon these things, when it was possible both to be haughty and to be reckoned among the courts and to advance to great wealth. But I, going round about foxes and lizards and beetles and snakes and lions, and what the leopard does, and how the stork is affectionate, and that the nightingale is sweet of mouth, and how the elephant is wise, and the kinds of fishes, and the migrations of cranes, and the natures of serpents, and all the rest that this work has laboriously gathered and keeps — I find it not dear to me to be reckoned among those rich men and tested against them; but if there are those whom both wise poets and men clever at seeing and observing the secrets of nature, and writers who have advanced their inquiry to the furthest, have judged worthy of themselves, among these I try, somehow or other, to reckon myself, and I wish to; and clearly I am a better counsellor to myself than their judgment is. For I would wish to gain one well-learned piece of knowledge rather than the much-sung riches and possessions of the very wealthy. And of these matters enough for now. I know too that some will not praise the following: that I did not separate my account according to each of the creatures, nor speak the particulars of each by themselves all together, but mixed up the various things variously, and went through many subjects, and here left off the account of these creatures, and there returned to speak other things about their nature. But I, first of all, in what is my own, am not the slave of another's judgment and will, nor do I say that I must follow another wherever he may lead me; and second, by the variety of the reading I hunt after attractiveness and flee the loathing that comes from like things, and so I thought I ought to weave and plait this work as a kind of meadow or seasonable garland out of the many colours, since the many creatures bring flowers, as it were. And if to huntsmen it seems somehow a piece of good luck to find a single creature, yet the tracks of so many, and the gathering of their members, I say, is no ignoble thing — that is, all that nature gave them and all that she granted to be tracked out. What against this are the Cephali and Hippolyti, and any other clever at pursuing wild beasts in the wild mountains, or again, of those clever in the water-hunts, Metrodorus of Byzantium, or Leonidas his son, or Demostratus, or any other most skilful hunters of fish, many, by Zeus? And as for painters, a horse painted most beautifully made them proud, as it did Aglaophon, or a fawn, as Apelles, or a sprouting little ox, as Myron, or some other thing. But if one man sets forth and brings to the light the works of so many — characters and shapes and wisdom and shrewdness and justice and temperance and courage and affection and piety, having hunted them out — how is he not already worthy of admiration? And having come to this point in my account, I am quite vexed, that we sing the piety of irrational creatures, but convict men of impiety. And this I shall not prove here; but it is most just to say besides the following, of which indeed at the beginning of these accounts I made mention: if I said these things, all that everyone, or at least the most, have said, it is not yet just to blame me; for I could not myself mould other creatures, but I displayed many that I came to know. Indeed, I have also told some things that no other has told, having come to them myself through this experience of mine; and truth is dear to me, both elsewhere and here not least. But how I told them, and with how much toil, and what the nobility of the diction is, and of the composition, and the beauty of the nouns and the verbs — those will know to whom I do not appeal as bad judges.

The raven is parched through the summer, punished by thirst, and cries out, calling its punishment to witness, as they say. And they give this reason. Apollo, whose servant it was, sent it to fetch water; but it came upon a deep field of corn, still green, and waited until the corn should grow dry, wishing to nibble at the grain, and so disregarded the command. And for this, in the driest season, it pays the penalty, thirsting. This seems a tale, but let it be told out of reverence for the god.

The kite is most unsparing in robbery. These, if they get the better of the bits of meat sold in the market, snatch them, falling upon them; but the meat from the sacrifice of Zeus they would not touch. And the mountain-falcon, falling upon birds, snatches away their eyes.

Chloris is the name of a bird, which would make its nest from nothing else but the so-called comfrey; and comfrey is a root hard to find and to dig up. For bedding it spreads under itself hairs and wool. And the female bird is so called, but the male they call chlorion, and it is ingenious in its life, good at learning whatever you will and steadfast in enduring the trial that comes with learning, whenever it is caught. And through the winter one would not see it free and at liberty, but when the spring turnings of the year begin, then it would appear. When Arcturus rises, it withdraws to its own haunts, whence it set out hither.

I shall need no older witness here, but I shall tell what I myself have known. A man, having caught a lizard, of those that are exceedingly green but rather full in body, and having pierced it with a sting made of bronze and so blinded the lizard, and having bored an earthenware pot of newly made ware with very fine holes, so as not to shut out the air yet not to give it a way of escape, and having poured in earth, and that very dewy, and put in the creature and a certain herb whose name he did not tell, and an iron ring set with a stone of jet, on which a lizard had been engraved—he covered the pot, sealing on it nine seals, of which he removed a seal each day for nine days. And having effaced the last of all he opens the vessel, and I myself saw the lizard looking, and it had most clear eyes, those that until then had been maimed. And we released it where it had been taken, but that ring the man who did these things said was good for the eyes.

About the hare too it occurs to me to say here such things as these. The hare does not come to its accustomed form before it has confused its tracks, here going in, there going out, in order to make disappear the plot of the hunters against it, the creature by a certain natural wisdom deceiving men most craftily.

The young offspring of wild animals are named in different ways, and most have a twofold appellation. The young of lions are called cubs and lion-whelps, as Aristophanes of Byzantium attests; those of leopards, cubs and arceli—though there are some who say that the arceli are a different kind from leopards. The young of jackals like to be called only cubs, and likewise those of tigers, and of ants and of panthers. It seems too that the offspring of lynxes are named in the same way. At any rate in the Dithyrambs ascribed to Lasus the lynx's young is so called. The young of apes we hear are called both cubs and ape-whelps; and the young of antelopes, foals; and if of oryxes too, I should not wonder, says the same Aristophanes. The young of dogs and of wolves would be called whelps, says he; and now the young of wolves are also called wolf-whelps, while the full-grown and largest would be called a lone-wolf. The young of hares are leverets; but the full-grown one the poets like to call a "cowerer," and the Lacedaemonians a "swift one." The offspring of foxes are called fox-whelps; but the mother herself is called the "cunning one" and the "burrower" and the "skulker." The young of wild swine they name moloubria; and you may hear Hipponax calling the boar itself a moloubrites. Some swine too are called "lone-ones." Gazelles they are accustomed to call zorcae and procae as well. The offspring of porcupines and such creatures are called obria; and Euripides mentions the name in the Peliades, and Aeschylus in the Agamemnon and the Net-Haulers. The young of birds and of snakes and of crocodiles some call psacali, among whom are the Thessalians. New-hatched birds they call ortaliches, and the chicks of fowls alectorides, and again goslings and shelduck-chicks and the like they form in the same way. Achaeus the tragic poet called the nestling of the swallow a "calf."

If one should crush sea urchins while they are still alive and in their shells and presenting their spines, and scatter them into the sea, leaving one fragment here and another there, they come together again and unite and recognize the kindred fragment, and clinging together grow into one. And they become whole again by some wonderful and peculiar nature.

The ichneumon is the same creature both male and female, having a share of both this nature and that, and nature has granted it both to beget and to bear with the same body. The defeated, after the battle, are assigned to the meaner sex; for the victors mount the vanquished and sow their seed into them. And these carry off, as the prize of defeat, the endurance of birth-pangs and becoming mothers instead of fathers. To the creatures most hostile to man, the asp and the crocodile, the ichneumon is the greatest enemy, and I have spoken above of their war. The ichneumons are said to be sacred to Leto and the Eileithyiae; and the people of Heracleopolis revere them, so they say.

The anthias-fish, when they are struck and caught, are the most pitiable of sights, and as they die they seem to lament themselves and in a way to supplicate, like men fallen among pitiless and most murderous robbers. For some of them, trying to escape, are then entangled in the nets, and as they try to leap over the ambush, the spear-point overtakes them; and others, fleeing this death, leap out onto the land that is until then hostile to fish, choosing the end of life apart from the sword, and very gladly.

The raven they say is a sacred bird, and they say it is the attendant of Apollo. For this reason they agree that it is good for prophetic signs, and those who understand the seats and cries and flights of birds, whether on the left hand or the right, take omens from its call. I hear besides that ravens' eggs dye the hair black. And whoever would dye his own hair must keep oil in his mouth with his lips closed; otherwise his teeth too are blackened along with the hair, and hard to wash and hard to cleanse.

Egyptian ravens, those that live along the Nile, seem at first to be suppliants of the voyagers, asking to receive something; and having received it they keep quiet, but failing to get what they asked, they fly along, and settling on the yardarm of the ship eat through and cut the knots of the ropes. And Libyan ravens, when men, fearing thirst, have drawn water and filled vessels, and setting them on the roofs have left the water to be kept fresh by the air, then, as far as their beaks reach down by stooping, use the drink; but when it has fallen low, they bring pebbles in their mouth and claws and throw them into the jar; and these, by their weight, are thrust down and settle, while the water, pressed up, floats to the top. And the ravens drink very ingeniously, knowing by some unspeakable instinct that two bodies do not occupy one place.

A bull whetted by anger and rampaging with its horn and borne along by an uncontrollable rush—neither does the herdsman check it, nor fear restrain it, nor anything else of the kind; but a man stops it and looses it from its onset by binding fast his own right knee with a band and meeting it.

To me, O men, it seems most shameful that there should be friendship among animals toward one another, not only among those of the same haunts nor among those of the same kind, but even among those that have no kinship with one another in the common species. At any rate sheep are friendly to goats, and there is friendship between dove and turtledove; and ringdoves and partridges are friendly toward one another; and we have long known that the halcyon and the cerylus long for each other; and the crow is friendly toward the heron, and the gull toward what is called the jackdaw, and the harpe toward the kite. But the crows and the owls wage everlasting and, so to speak, truceless war; and enemies are the kite and the raven, and the redstart against the turtledove, and the brenthus and the gull, and again the greenfinch against the turtledove, and the vultures and the eagles, and the swans and the snakes, and lions against the antelopes and bulls.
