Most hostile of all were the elephant and the snake, and the ichneumon against the asp, and the titmouse against the ass; for the ass brays, and the titmouse's eggs are broken, and the young fall out unformed; and the titmouse, avenging its young, leaps upon the sores of the asses, and eats them. And the fox hates the hawk, and the bull the raven, and the anthus the horse. And the educated man, who hears nothing in vain, must know that the dolphin too is at odds with the whale, the basses with the mullets, and the lampreys with the conger-eels, and others with others.

The mare, too, was a good mother and clever at remembering the colt born of her. Recognizing this, then, Darius the Lower used to bring into battle mares that had left their young at home fresh from the birth. And the colts, orphaned of their mothers, are reared on strange milk, just as men too are. So when the turning of the battle at Issus began to press the Persians, and Darius was being defeated, he mounted a mare, needing flight and swiftest safety. And she, by memory of the one left behind, as eagerly as her feet allowed, is celebrated as having snatched her master

That memory attends animals too, and that this also is peculiar to them, apart from the art and the wisdom in regard to it which certain charlatans boast that they have devised, these things prove. A man whose master was one of the Roman senate ran away—Androcles by name, a slave by fortune, for what crime, and how great, I cannot say. He came, then, to Libya, and left the cities behind, and, as the saying goes, marked his course by the stars, and advanced into the desert. Scorched by the abundant and fiery ray, he gladly ran beneath a cavernous rock and rested; but this rock was the lair of a lion. The lion, then, returns from the hunt, pierced through by a violent thorn and tormented, and meeting the young man it looked upon him gently, and began to fawn, and held out its foot, and entreated, as best it could, that the thorn be drawn out. At first the man cowered down; but when he saw the beast gentle and understood the trouble in its foot, he drew out what pained it from the foot, and freed it from its anguish. Delighted, then, with the cure, the lion, paying him his physician's fee, considered him guest and friend, and shared with him what it hunted. And the lion ate its share raw, as is the way of lions, while the man roasted his own; and they enjoyed a common table, each according to its own nature. For three years Androcles lived in this manner; then, grown over-shaggy and seized by a violent itch, he left the lion and gave himself up to fortune. Then, as he wandered, men seized him and, learning whose he was, bound him and sent him to Rome to his master. The master called the slave to account for the wrongs he had suffered, and the man was condemned to be given as food to wild beasts. And that Libyan lion too was somehow caught and let loose in the theatre, and the young man was brought out to be destroyed—he who had once been the housemate and tent-mate of that very lion. And the man did not recognize the beast, but the beast at once knew the man, and fawned upon him, and lowering its whole body cast itself at his feet. At last Androcles too recognized his own guest-friend, and embracing the lion as a comrade returned from abroad, he welcomed it. Then, since he seemed to be a sorcerer, a leopard too was let loose upon him. But as it rushed at Androcles, the lion, defending the man who had once healed it, and mindful of their common table, tore the leopard to pieces. As was likely, then, the spectators were astonished, and the giver of the show called Androcles, and learned the whole story. And a murmur spread through the crowd, and the people, having learned the truth, cried out that both the man and the lion should be set free as free men. Memory, then, is indeed peculiar to animals. And in harmony with what has been said, and to the same effect, there is the case of the man who slept in Samos at the foot of the "Gaping Dionysus," and was thought to know the den. Let this be heard from Eratosthenes and Euphorion and others who describe it.

To make the increase of their animals greater for themselves, their keepers rub the parts of the females—of ewes and goats and mares—at the time of mating, filling their hands with salt and natron. From this an appetite for love arises in them more strongly. Others anoint the same parts with pepper and honey, others with natron and the seed of the nettle; and some now anoint with horse-parsley and natron. From this irritation, then, the female flocks become incontinent of themselves, and go mad after the males.

To Lycaon the king of Emathia a son was born, named Macedon, after whom the country too was afterward called, no longer keeping its ancient name. To him in turn there was a son, brave and conspicuous for beauty, named Pindus; and he had other sons too, but these were foolish in soul and not strong in body, who afterward, in time, envying their brother both his virtue and his other good fortune, destroyed him, and destroyed themselves besides, paying the penalty according to Justice. For Pindus, perceiving the plot of his brothers against him, left the paternal kingdom, and dwelt in a country place, and was strong both in other ways, and a great huntsman. And once he was hunting fawns. They ran with all the speed of their feet, and he, pursuing, drove his horse at full gallop, and drew far away from his fellow-hunters; and the fawns, slipping into a hollow and very deep ravine and saving themselves from the sight of their pursuer, vanished. So Pindus, leaping down from his horse, tied it by the reins to one of the trees standing near, and himself set about searching the ravine and seeking out the fawns aforesaid. Then he heard a voice, and it said, "Touch not the fawns." So, when after looking all round he saw nothing, he feared the voice as having fallen upon him from some higher cause. And for that time he went away, leading his horse off; but on the next day he came alone, and did not enter the ravine at all, both in memory of the voice that had fallen upon his ears and out of fear. As he was turning over a plan within himself and was at a loss who it could have been that the day before had restrained him from his eagerness for the hunt, and as he looked round, as was natural, for either mountain herdsmen or other hunters, a great thing was seen — a serpent, dragging the greater part of its body, but raising up its neck a little toward him (and the neck together with the head was in size greater than a full-grown man); and being seen, it struck him with terror. Yet Pindus did not start in flight, but collecting himself, by cleverness he won the beast over; for of the birds he chanced to have caught he brought some, and offered them to it as gifts and as the ransom of his own life. The serpent, as though softened by the gifts and bewitched, as one might say, went off. This pleased the young man, and from then on, as a good man, he carried to the serpent, as a wage for his safety, the welcome first-fruits of whatever game he had, either of the mountain hunt or of the winged. And while his bringing of the aforesaid gifts was most effective, the blessings from the divinity began also to flourish for Pindus, and to advance day by day to greater grandeur; for as he hunted, good catches met him, both of the animals in the woods and of the birds. So he had great gain, and indeed his fame spread abroad that he went to grips with the beasts and took them unflinchingly; and he was great to look at too, and such as to astonish by the bulk of his body and his fine condition besides, and by his beauty he plainly inflamed all womankind and kindled them toward himself. And they came to his doors as though in Bacchic frenzy, all of the women that were unmarried; while those living with their husbands, guarded indeed by the law, yet enslaved by the fame of Pindus's beauty, would have preferred to live with him than to become goddesses. And most of the men too were amazed at him and loved him; his brothers alone were his enemies. And once they lay in wait for him as he hunted alone — and the hunt was near a river — then, falling upon him as he was bereft of allies, the three struck him with their swords, and he cried out. His comrade the serpent heard this; for the creature is sharp of hearing and very sharp of sight. So it came forth from its lair, and coiling about the impious men killed them, throttling them to suffocation; and it did not relax its watch until the kinsmen of the young man, longing for him, came, and found him lying there. They lamented indeed, but did not dare to approach to bury the corpse, out of fear of the guard. But the serpent, perceiving by some secret nature that it was keeping them off, went away at great leisure, leaving the dead man to receive the last kindness from his kin. So he was buried magnificently, and the river neighbouring on the murder was called Pindus, from the dead man and from his tomb. It is indeed peculiar to animals to repay favours to their benefactors, as has been said above, and not least now.

The bee-eater, they say, flies contrary to all other birds; for the rest dart forward and toward what is before their eyes, but it flies backward. And I am moved to marvel at the nature of this remarkable, strange, and unusual movement with which that creature darts.

Aristotle says that ravens know the difference between rich land and poor, and in the all-bearing and fruitful land they move in flocks and crowds, but in the barren and sterile by twos. And the young they have reared each makes an exile from its own nest; for which reason they seek their food, and do not feed those who gave them birth.

The leopard has five toes on its front feet, but four on its hind feet. The female is stronger than the male. And if it tastes unknowingly of the so-called leopard's-bane (it is a plant), having tracked out human excrement from somewhere, it saves itself.

Bears, when those of the hunters who fall on their faces and draw in their breath are smelt by them, leave them as dead; and this animal seems to loathe a corpse. Mice too hate those that die in their own dwellings and runs, and indeed the swallow casts out a dead swallow. And to the ants too most wise Nature has given the care of carrying out their dead and cleansing their own runs, since this too is peculiar to the irrational creatures—to carry their dead, those of the same kind and nature, more quickly out of sight. And the tales of the Ethiopians, which have no taste of Greek flattery or boasting, say that an elephant, seeing a dead elephant, would not pass it by without scooping up earth with its trunk and casting it on, as though performing some secret holy rite on behalf of the common nature; for not to do this is sacrilege. And it is enough for it to throw on even a branch, and it departs, having not dishonoured the common end of all. And this tale too has come to us. When elephants die of wounds, whether shot in war or having suffered this in the hunt, they take up the herb that is at hand or the dust at their feet, and look up to heaven, and throw up one of the aforesaid things, and in their own voice they wail and lament, as though calling the gods to witness the unjust and lawless things they endure.

from the height of the dangers pressing upon him. An old mule at Athens, released from its labours by its own master, as Aristotle says, did not release itself from love of toil and willingness to work as befitted its age. At any rate, when the Athenians were building the Parthenon, though it neither dragged nor bore burdens, yet it went uncalled and willingly, as it were a trace-horse, alongside the young mules carrying their loads along the road, escorting, as one might say, and urging on the work by walking together with them, like an old craftsman released by old age from working himself, but by experience and instruction at once spurring on and encouraging the young. So the people, learning these things, ordered the herald to proclaim that, whether it came to the barley-meal or approached the barley, it should not be fended off, but allowed to feed its fill, and that the people should pay the money in the Prytaneum—a kind of meals granted to an athlete now grown old.

Of the greatest sea-monsters not one approaches the beaches and shores and the so-called "scaly" and shallow places, but they inhabit the open seas. And the greatest are the lion and the hammerhead and the leopard and the blowers and the saw-fish and the so-called maltha; and this last is a hard creature to contend with, and unconquerable. The ram too is a dread animal and one that brings danger, even if it appears from afar, by the disturbance of the sea and the surge that it works. And the hyena—no good sight is this for seafarers. Of the "dogs," their difference and their strength I have told above.

In Claros too the Clarians and all the Greek people honour the son of Zeus and Leto. Accordingly the place there is untrodden by venomous beasts and most hateful to them, partly by the will of the god, but altogether also because the beasts shudder at him, inasmuch as he himself knows how to save, and indeed begot Asclepius, the saviour and the adversary of diseases. And Nicander too is my witness for what I say. Nicander says: "No viper, nor hateful spiders, nor the deep-striking scorpion lodges in the groves at Claros, since Phoebus, having covered the deep dell with ash trees, set the grassy floor far from biting creatures."

The moray, when she is filled with amorous impulse, comes forth onto the land and longs for the company of a bridegroom, and a very wicked one; for she goes to the lair of a viper, and the two embrace. They say also that the viper, in its frenzy, comes likewise to the sea for union; and as a reveller knocks at the door with his pipe, so that one too, hissing, summons his beloved, and she comes forth — nature bringing together into a like desire and the same bed creatures whose dwellings are apart.

The goby, the weever, and the flying-fish, by pricking, release venom of fishes, yet not to death; but the stingray kills at once with its sting. And Leonides of Byzantium says that a man inexperienced in the nature and discernment of fish, snatching a stingray from a net — the unlucky man thought it was a flatfish — put it in his bosom to carry and walked on, as having found something good and a snatch profitable to himself for selling. But the stingray, hurt at being pressed, struck and pierced him with its sting, and poured out the entrails of the unlucky thief. And the robber lay dead beside the stingray, a clear proof of what in ignorance he had done.

Horses, they say, have no lower eyelashes. So they say that Apelles of Ephesus is blamed, since in painting a certain horse he failed to observe this peculiarity of the animal. But others say that it was not Apelles who incurred this charge, but Micon, a good man at painting this animal, who erred only in the thing mentioned.

It is possible to recognize this too as peculiar to animals. We see the tame birds, those reared and kept under our feet, bold among horses and asses and oxen and camels; and if they are reared together with some gentle and tame elephant, they are not afraid, but go even between those very legs. And cocks even fly up onto their backs; so great is their boldness and fearlessness. But a weasel running past instils in them terror and strong fear. And of bellowing and braying they take no account, but at the mere squeak of the aforesaid weasel they shudder. Of geese and swans and ostriches they think little or nothing, but they dread a hawk, though it be very small. The cock by crowing frightens a lion and kills a basilisk; yet it cannot endure either cats or kites. The doves take heart at the cry of eagles and vultures, but no longer at that of hawks and sea-eagles. The flock and the kid and every foal go to the mother's teats the moment they are born, and indeed fill themselves by drawing at the udders; and the parent meddles not at all, but stands still. But all the cloven-footed animals offer their teats to their young lying on their backs—wolves and dogs and lionesses and leopards.

That Cleanthes of Assos was compelled, even unwillingly, to yield and concede that the animals too do not fail of reasoning, though he strongly and forcibly argued the contrary, such a history, they say, brought about. Cleanthes happened to be sitting, and indeed having an unusually long leisure. So there were many ants about his feet. And he sees, from one path, other ants carrying a dead ant to the dwelling of others not of their own kind, and standing on the edge of the anthill by the dead one, and others coming up from below and meeting the strangers as for some purpose, then going down again, the same ones, and this many times. And at last they brought a worm as a kind of ransom, and the others took it and gave up the dead one they had been carrying. And they received it gladly, as kinsmen recovering a son or brother. What then does Hesiod say to this, who says that Zeus distributed the natures, and so to fish and beasts and winged birds he gave to eat one another, since there is no justice among them, but to men he gave justice? But Priam would not say this, if indeed he too ransomed Hector with many precious and wondrous treasures from a man—man from man, and from the hero and offspring of Zeus, being himself too the offspring of Zeus.

The castorides are a sea creature, and on the headlands and the jutting rocks they let out a certain dread wailing, and howl most heavily. Whoever, then, hears this sound, escape is impossible for him, and not long after he dies. And the whale comes forth from the sea and warms itself in the ray. But the seals come out rather at dusk; though indeed even at midday they sleep out of the sea. This too Homer knew, and in the Odyssey he made Menelaus describe to Telemachus and Pisistratus this resting-place of theirs, when Menelaus recounted to them the events at Pharos and concerning Proteus the sea divinity, and the prophecy which that Proteus I spoke of prophesied to him.

I hear men say that in Eryx, where indeed stands the famous temple of Aphrodite, of which I made mention above when telling the peculiarities of the doves there, there is both much gold and very abundant silver and necklaces and rings of great value, but that these are inviolable and untouched through fear of the goddess, and that men of former times always held both the goddess aforesaid and her treasures in wonderful reverence. But I learn that Hamilcar the Libyan plundered these, and working them into gold and silver, then distributed them to his army, a wicked division; and that for this he was most painfully and grievously tortured and at once punished and hanged, and that all who had any share with him in the deed and the unrighteous sacrilege met with violent and dreadful deaths; and that his fatherland, blessed until then and seeming enviable, when a few of the sacred treasures had been brought into it, became enslaved. These things, though solemn, do not yet bear upon my present purpose; but this, which is in tune with the present discourse, shall be told. Every year and every day both the natives and the strangers sacrifice to the goddess. The altar is the greatest under the open sky; and though many victims are consecrated upon it, it burns all day long and into the night. But while it gives light, it shows neither charcoal nor ash nor the fragments of half-burnt brands, but is full of dew and of fresh grass, which grows up every night. The victims of each herd come of their own accord and stand by the altar, and it is the goddess first that leads them, then the power and the will of the sacrificer. If, for instance, you wish to sacrifice a sheep, behold, a sheep stands by the altar for you, and you must begin the lustral rite; but if you are among the wealthier and wish to sacrifice a cow, or even more, then concerning the price the herdsman will neither penalize you by exacting more, nor will you grieve him; for the goddess oversees the justice of the sale. And if you set down a fair price, you will have her gracious; but if you wish to buy more cheaply than is proper, you have laid down your silver in vain, for the animal goes away, and you cannot sacrifice. Let this too be told by us, after the foregoing, as peculiar to the animals of Eryx.

The marrow of a dead man's spine, they say, as it rots, turns into a serpent; and the beast comes forth, and the fiercest thing crawls out of the gentlest; and the remains of the good and noble are at rest, and have peace as their reward, just as the soul of such men has the things sung and hymned by the wise; but the spines of wicked men bring forth such creatures even after life. Either, then, the whole thing is a tale, or, if it is truly believed, the corpse of a wicked man, as I judge, has earned, as the reward of his character, to become the father of a serpent.

The raven — you would not call it less bold in daring than the eagles. For it too goes to grips with the creatures, not the smallest, but the ass and the bull; for it seats itself on their necks and pecks them, and of many the raven has even pecked out the eyes. And it fights too a strong bird, the one called the merlin; and when it sees the merlin fighting a fox, it gives aid, for it has a certain friendship toward the fox. And the raven was, it seems, the most full-throated and many-voiced of birds; for having learned, it utters even a human voice. And its cry is one thing when it plays, another when it is in earnest; but if it gives forth the things from the gods, then it utters a sacred and prophetic cry. And ravens know that through the summer they are troubled with a flux of the belly, and for this reason keep themselves untasting of moist food.

Nature has made the animals most various-voiced and, as one might say, of many sounds, just as she has made men also. The Scythian speaks one way and the Indian another, and the Ethiopian has a voice natural to him, and so do the Sacae; and Greek speech is one thing, and Roman another. So too the animals each send forth in its own way the sound and noise native to its tongue; for one roars, another lows, and there is the neighing of one and the braying of another, the bleating and the bleat of goats, and to some belongs howling, to others barking, and to another snarling; and screams and hisses and creakings and songs and melodies and warblings, and countless other gifts of nature, peculiar to the animals, some to some, some to others.

The deed itself reveals to us the name of the dipsas. And it is smaller in size than the viper, but quicker to kill; for those who fall victim to its bite are kindled to thirst and inflamed to drink, and gulp in great draughts, and most swiftly burst. And Sostratus says that the dipsas is white, but has on its tail two black lines. And I hear that some call them "burners," and others "scorchers"; indeed they pour a crowd of names upon this creature. It is called also "black-tail," they say, and "sand-walker"; and if you hear "sting-snake," understand that the same is meant by me. And I must sing too a myth about this animal, which I know from hearing, that I may not seem ignorant of it. Report says that Prometheus stole fire, and the myth says that Zeus was angry and gave to those who informed of the theft a drug that wards off old age. This, then, I learn, those who received it placed upon an ass. And the ass went forward carrying its burden, and it was the summer season, and the ass, being thirsty, came to a spring for the need of drink. So the snake guarding it fended it off and drove it away, and the ass, being tortured, gave it as a reward for its kindness the very drug it happened to be carrying. So an exchange takes place, and the one drinks, the other puts off old age, taking in addition, as the story goes, the ass's thirst. What then? Am I the maker of the myth? But I would not say so, since before me too Sophocles the tragic poet, and Dinolochus the rival of Epicharmus, and Ibycus of Rhegium, and Aristias and Apollophanes the comic poets, sing of it.

About the red mullet I have spoken above; but what I did not say, I shall now tell. At Eleusis it has honours from the initiates, and the account of this honour is twofold. Some say it is because it spawns three times in the year; others, because it eats the sea-hare, which is deadly to man. Perhaps I shall say something about the red mullet again.

The swallow signals the coming of the best season. And it is fond of man, and rejoices to share a roof with this creature, and comes uninvited, and when it is its pleasure and all is well, it departs. And men receive it according to the law of Homeric hospitality, which bids us both cherish the one present and send off the one who wishes to go.

Aristotle says that of animals some are viviparous, some lay eggs, and some bring forth worms; and that creatures bring forth living young — men and the rest that have hair, and the whale-like among the water-dwellers; and of these some have a blowhole but no gills, like the dolphin and the whale.

I have learned that wild asses no smaller than horses in size are found among the Indians. And they are white over the rest of the body, but have the head somewhat purple, and the eyes send forth a dark-blue colour. They have a horn on the forehead about a cubit and a half in length, and the lower part of the horn is white, the upper crimson, but the middle exceedingly black. From these variegated horns I am told the Indians drink—and not all of them, but the most powerful among the Indians—pouring gold around them at intervals, as though adorning with bracelets the fair arm of a statue. And they say that the one who drinks from this horn becomes a stranger and unacquainted with incurable diseases; for he would not be seized by convulsions, nor by the so-called sacred disease, nor be destroyed by poisons. And if he has previously drunk something harmful, he vomits it up and becomes whole again. It is believed that the other asses over all the earth, both tame and wild, and the other solid-hoofed beasts, have no anklebones, nor any gall by the liver; but Ctesias says that the Indian asses which have the horn possess anklebones and are not without gall; and the anklebones are said to be black, and if one were to crush them, they are such within as well. And these are the swiftest not only of asses, but of horses and deer; they begin their running quietly, but gather strength little by little, and to pursue them is, in the poet's phrase, "to chase the uncatchable." When the female has given birth and leads about her newborn, the fathers, pasturing with them, guard the young. The haunts of these asses are the most desolate of the Indian plains. When the Indians go out for their capture, they let the tender and still young ones graze behind, while they themselves fight in their defence, and go to meet the horsemen, and strike with their horns. And so great is the strength of these creatures that nothing struck withstands them, but yields and is cut through, and if it chances is crushed and rendered useless. Already too they have fallen upon the flanks of horses and split them open and poured out their entrails. Hence indeed the horsemen dread to come near them; for the price of coming near is for them a most pitiable death, and they perish, both they and their horses. They are dangerous at kicking too. And their bites reach so deep that they tear away all they have grasped. A full-grown one alive you could not take, but they are shot with javelins and arrows, and the Indians strip the horns from them when dead and treat them as I have said. The flesh of the Indian asses is uneatable; the reason is that it is naturally most bitter.

Throughout the land of Egypt asps make their dens near the Nile on both banks. And for the rest of the time they keep to their place and love it, as men love their own houses; but when the river is about to rise in the summer season, some thirty days beforehand the aforesaid asps move to the regions farther from the Nile, and creep into the overhanging banks, and indeed take their own offspring with them, having received this gift peculiar to themselves from nature: to know the yearly visitation of so great and so industrious a river, and to guard against the seizure and harm it brings. And the tortoises and the crabs and the crocodiles at the same season carry off their eggs to places untrodden and unreachable by the river; and from this those who chance upon the eggs of the aforesaid creatures already reckon how far the Nile, when it rises, will water their land for them.

If I should pass over a wise deed of the elephant, someone will say that I did not tell it from ignorance. And it is worth hearing, and therefore let us hear it. The man entrusted with the care of its feeding used to take away some of the barley, and by mixing in stones he rendered most of it uneatable to the elephant, but preserved the bulk of the measure before the master who inspected them both. And for a time he escaped notice. So the elephant, seeing the man who plotted against it boiling porridge, with its trunk took up a heap of the sand at its feet and threw it into the pot, and avenged itself in return for what it had suffered by what it did, most cleverly.

They fly when they are afraid, and spring out of the sea, the squids and the sea-hawks and the flying-fish. And the squids dart up to the greatest height with their fins, and lighten themselves aloft, and are borne along in shoals, in common, like birds; the flying-fish make their flight lower; while the hawks are borne a little above the brine, so that one can scarcely judge that they are not swimming but flying.

The goat has an advantage in the intake of breath, as the herdsmen's accounts say. For it breathes both through its ears and through its nostrils, and is the most perceptive of cloven-hoofed animals. The reason I do not know how to state; what I do know, I have stated. And if the goat too is a work of Prometheus, what he meant by making it so, I leave to him to know.

For the Mysians cattle bear burdens, and they are without horns. I mean that the herd is seen hornless no longer because of cold, but by the peculiar nature of these cattle; and the proof is at hand, for among the Scythians too cattle are not without the gift of horns. And I hear someone saying in a writing that there are Scythian bees too, which feel the cold not at all, and indeed that the Scythians, bringing it to the Mysians, sell honey not foreign to them but native, and combs of their own country. And if I say things contrary to Herodotus, let him not be angry with me; for the man who said these things declared that he was setting forth an inquiry, and not singing an untested hearsay to us.

Eudemus says that there are irrational animals which have a natural arithmetic without being taught, and he adduces as evidence the following about the animals in Libya. The name he does not give; but what he says is this. Whatever it catches, it makes into eleven portions, and eats ten of them, but leaves the eleventh (for whom, and with what notion, is worth considering) as a kind of first-fruits or a tithe, as one might say. So it is right to be amazed at this self-taught wisdom; for an irrational animal knows the unit and the dyad and the numbers that follow. But for a man, how many lessons are needed, and how many blows, that he may either learn these things well and rightly or often not learn them at all?

The river-horses are nurslings of the Nile; and when the crops are at their height and the ears are golden, they do not begin at once to crop and eat them, but passing outside the cornfield they reckon how great a measure will fill them, and then, having calculated what is enough for them, they fall to and retreat step by step as they fill, taking the river's stream at their back. And this has been thought out by them, so that if any of the farmers should come upon them to defend their crops, they might most easily run down into the water, these river-horses watching their enemies face to face, and not from behind.

The other dogs are clever at catching and tracking the wild beasts, but the Egyptian dogs are most skillful at fleeing. The dogs in the Nile, at any rate, fearing the creatures there, are led by thirst to drink, but fear does not permit them to drink quietly and to satiety. And for this reason they do not drink stooping, lest something creeping up from below should then snatch them away. So they run along the bank, and lap with the tongue, snatching, as one might say, or, by Zeus, even stealing the drink.

Fishes wander and roam, some in masses, like herds of cattle or ranks of soldiers going in squadrons and battalions, and some go in order in a column, and others—you would say they are companies. Others are numbered into tens and swim together in this way; and some swim by pairs. Others keep house in their lurking-places and live out their lives there.

They say that against the bite of the viper and of the other serpent there are antidote-drugs that do not fail. Some of these, I hear, are draughts, others ointments; and incantations too have soothed the venom of one anointed. But the bite of the asp alone, I hear, is incurable and beyond help. And the creature deserves to be hated for its fortune in evil. Yet there is a beast more abominable and more unguarded against than even this — the sorceress woman, such as we hear Medea and Circe to have been; for the venoms of the asps are the work of a bite, but theirs kill even by mere touch, they say.
Of sea-creatures I learn that the parrot-wrasse alone eats its food up again as it comes back, like the bleating beasts, which they also say chew the cud.

The Egyptians say (and philosophers do not lightly disregard them) that in a certain nome of Egypt, which they name after Heracles the son of Zeus, a beautiful boy, beautiful as an Egyptian, a keeper of geese, was loved by an asp, and indeed the love was marvellous on her part. Then, visiting her beloved, she would foretell to him in a dream the plots being craftily devised against him by another snake, which was, as one might say, her mate, the male trying to do this out of jealousy of the boy over his bride; and the boy, heeding her, was persuaded and kept on his guard. Now Homer gave a horse a voice, but nature gave one to the asp, "which cares nothing for laws," as Euripides says.

In the Mauretanian land the leopards do not attack the monkeys by main force or by such strength and might as they have. The reason is that the monkeys do not come to close quarters, but flee from them and run up onto the trees and sit there, guarding against their plots. But the leopard, then, was craftier than the monkey. See, at any rate, what kind of snares it contrives and weaves against them. Where a multitude of monkeys sit, there it comes and throws itself down under the tree, and lies on its back upon the ground, and swells out its belly, and lets its legs fall slack, and shuts its eyes, and presses in its breath, and lies there as if dead. The monkeys, seeing their bitterest enemy from above, think it is dead, and what they most wish, that they also believe. Yet they do not yet take heart, but make trial, and the trial is this: they send down one of themselves who seems most fearless, to test and examine the leopard's condition. He goes down not wholly without fear, but having run a little way then turns back, fear having checked him; and he comes down again, and having come near withdraws, and turns back once more, and examines the eyes, and tests whether it lets its breath go. And the leopard, keeping still most resolutely, instils in him little by little a sense of safety. And when he has approached and stayed by it unharmed, the monkeys aloft now take heart, and running down both from that tree and from the others that grow near, gathering in a crowd they go about it and dance round it. Then leaping upon it and mounting it they tumble and dance over it a mocking dance befitting monkeys, and after outraging it in various ways, they show forth the joy and pleasure they have, as over a dead thing. But it endures everything, and then, when it perceives that they are wearied with their dancing and their insolence, it springs up unexpectedly and leaping among them tears some with its claws and rends some with its teeth, and has a most abundant banquet and feast of its enemies. And nature bids the leopard endure patiently and stoutly and nobly, that it may prevail over the enemies who have outraged it, contending most enduringly and having no need to say, "Endure now, my heart." But the son of Laertes uncovered himself a little before the time, unable to bear the insolence of the serving-maids.

The hedgehog—not the sea one, but the land one—is in many other ways crafty, as I have already told; but a cunning trick of its which I have not mentioned shall now be told. When about to be caught, having rolled itself up it renders itself uncatchable, and then it presses in its breath and stays motionless and still and counterfeits the dead.

I learn that those skilled in herding, when they wish their animals to put on fat, take away their horns. And when they wish to make the he-goats more eager for mating, they anoint their nostrils with perfume, and their beards too they anoint with the same. And again they check excessive appetite, if one ties up the middle of their tails with a thread. Aristotle says that mares cast their foals if they smell overmuch the wick of a lamp that has been put out. And I hear that against the house-dogs, that they may not run away, this device has been contrived. Having measured their tail with a reed, they anoint the reed with butter, and then give it to them to lick all round. And they remain, they say, as though bound.

There are three kinds of sea-dogs. Some of them are very great in size, and would be reckoned among the strongest of the whales; the remaining two kinds are by nature mud-dwellers, and reach a cubit in size. Of these, the spotted ones would be called dogfish, and you would not be wrong to name the rest spurdogs. The mottled ones are softer in their skin and broader in the head; the others, hard in skin and with a head running to a point, have a colour inclining to white. They have spines growing on them, one on the ridge, as one might say, the other on the tail; and the spines are hard and unyielding, and carry a kind of venom. Each of these two tribes of small dogs is caught from the mud and slime, and it is not amiss to tell the manner of the catch. They let down as bait a white fish slit along the back. When one is caught and falls upon the hook, all the rest that see it leap upon it and follow it as it is drawn up from below, not held back even up to the ship, so that one might guess they do this out of jealousy, as though it had stolen from somewhere for itself alone some of the food; and several of them have often leapt into the ship itself, and been caught of their own will.
The dogfish gives birth through the mouth in the sea, and takes the young back in again, and brings them up by the same ways, alive and unharmed.

I have heard that camels live even fifty years, but I am told that those from Bactria go on even to twice that span. And the males being warlike, the Bactrians geld them, taking away their wantonness and lasciviousness, but preserving their strength. The females have the parts that kindle them to heat cauterized.

Among the Indians the elephants, when the Indians compel them to tear up some tree by the roots, do not first set upon it nor attempt the task before they have shaken it and considered whether it can be overturned or is wholly impossible.

The limpets—you could not tear them from the rocks, not even if you laid hold with the fingers of Milo, who most firmly and warily held the pomegranate, so that none of his adversaries could take it from his right hand. And whoever attempts to tear a limpet from the rock to which it clings is laughed at as he toils and provides amusement. At any rate he is unable to gain possession of what he is after. But scraped with iron it splits off from the rock at last.

These too are peculiar to the dog. They do not bark if anyone approaches carrying with him the tail of a weasel—a weasel which he has hunted, and having cut off the aforesaid tail then let it go alive. And an ass will not bray, if you hang a stone from its tail, as they say.

The sting of the sea-stingray is irresistible. For it has stung and killed on the instant, and even those of the fishermen who are clever at sea-matters shudder at this weapon of hers; for neither will another heal the wound nor will she who made it, since, as is likely, this was given to the Pelian ash alone.

A mouse's liver, very astonishingly and strangely, as the moon waxes, grows for itself a certain extra lobe daily until the full moon; then again it diminishes by the same reckoning as the month wanes, until it has slipped down into a shapeless body. And I hear that in the Thebaid, when hail has fallen, mice are seen on the ground, of which one part is still mud, the other already flesh. And I myself, driving from Italian Naples to Dicaearchia, was rained on by frogs, and the part of them at the head was crawling, and two feet drew it on, while the rest was dragged along still unformed, and seemed to be compounded out of some moist matter.

Eudemus says that a seal fell in love with a man accustomed to hunt sponges, and coming forth from the sea to where there was a hollow rock would consort with him. Of his fellow-craftsmen this man was the ugliest, but to the seal he seemed most beautiful. And there is perhaps nothing to wonder at, since men too have often fallen in love with the less beautiful, feeling nothing for the most beautiful, but neglecting them.

The deer in Syria are bred on the greatest mountains—Amanus and Lebanon and Carmel; and when they wish to cross the sea, the herd comes to the shores and waits for the dying-down of the wind, and when they perceive it blowing gentle and quiet, then they take heart for the deep. They swim in a row, and hold to one another, those following resting their chins on the loins of those in front; and the last, resting itself on the one before, then brings up the rear. They set out for Cyprus out of longing for the grass there; for it is said to be deep and to provide good pasture. And the Cypriots say that they dwell in a land of good soil, and dare to match their own fields against the cornlands of the Egyptians. Other deer too display this same swimming. The deer of Epirus, at any rate, swim across to Corcyra, and these lie facing each other across the strait.

The Libyans make war not only on their neighbours, that they may have more than they, but also on the elephants. And those animals know that the motive of the expedition against them is nothing else but their tusks. So those that have been maimed in one tusk stand at the front, the rest putting them forward, that some may receive the first onset and others defend themselves with the strength of their tusks unimpaired and equally matched—perhaps too philosophizing against the Libyans and showing them that they have not come to risk themselves for a great prize. They use the one tusk as a weapon, and keep it sharp, and the other as a mattock; for with it they dig up roots, and prising up trees they lay them down.

In the summer season, when the sun is very strongly at its height, the elephants anoint one another with thick mud, and this affords them coolness, and is more pleasant to these animals than any cavernous house or any tree overshadowing them with branches. These follow the scent strongly, and have a most keen perception. They go forward, making a way for one another, and the first—for they go in a column—perceiving the grass underfoot, and understanding from his touch of it that men have passed through, pulls up the grass and gives it to the one behind to smell, and that one to the one after him; and this passing-on, as one might say, goes through them all. And indeed, when it reaches the one bringing up the rear, he sounds out loudly, and they, as though soldiers receiving a watchword, then turn aside into the glens and thickets of the mountains, or the more hollow parts of the marshes, and indeed those of the plains that are thick with bushes. In any case, whatever men tread, this they flee; for they regard this animal as their bitterest enemy. And when their pastures fail them, some dig up the roots and feed on these too, while others go off seeking fodder. And the first of them who happens upon the prize turns back and calls his fellows and leads them to the find.

The horned viper is a slender creature. It is a serpent, and has two horns above its forehead, and the horns resemble those of the snail, though they are not soft as those are. So to the rest of the Libyans they are hostile; but they have a treaty with the people called the Psylli, who neither feel it themselves when bitten, and most easily heal those who have met with such a misfortune. And the manner is this: if, before the whole body has swelled, one of the men from there comes, summoned or by chance, then rinses out his mouth with water and washes his hands with other water, and gives both to the bitten man to drink, that man is restored, and is thenceforth free of all harm. There runs about also a Libyan story which says that a Psyllus suspected and hated his own wife as an adulteress, and indeed suspected the infant born of her as a bastard and counterfeit to his own race. So he made, they say, a most decisive test. Filling a chest with horned vipers, he threw in the infant, as a craftsman tests gold by fire, exposing the child by this placing. And the vipers at once rose up and grew savage and threatened their inborn malice; but when the child touched them, they withered, and from this the Libyan knew that he was the father not of a bastard but of a true-born child. This race is said also to be a match for the other venomous creatures and for the venomous spiders. And if the Libyans tell marvels of these things, let them know that they deceive not me but themselves.

The race of cattle was, it seems, useful for everything, both for partnership in farming and for the carriage of various loads. And the ox is good at filling the milk-pails, and adorns altars, and graces festivals, and provides a full feast. And even when dead the ox is a noble and praiseworthy thing. For bees grow out of its remains, a most industrious creature, and one that prepares among men the best and sweetest of fruits, honey.

Aristotle says that one struck by the water-snake at once gives off a most heavy smell, so that no one can come near him. The same author says that forgetfulness is poured over the one struck, and indeed a great mist over his eyes, and madness comes upon him and a very strong trembling, and he dies on the third day.

Not only, then, were the spiders weavers and handy after the manner of Athena Ergane and the goddess Penitis, but they are by nature also skilled in geometry. At any rate they keep the centre and make exact the circle from it and its circumference most strongly, and they need no Euclid at all; for they sit in the middle, in the centre, lying in wait for their own prey. And they are, so to speak, both noble weavers and handy at mending; and whatever you tear of their well-spun and well-threaded craft, they mend, and render it again unharmed and whole.

In the most violent winter, when the sea is in tumult, and the winds blow down harsh and violent, the fishes shudder at the sea that is at once their nurse and their friend. And some of them heap up the sand with their fins, and overshadowing themselves they keep warm beneath it, while others slip under some rock, and in shelter from the cold rest very gladly; and others, running down into the recesses of the deep, then turn aside the upper turmoil, going below and into the depth; for it is not, they say, so much above that the wave swells and beats in its rage. But at the beginning of spring, when the air has become bright, and the plants begin to flourish, and the meadows are thick with their native growth, the fishes, perceiving that the things of the deep are calm and fair, run up and leap, and swim near the land, as though come home from abroad.

The plotters and enemies of bees would be these: the so-called titmice and their nestlings, the wasps, the swallows, the serpents, the venomous spiders, and the shrew-mice. The bees fear these; so the bee-keepers drive them off from them either by fumigating with fleabane or by setting up, or strewing, poppy still green before the hives. These are hostile to the others mentioned; but the capture of wasps would be this. One must hang a basket-trap before the wasps' nest and put in it a thin sprat or a little sprat-fish and with these an iops or a chalcis; and the wasps, drawn by their inborn gluttony, the bait summoning them, fall in in throngs, and when the trap has surrounded them they can no longer fly back out. The lizards too plot against the bees, and the land-crocodiles; and against these the following destruction has been contrived. Steeping barley-meal in hellebore, or pouring spurge-juice over it, or scattering it with mallow-juice, they spread the barley-meal before the hives; which brings destruction to the aforesaid creatures when they have tasted it. And by casting mullein-leaves or nuts into the pond, the master of the bees most easily destroys the tadpoles. The venomous spiders are destroyed by night, when a burning lamp is set before the hives and vessels filled with oil are placed beneath the lamp; and they, flying toward the light, fall into the oil and perish; otherwise they could not easily be caught. The titmice, having tasted barley-meal soaked in wine, grow heavy-headed, then fall, and lying there flutter, and are ridiculous to capture, eager to fly up but unable even to stand at all. But the swallow, out of reverence for its music, they do not kill, though they might easily do so; it is enough for them to prevent the swallow from building its nest near the hives. And the bees, it seems, loathe all foul smell and perfume alike, neither enduring the ill-smelling nor welcoming the affected sweetness of fragrance, like decent and modest girls, abhorring the one and despising the other.

One must know that the oinas is a bird, and not, as some think, a vine. Aristotle says that it is larger than the ringdove, but smaller than the pigeon. There are, as I hear, certain "oinas-hunters" even at Sparta. It might also be said that the female hawk differs from the male hawk not only in kind but also in nature.

Without arithmetic the phoenixes know how to reckon the number of five hundred years, being pupils of most wise nature, and for this reason needing neither fingers nor anything else for the knowledge of arithmetic. The reason why they know this, and must know it, is a common tale. But that the time of the five hundred years is fulfilled, either some one or none of the Egyptians knows, and even these are very few of the priests. These, at any rate, cannot easily agree with one another about it, but some wrangle, disputing with each other that this divine bird will come not now but later, or that it ought to have come; but while they dispute thus, it, apart from them, marvellously signals the time and is present. And they, of necessity, must sacrifice and confess that they spend their leisure in the lecture-halls making the sun set, but do not know as much as the birds. But are not these things wise, by the gods—to know where Egypt is, and where Heliopolis, where it is fated to come, and where it must lay its father and in what tomb? But if these things do not seem marvellous, shall we call the doings of the market-place and of arms and the other plots of men against and upon one another wise? To me they do not seem so, O men who are emulators of Sisyphus and the Cercopes and the Telchines. And I speak to those who practice these things exactly; but to those uninitiated in the aforesaid evils I do not speak.

These three become the greatest of animals from the smallest: of the water creatures the crocodile, of the winged the great ostrich, and of the four-footed the elephant. Juba says that his father had a Libyan elephant many years old, descended from the higher members of its race; and that Ptolemy Philadelphus had an Ethiopian one, and that it too, having lived from far back, became most gentle and most tame, partly from its fellowship with men, partly from being broken in; and he sings that Seleucus Nicator possessed an Indian elephant, and indeed says that this one lived on to the reign of the Antiochi.

Cyrus the elder, as they say, prided himself greatly on his palaces in Persepolis, which he himself built, and Darius on the construction of the buildings at Susa; for he too made those famous works at Susa. And Cyrus the second, in Lydia, planted a garden with his own royal hands, in those delicate tunics and amid those delightful and most precious stones, and prided himself on this both before others of the Greeks and especially before Lysander the Lacedaemonian, when Lysander came to Cyrus in Lydia. And of these things the writers sing; but the buildings of the bees, being far wiser and more skilful, of these they took no account at all. For those men did what they did to the hurt of many; but nothing was more gracious than the bees, since nothing was wiser. For first they make the chambers of the kings, and these have spaciousness and are higher; and they throw a fence about them, to be, as it were, a wall and enclosure, dignifying by this too the royal dwelling. They divide themselves into three, and so also their dwellings into as many. The oldest live next to the court of the kings, the youngest dwell after these, and those in the bloom and prime of youth outside these, so that the oldest are the guards of the kings, and the young ones a fence for the youngest.

Cyanus is its name, a bird by nature, unsociable in its ways, hating the haunts of the city and the lodgings in houses, and shunning too the haunts in the fields and wherever there are huts and the steadings of men, but delighting in solitudes and taking pleasure in mountain peaks and sheer crags. Nor does it take delight in mainlands or in goodly islands, but in Scyros and any other like it that is exceedingly wretched and barren and for the most part bereft of men.

If the animals also know the power of reasoning and discrimination and of choosing this rather than that, we might fittingly call nature the invincible teacher of all things. To me, at any rate, a man who had tasted of dialectic and was somehow concerned with hunting told such a thing as this. There was a hunting dog, said he. So it went on the track of a hare. And the hare was not yet seen, but the dog, running on, comes upon a trench, and is at a loss whether it is better to pursue to the right or to the other side; and when it seemed to have weighed the matter sufficiently, it then leaped straight across. The man, then, who claimed to be both a dialectician and a hunter, tried somehow to draw from this a proof of what he had said. The dog, halting, considered and said to itself, "Either this way or that way or yonder the hare turned. But not this way nor that way; therefore yonder." And it did not seem to me to be quibbling; for the tracks not being seen on this side of the trench, it was left for the hare to have leaped over it. So with reason it leaped after it; for that dog was a tracker and keen of scent.

Those fishes which have a river neighbouring on their native sea, or some lake, when they are about to spawn, swim out of the brine, choosing the water that is unbroken by the waves and least troubled and beaten by the winds. For the peace of the waters is good for them to receive their offspring and to keep their young unharmed and unplotted-against, both in other ways and indeed through the absence and scarcity of beasts; and lakes and rivers somehow tend to have this freedom. For this reason the Euxine Sea too abounds in many fishes; for it has not learned to nourish monsters. And if anywhere it nourishes a seal and very small dolphins, yet from all the others the fishes there are in shelter.

One account says that the kings of these bees are without stings; but another says that very strong stings have grown on them, sharpened most valiantly, yet that they never use them either on a man or on the bees, but that the fear of them is merely feigned; for it is not lawful that the ruler and overseer of so many should do evil. And the experts in these matters agree that the other bees, in the sight of their own rulers, bend down their stings, as though withdrawing from their power and yielding it. And one might be astonished at either trait in those kings; for if they have nothing wherewith to do wrong, this is a great thing; but if, when they might do wrong, they do not, this is by far the better.

Finches, indeed, are wiser even than men at foreknowing the future. At any rate they know when winter is coming, and they have most providently guarded against the snow that is to be. And for fear of being caught they flee to the wooded places, and the thickets are, as one might say, their refuges.

The Massagetae, as Herodotus says, hang up the quiver before themselves, and then the male consorts with the female openly, even if all should see them, those men caring nothing. But the union of camels would never be done openly, nor in the sight, as it were, of witnesses; but whether we call it shame or a secret gift of nature, let us leave these things to Democritus and the others competent to examine and state the causes of things inscrutable and not to be compared. And indeed the herdsman too goes off somewhere, when he perceives the impulse of their coming together with one another, as one withdrawing for a bride and bridegroom passing into the chamber.
The sea-needles, being thin, and not having a womb capacious of embryos, do not endure the growth of the young within, but burst, and in this way they do not bear but cast forth their offspring.

Lycurgus enacts a most humane law, as I think: that the younger should give up their seats and the road to the elders, out of reverence for an age to which all pray to come, if indeed this is fated for them. But how could the noble son of Eunomus contend with and be matched against the laws of nature? The race of elephants, at any rate, attend to these things, O you Lycurguses and Solons and Zaleuci and Charondases, for whom they make no laws at all, and yet they do such things, and the young give up their food to the elders, and tend them when relaxed by old age, and rescue them from dangers, and when they have fallen into pits raise them up, throwing in armfuls and bundles of brushwood, which the others, using as steps, then climb up, being heavy with age. Where, now, has an elephant beaten its father with blows? Where, now, has a father among them disinherited his son? But to you perhaps, O men, I seem to be telling tales to craftsmen (if we wish to speak the truth)

It is said that the traces and tokens of the asp's bites are not very clear or easy to discern. And I learn the cause is this. The poison from it is most sharp and swiftest to run through. So the asp fastens on, but the venom does not stay on the surface, but slips down into the inner passages, and vanishes from the surface and the skin beneath the eye, and is thrust within. For this reason too the death of Cleopatra was not very easily recognized by those about Augustus, but late, when two punctures, hard to see and hard to detect, were observed, by which the riddle of the death was discovered. And besides, the traces of the asp's trail appeared, evident to those who have the knowledge of the movement of these animals.

and poets of the unbelievable myths. That the dog is a lover of its master, the things already told give proof, and one must add to them this too, no doubt. Gelon of Syracuse, sleeping most deeply, dreamed that he had been struck by Zeus's thunderbolt. And the apparition was a dream, but he cried out, though asleep, and that with a very sharp and piercing voice. So a dog reared by him, hearing the voice of its friend and rearer, as though Gelon were in danger of suffering something from a plot, leaping up with all its force onto the bed and standing over its rearer, barked most violently, as if to ward off the attacker. So Gelon awoke, both from fear and from the barking, casting off sleep, though it was very deep.

When Pompeius Rufus was aedile of the Romans, at the Panathenaea a man who was a drug-pounder and one of those who rear snakes for shows, with many others of the same craft standing by, put an asp to his arm as a proof of his skill, and was bitten. Then with his mouth he sucked out the venom. But not having water to gulp down after—for there was none at hand, although it had been prepared for him, the vessel having been overturned by a plot—since he neither washed out the poison nor rinsed it away, he ended his life, after the second day, I believe, in no pain at all, the venom having quietly rotted away his gums and his mouth.

A young snake becomes the foster-companion of a young child of Arcadian race, and that one too a native. So as they grew up together in age, the boy was now a youth, and the foster-companion was now exceedingly great. And they loved each other, but those related to the youth dreaded the size of the beast; for this creature, very quickly, you would see greatest in size, and most fearful to look upon. So while it slept with the boy upon the same bed, they took it up and carried it as far away as possible, and the boy got up, but the snake remained. And when it had reached the wood and the native herbs there, it stayed there, delighting in the food of snakes and choosing solitude before the haunts of the city and those in houses. And as time crept on it made the one a young man, and rendered the other a now full-grown snake. And once, going through a solitude, the Arcadian, the lover and beloved of the aforesaid creature, fell among robbers, and being struck with a sword cried out, as was natural, partly from pain, partly calling for allies. And the snake, then, was of animals the keenest of sight and the quickest of hearing. So it, having been reared with him, hears the voice, and hissing sharply, as though enraged, astonished them, and trembling seized them, and all that was villainous scattered, one here, one there; and indeed it destroyed some that it caught with a most pitiable death; but having cleansed the wounds of its old friend and escorted him past all that was beset with beasts, it went off departing to where they had set it out, neither angry over the casting-out, nor, like the wicked among men, overlooking in danger one who had until then been most dear.

When spring is at its height and the earth is flowering, the animals are filled with amorous frenzy and call to mind their matings, and are eager to couple with one another, both the mountain creatures and those that dwell in the sea and those that travel aloft. And of the fishes some rub off their eggs upon the sands, eggs that are dense and clinging to one another, while others, as they swim, then cast forth a very great quantity of eggs, and those swimming behind swallow most of them. And indeed the males go before and shed their milt, and the females following, gaping very greedily, fill themselves; and this is their mating. And that certain fishes even dwell together with their females as wives, and guard them, and that a kind of jealousy is kindled even in the kinds of fishes, I have told above.

The fox is a wicked creature, whence indeed the poets like to call it "the crafty one"; and the land-hedgehog is wicked too. And it lies curled up, having seen the fox come; and she, unable to gape and bite it, then urinated into its mouth; and it is choked, the breath being held within from the curling-up and the aforesaid liquid flowing in upon it; and indeed in this way one evil creature, the fox, getting round another evil one, the hedgehog, has caught it. And above another kind of catching has been told.

Aristotle says, and Democritus before him, and Theophrastus too in the third place says it, that fishes are not nourished by the salt water, but by the fresh water mingled with the sea. And since this seems somehow incredible, the son of Nicomachus, wishing to confirm what was said by the very facts, says that there is a drinkable water in every sea, and that it is proved thus. If one should make a vessel of wax, hollow and thin, and let it down empty into the sea, fastening it somewhere so as to be able to draw it up, when a night and a day have passed he draws it up filled with sweet and drinkable water. And Empedocles of Acragas too says that there is a sweet water in the sea, not visible to all, but nourishing to the fishes. And he gives a natural cause of this sweetening of the water in the brine, which you will learn from his work.

About the place called Conopion (it is a place of the Maeotis) the wolves keep faithfully by the line-fishermen and seafaring men, and if you saw them, you would not say they differed from house-watching dogs. So if these wolves get their portion of the sea-catch, they are peaceful and at truce with the fishermen; but if not, they tear apart their nets and make them disappear, and the wolves exact from them a penalty for their lack of a share.

Those initiated to the Two Goddesses would not, they say, eat the dogfish; for it is not a pure dish, since it gives birth through its mouth. But some say that it does not give birth this way, but that, fearing some of those that plot against its young, it swallows them down and hides them, and then, when the one that frightened it has passed by, disgorges them again alive. And the red mullet the same initiates would not taste, nor would the priestess of Hera at Argos; and the reasons I know I have told somewhere above.

The matings of the viper and the lamprey, and how they consort with one another—she coming forth from the sea, and he creeping out of his hole—I have not forgotten that I told in what went before. But what I did not say I would now say. When the viper is about to consort with her, that he may seem gentle, as befits a bridegroom, he vomits up and casts out his venom, and so, hissing softly, he calls his bride, as though striking up a kind of pre-nuptial wedding song. And when they have accomplished together the rites of their amorous eagerness, she rushes off to the waves and the sea, while he, sucking up his venom again, returns once more to his own haunts.
